True humility is not running yourself down and then shutting the door. True humility is opening up — opening to God so that grace flows in, and opening to others so that grace flows out. John 7:38 says, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”

Another picture from everyday life: have you ever noticed that the fuller the ear of rice, the lower it bows its head? The empty ears stand bolt upright. This isn’t poetic fancy; it’s physics — the greater the weight, the greater the turning force, and the deeper the stalk bends. Brothers and sisters, spiritual life is the same. Those who truly have substance within keep their heads low; it is those who are empty inside who need to keep their heads held high.

Psychology and Sayings

June Price Tangney, professor of psychology at George Mason University in the United States, pointed out in a 2000 study in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology that humility is often misunderstood as self-deprecation, but that in psychological terms humility includes an accurate assessment of one’s abilities and limitations, openness about one’s mistakes, not making oneself the centre of attention, and an appreciation of the worth of others.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes the Bible exactly. Romans 12:3 says, “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” Humility doesn’t say, “I’m good for nothing.” Humility is “thinking reasonably” — no more and no less, standing honestly in the place God has arranged for me.

The church father Augustine is generally credited with saying that if you ask the way to the truth, the first thing is humility, the second is humility, and the third is still humility. The saying has been handed down for sixteen hundred years because it names one thing truly: every step deeper into the spiritual life has only one entrance, and that is going low.

Applying the 321 Vision

321’s most central saying is: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order of James 4:7: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” First submit to God, then resist the devil. Many people skip the first sentence and go straight to the second, and the more they resist, the more exhausted they become. Because resistance without surrender is itself another form of pride — it is me doing the fighting, not God.

This is exactly what 321 calls the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When Jesus truly reigns as King in me, the “I” that wants to lift itself up naturally steps down from the throne. When the glory truly goes to Jesus, I no longer need to fight for my own pride.

And there is that reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. Proud people are always tired, because they must keep calculating, keep guarding themselves, keep maintaining an image. Humble people can rest, because the Lord says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Brothers and sisters, this is the way out.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message within the framework of 321, and you will see that it was one picture all along.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. When Eve wanted to be “like God,” Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7). The first Adam grasped; the last Adam let go. The pattern we are to learn is not grasping but letting go.

The Bible is my standard. Eve’s failure began with “Has God really said?” The moment people start correcting God’s word by their own feelings, the standard has changed hands. The world today offers a thousand explanations of sin; we have only one standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Galatians 5:16 says, “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” The way to deal with the lusts of the flesh is not to clench our teeth but to walk by the Spirit. This is what it means to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. The problem of sin is, in the end, a problem of the throne. Only one can sit on the throne. When I sit on it, sin has a foothold; when Jesus sits on it, sin loses its foothold.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Satan fell because he wanted glory for himself; humanity fell because it wanted glory for itself. Giving the glory back to Jesus is putting ourselves back in our originally intended position.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. What Jeroboam established was a system of his own — to secure himself, he was prepared to change even the worship of God. God’s system and man’s system differ in one thing only: who is at the centre.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the most important is the first — mindset. From “Sin was made by God; there’s nothing I can do” to “Sin is the result of pride, and I can choose humility.” Brothers and sisters, change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. When daily living changes, relationships change with it; and when relationships are right, ministry has a foundation.

The Priority of Relationships

First with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Proud people turn this exactly upside down — first they handle things, then they sort out people, then they soothe themselves, and only last of all do they grudgingly think of God. This morning, let’s put the order back the right way round.

A Shift in Perspective

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: no longer asking, “Why does God allow sin?” but asking, “What way out has God prepared for me?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: earthly logic is to climb upward; heavenly logic is to go down. The Lord says, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).

From the temporary to the eternal: everything pride fights over is very short-lived — winning an argument, saving face in a meeting. Nothing in eternity is won by fighting.

From the worldly to the godly: the worldly view values how much I have; the godly view values how much God gains.

The 920 Practice

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Brothers and sisters, set these nine graces side by side with the list of the deeds of the flesh we read a moment ago in Galatians 5:19–21: on one side the products of pride, on the other the fruit of the Spirit. Which will you bear today?

Pay special attention to “gentleness” and “self-control,” the two that pride fears most. Gentleness is not using your own strength to push people down; self-control is not letting your own desires be king. Once these two start to grow, pride can no longer keep its footing.

235 Relationships

235 reminds us: become a “2” — spiritual companions — with selfless people; establish the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Why do we need a spiritual companion? Because the greatest mark of pride is that it cannot see its own pride. You and I both need someone who can tell us the truth. Proverbs 27:17 says, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” Brothers and sisters, no one fighting alone can deal with pride, because the very thing that must be dealt with is the “I” that thinks it doesn’t need anyone else.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s work them out one by one through the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: pray every day, “Lord, keep me from making myself the centre; help me to fix my eyes on you.”

Information: first let the truth into your head. You have heard it today — God did not create sin; sin is the result of pride. Please memorise James 4:6.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your head into your heart. Ask the Lord to show you one concrete picture: at what moment this week was I making myself the centre?

Conviction: not just admitting, “That makes sense,” but saying, “This is addressed to me.”

Implementation: make this prayer the first thing you say when you open your eyes each morning. It needn’t be long — thirty seconds is enough — but do it every day.

Evaluation: before bed, take two minutes to look back — where was my focus today? On myself, on others, on my circumstances, or on Jesus?

Correction: if you find your focus has drifted, bring it back on the spot. Don’t wait until next week; don’t wait until the next meeting.

Repetition: forty days in a row. For a mindset to become life, it must be repeated; repetition is what turns it into instinct.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister, teach them this prayer, and remind each other.

Practice two: when you want to insist on your own way, stop first and ask, “Is this coming from pride, or from trust?”

Information: James 1:19 says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you hear this question in the three seconds before you’re about to explode.

Conviction: admit one thing — what I am insisting on is not necessarily the truth; very often it is only my pride and my face.

Implementation: decide on a specific action. When you feel the heat rise in your chest and your voice about to go up, take three deep breaths first and silently ask yourself the question.

Evaluation: once a week, take the chance to look back: how many times did I insist on my own way this week? How many of those turned out to be for the truth, and how many just to win?

Correction: if it was just to win, go back and apologise. You needn’t explain at length; “I had a bad attitude the other day — I’m sorry” is enough.

Repetition: don’t give up because you fail two or three times. The old self doesn’t die completely in one go.

Multiplication: share your failures and what you have learned in your small group. Your honesty will set others free to be honest.

Practice three: in relationships, learn to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble.”

Information: Philippians 2:3 says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to remind you by name — whose face comes to mind right now? The person you think of and immediately feel, “It’s obviously their fault.”

Conviction: believe one thing — relationships matter more than who is right; people matter more than tasks. Winning the argument and losing the relationship is the worst bargain there is.

Implementation: take the first step this week. A phone call, a message, a cup of coffee — any of these will do. The one who speaks first is not the one who loses; it is the one who is like the Lord.

Evaluation: after you have taken that step, note down what you really feel. Lighter, or more aggrieved? If more aggrieved, it shows I’m still seeking justice for myself.

Correction: bring that sense of grievance to the Lord and hand it over to him. 1 Peter 5:7 says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.”

Repetition: bowing your head once is not humility; bowing your head as a habit is humility.

Multiplication: when God uses you to restore a relationship, tell that testimony. Humility inspires humility — and that is where both sides begin to win.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take these two sentences home with you:

Pride takes us away from grace; humility brings us back to God.

Stop asking where sin comes from, and ask yourself: am I still holding on to “self”?

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have come a fair distance today. Let’s gather it up into a few sentences:

The starting point of sin is pride; the starting point of victory is humility. God did not create sin, nor did he create the fall. What God created was free will, so that we could choose him.

What enormous respect that is. God could easily have made a set of machines that never go wrong and kept the universe forever tidy. But he didn’t. He made children who can say “I will,” and in doing so he took the risk of hearing “I won’t.” And when we really did say “I won’t,” he did not destroy us. He sent his only Son, who walked a road exactly opposite to ours — we wanted to go up, he came down; we wanted to be king, he became a servant; we wanted to save our own lives, he gave up his.

Philippians 2:8–11 says, “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The highest place in the universe was won by walking the lowest road. And the Lord has already walked that road for us.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you.

First, admit it. Not admit, “I have a few small faults,” but admit, “There is a self inside me that wants to be king.” Call it by its name — pride.

Second, surrender. Let Jesus be King. Not his being your adviser, not his being your back-up plan, but his being King. Only one can sit on the throne. Please get up and let him sit down.

Third, choose. Today, in the place where it is hardest to bow your head, make one humble choice. A phone call, an apology, a moment of silence instead of self-defence.

May the selfless life grow up within us, and may revival begin in our hearts. For revival has never begun from the pulpit; revival begins from a heart willing to go low. May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)
“Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15)
practices: When you want to insist on your own way, stop first and ask
In relationships, learn to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

I confess that sin is not something you made; it is the pride in my heart that has taken me far from you. I confess that I often want to be my own king, to control my own destiny, to act as I please. Lord, please forgive me.
Cleanse me and refine me with your precious blood, and teach me humility. Take me down from my own throne, and let Jesus reign as King in every corner of my life.

Lord, I am willing to let go of “I have to be right” and choose “I am willing to be humble.” I am willing to lay myself down, choose obedience, and live in your grace and light. Holy Spirit, guide me every day, so that my focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on others, not on my circumstances.
Let the selfless life grow up within me, and let revival begin in my heart. To you be all glory, praise and honour, for ever and ever.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ecclesiastes 7:29 says, “Behold, I have only found this: that God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.” How have you answered the question, “If God is good, why is there sin in the world?” in the past? How has today’s message adjusted your view?

James 4:6–7 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Name one specific situation in which you are currently “insisting on your own way.” If you were to choose humility there, what first step could you take this week?
l073.title: Where Does Sin Come From?
l073.subtitle: Pride Is Where Sin Begins; Humility Is Where Victory Begins
l073.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Pride Doesn’t Appear Out of Nowhere
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to remember something — when was the last time you said to yourself, deep down, “I want”?

Was it last night, scrolling on your phone, when you saw someone’s holiday photos and the words “I want that too” rose up in your heart? Was it this month, when a colleague was promoted and the thought flashed through your mind, “That should have been me”? Or was it during some piece of service at church, when someone else was praised, and you smiled on the outside while a small thorn pricked you inside?

We rarely admit that we are proud. Because in our imagination pride looks like swagger, like looking down on everyone; and most of us seem quite polite, quite gentle, quite easy to get along with. But brothers and sisters, the pride the Bible speaks of often doesn’t look like that at all. The pride the Bible speaks of is often quiet, reasonable — even “perfectly sensible.”

The title of this lesson is “Where Does Pride Come From?” It is an important question, because anything whose root we cannot find, we will never be able to deal with.

When a tree grows crooked and you prune the branch, next year it grows back, because the root is still there. When someone loses their temper and apologises, the next time the same situation arises the same words come blurting out again, because the root is still there. Pride is the same. We can use willpower to hold down its outward expressions, but we cannot hold down its inward source.

So today we are going to dig down, all the way to the root.

The lesson states the answer clearly right at the start: pride does not appear out of nowhere. It has a root — sinful desire.

From the garden of Eden until today, human history has replayed the same tragedy again and again: believing Satan’s lie, thinking “I can control, I can decide, I can satisfy myself,” and then falling step by step into the snare of pride and sin.

Notice a truth of great importance in that sentence: the Bible shows that pride is not an inborn personality trait but a wrong choice of the free will.

This overturns what many people think. We often say, “I’m just a competitive sort of person — it’s my personality.” We treat pride as temperament, as a factory setting that cannot be changed. But the Bible does not say so. The Bible says pride is a choice — pride comes into being at the moment we choose to obey sinful desire, choose to believe a lie, rather than obey the truth.

That is bad news, and it is also good news.

The bad news is that we have no excuse. We can no longer say, “I was just born this way.”

The good news is that if it is a choice, then we can choose again. If pride was “chosen” in at a certain moment, then under the guidance of the Holy Spirit it can also be “chosen” out at another moment.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the starting point of what the 321 vision calls the fivefold change — when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. The first mindset we need to change today is this: pride is not my personality; pride is my choice.

Today we will walk three steps together. Step one: seeing that the root of pride is believing Satan’s lie. Step two: seeing that the driving force of pride is the push of sinful desire. Step three: seeing that the price of pride is the loss of freedom and blessing.

One is the point of ignition, one is the fuel, and one is the ruin left when the fire has passed.

May the Holy Spirit himself shine his light into our hearts this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, Three Eras, One Temptation
sections.html:
To make this lesson stand firm, let’s first set out the background. Today’s message stands on three books.

The first is Genesis.

Genesis 3 records the scene of humanity’s fall. Its author is Moses, and he was writing for the Israelites who had just come out of Egypt and were walking through the wilderness. This generation had seen the ten plagues with their own eyes and walked through the Red Sea, yet in the wilderness they complained again and again, demanded again and again, said “I want” again and again. Moses wrote down the story of Eden for them so that they would understand: the temptation you face in the wilderness today is the same temptation the first couple faced in the garden.

The second is James.

The author of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh. He came to faith only after Jesus’ resurrection and later became the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19). He calls himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1) — he could easily have said, “I am the Lord’s brother,” but he didn’t; he called himself only a servant. That in itself is a lesson in humility.

The letter is generally dated between AD 45 and 50, and may well be the first book of the New Testament to be completed. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish Christians scattered across the Roman Empire by persecution. They had lost their homes and their property, and in the lands where they lived as strangers they laboured and were oppressed.

In such circumstances, what are people most likely to say? Most likely, “I want.” I want back what I’ve lost; I want to prove myself to them. It was at just such a time that James wrote: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed” (James 1:14). He wanted to tell these suffering people: the real danger is not the swords of Roman soldiers but that force of “I want” inside you.

The third is 1 John.

The apostle John wrote this letter late in life, generally dated between AD 85 and 95, from Ephesus, to the churches of Asia Minor. The church was then facing the inroads of early Gnostic thought: some claimed to have attained a higher knowledge, yet did not live by love.

With three supremely concise phrases John takes the whole fallen world apart: “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

Brothers and sisters, look at the span of time across these three books. Moses wrote in the fifteenth century BC, James in the middle of the first century AD, John at the end of the first century AD. More than fifteen hundred years lie between them, across three utterly different settings — the wilderness, Jerusalem, Ephesus — and yet what they point to is the same source of disease.

In fifteen hundred years humanity changed its tools countless times; the human heart did not change even once.

That is why we still read Genesis 3 today. Because what that serpent said, it is still saying today.

sections.heading: 1. The Root of Pride: Believing Satan’s Lie
sections.html:
1. The serpent’s first words were a question

Genesis 3 opens like this: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, ‘Has God really said, “You shall not eat of any tree of the garden”?’” (Genesis 3:1)

The word “subtle” is the Hebrew ārûm (עָרוּם), and it is a fascinating word: in Proverbs it is repeatedly translated “prudent,” and in itself it is neutral, even positive. Satan’s attacks never come baring teeth and claws. He is “prudent,” clever, reasonable.

His first words are not a command but a question. He doesn’t say, “Go and eat.” He says, “Has God really said …?” He does not begin by attacking God’s authority; he begins by planting a question mark in the human heart — is God’s word really reliable? Is what God says really for your good?

Brothers and sisters, Satan never starts with behaviour; he starts with mindset. He knows that once the mindset is loosened, behaviour will follow sooner or later.

2. Then he turned the question mark into a lie

Next the serpent said, “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:4–5).

This is the first lie in human history. The Lord Jesus later said of the devil, “When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies” (John 8:44).

The heart of this lie is what the lesson points out: “You don’t need God; you can rely on yourself.”

Notice how the sentence is built. Satan didn’t say, “God doesn’t exist” — he never runs atheist propaganda, because that would be far too easy to expose. What he said was, “You will be like God.” He doesn’t ask people to deny God; he asks people to replace God.

“You will be like God, knowing good and evil” — in Hebrew usage, “knowing good and evil” is not just “recognising” information about right and wrong; it is the authority to “decide” right and wrong. The original word, yāda‘ (יָדַע), carries the sense of personal experience, control and possession. So what the serpent was really proposing was this: from now on you needn’t wait for God to tell you what is right and what is wrong — you yourself are the standard.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the 321 vision’s definition of pride — pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place.

Satan didn’t ask Eve to do a “bad thing.” He asked Eve to sit in a “seat that wasn’t hers.”

3. Why the lie succeeded

The lesson puts it profoundly: this lie struck at the deepest desires of the human heart — the desire for control, the desire to become better, the desire to become God.

Notice that the desire “to become better” doesn’t sound evil at all. In fact our education, our workplaces and our social media encourage that desire every single day.

But the problem isn’t “better.” The problem is “better by relying on whom?”

The passage goes on: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too” (Genesis 3:6).

Good for food — the lust of the flesh. A delight to the eyes — the lust of the eyes. To be desired to make one wise — the pride of life.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Genesis 3:6 and 1 John 2:16, fifteen hundred years apart, are the same list. John wasn’t inventing a new classification; he was reading Genesis.

The lesson says: Eve believed this lie and made a proud choice — she wanted to “decide for herself” what was right and what was wrong. That was the beginning of humanity’s fall.

4. Today’s serpent says the same things

The lesson reminds us that Satan still deceives us the same way today. He will never tell us outright, “Go and sin.”

He will say, “You deserve more.”

He will say, “You should satisfy yourself.”

He will say, “If you don’t look out for yourself, who will?”

Brothers and sisters, ask yourself honestly: where have you heard these three sentences?

The first is in advertisements. The second is in feel-good self-help. The third may have welled up from the bottom of your own heart, on the night you were most exhausted, most wronged, with no one to speak up for you.

These words sound very reasonable; they even sound as if they are protecting you. But the lesson hits the nail on the head: in reality they are amplifying the voice of “self.”

Satan’s greatest skill is not getting you to hate God but getting you to love yourself so much that God becomes optional.

So the lesson draws a crucial conclusion: pride does not start with outward behaviour; it starts at the moment the heart begins to believe the lie.

5. An example from life and a little supporting evidence from science

I often think of this picture. The bait on a fishhook is real. The fish isn’t fooled into eating something fake — it really does get to eat. The problem isn’t the bait. The problem is the hook hidden inside it, and the invisible line behind the hook.

What Satan offers is often real. The success he gives is real, the applause is real, the thrill is real. He never uses fakes, because fakes don’t catch fish. He just doesn’t tell you who is holding the other end of the line.

Science also offers some intriguing supporting evidence. From the 1990s the University of Michigan neuroscientists Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson put forward an important finding: in the brain, “wanting” and “liking” are handled by two different systems, and dopamine mainly drives “wanting,” not “liking.” This means a person can want something more and more while enjoying it less and less.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t using science to prove the Bible — the Bible doesn’t need science to prove it. But it does help us see that the voice of “I want” is naturally louder than the voice of “I have enough.” So we need all the more a truth from outside ourselves to correct the voice within.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

What happened in the garden of Eden was precisely the birth of the self-centred life. Before it, Adam and Eve’s world had only one centre — God. After it, their world had a second centre — themselves.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Brothers and sisters, the first lesson we need to learn this morning is to recognise voices. When a thought rises up, don’t rush to act on it. First ask: is this voice calling me back to my originally intended position, or calling me away from it? Is it telling me to be human, or telling me to be God?

For the 321 vision tells us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The moment our focus leaves Jesus, the first thing to take that place is always the self.

sections.heading: 2. The Driving Force of Pride: The Push of Sinful Desire
sections.html:
1. Two hunters’ verbs

James 1:14 says, “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed” (James 1:14).

This one short verse hides two extraordinarily vivid Greek verbs.

“Drawn away” is exelkō (ἐξέλκω), a hunting term meaning to lure prey out of the den where it hides.

“Enticed” is deleazō (δελεάζω), a fishing term whose root is “bait” — to lure a fish onto the hook with sweet-smelling bait.

Brothers and sisters, James is using pictures of hunting and angling. And notice one thing especially: the subject of both actions is not Satan but “his own lust.”

James has only just said, “Let no man say when he is tempted, ‘I am tempted by God,’ for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). He has blocked the first road of shifting the blame — we can’t blame God. And in this verse he quietly blocks the second road as well — we can’t blame it all on the devil.

Satan certainly lays bait, but if there were no appetite in us that “wants to bite,” the bait could not catch us. The Lord Jesus himself said, “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30). When Satan came to the Lord Jesus, he found nothing he could hook.

So the lesson is exactly right: Satan uses lies to ignite human desire, and that desire becomes the fuel of pride.

The lie is the match; desire is the firewood. Without a match the wood will not burn by itself; but without wood, strike the match a hundred times and it is only a brief flash.

2. The four stages of desire growing up

James goes on: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:15).

This is a very clear production line: desire, conception, sin born, death born.

Desire in itself is not yet sin, just as a passing thought is not yet sin. But if we keep it in our heart, talk with it and give it room, it “conceives.” And what has been conceived will surely be born.

Brothers and sisters, this is a frightening reminder and also one full of hope. Frightening because no sin appears from nowhere; every sin has its time of pregnancy. Full of hope because, if there is a time of pregnancy, there is time to turn back.

The question is: are we willing, at the very moment a thought arises, to bring it to the Lord?

3. Three desires, one triangular trap

Following 1 John 2:16, the lesson lists three common kinds of desire. Let’s first read the whole passage:

“Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:15–16)

First, the lust of the flesh — wanting sensual gratification.

Second, the lust of the eyes — wanting to possess more.

Third, the pride of life — wanting other people’s approval, honour and applause.

The phrase “pride of life” is, in the original, alazoneia (ἀλαζονεία), meaning “boasting, bragging, showing off what one has.” So it is not only about feeling inwardly that I am impressive; it is about “making sure others know I am impressive.”

Brothers and sisters, these three make up what the lesson calls “the triangular trap of pride.” The senses, possessions, applause — you may escape one of them, but it is hard to escape all three at once.

And Satan can make people fall into it with a single sentence, the one the lesson points out: “I don’t have it; I want it.”

The lesson gives three examples. Listen carefully:

“I don’t have money; I want more money” — and it turns into greed and anxiety.

“I don’t have status; I want to be noticed” — and it turns into comparison and rivalry.

“I don’t have love; I want others to satisfy me” — and it turns into lust and control.

Three sentences, three roads, all leading to the same place.

4. A deeper lie: “I have it, and I still want more”

The lesson goes on to point out another, deeper lie: “I have it, and I still want more.”

This is greed joined to pride, and it leaves people never content, never satisfied.

Brothers and sisters, the first lie deceives the poor; the second deceives the rich. The first says, “Once you have it, you’ll be fine.” The second says, “Just a little more and you’ll be fine.”

The American oil magnate John D. Rockefeller is commonly said to have been asked, “How much money is enough?” and to have answered, “Just a little bit more.” The source of the quotation is disputed, but it describes a real human heart with precision.

The Bible said it long ago: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 5:10).

Paul also warned Timothy: “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:9–10).

Notice the phrase “pierced themselves through.” No one else pierced them; they pierced themselves.

The lesson says: we think “a little more” will make us happy, but instead we end up bound by “more,” falling into loss of control and emptiness.

5. Confirmation from psychology: the hedonic treadmill

On this point psychology has produced fairly consistent findings.

In 1978 Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman published a famous study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They interviewed a group of major lottery winners and a group of people paralysed in accidents, along with a control group. They found that some time after their win, the lottery winners felt no significantly greater happiness in everyday life than ordinary people.

The study supported a concept Brickman and Donald Campbell had proposed in 1971 — “hedonic adaptation,” later often called “the hedonic treadmill”: we run forward with all our might, but the track is moving backwards at the same time, so we stay where we are.

In 2010 the Nobel laureates Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that in the United States of that time, although day-to-day emotional well-being rose with income, it levelled off at an annual income of around 75,000 US dollars. The exact figure has been debated by scholars since, but that “income and emotional well-being do not rise together without limit” is a fairly consistent finding.

Brothers and sisters, psychology can only tell us that the “treadmill” exists; it cannot tell us how to get off it. The Bible can.

Paul says, “But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that” (1 Timothy 6:6–8).

Contentment is not a personality trait; contentment is “learned.” Paul says, “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it” (Philippians 4:11).

“Learned” — the original carries the sense of “being taught, being trained.” Contentment is a compulsory course in God’s classroom, and the exam is taken many times.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is pushed along by “I want”; the selfless life is led along by “Lord, your will be done.”

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not emptying you out and leaving you to live in a void. Selflessness is asking the small self who has usurped the throne to step down, and letting the Lord who created the universe take his seat.

Self-centred people clutch a cup, afraid someone will snatch it; selfless people let go of the cup, because they have discovered they are standing on the shore of the sea.

The 321 vision also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry.

“I want” is a product of relying on the brain — calculating what I lack, comparing what I’m short of, scheming how to make it up. “I already have” is a product of relying on the heart — seeing what the Lord has already given, counting his grace, and the heart opens up.

Out of the heart flow the issues of life. When the heart is filled with “I want,” what flows out is anxiety; when the heart is filled with thanksgiving, what flows out is freedom.

sections.heading: 3. The Price of Pride: The Loss of Freedom and Blessing
sections.html:
1. An astonishing reversal

The lesson says: pride seems to make people gain, but in reality it makes them lose everything. It turns people from “the one in control” into “the one being controlled.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the sentence in the whole lesson that most needs to be seen.

What was Satan’s promise in Eden? “You will be like God” — you will have more power, more control, more freedom.

And the result? After eating the fruit, the first thing that happened was that their eyes were opened and they saw they were naked; the second was hiding; the third was shifting the blame.

More free? No. From that moment people began to be afraid, began to hide, began to accuse one another.

The lesson puts it superbly: when we keep saying “I want,” we become tied to the things we want.

2. Three chains

The lesson lists three kinds of bondage:

Those who want money become slaves of money.

Those who want power become prisoners of power.

Those who want lust become puppets of desire.

Brothers and sisters, this is not rhetorical exaggeration; it is the plain teaching of the Bible.

Paul says, “Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness?” (Romans 6:16)

The Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin” (John 8:34).

Notice Paul’s logic: people are not choosing between “being a slave” and “not being a slave”; they are choosing “whose slave to be.” No one is entirely their own master. You think you are riding the horse; very often the horse is riding you.

3. The illusion of freedom

The lesson goes straight to the point: Satan’s craftiest move is to make us think “I want” is freedom, when in fact “I want” is where bondage begins.

We can understand this through something we all know. Everything addictive — whether drugs, alcohol, gambling, or even the endless short videos on our phones that we never finish scrolling — shares one feature, called “tolerance.” The first time, a little is enough; later it takes more and more; in the end the same amount brings no pleasure at all and is used only to stop the discomfort. It begins with pleasure and ends with painkilling. That is the trajectory of “I want.”

In Book Eight of his Confessions, Augustine describes the process of his own bondage. He says that from a perverse will came lust; lust indulged became habit; and habit not resisted became necessity.

Sentences written sixteen hundred years ago read today as if they were describing us last night.

And at the beginning of the same book Augustine wrote the words that have shaped the church for sixteen hundred years: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

Brothers and sisters, this is the heart of the matter. Our hearts were made in the image of God; their capacity was prepared for God. However many things you pour in, they will never be full, because the empty space is God-shaped.

C. S. Lewis also makes a very sharp observation in Mere Christianity. He says that pride is essentially competitive: pride gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next person.

So, brothers and sisters, pride is bound to make people miserable. As long as there is one person in the world better than me, I cannot rest; and there will always be someone in the world better than me.

4. Pride’s five “I will”s

There is one passage in the Bible that shows the end of “I want” more clearly than any other. Isaiah speaks of the king of Babylon, and the church through the ages has also applied the description to the fall of Satan:

“You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, count them: how many times does he say “I will”? Five.

Five “I will”s, all the way up, rising higher and higher. And what does the next verse say? “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:15).

Solomon said it long ago: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

Pride’s sense of direction is always wrong. It thinks it is rising; in fact it is falling.

5. The law of sowing and reaping

The lesson quotes Paul’s warning. Let’s read the full passage:

“Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” (Galatians 6:7–8)

Paul uses a farmer’s picture. The one thing a farmer knows best is that you reap what you sow — and you always reap more than you sow.

Brothers and sisters, we often have a fantasy: I only indulge myself now and then; surely nothing will come of it. But a farmer never says, “I only scattered a few seeds carelessly; surely they won’t come up.”

The very nature of a seed is to grow. Sow a single seed, and when its time comes it grows into a whole field.

The lesson says: when we keep catering to our own desires, the end cannot be satisfaction; it can only be brokenness and destruction.

This is a loving warning, not a threat. Because God does not want us to come to that point.

6. The Lord who did not say “I want”

Brothers and sisters, at this point we must turn our eyes to an example of the complete opposite.

In the garden of Gethsemane, as the Lord Jesus faced the cross, he too had a will; he too had feelings. He said, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me.” But straight away he spoke the most powerful sentence in the whole universe: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39).

Satan said “I will” five times in heaven, and fell to Sheol; the Lord Jesus said once in the garden, “not what I desire,” and saved all humanity.

Paul describes him like this: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

“Emptied himself” — this is exactly what the 321 vision calls “selflessness.”

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: Jesus is my role model. When it comes to dealing with pride, our role model is not a set of techniques but a person — the Lord who laid down his rights, returned to his originally intended position, and obeyed to the very end.

7. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

We have all seen this law at work at home, at work and at church. One hard word is answered with a harder one; one person who won’t back down meets another who won’t back down, and in the end both lose.

But the reverse is just as true. When one person softens first, the atmosphere changes; when one person admits their own fault first, the other’s defences come down.

Humility is not losing; humility is letting Jesus win first.

The Bible says, “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5).

The word “resists,” Greek antitassomai (ἀντιτάσσομαι), is a military term meaning to draw up in battle array against. Brothers and sisters, what a sobering picture — God himself deploying his forces against the proud.

We truly do not want God standing on the opposite side from us.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: From “I Want” to “Your Will Be Done”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we have seen today and set it in order within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

In dealing with pride, not one of these three can be missing.

Jesus is my role model: in Gethsemane he showed us “not what I desire.” When I don’t know how to let go, I look at him.

The Bible is my standard: when Satan says, “You deserve more,” I need a word with greater authority to answer him. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, three times he said, “It is written.” Without a standard, I will take my feelings as my standard, and feelings always stand on the side of sinful desire.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: the power of sinful desire is too great to be overcome by willpower. Galatians says, “But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:8). What overcomes the flesh is not flesh trying harder, but the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The essence of pride is “I want to be king.” Brothers and sisters, a heart has only one throne. If Jesus is not sitting on it, I am. Every day we are making a decision about that chair.

And “let Jesus receive all the glory” is the most thorough cure for “the pride of life.” Because “the pride of life” wants applause; when I pass the applause on to Jesus, that ever-demanding appetite is cut off from its supply.

The Goal — establish God’s system.

Self-centred people establish “my system”: centred on me, using my methods, to achieve my goals. Selfless people establish “God’s system”: centred on God, using God’s methods, to accomplish God’s will. Here too our perspective shifts: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

John continues that passage: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:17).

Brothers and sisters, everything “I want” wants will pass away; what “your will be done” gains will remain forever.

Finally, let’s bring it down to 920 and 235.

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Notice the last fruit of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Self-control — this is exactly the fruit that deals with sinful desire. And it is “borne,” not “squeezed out.” Fruit is the product of life, not the product of effort.

235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, in dealing with pride, the worst thing is to fight alone. Because what pride does best is justify itself. We need a spiritual companion who can tell us the truth, a pair of eyes that can see our blind spots.

Pride grows fastest in the dark; in the light it won’t survive three days.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word without doing it is like seeing food and not eating it. The lesson gives us three very practical practices. Let’s look at them one at a time, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to root them deep.

Practice one: whenever “I want” rises up in your heart, stop and ask yourself, “Is this from God, or from sinful desire?”

This is a “pause button” practice.

Information: first remember today’s truth — sinful desire draws away and entices; it is like a hunter and like an angler, out to lure me from my hiding place.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let me truly see where that “I want” inside me is springing from. Information is knowing; revelation is seeing. Those who know will nod; those who see will weep.

Conviction: I admit wholeheartedly that if this “I want” isn’t dealt with, it will conceive, give birth to sin, and give birth to death.

Implementation: from today, set a three-second pause. When “I want” rises up, don’t decide, don’t place the order, don’t reply to the message, don’t answer back. Three seconds, and one sentence of prayer: “Lord, is this your will, or my sinful desire?”

Evaluation: before bed, take two minutes to look back — how many times did I press the pause button today? Which time did it work? Which time did I give way?

Correction: identify the times and situations when you are most likely to give way. Late at night? When you’re tired? After being put down? Then set up your defences in advance for those times.

Repetition: once doesn’t count, a week isn’t enough; this is a lifelong practice. Multiplication: teach this pause button to your family, your “2,” someone in your small group.

Practice two: spend a few minutes every day thanking God for the grace he has already given you, replacing “I still want” with “I already have.”

This is a “saying it differently” practice.

Brothers and sisters, our hearts cannot be filled with two kinds of words at once. The best way to drive out darkness is not to fight the darkness but to switch on the light.

The Bible says, “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

David says, “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Notice that David is giving orders to his own soul. He knew the heart does not give thanks automatically; it needs to be reminded and led.

There is solid research in psychology supporting this too. In 2003 Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published an experiment in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They divided participants into groups: one group wrote down five things each week they were grateful for, another five things that had annoyed them, and another simply five things that had happened. After several weeks, the group writing gratitude lists rated their lives more positively overall, complained of fewer physical symptoms and exercised more often.

One pen and five lines can change the angle from which a person sees the world. But brothers and sisters, Christian thanksgiving goes deeper than this. We give thanks not only because “it works well”; we give thanks because “he is worthy.”

The way to put it into practice is simple: each morning after reading the Bible, write down three specific graces. Don’t write something vague like “Thank you, Lord, for your grace.” Write, “Thank you, Lord, that this morning I could still get out of bed on my own.”

After a week, look back and you will find the theme of your thanksgiving list beginning to change — from “things going smoothly” gradually towards “who he is.” That is your perspective shifting from the earthly to the heavenly.

Practice three: when you want to grab hold of something, choose to let go, and let God satisfy you.

This is a “loosening your grip” practice.

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

“Deny himself” — this is selflessness. And denying of self is never an abstract state of mind; it always comes down to something concrete.

Letting go might mean letting go of a conversation you’ve been determined to win; it might mean letting go of a position you’ve always wanted and putting it into God’s hands; it might mean letting go of a person you’ve been clutching tightly, no longer using your emotions to control them; or it might mean letting go of that app on your phone you know you shouldn’t open again.

What does David say? “Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup. You made my lot secure. The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places. Yes, I have a good inheritance” (Psalm 16:5–6).

Hebrews also says, “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5).

Brothers and sisters, listen to the logic: I can be content not because what I have is enough, but because the One who has me is good enough.

And God never leaves us to struggle without a way out: “No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Letting go is not falling; letting go is landing in his hands.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, please keep these two sentences from the lesson in your heart and take them home with you.

Satan’s lie is: “I don’t have it; I want it.”

God’s truth is: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 23:1).

Notice that David doesn’t say, “I have everything.” He says, “I shall lack nothing.”

The difference between the two is enormous. “Having everything” is a warehouse; “lacking nothing” is a relationship. A warehouse can be emptied; the shepherd will not walk away.

David was a shepherd in his youth, and he knew all too well what kind of animal a sheep is — slow-witted, easily lost, with almost no means of defence. A sheep’s only security is its shepherd.

So what this sentence really means is: because he is here, I no longer need to say “I want.”

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have walked three steps.

Step one: the root of pride is believing Satan’s lie — the problem lies in our mindset.

Step two: the driving force of pride is the push of sinful desire — the problem spreads like fire into our life.

Step three: the price of pride is the loss of freedom and blessing — the problem shows itself in our daily living.

And the lesson’s conclusion gathers everything into one sentence: pride begins with “I want”; humility begins with “Lord, your will be done.”

Brothers and sisters, behind every choice lies a spiritual battle.

Don’t underestimate that one small thought in the early morning. Don’t underestimate that “I deserve it.” Don’t underestimate that “just this once won’t matter.”

Every thought is a vote — a vote for myself as king, or a vote for Jesus as King.

The Bible says, “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7).

Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can we resist the devil. Many people get it backwards, resisting the devil with all their might while never being willing to submit to God, and they end up fighting themselves to exhaustion.

Because the strength to resist the devil comes from submitting to God.

So this morning I want to issue three calls to you, brothers and sisters.

First, if there is an “I want” that keeps coming back in your heart right now, please don’t step around it any more. Today, call it by name, bring it to the Lord, and say to him, “Lord, this is my sinful desire; please deal with it.”

Second, if you have been bound by something for a long time — so long that you think that’s who you are — brothers and sisters, that is not who you are. The Lord Jesus said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly” (John 10:10). He did not come to confiscate your joy; he came to give back what was stolen from you.

Third, if today you feel you’re doing fine, with no real problems — please be especially careful. Because that is exactly where pride most loves to hide. Ask the Lord to search you.

Let us no longer believe the lie, no longer obey sinful desire, but answer God’s truth with humility, letting the selfless life replace the pride of “I want,” and entering into true freedom and satisfaction.

May Jesus reign as King in our hearts.

May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)
“For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare this together with me:
Lord, I will no longer believe Satan’s lies;
I will no longer let “I want” define my life;
For you have given me all I need; you are my greatest satisfaction.
Keep me far from pride, living in humility and thanksgiving.
practices: Whenever “I want” rises up in your heart, stop and ask yourself
Spend a few minutes every day thanking God for the grace he has already given you, replacing “I still want” with “I already have”
When you want to grab hold of something, choose to let go, and let God satisfy you
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we come before you and confess that we say “I want” to ourselves far too often.

We ask your forgiveness. Forgive us for setting you aside and sitting on that throne ourselves; forgive us for believing Satan’s lie that we could live better apart from you; forgive us for using the three words “I deserve it” to justify so many things we should never have wanted.

Lord, shine your light on the sinful desires within us. They hide so deep that even we cannot see them. Holy Spirit, like a lamp, shine into every corner of our hearts, so that we see the thoughts that are already conceiving, and hand them over to you before they give birth to sin.
Lord Jesus, you are our role model. In Gethsemane you said, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” Put these words into our hearts, and make them the first prayer of every day.

Lord, we also ask you to heal our discontent. Help us see that what we lack is not things, but you. Let us taste your goodness afresh, so that we can say from the heart: Yahweh is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.
Give us spiritual companions who can speak the truth to one another, remind one another and hold one another up, so that we do not wrestle with pride alone in the dark.
In every relationship, help us live out the selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit — especially the fruit of self-control.
Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory go to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.” (James 1:14) Please share honestly: over the past week, what is the “I want” that has come up most often in your heart? Do you think it comes from God, or from sinful desire? How do you plan to deal with it?

“Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) Share something you once held on to tightly but later learned to let go of. After you let go, how did God provide for you? If there is still something you are holding on to now, are you willing to hand it over to God today here in your small group?
l074.title: Where Does Pride Come From?
l074.subtitle: Sinful Desire Is the Fuel of Pride
l074.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: The Hand That Wouldn’t Let Go of the Peanuts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today let’s think together about something very small that nevertheless decides whether our whole life is lived in freedom or in bondage — when, at last, we’re willing to open our hands.

Let me begin with an old, much-told story. A man sets out to catch a monkey. He uses no net and no gun — just a wooden box with a very narrow opening and a handful of peanuts inside. The monkey reaches in and grabs a fistful of peanuts, but a fist full of peanuts is bigger than the opening, and no matter how it pulls, it can’t get its hand out. The hunter walks up; the monkey shrieks in panic and tugs with all its might, yet it simply will not let go. It isn’t the box that has trapped it. It’s trapped by its own hand — the moment it lets go of those peanuts, it’s free to leave.

Brothers and sisters, we are so often just like that. What really traps us is seldom our circumstances; far more often it’s that hand of ours that refuses to open. What holds us captive is not what we lack, but what we can’t bear to give up.

In the last lesson we saw that pride springs from Satan’s lies and from human desire. Satan keeps whispering two sentences into people’s ears: “I don’t have it — I want it.” And once they have it, he switches to another: “I have it — and I want more.” Those two sentences push people into a cycle that never stops — discontent, wanting, getting, discontent again, wanting again. That cycle has no terminus. There’s only ever a next stop.

But our Lord Jesus walked the exact opposite road. He was not mastered by the lie of “I want.” What he chose was “I don’t want.” This is the principle of humility, and it’s the secret of overcoming pride.

Psychology has looked closely at this hand that won’t let go. In 1990, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler published the famous “mug experiment” in the “Journal of Political Economy.” They gave a coffee mug at random to half the participants and then let the two groups trade freely. The result: the people who had been given a mug asked, on average, more than twice what those without a mug were willing to pay. The very same mug meant nothing to me yesterday, yet today, simply because it is “mine,” its value has doubled. This is what’s called the “endowment effect.”

Brothers and sisters, the moment we hang the label “mine” on something, its price changes — and so does our heart. The thing hasn’t grown heavier. We’ve just started gripping it tighter.

So in today’s lesson we’ll follow the text and walk, step by step, along four stretches of road. First, the role model of Jesus — “I have it, but I don’t want it.” Second, Satan’s principle — “I want,” the mindset of possessing. Third, desire is the entry point of pride — a small desire, a big breach. Fourth, the way to overcome pride — the choice of humility.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Joy Sent from Prison
1. Author, Date and Recipients
sections.html:
The theme passage of this lesson comes from Philippians chapter 2. Its author is the apostle Paul. It’s generally held that the letter was written between AD 60 and 62, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome. A man in chains wrote a letter in which “joy” and “rejoice” appear more than a dozen times. Brothers and sisters, that in itself is a sermon: freedom isn’t found in our circumstances; freedom is found in a heart that no longer grasps for itself.

The church that received it, in Philippi, was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). Philippi was a Roman colony, home to many retired soldiers; its residents held Roman citizenship, and the city was intensely class-conscious — everyone cared about title, status and honour. To people like these, Paul wrote: have the same mind that was in Christ Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. The Context: A Small Crack in a Church
sections.html:
Why does Paul insert this most exalted passage about Christ just here? Because a small crack had appeared in the church at Philippi. In chapter 4 Paul names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two co-workers were at odds. He also urges them: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3-4)

Brothers and sisters, notice the word “conceit,” which the Chinese Union Version renders “coveting empty glory.” The Greek is κενοδοξία (kenodoxia), formed from “empty” (kenos) and “glory” (doxa) — literally “empty glory.” People fight and scramble, and what they end up clutching is so often an empty shell. And right after this, Paul uses the same root to describe the Lord: “emptied himself” — in Greek ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), “to pour oneself out until empty.”

People strain with everything they have to fill themselves with “empty glory,” while the Lord willingly “emptied” himself. One single root nails down the message of the whole letter: a church’s problem isn’t its structures; it’s a question of who is willing to empty themselves first.

sections.heading: 3. The Theme Passage, Phrase by Phrase
sections.html:
“Existing in the form of God” — the Greek for “form” is μορφή (morphē). It doesn’t mean outward appearance; it means the true expression of an inner essence. Jesus isn’t merely like God. He is God.

“Didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped” — the Greek for “a thing to be grasped” is ἁρπαγμός (harpagmos), meaning “a prize of war held tight and never released.” Jesus’ equality with God was his by right, not something he had seized; and precisely because it wasn’t seized, he had no need to cling to it. Brothers and sisters, there’s a very deep truth here: the more truly you possess something, the less you need to clutch it; the more insecure a person is, the tighter they grip.

“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” — the Greek for “servant” is δοῦλος (doulos), a person with no sovereignty of their own at all. He didn’t lose his divinity; he added the identity of a servant. He didn’t become less; he laid himself down.

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” — in the Roman world, the cross was a punishment reserved for slaves and rebels. Those people in Philippi who prided themselves on their Roman citizenship must have been shaken to hear these words: the direction we strain so hard to climb is the very direction our Lord went down, all the way down.

This is the key to the lesson. Satan’s route runs upward: I want, I want, I want. Jesus’ route runs downward: emptying himself, humbling himself, obeying, even to death. And God’s response is: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” (Philippians 2:9)

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Role Model of Jesus — “I Have It, but I Don’t Want It”
sections.html:
1. He Already Had Everything

First we need to see one thing clearly: when Jesus said “I don’t want it,” it wasn’t because he didn’t have it. He is the One who possesses all things. “All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.” (John 1:3) All the glory and authority of heaven were already his.

That is exactly why his “I don’t want it” carries such weight. When someone who has nothing says “I don’t want it,” it may be nothing more than resignation. When someone who has everything says “I don’t want it,” that is true denying of self. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

2. The First Showdown in the Wilderness

When the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, Satan played his biggest card: “Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory. He said to him, ‘I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.’ Then Jesus said to him, ‘Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.”’” (Matthew 4:8-10)

Brothers and sisters, look closely at this deal: what Satan offered was “possession,” and the price he demanded was “worship.” He never tells people outright to worship him; he just keeps whispering in their ear, “You could have it.” The Lord’s answer was absolutely decisive. It wasn’t that he lacked the power to gain the kingdoms of the world; it was that he refused to gain them Satan’s way.

This is the first layer of “I have it, but I don’t want it”: I refuse to use methods that don’t fit God’s heart to get even what is rightly meant to be mine.

3. The Final Time, in Gethsemane

But the deepest “I have it, but I don’t want it” came in the Garden of Gethsemane. “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord didn’t pretend not to be in anguish. He said, “Let this cup pass away from me” — that was a real struggle. But then he said, “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” Denying of self doesn’t mean feeling nothing. Denying of self means handing over the sovereignty even while you feel it all.

4. Children Are a Blessing, Not a Possession

Let me be clear first: “I don’t want it” is not a denial of blessing, still less a gloomy rejection of life. What it deals with is the heart that rewrites God’s grace into “my property, my pride.” The text gives an example very close to home: our children. “Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” (Psalm 127:3) Children are entrusted to us by God; they are a blessing. But the moment we treat our children as “my property, my pride, my face,” the trouble begins.

Without realising it, we start treating our child’s grades as our own report card and our child’s career as our own business card. So love turns into control, and care turns into pressure; what the child feels is not being loved, but being graded.

Scripture shows us two parents who did the opposite. Hannah prayed for years before she received Samuel, and as soon as he was weaned she brought him to Shiloh: “I prayed for this child, and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I have also given him to Yahweh. As long as he lives he is given to Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 1:27-28) Abraham took Isaac up Mount Moriah, and God said: “For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” (Genesis 22:12)

Brothers and sisters, neither of them failed to love their child. They simply knew all too well whose child it was. Those who let go are the ones who gain; those who cling are the ones who lose. It’s the same with marriage, with ministry, with wealth and career — the moment we want to “possess,” the struggle begins; the moment we’re willing to “let go” and let Jesus take over, everything finds its order again.

5. Two Convictions That Overcome

The text gives us one very powerful sentence: “Whether I have it or not, I can still not want it.” There are two practices here —

“I don’t have it, and I don’t want it” — this is contentment. “But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.” (1 Timothy 6:6-8)

“I have it, but I don’t want it” — this is denying of self. “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Once we’ve learned both, Satan’s deceptions lose their power. For every bait he uses hangs either on “you don’t have it” or on “you could have more.” A person who neither fears going without nor craves having more gives him nowhere to set his hook.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is that hand clutching the peanuts; selflessness is the moment we willingly let go. And let me stress this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Satan’s Principle — “I Want”: The Mindset of Possessing
sections.html:
1. Five Times “I Will”

“I want” is the language of pride and the seed of desire. Its earliest and clearest appearance came at the moment the archangel fell: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13-14)

Brothers and sisters, count them: in just two verses, five times “I will.” Satan’s fall didn’t begin with some great sin; it began with “I want.” The 321 vision puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Then in Eden the same script was handed to humanity, word for word: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate.” (Genesis 3:6) “Good for food” is the lust of the flesh; “a delight to the eyes” is the lust of the eyes; “to make one wise” is the pride of life. John sums up these three in exactly the same way: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

2. Want to Possess, and You’ll Be Bound by What You Possess

The text puts it with great insight: “I want” drives people to pursue possessions, and in the end they are bound by the very things they possess.

Want money, and money will control you. Want a reputation, and you’ll be tied up by other people’s opinions. Want relationships, and you’ll be held hostage by your feelings.

Brothers and sisters, someone who cares about money sees their face fall every time the stock market falls; someone who cares about their reputation can lose a whole night’s sleep over a single online comment. How clearly the Lord said it: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

3. Why “Wanting” Never Stops

Neuroscience offers a piercing piece of corroboration here. After years of research, Professors Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson of the University of Michigan proposed that “wanting” and “liking” in the brain are two different systems, and that dopamine mainly drives “wanting,” not “liking.” In other words, the brain can crave something intensely and then, once it gets it, not be all that happy.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly what “I want” looks like? While we’re chasing it, our heart races; once we’ve got it, the thrill lasts three days. After three days, our eyes start searching for the next target.

Psychology also has a famous observation called “hedonic adaptation.” In 1978, Philip Brickman and his colleagues published a study in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” comparing big lottery winners with ordinary people. They found that the happiness of winning fell away quickly, and the winners’ everyday happiness was not much higher than that of the control group. In 2010, Kahneman and Angus Deaton published research in the “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” showing that higher income does improve day-to-day emotional well-being, but beyond a certain level the gains clearly level off.

Three thousand years ago Solomon had already said: “He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 5:10) What decades of scientific research have concluded, Scripture said in a single sentence.

4. Money as an Example

The text uses money as a particular example: if we want to possess it, money will rule us; but if in our hearts we “don’t want to possess,” money can’t bind us. Such people are free to give generously and use their wealth to advance God’s kingdom, rather than being held captive by it.
