Paul’s words deserve to be read slowly, word by word: “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.” (1 Timothy 6:9-10)

Notice that Scripture doesn’t say “money is the root of evil”; it says “the love of money” is. The problem isn’t in our wallet; it’s in our heart. Money in our hand is a tool; money in our heart is a master.

The eighteenth-century evangelist John Wesley left us three sentences in his sermon “The Use of Money”: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can. As his own income grew, his standard of living stayed the same, and he gave away all the rest. In the nineteenth century, George Müller (1805–1898) of Bristol in England cared for more than ten thousand orphans in his lifetime, yet resolved never to ask anyone for money — he asked only God, in prayer. The man who didn’t cling to money became a blessing to countless children.

Psychology confirms this path too. In 2008, Elizabeth Dunn, Michael Norton and their colleagues published a study in the journal “Science”: people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent the same amount on themselves. Once again the Lord Jesus’ words prove true: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

5. Applying the 321 Vision

Brothers and sisters, behind “I want” and “I don’t want” lie two different perspectives. The 321 vision says we must shift from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Seen from an earthly, temporary perspective, letting go is a loss. Seen from a heavenly, eternal perspective, letting go is storing things in the safest place there is. “But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:20-21)

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Desire Is the Entry Point of Pride — A Small Desire, a Big Breach
sections.html:
1. The Production Line of Sin

Scripture describes how sin comes into being almost like a production line: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14-15)

Brothers and sisters, notice the four stages: desire, conception, sin, death. Not one step happens suddenly; at every step there’s a chance to call a halt. Sin doesn’t appear overnight. Sin is fed until it grows up.

“Drawn away” and “enticed” are both fishing terms in Greek: “drawn away” (ἐξέλκω) is luring a fish out of its hiding place, and “enticed” (δελεάζω) is tricking it onto the hook with bait. Brothers and sisters, Satan never fishes with a bare hook; there’s always something on it that we genuinely want.

2. Little Foxes and Small Breaches

Pride doesn’t necessarily begin with big things; more often it slips in through “a small desire.” That little bit of “wanting,” that faint trace of “resentment,” can become Satan’s breakthrough point.

“Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom.” (Song of Songs 2:15) Brothers and sisters, Scripture doesn’t say lions ruin the vineyard; it says little foxes do. When a lion comes, everyone runs; when a little fox comes, nobody pays any attention. Yet when the vines are in blossom, the damage a little fox does is deadly.

Paul gives the same warning: “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil.” (Ephesians 4:26-27) The Greek for “place” is τόπος (topos) — “a spot, a space.” The devil doesn’t need us to throw the whole door open. All he needs is a crack.

3. Judas: A Mirror

He had been a disciple, chosen personally by Jesus (Mark 3:19), the one among the Twelve who kept the money. John honestly records his problem: “Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it.” (John 12:6)

Brothers and sisters, notice: this wasn’t one massive embezzlement. He “used to steal what was put into it.” A little at a time. And every time, he could convince himself: this is for the Lord’s work too; I give so much; taking a little isn’t going too far. That’s exactly how a small desire grows up.

Then that “thought” came in: “During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him.” (John 13:2) Brothers and sisters, notice the order — first the desire for money had been stored inside him for a long time; only later did the devil put in a specific intention. The breach was one he opened himself; the enemy merely walked in.

How many chances did Jesus give him? The Lord washed the disciples’ feet, Judas’ feet included (John 13:5). The Lord also handed him the dipped piece of bread — in the banquet culture of the time, handing someone that morsel was the highest mark of honour and acceptance: “So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.” (John 13:26)

The Lord had shown love to the very uttermost. And yet Scripture goes on: “After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him.” (John 13:27) Between “put into his heart” and “entered into him” there stood just one more choice — and still he would not choose humility and repentance.

And how did it end? Thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), and then: “He threw down the pieces of silver in the sanctuary, and departed. He went away and hanged himself.” (Matthew 27:5) Brothers and sisters, he never got to spend a single coin of that money. What desire promises, it never pays out.

Peter fell too; he denied the Lord three times. But Peter “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75) — he turned back. Both men failed. The difference wasn’t the size of the failure; it was where each went after he fell: one toward humility, the other toward despair.

4. The Lesson of Delayed Gratification

In the 1960s and 70s, Professor Walter Mischel of Stanford University in the United States ran the famous “marshmallow experiment.” A child had one marshmallow placed in front of them; if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Some children couldn’t hold out for more than a few dozen seconds; others turned their heads away, sang songs, or sat on their hands, and lasted the full fifteen minutes.

I should add that a large-scale replication published in 2018 by Watts, Duncan and Quan in “Psychological Science” found that family socio-economic background accounted for a substantial part of the differences, and that the long-term predictive power claimed early on was not as strong as once thought. Still, the experiment itself reveals something important: in the face of temptation, what works best isn’t gritting your teeth, but taking your eyes off the marshmallow.

Brothers and sisters, that’s exactly what Scripture has always taught. In dealing with desire, the crucial thing isn’t to wrestle it with clenched teeth, but to turn our focus to Jesus. “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:2) The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Stare at the marshmallow and you’ll lose every time; look to Jesus and you’re free.

5. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. What makes desire so terrifying is that it works as this fivefold change in reverse — one small desire left unaddressed first distorts the mindset, then corrodes the life, then wrecks relationships, and finally destroys the ministry. Judas is the case study of someone who went all the way down that road.

That’s why the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Judas had a ministry. He was one of the twelve apostles; he preached and he cast out demons. But in his life there was a breach that was never dealt with. Brothers and sisters, if the life isn’t dealt with, the bigger the ministry, the harder the fall.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Way to Overcome Pride — The Choice of Humility
sections.html:
1. Root and Fruit

The text puts it very concisely: the root of pride is “I want”; the fruit of humility is “I don’t want.”

2. “I Don’t Want It” Is an Active Declaration of Faith

Choosing “I don’t want” is not passive; it is an active declaration of faith: “Lord, I will not live for myself. Come and reign.”

There is a kind of “not wanting” in this world that is really pretending not to want what we can’t have — disappointment in disguise. A Christian’s “I don’t want” is something else entirely. I don’t want it because I have someone far better; I let go because there is a steadier pair of hands to catch me.

“I don’t want” is not negativity; it is actively trusting in God’s provision. “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.’” (Hebrews 13:5)

Paul could not have put the secret more plainly: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:11-13)

Notice the words “I have learned.” Contentment is not an inborn temperament; contentment is a lesson learned. Brothers and sisters, if it can be learned, then there is a curriculum, there is practice, there are exams — and it also means that every one of us can learn it.

3. When We Let Go, God Goes to Work

The text says: when we are willing to let go, God goes to work; when we choose humility, God raises us up. This is not a motivational slogan; it is a promise Scripture makes again and again.

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:6-7)

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first submit to God, and only then can we resist the devil. Many people try to resist the devil directly without first submitting to God, and the harder they try to drive him off, the more exhausted they become. Submission is the foundation of resistance.

“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Our part is simply to go low; lifting us up is God’s part.

4. The Logic of a Grain of Wheat

The Lord used a picture every farmer understands: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat held in your hand is perfectly safe — and it will only ever be one grain. Put it into the soil and it seems to lose everything, yet in exchange it yields a whole field of wheat. Brothers and sisters, hold on, and you keep one grain; let go, and you gain a field. That is the arithmetic of the kingdom of heaven.

5. Words of Wisdom and a Reminder

The English writer C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind, and as long as a person is proud, he cannot know God.

Augustine opens his Confessions by saying to God: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly why “I want” can never stop — our hearts are too big; nothing created can ever fill them. Only God himself can give them rest.

6. Applying the 321 Vision

At this point all of 321’s Three Foundations come together. Jesus is my role model — he had it, but he didn’t want it. The Bible is my standard — not my feelings, but God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — what I can’t give up in my own strength, I can give up by the Holy Spirit. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16)

The Two Core Values are here too. Let Jesus be King — saying “I don’t want” is giving up the throne to him. Let Jesus receive all the glory — no longer coveting that hollow, empty glory. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he existed in the form of God, yet emptied himself. The Bible is my standard — we judge not by what the market says, but by what God’s word says. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the strength to let go isn’t willpower; it’s the power of the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — when a heart is still saying “I want,” it’s we ourselves who are sitting on the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when we stop fighting over that empty glory, the true glory goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A crowd of people all saying “I want” can only build a Tower of Babel; only people who have learned to say “I don’t want” can build God’s house together.

sections.heading: 2. Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place — that is the road of Satan’s five “I will”s. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God — that is the road of the Lord Jesus, who “emptied himself.”

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This is the most common tragedy in families: both people want to win, so both people lose. The moment one of them is willing to say first, “I don’t need to win this time,” that home begins to come back to life.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today there’s just one mindset to change: from “possessing is gaining” to “letting go is gaining.”

Our perspective must shift as well: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Through earthly eyes, “I don’t want it” is a loss; through eternal eyes, “I don’t want it” is depositing things into an account that can never decay.

sections.heading: 4. The Priority of Relationships and the 920 Practice
sections.html:
The 321 vision says relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson is exactly what people who have reversed that order most need to hear. Many people grab hold of things first, then people, then themselves, and only at the very end think of God — so they grasp at everything and are worn out by everything.

The 920 practice is very practical here: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” As we practise living out the selfless “0” before them, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23) — which of them doesn’t grow precisely in the moments we say “I don’t want”? Patience is “I don’t want to explode right now”; self-control is “I don’t want to follow my cravings.”

And 235 relationships remind us: don’t try to tough it out alone. Find a brother or sister who is equally willing to be selfless to be your “2,” and remind each other about that clenched hand; then build your “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and pass this lesson on; and finally become a “5,” a team of spiritual comrades. For one person to let go is hard; when a whole group lets go together, it becomes revival.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The text gives us three practices for daily living. We don’t just want to know them; we want to walk them through the eight stages — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they truly become life.

Practice 1: Examine the “I want” in your heart every day

Every day, examine the “I want” in your heart and say to the Lord: “Lord, I give this to you. I refuse to be controlled by it.”

Information: Today we’ve learned that “I want” is Satan’s principle and “I don’t want” is Jesus’ principle.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show me the truest “I want” in my heart. It might be a position, a word of affirmation, a relationship, a sum of money, or an apology from someone else.

Conviction: I believe what the Lord says is true — clinging only binds me; letting go is what sets me free.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three quiet minutes writing down the biggest “I want” in your heart that day, then say to the Lord in specific terms: “Lord, I give this one to you. I refuse to be controlled by it.”

Evaluation: In the evening, look back — did it lead me around by the nose today? Which moment, which remark, pulled me back into “I want”?

Correction: Don’t condemn yourself and don’t make excuses; confess, and hand it over once more (1 John 1:9).

Repetition: Forty days in a row. A change of mindset takes repetition; one moment of being moved won’t change a lifetime of habit.

Multiplication: Tell a brother or sister about this practice, and ask each other once a week: “This week, did you hand it over?”

Practice 2: Ask yourself, “Who am I wanting this for?”

When you’re struggling over possessions, relationships, ministry or position, ask yourself: “Who am I wanting this for?”

Information: Motive determines nature. The very same thing, done for God, is service; done for ourselves, it’s ambition.

Revelation: Ask God to expose my hidden motives. “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9)

Conviction: I admit that even within my most spiritual actions an “I want” may be hiding.

Implementation: At the very moment of each struggle, stop for three seconds and ask: “Who am I wanting this for?” If the answer is “for my own face,” hand it over right there and then.

Evaluation: Once a week, take stock — what was my fiercest struggle this week? What did I really want underneath it?

Correction: Take the part that is “wanting it for myself” and concretely turn it into “wanting it for God’s kingdom.” For example: not asking the Lord to let me be seen, but asking him to use me, even if no one sees.

Repetition: Practise it again and again in the same area until the response becomes instinct.

Multiplication: When someone near you is caught in a struggle, don’t rush to give advice; first sit with them and ask, “Who are you wanting this for?”

Practice 3: Write down one thing you’re willing to let go of

Write down one thing you’re willing to “let go” of, and pray over it, entrusting it to the Lord.

Information: Letting go isn’t giving up; it’s transferring sovereignty.

Revelation: Be still before the Lord and let him point out that one thing — usually the very thing you least want to write down.

Conviction: Believe he can catch it. “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” (Psalm 37:5)

Implementation: Write it down today, and write it clearly — the date, the matter, the person; a vague entrusting is no entrusting at all.

Evaluation: Take it out again a month later — have I really let go? Have I quietly taken it back?

Correction: If you’ve taken it back, let go of it once more. Every year Hannah made a little robe and brought it to Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:19) — letting go doesn’t cut off love; it puts love back in its proper place.

Repetition: Rewrite your list every quarter. You’ll find you can lay down more and more, and the space in your heart keeps growing larger.

Multiplication: Tell someone who is struggling right now the story of how God worked after you let go. Your testimony is their Information.

A Gentle Reminder: Two Sentences, Two Roads

Satan says: “I don’t have it — I want it.”

Jesus says: “I have it, but I don’t want it.”

The first brings bondage; the second brings freedom.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, which of the two is your heart repeating?

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Gaining Everything by Not Wanting
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that monkey’s hand at the beginning. It wasn’t the box that trapped it. It was trapped by its own hand.

Pride ensnares us in the net of “I want”; humility brings us into the freedom of “I don’t want.” Jesus lived out, with his own life, the role model of “I have it, but I don’t want it,” and revealed that true glory lies not in possessing, but in laying down.

That’s why Scripture says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9-11)

The end of this road is not “now I have nothing left.” The end of this road is “to the glory of God the Father.” Brothers and sisters, laying down is not the end; laying down is the beginning of letting Jesus reign as King.

This morning I want to invite you to make one very concrete decision: hand over the fistful of peanuts in your hand. It might be a position you’ve clung to for years; it might be someone you’ve never been willing to forgive; it might be a life you’ve designed in advance for your child; it might be a sum of money you’re afraid to give; or it might simply be an “I’m sorry” you’ve been waiting for someone else to say first.

Let us follow his example: choose humility, choose denying of self, gain everything in “not wanting,” and enter true fullness in “letting go.” Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5-8)
declarations: Lord, you are the satisfaction of my whole life.
I no longer chase worldly possessions, nor do I live for myself.
I choose “I don’t want,” and let you reign,
that my heart may find freedom and peace in you.
practices: Write down one thing you’re willing to let go of
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Your Son existed in your form, yet emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and walked the road of the cross. Lord, only this morning have we seen that true glory lies not in possessing, but in laying down.

Lord, forgive us. There’s so much “I want” in our hearts — I want to be seen, I want to be affirmed, I want to be in control, I want everything to be all right. Shine your light on that hand inside us that refuses to open.

Lord, we open our hands now. We give our children back to you, our marriages back to you; our careers, our money, our reputations, our places of ministry — we give them all back to you. We also bring before you that trace of resentment, that little desire; wash it clean with your precious blood, so that we no longer give place to the devil.

Holy Spirit, guide us every day, so that we no longer rely on the brain and ourselves, but rely on the heart and on you. In every moment of struggle, help us to say: “Lord, I don’t want it — what you want is enough.”
May our homes be restored because someone let go first; may our churches be united because someone humbled themselves first; may your kingdom come, and your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5-7) The Lord Jesus possessed everything, yet chose “I have it, but I don’t want it.” In your life right now, what is something you “have” but have been gripping tightly? If you were to open your hand after the Lord’s example, what would you be most afraid of losing?

“Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15) Judas’ breach began with that little bit he “used to steal.” Think honestly: is there a little fox in your heart that you’ve been treating as “nothing much”? What concrete action will you take this week to catch it?
l075.title: I Have, and I Don’t Want
l075.subtitle: Where Does Pride Come From? (Part 2): From “I Want” to “I Don’t Want”
l075.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: We Know It’s Wrong — So Why Are We Still Led Away?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today let’s be still together before the Lord and think about a question no Christian can escape, yet one we often struggle to put into words: where, exactly, do sinful desires come from?

Let me start with a scene. There’s a brother who has believed in the Lord for more than ten years. He’s devout and faithful; he never misses a Sunday, and he’s always first to arrive at small group and last to leave. One day he sees a message in a group chat: a younger man he once mentored is being greatly used by God — his church is growing, his ministry is expanding, and he’s even been invited to share from the platform. The brother taps a “blessings” sticker and types, “Thank the Lord, glory to God.” But the moment he puts his phone down, his heart feels hollow and sour, with an ache he can’t quite name. He even startles himself: how can I be like this? Didn’t I hand myself over to the Lord long ago?

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had an experience like that? You know full well you shouldn’t compare, yet your heart starts comparing all by itself. You know full well you shouldn’t covet, yet your eyes stay glued right there. You truly want to love the Lord, yet when it really counts you’re shockingly weak. We often think the problem is that “the environment is too alluring,” “the temptation is too strong,” “that person went too far.” But Scripture pulls our gaze from the outside back to the inside, and tells us something that cuts deep and yet sets us free —

The power of sin isn’t out there; it lies in the desires in our hearts that have not yet been dealt with.

James puts it with great precision: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.” (James 1:14) Notice the words “his own.” The bait of temptation may be set by someone else, but the line that pulls us out is tied to something in our own hearts. However strong the temptation outside, if there’s no matching desire inside, it can’t hook us. Before his suffering, the Lord Jesus said to his disciples: “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30) Satan came, and found nothing at all in the Lord to hang a hook on — so he came away with nothing.

And this is the great hope today’s lesson brings us: if sinful desire has a “source,” then it can be “dealt with.” We no longer have to live in the cycle of “fight and fail, fail and fight again.” We no longer have to grit our teeth and hang on by sheer willpower. When we understand where desire comes from, how it gets in and how it grows, we can guard against it and refuse to be held hostage by it — and instead overcome through Jesus.

Today we’ll walk five steps together. First, if we still react to sin, there is still desire in our hearts. Second, desire originates in an unthankful heart. Third, thanksgiving shuts the door on desire. Fourth, desire enters through what we see and hear. Fifth, the heart flows from seeing to thinking, from thinking to speaking, and from speaking to doing.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Family Letter to Suffering Believers
sections.html:
To understand James 1:14-15, we first need to get to know this letter.

The James who wrote it was, according to the consistent view of church history, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh (Matthew 13:55 names Jesus’ brothers: “James, Joses, Simon, and Judas”). The Gospels tell us that while the Lord was on earth, even his own brothers didn’t believe in him (John 7:5); but the risen Lord appeared personally to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and this younger brother became a disciple, later a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9; Acts 15:13). Interestingly, at the start of his letter he doesn’t call himself “the Lord’s brother”; he simply says, “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). That in itself is a lesson in selflessness: he laid down a family connection he could have boasted about, and returned to his originally intended position as a servant.

Most evangelical scholars date the letter to around AD 45–50, which may well make it the earliest-written book of the New Testament. It is addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings” (James 1:1) — that is, the Jewish believers scattered abroad by the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1). They were refugees, far from home, living as strangers in foreign places; the gap between rich and poor was vast, their wages were held back by fraud (James 5:4), and they were looked down on by the rich in the synagogue (James 2:6).

Notice their situation: they weren’t sinning out of boredom in easy times; they were struggling in want, injustice and affliction. And James chapter 1 opens with: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James 1:2). Where the Chinese Union Version reads “trials” here and “temptation” in verse 14, the Greek uses words from the same root, peirasmos. The very same hardship, seen from God’s side, is a “trial,” meant to refine our faith; seen from Satan’s side, it’s a “temptation,” meant to make us stumble. The difference isn’t in the circumstances; it’s in how we respond inside to those circumstances.

So James goes on to shut the mouths of those who shift the blame: “Let no man say when he is tempted, ‘I am tempted by God,’ for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.” (James 1:13) Then in verse 14 he points to the real source: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.”

Several Greek words here are wonderfully vivid. “Lust” is epithymia, formed from an intensifying prefix and a word for “strong passion.” In itself it’s a neutral word — the Lord Jesus himself used it when he said, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). But when that longing breaks away from God and centres on “self,” it becomes the engine of sin. “Drawn away” is exelkō, meaning to “drag out” prey from its hiding hole; “enticed” is deleazō, whose root is “bait” — exactly the picture of baiting a fishhook. Brothers and sisters, Satan never fishes for people with a bare hook; he always wraps the hook in bait. And that bait is always designed to match the appetite already in your heart.

Verse 15 is even a picture of childbirth: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” “Conceived” (syllambanō) and “produces” (apokyeō) are both obstetric terms. Sin doesn’t fall out of the sky; sin is “born” — and the mother who gives birth to it is desire. This reminds us, too, that pregnancy is a process, so there are chances to stop it along the way.

Finally, notice what follows immediately in verses 16 and 17: “Don’t be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:16-17) Brothers and sisters, this sequence is so important! Right after describing desire giving birth to sin and sin giving birth to death, the Holy Spirit, through James, immediately turns our eyes to “all God’s goodness.” This is the very heart of today’s lesson: the deepest antidote to desire is to see and count God’s grace — thanksgiving.

sections.heading: 1. If We Still React to Sin, There Is Still Desire in Our Hearts
sections.html:
1. The Dead Don’t React

In Romans chapter 6, Paul writes down the Christian’s secret of victory: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) Look further back, to verse 2: “We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?” Verse 6 makes it even clearer: “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.”

A dead person has one defining feature: they don’t react. However much you stimulate them, they feel nothing at all.

In medicine, the most basic tool for judging a person’s level of consciousness is the “Glasgow Coma Scale,” introduced in 1974 by two doctors at the University of Glasgow, Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett. It assesses three things: eye-opening response, verbal response and motor response. The medical staff call the patient’s name and apply stimuli to see whether there’s any response. A response means the person is still alive; the weaker the response, the deeper the loss of consciousness.

Brothers and sisters, move that measuring stick into the spiritual world and it becomes a brutally honest mirror: whatever sins I still react to show me where my “self” is still alive and well.

2. Measure Yourself Honestly

The text lists three examples. Let’s hold them up, one by one, against our own hearts.

First, feeling envy when you hear of someone else’s success. Not that you refuse to bless them out loud, but that sour twinge inside. When Saul heard the women singing, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands,” Scripture records: “Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, ‘They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?’ Saul watched David from that day and forward.” (1 Samuel 18:8-9) That sour twinge is the measuring stick.

Second, being stirred by the temptation of money. Not that you actually reach out and take it, but that your heart has already done the sums: “Nobody would know if I did this, would they?” Achan said: “When I saw among the plunder a beautiful Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels, then I coveted them and took them. Behold, they are hidden in the ground in the middle of my tent” (Joshua 7:21). First he “saw,” then he “coveted,” and finally he “took” — the order is crystal clear.

Third, being easily offended in relationships. One remark, one facial expression, one gathering you weren’t invited to, and you’re out of sorts all day. Behind being offended, it’s usually not that the other person is so terrible; it’s that the “self” in us that says “I deserve to be respected, seen and affirmed” has been touched.

3. Not Suppression, but Uprooting

So what do we do? The text says something extremely important: overcoming sin isn’t suppression but uprooting; it isn’t by willpower, but by the life of Jesus putting “self” utterly to death.

The difference between suppressing and uprooting is like dealing with the weeds in a garden. Suppressing is taking shears and trimming the weeds level; the garden looks neat, but the roots are still in the soil, and when the spring rain comes they all shoot back up. Uprooting is pulling them out roots and all. Psychology gave us this warning long ago: in 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner (then at Trinity University in Texas, later at Harvard) conducted the famous “white bear experiment.” He asked participants “not to think about a white bear,” and they ended up thinking about white bears more often than those who were allowed to think about them. This “ironic rebound effect” tells us that suppression alone often makes the thought stronger.

The way of Scripture isn’t suppression; it’s dying and living with Christ. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Trace any sinful desire all the way down and you’ll find that same “I want.” And what deals with “I want” isn’t a harder “I don’t want” — that’s still “I.” It’s letting “self” die completely on the cross and letting Christ live in me. Selflessness is not becoming nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. The one who trims weeds spends a lifetime trimming; the one who lets Christ be King hands the garden over to its Gardener.

So the first step isn’t to rush to change our behaviour; it’s to be honest: Lord, where do I still react? Shine your light on me. That is where change begins.

sections.heading: 2. The Origin of Desire: An Unthankful Heart
sections.html:
1. One Verse Lays Bare the Mechanism of the Fall

How does desire begin? In Romans chapter 1, Paul traces the source of human corruption and writes a key verse:

“Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.” (Romans 1:21)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order here. Humanity’s fall didn’t begin with murder and arson; it began with two things: not glorifying God, and not giving thanks to God. Only then did their reasoning become vain and their hearts darkened, and only from Romans 1:24 onward do all the various corruptions appear. In other words, “unthankfulness” is the first domino to fall.

The Greek for “give thanks” is eucharisteō, formed from “good” (eu) and “grace” (charis) — meaning “to treat the grace you have received well.” The church’s later name for the Lord’s Supper, the Eucharist, comes from this word. Its opposite, “unthankful,” is acharistos. Describing the scene of the last days, Paul says: “For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:2) — “unthankful” is exactly this word, and the very first item at the head of that list is “lovers of self.” Unthankfulness and the self-centred life are forever twins.

2. The Unthankful Keep Their Eyes on What They Don’t Have

The text says something worth copying into your notebook:

Thankful people focus on “the grace they already have”; unthankful people focus on “the desires they don’t yet have.”

Looking at the same glass, the thankful see the water in it, while the unthankful see the empty half. Living through the same day, the thankful count ten things they’ve been blessed with, while the unthankful remember the one thing that went wrong.

Psychology describes this phenomenon very clearly. In 1954 the psychologist Leon Festinger proposed “social comparison theory”: when people lack an objective standard, they automatically measure themselves against others. The trouble is that we almost always make “upward comparisons” — we compare ourselves with people who are better off. Today’s social media gathers the world’s most glamorous moments onto one small screen and delivers them right before your eyes, so “upward comparison” goes from an occasional thing to dozens of times a day.

There’s another phenomenon called “hedonic adaptation.” In 1978, Philip Brickman and his colleagues published a well-known study in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” comparing the happiness of lottery winners, ordinary people and accident victims who had been paralysed. They found that some time after winning big, the winners’ pleasure in everyday life was no higher than that of ordinary people — if anything, slightly lower. The more we get, the higher the bar rises. This is why the unthankful can never be filled — because “I want” is a bottomless pit.

The Israelites are the most painful example. They had seen with their own eyes the Red Sea parting and manna falling from heaven, yet Scripture says: “The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly; and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, ‘Who will give us meat to eat?’” (Numbers 11:4) Looking back on this history, the psalmist says: “They soon forgot his works. They didn’t wait for his counsel, but gave in to craving in the desert, and tested God in the wasteland. He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul.” (Psalm 106:13-15)

“They soon forgot his works” — that’s unthankfulness. “Gave in to craving” — that’s sinful desire. The order couldn’t be clearer.

3. The Trap of “I Ought to Be Better”

The text makes a very perceptive observation: when we say “I ought to be better” or “I ought to have more,” we have in fact already opened the door to desire.

Brothers and sisters, we need to discern this sentence carefully so we don’t misunderstand it. Pursuing growth isn’t sin; Paul says, “I press on toward the goal” (Philippians 3:14). The question is what motive lies behind that “ought.” If it comes from God’s calling, a desire to be renewed for God’s glory, that’s a holy longing. But if it comes from “I’m not as good as others,” “I can’t accept this,” “I want to be seen,” then it’s desire dressed up in spiritual clothing.

The very same words, “I want more anointing,” can be hunger for God or they can be ambition; the very same words, “I want to grow this ministry,” can be vision or they can be vanity. The way to tell is simple. Ask yourself: if this succeeds, who gets the glory? If someone else did it, and did it better than me, would I be genuinely glad?

And once “I want” gets in, Satan gains a foothold of authority. For pride is the very essence of Satan: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13-14) Five “I will”s in a row — that’s Satan’s signature.

So let’s hold on firmly to the text’s conclusion:

Unthankfulness → discontent → “I want” → desire → sin.

4. A 321 Insight

In the 321 vision, this chain is how the self-centred life operates. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. At its core, unthankfulness is refusing to admit that “everything I have, I have received.” So we quietly put ourselves in God’s place and start judging whether God has given us enough, whether he’s been fair.

Paul goes straight to the heart of it: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

Brothers and sisters, giving thanks is returning to our originally intended position; and when we return to our originally intended position, desire loses its footing.

sections.heading: 3. Thanksgiving Shuts the Door on Desire
sections.html:
1. The Lord Jesus Cares Deeply About Thanksgiving

The text reminds us that Jesus cares deeply about thanksgiving. Luke’s Gospel records that the Lord healed ten men with leprosy; they went to show themselves to the priests as he told them, and on the way they were cleansed.

“One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan. Jesus answered, ‘Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine? Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?’” (Luke 17:15-18)

Notice two details. First, all ten were healed — God’s grace is universal; but only one came back — thanksgiving is rare. One in ten. That ratio probably hasn’t changed much in two thousand years.

Second, the Lord speaks of someone who “returned to give glory to God.” In Scripture, giving thanks and glorifying God are two sides of the same thing, just as Romans 1:21 sets “didn’t glorify him as God” and “didn’t give thanks” side by side.

The Lord’s question — “But where are the nine?” — isn’t only a rebuke; even more it’s an aching heart and a reminder. He longs for all his children to live in thanksgiving. For he knew that although the leprosy on those nine had been healed, the door of their hearts was still open. Only to the one who came back did the Lord say: “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you.” (Luke 17:19) The Chinese Union Version reads “your faith has saved you,” and the original word (sōzō) is richer than “cleansed” — he wasn’t only healed in body; he was saved as a whole person.

2. Giving Thanks in Everything Is God’s Will

Paul reminds the church in Thessalonica:

“Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

Brothers and sisters, many people spend their whole lives asking, “What is God’s will for me?” Here it is, written plainly. And notice, the verse says “in everything give thanks,” not “give thanks for each thing in itself” — cancer isn’t a good thing, betrayal isn’t a good thing, and we don’t need to pretend they are. “In everything give thanks” means giving thanks in the midst of each thing, because I believe God reigns, and even in adversity he is preparing the best outcome for me.

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

So thanksgiving isn’t an optimistic personality; it’s an act of faith. It isn’t blind positivity; it’s treating God’s faithfulness as fact.

3. The Science of Gratitude: A Design God Built In When He Made Us

Modern psychology’s research on gratitude happens to confirm the wisdom of Scripture. In 2003, Robert Emmons of the University of California, Davis, and Michael McCullough of the University of Miami published an experiment in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.” They divided participants into groups: one wrote down five things they were grateful for each week, one wrote down five hassles, and one wrote only about neutral events. After ten weeks, the gratitude group was noticeably more satisfied with life as a whole, more optimistic about the coming week, complained of fewer physical symptoms, and even spent more time exercising.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t because gratitude has some magic power; it’s because the One who created us designed us from the start to be healthy only when we live in thanksgiving. Use the machine according to the manual and it runs smoothly; ignore the manual and it breaks down.

We can see the same order in Philippians: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6-7) “With thanksgiving” is the condition; “will guard your hearts and your thoughts” is the result. The original word for “guard” (phroureō) is a military term, meaning “to station troops at the city gate.” Brothers and sisters, a prayer of thanksgiving is asking God’s peace to stand sentry at the door of your heart!

4. Shift the Focus, and Desire Has Nowhere to Take Root

The text puts it beautifully: a thankful heart turns our focus from “self” to God, and once the focus isn’t on “self,” desire can’t take root.

This is the very core of the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Think of Peter walking on the water. While his focus was on the Lord, he walked on the water; “but when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink” (Matthew 14:30). The moment his focus shifted, gravity took over again. Desire works the same way: as long as our focus stays on “what I have, what I lack, who I have more than, who I have less than,” desire has soil to grow in; the moment our focus returns to the Lord, that soil is taken away.

Paul says: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) This is the shift of perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

And thanksgiving is the most practical button for making that shift. Because you can’t count God’s grace and complain about God’s unfairness at the same time. At the opening of his “Confessions,” Augustine says: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Thanksgiving is letting the heart come back to rest in God.

sections.heading: 4. How Desire Gets In: What We See and What We Hear
sections.html:
1. Satan’s First Tool Is “Speech”

Through which door does desire come in? The text points out: through what we see and what we hear.

Look at the Garden of Eden. Satan didn’t make Adam and Eve sin by force; he did it by “speaking.” First he asked: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) That question was meant to shake the accuracy of God’s word. Next he said: “You won’t really die” (Genesis 3:4) — an open denial of God’s word. Finally he threw out that deadly bait:

“For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The heart of the bait is “you will be like God” — that’s the pride of “I want to take God’s place,” the very same old road by which Satan himself fell. He can’t create new temptations; all he can do is dig, right in front of your feet, the same pit he himself fell into.

Then the text describes Eve’s response:

“When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.” (Genesis 3:6)

“Saw” — the door of the eyes swung open. “Good for food” — the lust of the flesh. “A delight to the eyes” — the lust of the eyes. “To be desired to make one wise” — the pride of life. Compare the words of the apostle John: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16) Brothers and sisters, humanity’s very first sin already put on full display all three forms that every later temptation would take.

There’s also a Hebrew clue well worth noticing. “To be desired” is the Hebrew chamad, and this word later appears in the Ten Commandments: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.” (Exodus 20:17) “You shall not covet” is lo tachmod, from the same root. In other words, the last of the Ten Commandments — the only one that takes place entirely inside the heart, invisible to anyone else — is aimed squarely at that very act in Eden of “seeing it and desiring it.”

2. Today’s Eden: The Screen

Satan hasn’t changed his methods today; he’s only changed his equipment. Through media, advertising, images and sounds, he keeps stimulating our five senses, so that we “see” and “hear” the world’s temptations.

From the standpoint of neuroscience, the eye truly is the widest door. The human retina has about 120 million rod cells and 6 million cone cells, and each optic nerve is made up of roughly a million nerve fibres. Scientists estimate that a considerable proportion of the human cerebral cortex (studies often mention around a third of cortical areas) is involved in processing visual information. God made the eyes so that we might see his glory; but if no one guards it, that same window will let a thief climb in.

That’s why the Lord Jesus said: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22-23)

When these influences enter our thoughts, they become desires; and if desires aren’t stopped, they become actions — that is, sin. In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord put it very sternly:

“But I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (Matthew 5:28)

In Greek, “gazes” here is an ongoing action — not an accidental glance, but lingering there, looking again and again. Brothers and sisters, the first look is usually not the sin; the second look is. There’s a long-circulated saying, generally attributed to Martin Luther: you can’t stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair.

3. Making a Covenant with Our Eyes

So how do we actually guard ourselves? Scripture gives us examples.

Righteous Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) Notice, he didn’t just “try to be careful”; he “made a covenant” — he made the decision before anything happened.

The psalmist prayed: “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” (Psalm 119:37)

David resolved: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” (Psalm 101:3)

Brothers and sisters, the work of guarding the door must be done at the door; don’t wait until the thief is inside the house before you act. This is also what the 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Relying on our own brain and our own self-control to wrestle with images that are already inside our hearts is the most exhausting way to fight, and the one most likely to fail; relying on the Holy Spirit to stop them at the door is actually light work. Rely on the heart and there’s joy; rely on the brain and there’s worry.

At the same time, we must actively replace them with good pictures. Paul says: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8) An empty house is the easiest to take over; only a heart filled with God’s word can hold its ground.

sections.heading: 5. The Flow of the Heart: From Seeing to Thinking, from Thinking to Speaking, from Speaking to Doing
sections.html:
1. Four Stages, One Slope

The text sets out the formation of desire as a clear process. Brothers and sisters, please remember these four steps:

Step one, seeing: the outward stimulus.

Step two, thinking: desire forming in the heart.

Step three, speaking: it comes out of our mouths.

Step four, doing: it is put into action.

This isn’t a cliff you go over in a single leap; it’s a slope you slowly slide down. Precisely because it’s a slope, at every bend we still have the chance to hit the brakes; and precisely because it’s a slope, the later we brake, the harder it is to stop.

Let’s look once more at Achan’s confession: “When I saw among the plunder a beautiful Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels, then I coveted them and took them. Behold, they are hidden in the ground in the middle of my tent” (Joshua 7:21). Saw, coveted, took — three steps, and a whole family’s lives were gone.

David too: “At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at. David sent and inquired after the woman.” (2 Samuel 11:2-3) He saw, he inquired, he sent for her — at every step there was still room to turn back, yet he didn’t stop at a single one.

2. What Fills the Heart Comes Out of the Mouth

The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34)

This sentence is the most accurate spiritual diagnostic instrument there is. You don’t need to guess what’s in your heart; just listen to what you’ve said this week and you’ll know. If the heart is full of desire, the mouth will naturally be full of complaining, comparing and criticising; if the heart is full of God’s word, the mouth will be full of grace and praise.

Psychology has reached a similar conclusion. In the 1960s, Aaron Beck of the University of Pennsylvania developed cognitive behavioural therapy, whose core insight is this: what shapes our emotions and behaviour is often not the event itself, but our interpretation of the event and our inner automatic thoughts. Change the automatic thoughts, and emotions and behaviour change along with them.

But Scripture said it earlier, and deeper. Solomon says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The Hebrew word for “keep,” natsar, means “to guard, to watch over,” and is used of the sentry on a watchtower. The heart is the wellspring of a whole life, so it deserves the highest level of guard.

3. Throwing Down and Taking Captive

So what if a thought has already got in? Paul gives us the tactics:

“Throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:5)

“Throwing down” and “bringing into captivity” are both terms of war. “Bringing into captivity” in the original means marching prisoners of war back under escort. Brothers and sisters, when a thought comes, we don’t passively wait for it to leave; we actively seize it, bring it before Christ, and make it surrender.

The practical exercise can be very simple. When a thought of comparison rises, say aloud at once: “Lord, thank you — what you’ve given me is enough.” When a complaining thought rises, immediately count three graces. When an impure image rises, immediately get up, change your surroundings, and open your mouth in praise.

This is the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Everything begins with the mindset, and the battlefield of the mindset is in our thoughts.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Reign as King at the Door of My Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place what we’ve learned today within the 321 framework, it becomes clearer still.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, he answered Satan three times with “It is written.” He didn’t negotiate with desire; he shut the door with the word of God. The Bible is my standard — every pathway we’ve seen today is something Scripture itself says, not some human insight. The Holy Spirit is my guide — what guards our hearts and thoughts is not my willpower, but the Holy Spirit who lives within us.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the key to the door of my heart is placed in his hands, not in the hands of my self-control. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so when grace comes to me, like that Samaritan I “turn back, glorifying God with a loud voice.”

The Goal: establish God’s system — a thankful person carries thanksgiving into the family, into the small group, into the workplace; and a group of thankful people together is what God’s system looks like on earth.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The engine of desire is “I want,” and the root of “I want” is the self-centred life. So the most thorough way of dealing with desire isn’t managing our cravings; it’s letting “self” die completely. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Peter says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5) Thanksgiving is the most natural expression of humility — because a thankful person admits: everything I have, I have received.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a home where everyone keeps their eyes on “I give more than you do,” everyone loses; where everyone says “thank you” first, relationships come alive.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Don’t rush to cover up the desires in your heart with more service; that only buries the problem deeper. Let the life be dealt with first; then relationships are healed, and only then does ministry have a foundation. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson is repairing exactly the first two — with God, by learning to give thanks; with ourselves, by honestly facing our own reactions.

The 920 practice is very practical here: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” When the person who most easily makes me envious, or most easily offends me, shows up in front of me, that is the very place to practise selflessness (the “0”). We don’t just grit our teeth; we take them as a lesson God has given us, give thanks for them and bless them, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). You’ll notice that the last of the nine is “self-control” — and self-control isn’t the product of white-knuckled endurance; it’s fruit borne by the Spirit.

Our 235 relationships are our protection too. Desire fears the light most of all and loves to hide. Find a selfless spiritual companion to be your “2,” and be open with each other and pray for each other; within the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, be shepherded and shepherd others; and fight shoulder to shoulder in the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team. “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9) Someone who takes on desire alone doesn’t have good odds; someone with companions goes far.

A shift of perspective is the key to this lesson. From man’s perspective, I lack a great deal; from God’s perspective, I’ve already been blessed in Christ “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). From an earthly view, others have more than I do; from a heavenly view, my name is written in heaven. From a temporary view, I’m being badly treated right now; from an eternal view, “our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Walking the Whole Way Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The text gives us four practices. The 321 vision tells us that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to work these four practices in solidly.

Practice 1: Practise thanksgiving — every day, list three things you’re thankful for, and thank God for them

Information: First know the facts — “unthankfulness” is the starting point of desire (Romans 1:21), and “in everything give thanks” is God’s will (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this from knowledge into sight. Be still for three minutes and ask the Lord to show you: what have I recently been complaining to God about?

Conviction: Admit that I need to change, and confess to God: I’ve been unthankful because I’ve taken grace for granted.

Implementation: Starting today, before bed each night, write down three specific things you’re thankful for. Don’t write a vague “thank you, Lord, for all your grace”; write “today so-and-so did such-and-such for me.”

Evaluation: A week later, look back and ask yourself: could I write them? Which days couldn’t I? What was I busy with on those days?

Correction: If you couldn’t write them, move the time earlier, or make it the first thing you do in the morning; if what you wrote was too vague, require yourself to name the person, the event and the time.

Repetition: Keep it up for forty days. Turning a behaviour into a habit takes repetition, not enthusiasm.

Multiplication: Do it with your family — around the dinner table, each person shares one thing they’re thankful for; do it with your small group.

Practice 2: Guard your eyes — avoid watching content that stirs up desire

Information: Know the pathway — “seeing” is the entry point of desire (Genesis 3:6; Matthew 5:28).

Revelation: Ask the Lord to shine his light, and honestly list your own “minefields”: What time of day? Which platform? In what emotional state are you most likely to give way?

Conviction: Admit that I can’t win on my own; I need the Lord, and I need boundaries.

Implementation: Like Job, make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1). In concrete terms: leave your phone outside the bedroom at night; unfollow accounts that stir up comparison; install filtering tools; keep the door open when you’re alone.

Evaluation: Once a week, take an honest look — without self-condemnation, and without covering up.

Correction: If you find you’re especially weak at a certain time of day, plan something else for that time — go for a walk, phone someone to check on them, listen to worship songs.

Repetition: Boundaries have to stay in place long-term; setting them once isn’t enough.

Multiplication: Keep watch with your spiritual companion, and ask each other, “How did this week go?”

Practice 3: Turn to praise — when you feel like complaining or envying, replace it with praise at once

Information: “Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) The mouth is the heart’s exit — and it can also become the heart’s entrance.

Revelation: See that complaining is really a declaration of belief — a declaration that God hasn’t treated me well.

Conviction: Decide that complaining will no longer be legal in my mouth.

Implementation: Keep three songs and three verses ready in your heart, and the moment the thought comes, open your mouth. For example: “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2).

Evaluation: Keep a record of how many times this week you complained out loud, and how many times you turned it into praise.

Correction: If you keep complaining about the same person, pray specifically for that person and bless them, until your heart truly softens.

Repetition: Let “Thank you, Lord” become your catchphrase.

Multiplication: Set up a “no-complaining dinner table” at home, and in your small group set the order “thanksgiving first, then intercession.”

Practice 4: Meditate on the Lord’s grace — think about the blessings God has already given you, not about what you lack

Information: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17).

Revelation: Ask the Lord to open your eyes to the graces you’ve taken for granted: breath, family, food, salvation.

Conviction: Admit that everything I have, I have received (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Implementation: Every morning, take five minutes to meditate quietly on one thing God has done in your life, thinking through the details.

Evaluation: Notice whether your day is any different after you’ve meditated.

Correction: If you get easily distracted while meditating, write it down with pen and paper, or read it aloud.

Repetition: Make meditation part of your morning devotion.

Multiplication: Speak out what God has done in you and bear witness — your testimony will become a seed of thanksgiving for someone else.

Brothers and sisters, the stages of the eight that are most easily skipped are Evaluation and Repetition. We often hear something and are deeply moved (Information, Revelation), and decide to change (Conviction), and do it for three days (Implementation) — and then it’s gone. May the Lord give us perseverance, so that these four practices run their full course in us, all the way to Multiplication — because a victorious life will always multiply victorious lives.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Thankful people don’t fall into temptation; for unthankful people, desire can get in at any time.

“In everything give thanks” is the most powerful prayer for shutting the door on desire.

Brothers and sisters, please take these two sentences home with you. Not because they’re slogans, but because they describe how it works. When the door is open, the thief comes in; when the door is shut, the thief can’t get in. And the key that shuts that door is called thanksgiving.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we’ve seen together that sinful desire doesn’t appear suddenly. It begins with “an unthankful heart.”

When we forget God’s grace, our focus turns to ourselves; when our focus turns to ourselves, desire gains a foothold; when desire has conceived, it bears sin; and sin, when it is full grown, produces death. This is a downhill road.

But thank the Lord, there’s another road. When we learn to give thanks and see the abundance God has already given, the door shuts; when the door shuts, desire can’t get in; when desire can’t get in, “self” shrinks day by day; and as “self” shrinks, Christ grows larger within us. This is an uphill road, and it leads to freedom.

So this morning I want to invite you to make a decision. Not the decision “I’ll try harder to resist sin” — that’s still relying on yourself — but the decision to let Jesus reign as King at the door of your heart. Hand him the door of your eyes, the door of your ears, the door of your thoughts, the door of your tongue, one by one. Tell him: Lord, from today on, this door is yours to keep.

Let’s live in thanksgiving, shut the door on desire, and live in the freedom of selflessness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. May our lives become a truly blessed testimony, and may all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14-15)
declarations: Lord, thank you — you are my every provision and my full satisfaction.
I no longer focus on what I don’t have, but give thanks for what you have given.
Help me to guard my eyes and my thoughts,
that I may find freedom in thanksgiving and victory in humility.
practices: Guard your eyes — avoid watching content that stirs up desire
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, you have shone your light into our hearts through today’s word. We confess that there is still much in us that reacts to sin — those sour twinges, those stirrings, those moments of feeling offended all remind us that “self” is still alive. Please forgive us.

Lord, we also confess that we are often unthankful. We count our lack more than we count your grace; we fix our eyes on what others have and forget what you have already given us. Cleanse us, and turn our eyes from “what I don’t have” to “what you have given.”

Help us to guard the doors of our eyes and our ears. When images come, when sounds come, when thoughts come, may the Holy Spirit stop us at the door, so that we can bring every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.

Lord, fill our hearts with your word, fill our mouths with praise, let thanksgiving flow out of our daily living, let our relationships be reconciled through thanksgiving, and let our ministry be blessed through selflessness.
Reign as King in our hearts, until the fruit of our whole lives is given back to you.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) This week, which kind of sin do you “still react to”? Is it envy, greed, or being easily offended? Please share honestly and pray for one another, asking the Lord to let that part of your “self” die completely.

“Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.” (Romans 1:21) Think back to the last time an “I want” welled up in your heart. If you trace it back, was there something you had forgotten to thank God for? Name three things you can give thanks for today, and remind one another to turn thanksgiving into a daily practice.
l076.title: Where Do Sinful Desires Come From?
l076.subtitle: Closing the Door on Sinful Desire with Thanksgiving
l076.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Whose Hand Is on the Door Handle?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are going to face together a question that no Christian can find a way around.

In our last lesson we came to understand one thing together: sinful desire is the doorway to sin. Satan doesn’t begin by asking us to commit murder or arson. He simply sows, very lightly, beside our eyes and our ears, a single seed of “I want.” That seed is so small that we often think, “What harm can this do?” But once the seed falls into the soil of the heart, it sprouts.

And so the question arises. When sinful desire has already entered our thoughts — when it has even begun to take shape and to have an outline — what are we to do?

A brother once described his struggle like this: “Every night I go to war with myself. I tell myself a hundred times, ‘Don’t think about it,’ and then I spend the whole night thinking about it. The harder I push it down, the higher it bounces back. By dawn I’m exhausted, and that thought is still sitting there in my heart, perfectly comfortable.”

Brothers and sisters, have you heard a struggle like that? Perhaps you are in the middle of it yourself. It isn’t that you are ungodly; it’s that you are trying too hard. It isn’t that you don’t want to overcome; it’s that you are using the wrong method.

In this lesson the Bible wants to tell us a supremely important truth: the key to overcoming sin is not suppression but shutting the door; not rejection but replacement.

Notice these two contrasts. Suppression is pressing your hand against the door. The person outside keeps knocking, so you keep pressing, until your hand trembles and your heart panics. Shutting the door is latching it, locking it, and then turning round to do something else.

Rejection says to the lie, “Go away,” while your eyes are still fixed on the lie. Replacement invites the truth in to sit at the very centre of your heart — and the lie simply has no place left.

You can never sweep the darkness out of a room with a broom. The more you sweep, the more tired you get, and the darkness is still there. But just flip the switch, and the moment light comes in, the darkness is gone. Darkness isn’t driven out; darkness is replaced by light.

Brothers and sisters, our heart is not a vacuum. It is a room that will always be filled with something. The question has never been “Will it be filled?” but “What will fill it?”

So every day, every moment, we stand before a choice: let sin come in, or let Jesus reign.

The door handle is not in Satan’s hand; the door handle is in ours. That is the first piece of good news today, and the most important.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Apostles, One Battlefield
sections.html: Our two theme passages today come from Paul’s letter to the Romans and from the letter of James. The two writers had different backgrounds and wrote to different readers, yet they point to the same battlefield — the human heart.

sections.heading: 1. Romans 6: A New Identity under Grace
sections.html:
Romans is the work of the apostle Paul, generally thought to have been written between AD 56 and 57 in Corinth, in Greece. Paul was about to take the collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, and on the way he wrote to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited in person, to prepare for a future visit.

Rome was the capital of the world at that time, a city of a million people, yet its moral condition was utterly corrupt. The bloodshed of the arena and the debauchery of the idol temples lay right beside the streets the believers walked every day. The Christians of Rome did not come to faith in a greenhouse; they followed Jesus in a city where sinful desire was publicly celebrated.

In chapters 1 to 5 Paul makes one thing plain: under the law no one can save himself; we are justified by faith alone. Then, at the start of chapter 6, a sharp question appears: since grace is so abundant, may we go on in sin so that grace may abound? Paul answers at once: “May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?” (Romans 6:2)

He goes on: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11)

Look carefully at the order: first a new identity, then new action. “Consider yourselves dead” in verse 11 is identity; “don’t let sin reign” in verses 12 and 13 is action. Paul is not telling us to fight our way into a new identity by willpower; he is telling us to act in keeping with the new identity we have already received.

The Greek word for “present” is paristēmi, which originally means “to place beside, to hand over, to offer.” It was often used of leading a sacrificial animal to the altar, and also of handing weapons over to a commander to await his orders. The Greek word for “instruments” is hopla, which means “weapons, armaments.” Paul’s picture is vivid: your eyes, ears, tongue, hands and feet are all weapons, and every morning they must be handed to a commander — if not to sin, then to God.

So Romans 6:13 is not an abstract exhortation; it is a military order. Today, to whom will you hand your weapons?

sections.heading: 2. James 1: Faith Matures under Trial
sections.html:
Evangelical scholars generally hold that the author of the letter of James is James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh.
