At first he did not believe (John 7:5); after the Lord rose, he appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became one of the pillars of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9).

James is quite possibly one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written, around AD 45 to 49, addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution. They were displaced, oppressed by the rich, their faith shaken by trials.

James opens by speaking of trials, and then makes a very important distinction: the trials outside us are permitted by God and can refine us, but the temptation within us does not come from God. “Let no man say when he is tempted, ‘I am tempted by God,’ for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.” (James 1:13–14)

The Greek for “drawn away” is exelkō, which originally means “to drag prey out of its hiding place”; “enticed” is deleazō, whose root is the word for “bait.” James’s meaning is clear: Satan is the one who sets the bait, but the fish that takes the hook is the sinful desire within us. If there is no mouth to bite, the bait catches nothing.

Only then comes that startling sentence in verse 15: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” A whole string of words about pregnancy and birth shows that sinful desire is not static; sinful desire grows.

Put the two passages side by side and the picture is complete: James speaks of what is “conceived within,” Paul of what is “presented outwardly”; and between the two stands you — someone with the power to choose.

Today, following the four key points of the lesson text, we will learn step by step how to shut the door on sin and open the door to God.

sections.heading: 1. Shut the Door on Sin: Do Not Present Yourself to Sin as an Instrument of Unrighteousness
sections.html:
Paul says: “Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.” (Romans 6:13)

Notice the most important words in this verse: “do not.” Since God says “do not,” it means we are able not to. God never commands us to do something he has not given us the power to accomplish.

This brings us to the first key realisation today: whether or not sin reigns in us is a decision that lies in our hands.

The verse before puts it even more directly: “Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts.” (Romans 6:12) That word “let” is beautifully chosen: sin cannot seize the throne by force; it has to wait for you to let it. Satan has no key — only a hand to knock with. The door is locked from the inside.

That is why Paul can dare to say in the next verse: “For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.” (Romans 6:14)

If we choose indulgence, we open the door to sin; if we choose holiness, we shut the door on sin. This isn’t a slogan. It is a concrete choice made dozens of times a day.

Sin Works in Three Stages

The lesson text divides the working of sin into three stages. They are like dominoes: each one knocks over the next.

Stage one: careless looking and careless listening. Outward enticement enters our thoughts through the eyes and ears.

Stage two: careless thinking. Sinful desire is nurtured and conceived in the heart.

Stage three: careless doing. Sinful desire matures and gives birth to sinful acts.

This is a replay of Genesis 3: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate.” (Genesis 3:6a)

First “saw” — the eyes; then “to be desired” — the thinking of the heart; and finally “took some of its fruit, and ate” — the action of the hand. From eye to heart, from heart to hand: humanity’s first fall travelled exactly this road.

First John sums up this road even more precisely: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

These three stages have one thing in common: the further along you go, the harder it is to turn back. At stage one, all you need do is turn your head or switch off the screen, and it’s over. By stage three, what you pay is tears, cost, even a lifetime of regret.

There is an often-quoted saying, generally attributed to Martin Luther: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. A thought flying past is not sin; letting it settle, build a nest and hatch a brood — that is our responsibility.

The Gatekeeper’s Standard: The Three Foundations

On the other hand, if we watchfully guard our eyes and ears and do not let wrong voices into our hearts, sinful desire has no room to survive.

King Solomon put it urgently and weightily: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The Hebrew for “keep” is natsar, which originally means “to watch, to guard, to stand sentry like a soldier guarding a city.” The heart is not a garden; it is a city. A city has gates, and gates need sentries.

A gatekeeper without a standard doesn’t know whom to let in and whom to keep out. The Three Foundations of Kingdom 321 are the clearest standard at the gate of the heart:

Jesus is my role model — Would he watch this? Would he listen to this? Would he respond like this?

The Bible is my standard — Is this content in line with God’s word?

The Holy Spirit is my guide — Do I have peace in my heart? Is the Holy Spirit holding me back?

Add to these the Two Core Values and the Goal: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory, in order to establish God’s system, so that people may see Jesus in it.

And so gatekeeping comes down to a very simple three-question test: whatever cannot glorify God, cannot build up life and cannot bring peace, we will not watch, will not listen to and will not dwell on.

Job made a covenant: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) David too said: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” (Psalm 101:3a)

Neither of them waited until temptation came before beginning to struggle; they made the covenant before temptation ever arrived. The work of gatekeeping is done in times of peace.

An Illustration from Daily Life and a Reminder from Science

The purpose of a fly screen is not to chase mosquitoes once they’ve flown in, but to keep them from getting in at all. No sensible homeowner would tear down the screens and then battle all night until dawn with an electric swatter. Yet that is exactly how many Christians live their spiritual lives — every screen torn down, and then they blame the mosquitoes for being so many.

Cognitive science has a reliable finding: human attention is a limited resource. The amount of information our senses take in every second is enormous, yet what makes it into consciousness is pitifully small. The filter theory of the British psychologist Donald Broadbent (1958) explains exactly this: before information enters consciousness, it first passes through a sieve.

When God made us, he already gave us a sieve. The problem is that we have made the holes far too large.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision says that change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. All change begins with the mindset.

“Shutting the door on sin” is first of all not a behaviour but a turnaround of mindset. The old mindset says, “I can’t control myself”; the new mindset says, “Sin will not have dominion over me.” The old mindset says, “One look won’t hurt”; the new mindset says, “My eyes are a weapon, and today I hand them to God.”

This is also a shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Sinful desire offers you only temporary pleasure; God wants to give you eternal freedom.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please latch that door in your heart and say: Lord, I hand you the key to this door.

sections.heading: 2. Deal with Sinful Desire Early: Don’t Let It Conceive and Grow
sections.html:
James says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15)

Here the Bible uses a deeply sobering image — an embryo. A fertilised egg is about a tenth of a millimetre across, almost invisible to the naked eye, and it looks completely harmless; yet it implants, divides, grows a heartbeat and limbs, and finally becomes a life that breathes and cries.

Sinful desire is just like that. At first it is tiny — so tiny you think, “I’m only thinking about it.” But if it isn’t dealt with, it gradually grows, until finally it becomes sin in action, and even brings death.

Notice that James’s wording has four stages: conceived, bears sin, full grown, produces death. It is a one-way street, and the further you go, the faster you move.

Having a Sinful Desire Is Not the Same as Having Sinned

There is a very important distinction to be made here, because many sensitive believers have been accused by Satan on precisely this point for years: having a sinful desire does not mean you will necessarily sin; the key is whether we deal with it in time.

“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” (Hebrews 4:15) The Lord was tempted yet did not sin, which shows that being tempted is not in itself sin.

So when a thought suddenly appears, you don’t need to condemn yourself at once and say, “I’m finished.” You only need to deal with it at once.

Satan loves two sentences above all: one is “It doesn’t matter,” the other is “I’m finished.” The first makes you indulge; the second makes you despair. Both roads lead to the same place.

The Earlier You Deal with It, the Easier It Is

Doctors often tell expectant mothers a plain truth: the longer a pregnancy goes on, the harder it is to intervene. Sinful desire is the same — the earlier you remove it, the easier; the later you remove it, the more painful.

So when you find your heart beginning to “think carelessly,” don’t wait, and don’t bargain with it. Act immediately: clear it out at the stage of thought, and don’t let it grow into sin.

Many people fail, not because they don’t want to overcome, but because they are too self-confident. They think they can negotiate with sinful desire, sit with it for a while and then leave. Joseph didn’t do that: “She caught him by his garment, saying, ‘Lie with me!’ He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” (Genesis 39:12) He didn’t even keep his garment. No debate, no analysis. He ran.

Paul gave Timothy the same command: “Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” (2 Timothy 2:22) Not “Face them,” but “Flee.” Some battles are fought with your feet.

Supporting Evidence from Science and an Illustration from Daily Life

In The Organization of Behavior, the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb (1949) set out a famous principle, later often summed up as “neurons that fire together wire together”: when two groups of neurons are repeatedly activated at the same time, the connection between them grows stronger and stronger.

The meaning is very clear: every time you think about that thing, that neural pathway gets a little thicker; every time you don’t, that path becomes a little more overgrown. The first time is hard; the tenth time becomes habit; the hundredth time becomes character.

Thank God, neuroplasticity works both ways — old paths become overgrown, and new paths can be trodden out. This is what Paul means by being “transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2).

Here is another comparison. A tile on the roof has come loose. Fix it today, and it takes a ladder and ten minutes. Leave it three months, and rainwater soaks into the ceiling. Leave it three years, and the beams have rotted. A tile won’t slip back into place just because you don’t look at it — and neither will sinful desire.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. However great a ministry may be, if there is an unresolved sinful desire inside, it is like a ship with drums and gongs sounding on the deck and a small hole in the hull.

The 321 vision also says the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. Dealing with sinful desire early belongs to the “relationship with ourselves” — facing ourselves honestly, without whitewashing, without delay, without self-deception.

David’s prayer is the best model: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please be still for thirty seconds and ask the Holy Spirit one question: Lord, is there a thought in me right now that I haven’t yet dealt with?

sections.heading: 3. The Key Strategy for Removing Sinful Desire: Replacement, Not Rejection
sections.html:
Many Christians often say, “I must reject sinful thoughts.” It sounds very spiritual, but in practice it often fails. Why?

Because the more we “reject,” the stronger the thought becomes. Rejection itself keeps us focused on Satan’s words; the more we try to suppress, the more we are controlled.

You can try it right now: from this second on, whatever you do, do not think of a white bear. What happened? A white bear appeared in your mind.

The White Bear Experiment: The More It’s Forbidden, the More It Appears

This is no joke. In a study published in 1987 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues asked participants not to think of a white bear for five minutes, and to ring a bell whenever they did. The group told to suppress the thought not only rang the bell again and again during the suppression period; afterwards, when they were allowed to think freely, they thought of the white bear far more often than the control group. Wegner called this the “rebound effect,” and proposed the “ironic process theory”: when you try hard not to think of something, the mind starts two processes at once — one that turns attention away, and another that keeps checking, “Have I thought of it again?” That very act of checking is itself thinking about it.

Brothers and sisters, someone who keeps checking “Am I thinking about that thing?” is someone who keeps thinking about that thing. By suppression alone, we will never win.

The Bible’s Strategy: Not Rejection but Replacement

The Bible’s strategy is not “rejection” but “replacement” — replacing Satan’s words with God’s words.

The lesson text gives us three very practical pairings:

When Satan says, “You’re not good enough,” I replace it with God’s word: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

When Satan says, “You don’t have enough,” I declare: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1)

When Satan says, “Nobody loves you,” I declare: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20b)

Notice: these three sentences are not motivational sayings; they are words God himself has spoken. Self-comfort will be defeated by reality, but God’s word never fails.

Our mind can only dwell on one thing at a time. When truth comes in, lies are naturally driven out. Rejection only holds things down for a while; replacement clears them out completely.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Danger of an Empty House

The Lord Jesus told a parable that shows exactly the danger of “driving out without filling up.”

“When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” (Matthew 12:43–45a)

Look at that house: empty, swept, put in order — very beautiful, but empty. If a house stands empty, the former occupant will come back, and bring more with him. Simply “giving up” is not enough; we must “exchange.”

Paul says it most fully: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

Put away, be renewed, put on — it is one complete set of movements. No one takes off their clothes and goes out without putting any on. Someone who only takes off and never puts on will end up standing naked in the cold wind, and will pick the old clothes back up and wear them again.

He also says: “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.” (Romans 13:14) If you have put on Christ, sinful desire has no room to make provision.

A List of Positive Thoughts

So what should the heart hold? Paul wrote out a list:

“Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

Notice the final words: “think about these things.” God is not telling us “don’t think about”; he is telling us “do think about” — this is a positive command, not a prohibition. Paul also says: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) Only when we first set our minds on the things above does the second half hold true.

This was exactly the Lord Jesus’ method when he was tempted in the wilderness. Three times he was tempted, and not once did he say, “I don’t want to.” Each time he said, “It is written”: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.” (Matthew 4:4b) “You shall not test the Lord, your God.” (Matthew 4:7b) “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.” (Matthew 4:10b)

The Lord did not debate with Satan; he simply quoted Scripture. He did not push temptation down by willpower; he crowded temptation out with the word of God.

An Illustration from Daily Life and Supporting Evidence from Research

From the late 1960s, the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel conducted the famous “marshmallow experiment”: eat now and you get one marshmallow; wait until the researcher comes back and you get two. The interesting thing was not how many children managed to wait, but how they did it. Mischel found that almost none of the children who waited successfully did so by staring at the marshmallow and gritting their teeth. They sang, turned round, covered their eyes, imagined the marshmallow was a white cloud. They didn’t reject it; they diverted and replaced. Mischel’s conclusion is worth remembering: the key to self-control lies not in the strength of willpower but in where attention is placed.

“proving what is well pleasing to the Lord.” (Ephesians 5:10) Focus determines the outcome — the focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances.

God’s word is living water. You don’t have to wrestle with the darkness; just turn on the tap and let clean water keep flowing in, and the muddy water will naturally overflow and run out.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be glad, rely on the brain and you will worry. “Rejection” relies on the brain and ourselves — on willpower, on gritted teeth. “Replacement” relies on the heart and the Holy Spirit — on God’s word, on the Holy Spirit, on the presence of Christ.

The 321 vision also says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. This is the deepest level of “replacement” — not just exchanging one thought, but exchanging one master. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20a)

Selflessness is not emptying yourself into an empty house — that would only invite seven spirits more evil. Selflessness is being filled with Christ; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless.

sections.heading: 4. Replace Sinful Desire with Thanksgiving, and Pride with Humility
sections.html:
So what exactly are we to replace it with? The lesson text hands us two of the sharpest swords: thanksgiving and humility.

Thanksgiving Takes On “I Want”

Sinful desire begins with “I want,” but thanksgiving says, “Lord, thank you — I already have.”

Look at the direction. The eyes of “I want” look at what we don’t have; the eyes of “thank you” look at what we already have. The same situation, looked at from a different direction, produces a completely different state of heart.

Paul links this principle with peace: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7)

Notice the words “with thanksgiving.” Prayer can turn into a complaints meeting, or it can become a thanksgiving service — and this is where the difference lies.

Paul is even more direct: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:18) We often say, “I don’t know what God’s will is.” This verse tells you: give thanks in everything — that is God’s will.

David too reminded himself: “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits.” (Psalm 103:2) Ingratitude is not someone else’s problem; it is my own heart that needs reminding.

A Reliable Study

In a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Robert Emmons of the University of California, Davis, and Michael McCullough of the University of Miami randomly divided participants into three groups: one wrote down five things they were grateful for each week, one wrote down five hassles, and one simply recorded ordinary events. After ten weeks, the gratitude group scored significantly higher than the other two on overall well-being and optimism about the future; they even exercised more and reported fewer physical complaints.

Thanksgiving is not self-hypnosis; it is seeing afresh the grace we have already received. Someone put it well: if God gave you tomorrow only what you thanked him for today, what would you have left tomorrow?

Humility Takes On Pride

The root of sinful desire is pride — the feeling that “I deserve more.” Humility says, “Lord, I am willing to be less, so that you may be more.” This was the very heart of John the Baptist: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Bible repeats the same sentence twice, which shows how important it is: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6b; 1 Peter 5:5b)

The Greek for “resists” is antitassomai, a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against, to set the ranks in order to face an enemy.” Picture it: a proud person, and God himself drawn up in battle formation opposite him. There is no harder battle in all the world.

James goes on: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil.

The British writer C. S. Lewis points out in Mere Christianity that pride is the utterly anti-God state of mind; it is especially dreadful because its essence is comparison — as long as anyone is better than I am, I can have no rest.

The prayer at the opening of Augustine’s Confessions goes straight to the point: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Sinful desire can never be satisfied, because we are trying to fill a place prepared for God with things that are finite.

Two Concrete Methods

There are two practical ways to overcome sinful desire: first, replace “I want” with thanksgiving, often reflecting on the grace God has already given; second, replace “self-gratification” with humility, laying down the desire to satisfy ourselves and turning instead to satisfy God’s heart.

The Lord Jesus is the most perfect role model: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7)

The Greek for “emptied himself” is kenoō, meaning “to pour oneself out.” The Lord Jesus was not emptied by someone else; he emptied himself. It was an active, willing choice of love.

Between “satisfying ourselves” and “satisfying God,” the choice decides the outcome: choose to satisfy yourself, and sinful desire grows; choose to satisfy God, and life is set free. The Lord Jesus said: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:32)

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, sinful desire damages not only our relationship with God but also our relationships with others. When I “want,” other people become tools for getting what I want; when I “give thanks,” other people become once again gifts God has given me. This is exactly what the 321 vision means by “people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.”

This is also what the 920 practice is about: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2,” and before them we live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a)

Look at the last fruit: self-control. Self-control does not come from gritting our teeth; it is fruit the Spirit bears. That is why Paul says: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) The ultimate answer to sinful desire is not a stronger will but a fuller measure of the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Shutting the Door to Building Up
sections.html:
Place today’s four key points into the overall blueprint of the 321 vision, and a fuller picture appears.

The Three Foundations: The Gatekeeper’s Standard

Jesus is my role model. Three times the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, and three times he said, “It is written.” He did not suppress; he replaced with the word of God. This is the perfect demonstration of the “replacement strategy.”

The Bible is my standard. The opponent of sinful desire is not our will but God’s word. “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11) Not placed on a bookshelf, but hidden in the heart. Whatever is hidden in your heart is what you will bring out at the critical moment.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Self-control is the fruit of the Spirit, not an achievement of the flesh.

The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King

The flip side of “don’t let sin reign” is “let Jesus reign as King.” There is only one throne in the heart: if sin is not sitting on it, the Lord is.

So shutting the door on sin is not only defence; it is a coronation. We are not guarding an empty city; we are welcoming a King into the city.

When Jesus reigns as King, all the glory goes to him. Victory is not our achievement; it is his doing.

The Goal: Establish God’s System

People who overcome sinful desire are not only set free themselves; they become living stones in God’s system on earth. Sinful desire makes people isolated, hidden, living a double life; holiness makes people transparent, connected and able to be built up.

So dealing with sinful desire has never been a private matter. Your victory is a blessing to your family; your hiddenness is a breach in the whole system.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

“I want” is the language of the old self; “Your will be done” is the language of the new self. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless.

Thanksgiving and humility, those two swords, are the two hands that escort “self” down from the throne: thanksgiving acknowledges, “All I have, I have received”; humility acknowledges, “All I am is grace.”

The Fivefold Change

Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

A change of mindset: from “I must suppress” to “I will replace.”

A change of life: the heart is gradually filled with God’s word and no longer left empty.

A change of daily living: what I watch, what I listen to and what I think about all now have a standard.

A change of relationships: no longer treating people as tools for satisfying myself, but as those whom God loves.

A change of ministry: only a vessel that is clean within is one God dares to use greatly.

A Shift of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: man says, “This is what I deserve”; God says, “This is what I give you.”

From earthly to heavenly: sinful desire looks at what is in front of it; faith looks to that better homeland.

From temporary to eternal: the pleasure sinful desire gives is counted in minutes; the joy God gives is counted in eternity.

From worldly to godly: the world says, “Satisfy yourself”; the Bible says, “Satisfy God’s heart.”

235 Relationships: Don’t Fight Alone

The environment sinful desire loves most is darkness and loneliness.

That is why the Bible says: “Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.” (James 5:16)

The 235 relationships of the 321 vision are designed for exactly this: become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone selfless; establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

A single log is hard to keep burning; a pile of logs blazes. Ecclesiastes says: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12)

sections.heading: 6. Practice for Daily Living: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us four practices. We will use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to root them in us one by one.

Practice 1: Spiritual Gatekeeping

Every day, check what you have watched and what you have listened to, and whether it glorifies God.

Information: I know the three stages of sin are careless looking and listening, careless thinking and careless doing, and that the entrance is through the eyes and ears.

Revelation: The Holy Spirit shows me that one of my habits is exactly the door that has been left unshut for years.

Conviction: I no longer say, “One look won’t hurt.” I believe that out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

Implementation: Set boundaries today. Leave your phone in the living room an hour before bed; cancel one subscription that feeds sinful desire; stick Job 31:1 beside your screen.

Evaluation: Every evening, be still for three minutes and ask yourself: today, where did my eyes and ears linger longest?

Correction: Whichever door is loosest, start by locking that one. Don’t try to repair ten doors at once.

Repetition: Forty days in a row. Gatekeeping is not a one-off decision; it is a way of life.

Multiplication: Tell a spiritual companion about your boundaries, and invite them to set their own.

Practice 2: Renewing Our Thoughts

Replace a wrong thought with a verse of God’s word, and declare it again and again.

Information: I understand that “rejection” causes a rebound, and only “replacement” clears things out.

Revelation: The Holy Spirit points out the lies that most often appear in my heart — “I’m not good enough,” “God doesn’t care about me,” “I can’t change anyway.”

Conviction: I believe God’s word is truer than my feelings.

Implementation: Write the lie on the left side of a sheet of paper and a corresponding verse from the Chinese Union Version on the right, and declare it aloud ten times a day.

Evaluation: After a week, check: has that lie been appearing less often?

Correction: If the verse isn’t a close enough fit, change it. The verse has to be aimed right at the wound for healing to happen.

Repetition: Keep going until, half asleep, what comes out of your mouth is God’s word and not the lie.

Multiplication: Share your “lies and truths” chart with your small group, and help another brother or sister.

Practice 3: Replacing with Thanksgiving

Whenever temptation comes, immediately name one thing you are thankful for.

Information: Sinful desire begins with “I want”; thanksgiving runs in exactly the opposite direction.

Revelation: The moments I am most easily tempted are often the moments I feel most that “I lack.”

Conviction: I believe, “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Implementation: Make a rule — the moment the thought comes, immediately thank God aloud for one specific thing, naming the person and the event.

Evaluation: Tally it up each week: how many thanksgivings did temptation prompt me to speak this week? Temptation becomes an alarm clock for counting blessings.

Correction: If thanksgiving grows hollow and repetitive, switch to “one new thing today.”

Repetition: Keep going until thanksgiving becomes your first reaction under pressure.

Multiplication: Start “taking turns to give thanks” in your family or small group, so that thanksgiving becomes the very air the group breathes.

Practice 4: Humble Submission

In every choice, ask yourself: “Does this satisfy me, or does it satisfy the Lord?”

Information: The root of sinful desire is pride, and God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

Revelation: The Holy Spirit shows me that what I have been insisting on was never really the truth — only my own face.

Conviction: I believe “He must increase, but I must decrease” is not a loss but a gain.

Implementation: Today, in one decision, choose “you more, me less” — give up a seat, let go of one chance to win an argument, be the first to apologise.

Evaluation: Was there a moment today when I was “seizing rights” rather than “returning to my originally intended position”?

Correction: When you find pride, admit it at once and turn back at once. Don’t let it pile up until tomorrow.

Repetition: Once a day. Humility in small things adds up to obedience in great things.

Multiplication: Bring someone along to practise 920 with you — before every “2,” live out the life of “0,” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

sections.heading: 7. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, before you go, please take these three sentences home with you:

Rejecting Satan’s words still leaves us thinking about them.

Only by replacing them with God’s words can we be truly free.

Thanksgiving and humility are the twin swords against sinful desire.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end today we have said just one thing: the power of sinful desire comes from “I want”; the power of holiness comes from “Lord, I don’t want it.”

Overcoming sin does not come by suppression but by replacement. When we let the truth in, lies naturally flee.

Let us practise “shutting the door on sin and opening the door to God” — choosing thanksgiving, choosing humility, choosing to satisfy God’s heart. This is the victorious life, and the road we must travel towards selflessness and revival.

Remember that empty house. The Lord Jesus doesn’t want you to be an empty house, swept clean; he wants to move in: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.” (Revelation 3:20)

Brothers and sisters, this morning, don’t just shut one particular door — open the door of your heart to the Lord.

May sin not reign in your heart today; may Jesus reign as King.

May every victory you win today give the glory to Jesus — not to your willpower, your methods or your efforts. For “So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16).

May we together establish God’s system, and together become overcomers.

keyVerses: “Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.” (Romans 6:12–13)
“Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15)
declarations: Please declare with me:
Lord, I will no longer let sin reign in me;
I choose to shut the door on sin and open the door of thanksgiving.
May your word replace Satan’s lies,
and let my heart be filled with your truth alone.
I will replace pride with humility, and sinful desire with thanksgiving,
and live a life that is free, holy and yours.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you for shining your word into our hearts this morning.
Lord, we confess that we so often wrestle with sinful desire in our own strength — the harder we push it down, the more tired we get; the more we fight, the more we lose. Please forgive us.
Today we hand you the key to the door of our hearts. Help us to keep watch at the gate, and not to let in any voice that cannot glorify you, cannot build up life and cannot bring peace.
Give us sensitive hearts, so that the moment we notice “careless thinking,” we come straight to you to deal with it — without delay, without bargaining, without deceiving ourselves.
Lord, fill us with your word; let the truth dwell in every room of our hearts, leaving no empty space for the enemy.
Give us thankful hearts, so that before “I want” can grow, we have already said, “Lord, thank you.”
Give us humble hearts, willing to say, “You must increase, but I must decrease.”
Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Please share honestly: over the past week, which “door” have you guarded least well? What concrete boundary do you plan to set, starting today?

“that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:22–24a) What lie appears most often in your heart? Which verse from the Chinese Union Version will you use to replace it? Write it down, and declare it aloud once in your small group.
l077.title: Close the Door to Sin, Open the Door to God
l077.subtitle: Where Do Sinful Desires Come From? (Part 2)
l077.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Are Those Three Words So Hard to Say?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we are going to face together a very ancient sickness that has never gone out of date, and receive together a very simple yet supremely effective medicine. The sickness is called pride; the medicine is called humility.

Let me begin with a true story. In the United States, medical malpractice disputes have long been the heaviest burden hospitals carry. The traditional approach was this: when something goes wrong, admit nothing at first and hand everything over to the lawyers. But in 2001 the University of Michigan Health System decided to do the opposite — when a medical error had genuinely occurred, it would take the initiative to explain the truth to the patient and family, apologise sincerely and offer compensation.

Many predicted the hospital would be sued into collapse. And the result? In 2010 Kachalia and colleagues published the data from before and after the programme in the Annals of Internal Medicine: new claims fell from 7.03 to 4.52 per 100,000 patient encounters; cases that actually went to litigation fell from 2.13 to 0.75; and the median time from claim to resolution shortened from 1.36 years to 0.95 years.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? One honest “I was wrong” is more powerful than an entire team of lawyers. Bowing your head is not a loss; bowing your head is the way out.

Yet we all know how hard those three words are to say. A husband and wife quarrel; both badly want to make up, yet neither will speak first. Between parents and children there is love in both hearts, yet all that comes out of their mouths is “What did I do wrong?” Two co-workers in a church fall out over some small matter and stay frozen for years. It isn’t that we don’t know how to apologise; it’s that we can’t bear to bow our heads.

The introduction to the lesson text puts it with great precision: pride drives people away from God; humility brings people back before him. From the fall of the archangel and the sin of Adam to our own weaknesses and failures today, the root of sin has always been the same — pride.

The Bible records how that anointed cherub who covers (Ezekiel 28:14) fell. The prophet Isaiah, speaking through the mouth of the king of Babylon, utters words that shake the heart: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ ” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, count them: how many times does he say “I will”? Five. Five “I will”s, and an archangel was hurled down from heaven. Pride has never been “I did something bad”; pride is “I want to sit in the seat that doesn’t belong to me.”

In the Garden of Eden, the serpent’s words to the woman used the same recipe: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Humanity’s fall did not begin with a piece of fruit; it began with a thought — I don’t have to depend on God; I can manage on my own.

The English writer C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. He was right. For pride is the only sin that the more it grows, the less you can see it in yourself. A greedy person knows he is greedy; an angry person knows he is angry; only the proud person always thinks it is someone else who is proud.

So how is this deepest root of humanity’s sickness to be treated? The Bible gives only one answer, and it has never changed from Genesis to Revelation — humility is the antidote to pride. Only the humble can receive salvation, obtain forgiveness and enter revival.

In the 321 vision we put it even more directly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights that are not ours and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Today, following the three key points of the lesson text, we will walk step by step along this road home: first, humility is the starting point of salvation; second, the humble are forgiven and the proud are rejected; third, humility brings revival and healing.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Younger Brother Who Called Himself a Servant
1. The Author, Date and Readers of James
sections.html:
Our theme verse comes from the letter of James. Its author is generally held to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. At first he did not believe in the Lord; John’s Gospel says it plainly: “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” (John 7:5) But after the Lord rose, he appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and this younger brother was utterly changed. He went on to become a leader of the church in Jerusalem, called by Paul one of the pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9), and gave the ruling at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:13–21).

Notice how he introduces himself: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings.” (James 1:1) Brothers and sisters, he could perfectly well have written “James, the brother of the Lord” — the most dazzling title in the whole church. He didn’t. He wrote “servant.” The Greek is δοῦλος (doulos): a slave. How deeply a person knows Jesus can be seen from what he calls himself. This book about humility begins teaching humility from its very first verse.

There is another account from church history. Hegesippus, in the second century, left a passage that the church historian Eusebius preserved in his Ecclesiastical History, saying that James was constantly on his knees praying for the people, so that his knees grew calloused, hard as a camel’s. Though this account belongs to tradition, it fits the spirit of the letter of James: the truly humble person is someone on their knees before God.

The letter of James is generally thought to have been written between AD 45 and 50, and is quite possibly the earliest book of the New Testament to be completed. Its readers were “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” — Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived in poverty, persecution and trial, and yet in the church there had arisen favouritism, rivalry and mutual criticism.

sections.heading: 2. The Setting of James 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4, where our theme verse is found, opens with a very pointed question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1) Brothers and sisters, the root of conflict in the church is rarely in the matter itself; mostly it lies in the heart. James goes on: “You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” (James 4:2)

Then we come to our theme verse today: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (James 4:6) That phrase “it says” introduces a quotation from Proverbs 3:34. The apostle Peter quotes the same sentence: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (1 Peter 5:5) Two pillars of the Jerusalem church, independently quoting the same Old Testament verse — this in itself is a reminder: this is not James’s personal opinion; it is an unchanging law of the kingdom of God.

sections.heading: 3. Three Key Words in the Original
sections.html:
The first word is “proud,” Greek ὑπερήφανος (hyperēphanos), made up of two roots, “above” (ὑπέρ) and “to appear” (φαίνομαι). Literally it means “to make oneself appear higher than others.” The core of pride is not being highly capable; it is wanting to be seen as higher than others.

The second word is “humble,” Greek ταπεινός (tapeinos), whose verb is ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), meaning “to lower, to bring down, to place beneath.” Interestingly, in Greco-Roman culture this word originally carried a negative sense, describing someone base and lacking ambition. It was the Bible that turned it upside down and made it the highest virtue of the kingdom of heaven — what the world regards as shameful, God has made glorious.

The third word is “resists,” Greek ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, this is a fearful thing to read: God does not merely disapprove of the proud; he draws up his ranks against them as an enemy. There is no battle in all the world with less hope of victory than standing in battle against God.

sections.heading: 4. The Background of Two Other Key Passages
sections.html:
2 Chronicles 7:14, quoted in the lesson text’s third key point, is set at Solomon’s dedication of the temple. After the temple was completed, fire fell from heaven and the glory of Yahweh filled the house, “Yahweh appeared to Solomon by night” (2 Chronicles 7:12) and spoke those words that countless intercessors have quoted. Notice: these words were not spoken to the Gentiles but to “my people, who are called by my name.” Revival has never begun in the world; it begins in the house of God.

Luke 14:11, quoted in the lesson text’s first key point, has an equally important background. Jesus was eating at the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees, and “he noticed how they chose the best seats” (Luke 14:7). So he told a parable, ending with: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) This saying appears twice in Luke’s Gospel; the other time is after the parable of the tax collector and the Pharisee at prayer (Luke 18:14). Once at the dinner table, once in the temple; once about our seat before people, once about our standing before God. What the Lord is saying is that it’s the same everywhere: in the kingdom of God there is only one way up, and that is to go down first.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Humility Is the Starting Point of Salvation
sections.html: The lesson text’s very first sentence makes the truth plain: salvation does not depend on effort; it begins with humility. If a person will not bow their head and admit they are a sinner, they cannot be saved.

sections.heading: 1. A Law Laid Down by the Lord Himself
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11) Brothers and sisters, this is not an exhortation; it is a law. Like gravity, it is always at work whether you believe in it or not. When people grasp upwards, God brings them down; when people bow down, God lifts them up.

The clearest demonstration of this law is the parable in Luke 18. Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and prayed to himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.” (Luke 18:11–12)

Every word he said was true. He really did fast, he really did give, he really was no extortioner or adulterer. So where was the problem? The problem was that the word appearing most in his prayer was “I” — and while he stood before God, his eyes were fixed on the man beside him. Brothers and sisters, there is a very reliable test for pride: when you are before God, who are you thinking about?

And the other man? “But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ ” (Luke 18:13)

For “be merciful to me” the Greek uses ἱλάσθητί (hilasthēti), from the same root as “atoning sacrifice”; literally it means “be propitiated towards me — grant me the grace of atonement.” And “a sinner” carries the definite article in the original: “me, the sinner” — not one sinner among many, but the sinner. He made no comparison, he offered no explanation; he admitted one thing only: I need God.

The Lord’s conclusion is: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the one who walked out of the temple that day declared righteous by God was not the one with the higher moral score, but the one willing to bow his head. The door of salvation is very wide — wide enough for anyone to come in; but the door is very low — low enough that everyone must bow their head.

sections.heading: 2. Adam’s Tragedy: From Hiding to Shifting the Blame
sections.html:
The lesson text takes us back to the Garden of Eden. After Adam sinned, his first reaction was not to confess but to hide. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

God came looking for him and asked the first question in the Bible: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’ ” (Genesis 3:9) Brothers and sisters, of course God knew where he was. When God asked “Where are you?” it wasn’t to locate him but to give him a chance to turn back. God was saying: Come out, child; let’s talk.

How did Adam answer? “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’ ” (Genesis 3:12)

With that one sentence he passed the blame on twice: first to the woman, then to the God who had given him the woman. The lesson text is right — pride cost him the chance to repent. God meant to give him forgiveness; he wanted to give God excuses.

Brothers and sisters, have we made any progress since Adam? When a child breaks a cup, the first words are often “It wasn’t me.” When husband and wife clash, the first words are often “You started …” The mistake itself won’t destroy a person; covering up the mistake will. That is why the Bible says: “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” (Proverbs 28:13)

sections.heading: 3. Confirmation from Psychology: We Are Born Self-Justifiers
sections.html:
Psychology observed this long ago. In 1975 Dale Miller and Michael Ross published a paper in the Psychological Bulletin reviewing a large body of experiments, pointing out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: when they succeed, they attribute it to their own ability; when they fail, they attribute it to circumstances or other people.

A little earlier, in 1957, Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when my behaviour contradicts my self-image of “I am a good person,” my mind becomes very uncomfortable; and to get rid of that discomfort, the easiest thing to do is not to change my behaviour but to change my story — to find myself a reason. In their 2007 book, the social psychologists Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson called this mechanism “self-justification”: the longer we justify ourselves, the further we drift from the facts.

Brothers and sisters, psychology tells us the true condition of the human heart; the Bible tells us the way out. Science can describe the symptoms; only the gospel can heal the root of the disease. It isn’t that we are unable to admit our mistakes; it’s that we won’t pay the small price of a little face.

sections.heading: 4. Turning Back Is the Fastest Way
sections.html:
In Mere Christianity C. S. Lewis offers a fine comparison: we all want progress; but if you are on the wrong road, progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road — and in that case the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had this experience? You get on the motorway, drive for twenty minutes, and only then realise you are going the wrong way. The biggest struggle at that moment isn’t the cost of the petrol; it’s the thought, “I don’t want to admit I went the wrong way.” So you console yourself: I’ll drive on a bit and see. And the result? The further you drive, the further away you get.

Confession is the act of taking the exit. It takes a few minutes, but it can save you hours. John puts it very clearly: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

The lesson text says: but Jesus has opened the way home for sinners. As long as we are willing humbly to admit, “Lord, I was wrong,” he forgives at once, heals, and lets us stand up again.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: From Information to Revelation
sections.html:
In the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset, the first stage is Information and the second is Revelation. Information is “I know pride is bad”; Revelation is “Lord, I see that I am that proud person.” How many people stay at the first stage all their lives — hearing sermons for decades without ever once being truly searched by the light.

Brothers and sisters, the work of the Holy Spirit is precisely to turn information into revelation. The Lord said: “When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment.” (John 16:8) The Chinese Union Version renders “convict” as “cause them to reprove themselves” — notice that phrase. The Holy Spirit never deals with us by humiliating us; he shines the light in, so that we see for ourselves, admit for ourselves, turn back for ourselves. This is the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not circumstances. The Pharisee’s focus was on himself and on others; the tax collector’s focus was on God. So one went home empty-handed, and one went home justified. Pride makes people perish; humility gives people life.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Humble Are Forgiven; the Proud Are Rejected
sections.html: The lesson text says that the contrast between Saul and David is the most vivid example. Both men were kings of Israel, both were chosen by God, both sinned. Yet their ends were completely opposite. The difference lay not in how heavy the sin was, but in how soft or hard the heart was.

sections.heading: 1. Saul: Pride Wrapped in Pious Reasons
sections.html:
Saul disobeyed God’s command twice. The second time, God commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but he kept King Agag and the best of the cattle and sheep. When the prophet Samuel arrived, what were Saul’s first words?

“Samuel came to Saul; and Saul said to him, ‘You are blessed by Yahweh! I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:13)

Brothers and sisters, how spiritual that sounds! A blessing, and a report of obedience. But Samuel said: “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?” (1 Samuel 15:14) The truth doesn’t change because of how we describe it; the sheep were still bleating.

Saul went on to explain: “They have brought them from the Amalekites; for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the cattle, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God. We have utterly destroyed the rest.” (1 Samuel 15:15) And later: “But the people took of the plunder, sheep and cattle, the chief of the devoted things, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God in Gilgal.” (1 Samuel 15:21)

Look at the three tactics in these words. First, he shifts the blame onto the people. Second, he dresses up the motive as piety — it was meant as an offering to God. Third, notice his wording: “Yahweh your God,” not “my God.” Brothers and sisters, when people are making excuses, even the way they address God gives the truth away.

The lesson text hits the nail on the head: he would not admit his error, but instead used “pious reasons” to cover his pride. This is the hardest pride of all to detect — wrapping my own will up as God’s will.

Samuel’s answer is among the weightiest words in the Old Testament: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:22–23)

There is a startling verbal correspondence here. The Hebrew for “rejected” is מָאַס (ma’as), meaning “to refuse, to cast away.” The same word appears twice in this verse: you have rejected Yahweh’s word, and Yahweh has rejected you from being king. Brothers and sisters, how exact God’s justice is — as we treat God’s word, so God treats our position.

Someone may ask: didn’t Saul later say, “I have sinned”? Yes, he did. “Saul said to Samuel, ‘I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:24) But read on: “Then he said, ‘I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship Yahweh your God.’ ” (1 Samuel 15:30)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What he really cared about was not God’s heart but saving face in front of everyone. His confession was to hold on to his throne. That is not repentance; that is public relations. And so God rejected him and took away his kingship.

sections.heading: 2. David: A Crushed Heart
sections.html:
David’s sin was even more serious. He committed adultery, then arranged the murder of the loyal Uriah, and kept it hidden for nearly a year. The prophet Nathan came and told a parable about a poor man and his little ewe lamb, then pointed at him and said: “You are the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7)

David’s response was a single sentence: “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ Nathan said to David, ‘Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.’ ” (2 Samuel 12:13)

No explanation, no “but,” no “the people.” One sentence of confession, one sentence of forgiveness. Brothers and sisters, God’s forgiveness is never slow; what is slow is our bowing of the head.

David wrote that experience into Psalm 51. He says: “For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.” (Psalm 51:3) And again: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

The Hebrew for “broken” is שָׁבַר (shavar), meaning “shattered, snapped”; “contrite” is דָּכָה (dakah), meaning “crushed, ground down.” Both are heavy words. God doesn’t want us to make our offerings look impressive; God wants a heart that is truly broken. The lesson text puts it well: God does not look at how heavy the outward sin is, but at whether our heart has truly repented.

Brothers and sisters, look at the contrast: Saul offered the best of the cattle and sheep, and God did not accept it; David offered only a broken heart, and God accepted him completely. For an offering can be a bargaining chip I use in exchange, but a broken heart is the surrender of my whole self.

Scripture also says: “For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.’ ” (Isaiah 57:15) God dwells in two places: the high and holy place, and a contrite and humble heart. Brothers and sisters, your heart can become God’s dwelling place.

sections.heading: 3. The Prodigal Son: The Father Interrupted His Bargain
sections.html:
The lesson text says that the story of the prodigal son confirms this truth once again. The prodigal came to his senses in the pigsty and said: “I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.’ ” (Luke 15:18–19)

He prepared three sentences. The first: I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. The second: I am no more worthy to be called your son. The third: make me as one of your hired servants.

But look at what happened when he actually came home. “He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20) And then: “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ ” (Luke 15:21)

Brothers and sisters, the third sentence has vanished. The father didn’t let him finish. Why? Because the first two sentences were repentance, and the third was a bargain — I’ll work, you feed me. The father didn’t want a hired servant; the father wanted a son.

The lesson text says: he made no excuses and hid nothing; he simply came home humbly. The father had long been waiting at the door; he embraced him and restored him. It is never too late to repent, as long as we are willing to turn back in humility.

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “ran.” In the culture of the ancient Near East, an elderly man of standing did not run; to run he had to hitch up his robes, which was unseemly. Yet this father ran. He would rather lose his own dignity than let his son be shamed at the edge of the village. This is our God — he is more eager to forgive than we are to be forgiven.

sections.heading: 4. Confirmation from Psychology and Daily Life
sections.html:
In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning published a famous study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They found that across several tests, the group with the least ability actually rated their own performance the highest. This phenomenon later became known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect.” The reason is simple: if a person doesn’t even know what they lack, they have no way of knowing that they lack it.

Brothers and sisters, this was exactly Saul’s situation, and it is often ours too. The most dangerous thing about pride is not that it makes me go wrong, but that it keeps me from seeing that I have gone wrong. That is why David prayed: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Here is another example from daily life. Two patients walk into the consulting room. The first says, “Doctor, I’m fine — just a bit tired lately.” The second says, “Doctor, it hurts here. It’s hurt for three months and I can’t sleep at night.” Which one can the doctor treat? Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that the doctor plays favourites; the first patient never handed over his illness at all. The Lord Jesus said: “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.” (Matthew 9:12) It isn’t that the Lord won’t heal the proud; it’s that the proud won’t admit they are sick.

It is generally said that Augustine, in the history of the church, was once asked what the most important lesson of the Christian faith was, and he answered: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. The saying comes from his letter to Dioscorus. Sixteen hundred years have passed, and the answer hasn’t changed.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Pride Makes Both Sides Lose; Humility Lets Both Sides Win
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a very important saying: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

The conversation between Saul and Samuel is pride provoking pride in action: one excuse draws a rebuke, the rebuke draws a harder excuse, and in the end the throne is gone, and the prophet “came no more to see Saul until the day of his death” (1 Samuel 15:35). By contrast, Nathan says one sentence, “You are the man,” David says one sentence, “I have sinned against Yahweh,” and both men are preserved — and God’s name is preserved too.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. David’s mindset changed — he no longer asked, “How do I get out of this?” but “O God, how do I come back before you?” And so his life was restored, and his psalm has become, for three thousand years, the prayer of countless multitudes of penitents.

This is also what the 321 vision calls the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. Saul kept dealing with “people” and “things” — how the people saw him, how to keep his throne. David dealt with God first — I have sinned against Yahweh. Turn the order upside down and everything falls; put the order right and everything comes right.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Humility Brings Revival and Healing
sections.html: The lesson text says: humility is not only a personal transformation; it is the turning around of a nation. This is a very great promise, and a very solemn order of priority.

sections.heading: 1. The Order of Revival: Humbling Ourselves Comes Before Prayer
sections.html:
God says to his people: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

Brothers and sisters, notice the four actions here: humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn from their wicked ways. The lesson text makes a very good point — the first step on God’s road to healing is not “pray” but “humble themselves.”

Why? Because without a humble heart, prayer is merely a form. Someone who still thinks he is right can easily turn prayer into notifying God: Lord, I’ve already decided to do this; please bless it. That isn’t prayer; that is filing a report. The lesson text says it well: humility leads us to admit our limits and let God be Lord again; humility makes us willing to lay down our own will and turn to God’s will.

The Hebrew for “humble themselves” here is כָּנַע (kana‘), meaning “to bring oneself low, to bend the knee, to bow down in submission.” The word was originally military, describing a city or a nation yielding and surrendering in war. Brothers and sisters, how vivid this is — true humbling of ourselves is raising our hands in surrender before God and saying: Lord, I’m done fighting, I’m done striving; you fight this battle.

God’s response is: I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin and heal their land. When we come down an inch, God comes near a mile. This is the law of God’s kingdom.

sections.heading: 2. Nineveh: A City That Bowed Its Head
sections.html:
The lesson text gives Nineveh as an example. Let’s first make the background clear. Nineveh was the great city of the Assyrian Empire, on the east bank of the Tigris, its ruins near today’s Mosul in Iraq. Assyria was the most brutal military power of the ancient Near East, notorious for torture. Jonah refused to go, not because he was timid, but because he did not want God to forgive such an enemy (Jonah 4:2).

Jonah ministered around the eighth century BC, in the time of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Nineveh finally fell to the combined forces of the Medes and the Babylonians in 612 BC, and with that the Assyrian Empire came to an end. In other words, the message of repentance Jonah preached won that city more than a hundred years of forbearance.

Jonah proclaimed God’s judgement: “Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried out, and said, ‘In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!’ ” (Jonah 3:4)

Brothers and sisters, notice that this was a message with no comfort, no way out and no “unless.” Jonah spoke only of judgement, not of grace. Yet Scripture says: “The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.” (Jonah 3:5)

Even the king did the same: “The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.” (Jonah 3:6)

Brothers and sisters, there are four actions in this verse, and every one of them goes downwards: he rose from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth and sat in ashes. From the highest seat all the way down into the ashes. This is the picture of humbling oneself.

And the result? “God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.” (Jonah 3:10)

The lesson text puts it superbly: humility can turn judgement into blessing and crisis into opportunity. The fate of a whole city turned on whether one king was willing to leave his throne. Brothers and sisters, the fate of a family also often turns on whether one person is willing to bow their head first.

sections.heading: 3. Confirmation from Church History: Every Revival Begins with Confession
sections.html:
Open the history of the church and you will find that every true revival began not with eloquence but with people going down on their knees.

In the autumn of 1904 a revival broke out in Wales that touched the whole world. What the young preacher Evan Roberts proclaimed was not lofty words or great wisdom, but four simple demands: confess and put away every known sin; remove everything doubtful from your life; obey the Holy Spirit’s leading completely; confess Christ publicly. Within a few short months, according to church records of the time, about a hundred thousand people turned to Christ; in many places the taverns closed, and the moral climate of society was transformed.

In January 1907 the same thing happened in Pyongyang on the Korean peninsula. At the Presbyterian winter Bible conference, a local elder, Kil Sun-Joo (later that year one of the first Korean ministers to be ordained), confessed before everyone that he had wronged the estate of a friend who had died, and was willing to make restitution. That confession was like a key that opened the floodgates: the whole congregation fell on their faces, weeping and confessing their sins, and the meeting went on late into the night. This revival came to be called “the Korean Pentecost,” and laid the foundation of the Korean church for the century that followed.

Brothers and sisters, notice what they have in common: the starting point of both revivals was not someone preaching a great sermon, but someone saying in front of everyone: I was wrong.

sections.heading: 4. Two Lessons from the Natural World
sections.html:
God has also written truth into the things he has made.

The first lesson: water flows downhill. All the water in the world flows to the lowest places; high ground cannot hold water, and only a low-lying basin can collect it into a lake. Grace is the same. God’s grace, like water, always flows towards the lowest heart. If you exalt yourself, grace slides right off you; if you bow down low, grace gathers in you into a deep pool.

The second lesson is a warning. Israel has two lakes, both fed by the Jordan River. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has clear water and abundant fish; in the south, the Dead Sea lies about 430 metres below sea level, the lowest point on the earth’s land surface, with a salt content about ten times that of seawater, and almost nothing can live in it.

The same source, both of them low-lying — so why does one have life and the other none? The difference is this: the Sea of Galilee has an inflow and an outflow; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out.

Brothers and sisters, this reminds us that being low is not the same as being humble. There is a kind of “lowness” that is self-pity and self-enclosure, only taking in and never giving out — a Dead Sea kind of lowness. True humility is open towards God and flowing towards others — having received grace, we let grace flow on. That is why the lesson text’s gentle reminder is so precise: true humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God.”

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a very clear order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

2 Chronicles 7:14 is the very prototype of this order. God didn’t say, “If you plan, publicise and mobilise”; God said, “If you humble yourselves, pray, seek my face and turn from your wicked ways.” First deal with life, then with relationships, and only last of all does it reach the land — that is, ministry and the environment. Revival is not making events bigger; revival is turning human hearts around.

Brothers and sisters, this also brings us to the 321 vision’s “920 practice”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; as I practise living out a selfless life before them, I bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice that the last one is “self-control,” and humility is the very root of self-control: only someone willing to surrender can rein in their tongue and their temper.

Next come the “235 relationships”: become a “2” with someone selfless, spiritual companions to one another; establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, not one of these relationships can a proud person build. For the proud have only an audience around them, not companions; only subordinates, not children.

The lesson text says: today God is still looking for a people willing to be humble. When the church is willing to admit its weakness, when believers lay down their self-righteousness, revival will come to this land. This is precisely the Goal of the 321 vision — to establish God’s system. God’s system is not built on capable people; it is built on people who are willing to kneel.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Humility Is Returning to Our Originally Intended Position
1. The Three Foundations
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model. Paul wrote the most complete model of humility in the New Testament: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8) Brothers and sisters, look at this road: from the form of God to the form of a servant; from the throne of heaven to the cross.
