He was already in the highest place, yet he walked all the way down to the lowest. It wasn’t that he couldn’t contend; it was that he had no need to. He also said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) This is the only time the Lord directly describes his own heart — gentle and humble.

The Bible is my standard. Not one of the truths we have looked at today is human reasoning: Luke 14:11 is a law spoken by the Lord himself; James 4:6 quotes Proverbs 3:34; 2 Chronicles 7:14 is the procedure for revival laid down by God himself. Brothers and sisters, we don’t humble ourselves according to our feelings; we return to our originally intended position according to God’s word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. True confession is never forced out of us by people; it is drawn out by the light. The Lord said that when the Holy Spirit comes, he will make the world “reprove themselves,” as the Chinese Union Version puts it (John 16:8). Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you will worry, rely on the heart and you will be glad. We don’t need to fake humility by willpower; we need only open our hearts to the Holy Spirit every day.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King. What is the essence of pride? It is “I want to sit in that seat.” The archangel said “I will” five times; Adam wanted to be “like God, knowing good and evil”; Saul wanted to be honoured “before the elders of my people.” The essence of humility is giving that seat back to Jesus. When Jesus reigns as King, I don’t have to be king; and once I don’t have to be king, I am free.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The moment people compete for glory, relationships break; the moment people give the glory to the Lord, relationships are restored. John the Baptist said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Brothers and sisters, this is not a declaration of loss; it is a declaration of freedom.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html: The Babylonian system is a system of climbing upwards — “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). God’s system is a system of going downwards — “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). Brothers and sisters, these two systems press completely opposite direction keys. Every day we are adding bricks to one system or the other.

sections.heading: 4. The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness
sections.html:
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Brothers and sisters, remember: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A cup of water poured into the ocean has not disappeared; it has gained the whole ocean.

sections.heading: 5. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. There is only one mindset this lesson sets out to change: bowing your head is not losing; bowing your head is the way to life.

Our perspective must also shift in four directions: from man’s to God’s — Saul cared how people saw him, David cared how God saw him; from earthly to heavenly — the king of Nineveh laid down his earthly throne and saved the whole city; from temporary to eternal — a moment’s face cannot buy eternal forgiveness; from worldly to godly — the world says you only get by fighting, God says you receive by letting go.

sections.heading: 6. The Path of Serving
sections.html: The 321 vision’s Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides; the Bible gives understanding; our life imitates Jesus; in service we let Jesus reign as King; and in the end we give all the glory to God. Brothers and sisters, every step of this road requires a bowing of the head.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Making Humility Part of Everyday Life
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us four concrete practices. Let’s look at them one by one, and use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Daily Self-Examination

At the end of the day, ask yourself: “In what things was I still proud today? Am I willing to admit it humbly?”

Brothers and sisters, I suggest you check yourself with three very concrete questions. First, did I put someone else down in my heart today? Second, was there something I said today that I knew would hurt, and said anyway? Third, did I take the credit for something today? You can write three lines on your phone or in a notebook — it needn’t be long. David’s prayer is the best model: “Search me, God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23)

Practice 2: A Prayer of Repentance

Take time to come before the Lord alone, admit your wrongs, and ask the Lord to shine his light on you and cleanse you.

Be specific in confession. Don’t just say, “Lord, forgive me all my sins” — that is too general, and general confession doesn’t bring real change. Say: “Lord, what I said to my husband at half past eight this morning was proud. Please forgive me.” Brothers and sisters, the more specific, the more free. For God’s forgiveness is specific: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Practice 3: Learning to Submit

When someone reminds or corrects you, don’t justify yourself or argue; listen first and examine yourself first.

This is the hardest of the four practices. Let me give you a very practical method called “three seconds and two words.” When someone points out a problem in you, stay quiet for three seconds and don’t answer straight away; then say two words: “Thank you.” When you have calmed down, then work out how much of it is true. Brothers and sisters, the Bible says: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1) And: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19) Being swift to hear is where humility begins.

Practice 4: Interceding for the Nation

Pray humbly for the church, for families and for the nation, asking God to heal the land.

Brothers and sisters, the easiest trap to fall into in intercession is using prayer to accuse: Lord, please deal with those people. But 2 Chronicles 7:14 says, “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves.” When Daniel confessed on behalf of Israel, he said, “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely” (Daniel 9:5) — he counted himself in. Nehemiah did the same: “Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.” (Nehemiah 1:6) True intercession stands in the gap, not on the high ground.

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages

The 321 vision says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s walk today’s lesson through them.

Stage one, Information. Today we have received clear information: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6); salvation begins with bowing the head; revival begins with humbling ourselves.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation, so that, like David hearing “You are the man,” we see the specific pride in ourselves. Information without revelation only adds knowledge; it doesn’t change life.

Stage three, Conviction. Agree in your heart, truly: God is right and I am wrong; bowing the head really is the way to life. Conviction is not emotional excitement; conviction is a settled resolve.

Stage four, Implementation. Go today and do the hardest thing — make that phone call, say that “I’m sorry,” write that message. Brothers and sisters, if humility doesn’t land in a concrete action, it is only a feeling.

Stage five, Evaluation. Afterwards, look back: when I apologised, did I add, “But you also …”? That “but” is pride slipping back in through the back door.

Stage six, Correction. When you spot it, adjust. Next time, take out the “but,” and let the full stop come straight after “I’m sorry.”

Stage seven, Repetition. Humility is not a one-off decision; it is a lifelong practice. The Lord Jesus spoke of taking up one’s cross daily (Luke 9:23); in the same way, humility is a daily lesson. Bowing the head once is a moment of being moved; bowing the head every day is life.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When your family, your colleagues, your brothers and sisters see that you really are different, you can pass this life on. This is the “3” of the 321 vision — spiritual parents bringing forth spiritual children. Brothers and sisters, we are not trying to train a group of people who understand the teaching on humility; we are trying to multiply a group of people who live out a humble life.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson text leaves us three reminders, worth copying out and putting up somewhere you will see them.

First, pride drives people away from God; humility draws God near to people.

Second, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Third, true humility is not putting ourselves down, but admitting, “I need God.”

Brothers and sisters, remember this third one especially. Humility is not self-negation; it is not telling everyone you meet, “I can’t, I’m not worthy” — that can sometimes be another form of self-centredness. True humility is accuracy: knowing accurately that God is God and I am human; knowing accurately that I have gifts God has given me, and also the limitation that apart from him I can do nothing (John 15:5). Let God be God and let man be man — this is returning to our originally intended position.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us come back to the lesson text’s closing words. Humility is medicine for the soul, the antidote to pride. Pride makes people fall; humility makes people receive grace. Pride shuts the gate of heaven; humility opens it.

This morning I invite you to be still and ask yourself three questions.

The first question: before God, when was the last time I sincerely said, “Lord, I was wrong”?

The second question: before people, is there someone right now to whom I know in my heart I owe an apology, and I keep putting it off?

The third question: in my affairs, is there something I keep propping up by my own methods, and have never truly entrusted to God?

Let us learn, like David and like the prodigal son, not to run away and not to make excuses, but simply to return to the Father’s embrace. Like the king of Nineveh, let us be willing to come down from the throne. Like our Lord, who was in the form of God, yet willingly took the form of a servant.

When we are willing to be humble, God himself goes to work — dealing with our sin, restoring our life, and making revival begin with us and reach the whole land.

Brothers and sisters, let us begin right here today: laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position; letting God be God and letting man be man; letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ ” (James 4:6)
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” (James 4:10)
“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11)
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, I confess that I often cover my weakness with pride, disguise my mistakes with excuses, and use busyness to escape your searching light. Today I will hide no longer; I choose to be humble before you.
Forgive me and renew me; bring me back into your embrace. Take away those five “I will”s from my heart, and set your throne once again at the centre of my life.
Give me a broken and contrite heart, ears that are swift to hear and a tongue slow to speak, and the courage to be the first to bow my head.
May your grace come upon me, and upon my family, my church, this city and this nation. Heal our hearts, forgive our sins, and bring heavenly revival.
May all the glory be yours, for you are worthy. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Saul said, “I have sinned,” yet God still rejected him; David said, “I have sinned against Yahweh,” and God forgave him at once. Compare 1 Samuel 15:30, “Then he said, ‘I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship Yahweh your God,’ ” with 2 Samuel 12:13, “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ ” What is the difference between these two confessions? In your own experience, have you ever made a “Saul-style confession”?

2 Chronicles 7:14 says: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” Why does God put “humble themselves” before “pray”? This week, towards which specific person or in which specific matter will you bow your head first, so that your prayer is more than a mere form?
l078.title: Humility Is the Antidote to Pride
l078.subtitle: Admitting I Need God; Letting God Be God and Man Be Man
l078.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Doesn’t God Simply Strike Satan Down?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Let’s begin today by facing a question many believers have asked in their hearts but hardly dare say out loud: if God is almighty, why doesn’t he simply wipe Satan out in one stroke? Why let this spiritual war drag on for thousands of years, and let the world suffer so much?

The question is not irreverent. In fact, it is a key. Because when we honestly keep asking, we discover this: it isn’t that God “can’t beat” Satan; it’s that God “doesn’t fight that way”. If the almighty God chose to destroy Satan by sheer power, it wouldn’t take him a single second. But he didn’t do that. He chose the road that looks slowest, weakest and least like victory — he sent his only Son into the world as a man, born in a manger, raised in a carpenter’s home, and in the end nailed up between two robbers.

This is the most staggering truth in the gospel: God did not overpower Satan with might; he defeated him with love and obedience.

Let me begin with a scene from everyday life. A father told me that he and his teenage son had been locked in a cold war for three months. He said, “I’m his father. I raise him, I provide for him, I’ve given everything for him — don’t I have the right to make demands of him?” I asked him, “What is it you want? For him to bow his head, or for him to come home?” He was stunned. Because he realised that every time he had opened his mouth in those three months, he had been fighting over “whether I have the right”, and not once had he been fighting over “how I can win his heart back”.

Brothers and sisters, authority can bring people to their knees, but only humility can bring the heart to true surrender. This continues the truth we saw in the last lesson: humility is the antidote to pride. Today we go a step further and see that humility is not merely a virtue — humility is God’s strategy; it is not merely good character — humility is the strategy that wins.

Last time we saw that pride is the root of all evil, the cause of Satan’s fall and the source of humanity’s sin. Today we ask: how, then, does God deal with pride? The answer astonishes us: God doesn’t crush pride with a greater pride; God dissolves pride with humility.

It is commonly held that when the church father Augustine was asked in a letter what matters most in the Christian faith, he answered: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. It sounds like exaggeration, but it is profound. For in the kingdom of God, humility is not one virtue among many; humility is the soil in which every other virtue grows. Without humility, even our zeal, our gifts and our service will slowly turn into tools for self-exalting.

In this lesson we will look together at three things: first, God does not destroy Satan by authority but overcomes him by humility; second, humility is God’s strategy for overcoming Satan; third, humility is the strongest weapon in relationships.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: How Philippians 2 Came to Be
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from Philippians chapter 2. To understand it accurately, we need to know where it came from.

The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, in what is now northern Greece. Acts 16 records that on his second missionary journey Paul, called by a vision in the night, crossed the sea into Macedonia, and Philippi became the first church he planted in Europe. Its first believers included Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, and the jailer whose whole household came to the Lord after the earthquake. The letter is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, while Paul was a prisoner in Rome awaiting Caesar’s judgement.

Notice the contrast: a prisoner bound in chains, with an uncertain future, wrote the most joyful book in the New Testament. The word “joy” recurs more than ten times in just four chapters. Paul isn’t talking about humility from a place of ease; he is talking about it from a prison cell. He isn’t talking about lowliness amid applause; he is talking about it in chains. That is what gives his words their weight.

So why did Paul write this passage in chapter 2? Because although the Philippian church loved the Lord, gave generously and stood firm under persecution, it had a hidden worry: factions and quarrels were beginning to appear among them. In chapter 4 Paul even names two co-workers, Euodia and Syntyche, and urges them to “be of the same mind in the Lord”. So at the very start of chapter 2 Paul says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4).

Then Paul does something extremely important: instead of carrying on with argument, he lifts up Jesus Christ and says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). And then comes our key passage today — the section church history calls the “Christ Hymn”. Many scholars believe it was very likely a song the early church sang in worship, which Paul quoted here. In other words, the early church did not treat “emptying himself” as an obscure theological term; it was a confession of faith they sang into their very lives.

The structure of the passage is crystal clear — a deep “V”: down from the glory of heaven, all the way to the manger, to the form of a servant, to death on the cross; then up from the dead, exalted by God to the highest place, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses. Every step down was one he chose himself; every step up was one God did for him. This is one of the most important spiritual laws in the whole Bible: whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Two other passages we will use today also need some background. Isaiah 14 is a lament over the king of Babylon, in which the prophet mocks how this arrogant monarch fell from the heights. Yet as the church through the ages has read it, they have seen behind its five “I will”s a shadow far older than the king of Babylon — the very pride that brought humanity down. Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians facing persecution and tempted to retreat into the rituals of the old covenant; the author wants them to see that the Jesus who humbled himself is the very author and perfecter of their faith.

With this background, we can now turn to today’s three key points.

sections.heading: 1. God Does Not Destroy Satan by Authority but Overcomes Him by Humility
sections.html:
Ever since the creation of the world, Satan has been challenging God’s authority. The prophet Isaiah left us this famous description:

“How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:12–14)

Brothers and sisters, count how many times “I will” appears here. Five, no less. “I will ascend into heaven”, “I will exalt my throne”, “I will sit on the mountain of assembly”, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds”, “I will make myself like the Most High”. The grammar of pride is always the first person; the direction of pride is always upward; the goal of pride is always “like the Most High” — that is, to leave our originally intended position and try to take God’s place.

The Hebrew verb for “ascend” here is alah, which is in itself a neutral word; the Bible also uses it of a burnt offering “going up”. The same movement — what matters is not high or low, but who is lifting me up. When God lifts a person up, it is grace; when a person lifts himself up, it is rebellion.

But look at the next verse: “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:15). Five “I will”s pointing upward, answered by a single sentence of God’s judgement pointing down. This is exactly what Proverbs says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

Here is the question: if God has long since pronounced the sentence, why doesn’t he carry it out at once? Why has God tolerated Satan troubling the world for so long? The answer lies not in any limit to God’s power but in the depth of God’s purpose. What God wants is not merely to eliminate an enemy, but to display once and for all, before the whole universe, that “the way of pride is the way of death, and the way of humility is the way of life”.

So God did not erase Satan with a thunderbolt of power. Instead, he sent his Son into the world as a man:

“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

Two key Greek words here deserve our attention. The first is “emptied himself”, kenoo in the original, meaning to pour out, to make empty. Note carefully: what Jesus emptied was not his divinity — he did not stop being God. What he laid aside was the use of the glory and rights of equality with God. The second is “a thing to be grasped”, harpagmos in the original, meaning something clutched tightly, held on to like plunder that one refuses to let go. Satan’s problem was that he wanted to “seize” a position that never belonged to him; Jesus’ beauty is that he did not cling even to what was rightly his.

Brothers and sisters, do you hear the contrast? One grabs what he does not have; the other lets go of what he already has. One falls because he grasps; the other is exalted because he lets go.

So look at this picture: Satan, who wanted to exalt himself, fell through pride; Jesus, who was willing to lower himself, was exalted through humility. This is a fixed and unshakeable law of the spiritual world — pride drags us down, humility lifts us up. The Lord Jesus himself put this law as plainly as it can be put: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Let me illustrate with a picture from nature. Water by its nature flows downward, and so all the rivers of the earth gather into the sea; and the sea can hold every river precisely because it lies lowest of all. The mountaintop, by contrast, may look highest, yet it cannot keep a single drop of water. People are the same: the lower someone’s position, the more life they carry; the loftier someone’s posture, the less remains with them.

Psychological research confirms this from another angle. In a 1996 study published in Psychological Review, the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues proposed the idea of “threatened egotism”, arguing that aggression and violence often come not from low self-esteem but from a highly favourable view of oneself that has been challenged or offended. In other words, the more someone needs to defend the image that “I’m really something”, the more violently they react once it is questioned. This shows exactly why, if you use authority to crush pride, what you get is not surrender but a fiercer backlash.

Let’s connect this truth with the 321 vision. 321 tells us that the problem of the old self is the self-centred life, and the way out for the new self is selflessness. Satan’s five “I will”s are the self-centred life at its extreme; Jesus’ “emptying himself” is selflessness at its height. And selflessness is not turning ourselves into zero, into nothing; it is placing ourselves in God’s hands, entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

So God’s strategy has never been “force against force” but “humility overcoming pride”. Not by arguing, not by power, not by emotion, but by obedience, trust and the lowliness of love. Brothers and sisters, if this truly turns around in our mindset, the way we relate to people will be completely different.

sections.heading: 2. Humility Is God’s Strategy for Overcoming Satan
sections.html:
In this second key point, we want to see more deeply that humility is not God’s last resort; humility is God’s strategy.

God does not subdue pride with intimidation, because pride is never crushed into submission; it is only provoked into resistance. A law of physics can help us understand this. Newton’s third law of motion says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. However hard you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. The human heart is the same. However forcefully you bear down on people, they push back with just as much resistance. This is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

So God did something no one expected. He had the eternal Son become flesh, become a baby:

“But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone.” (Hebrews 2:9)

The Lord who created the angels now became a man made a little lower than the angels. This was no mistake; this was a plan. For verse 14 goes on to give the reason: “Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14).

Notice the phrase “through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death”. To abolish death, God’s method was — death; to overcome the one who held the power of death, God’s weapon was his own dying. In human logic this makes no sense at all; in God’s wisdom it is brilliant.

The cross looked like defeat; in fact it was the starting point of victory. On that day the sky went dark, the disciples scattered, the religious leaders jeered and the Roman soldiers divided his clothes. Satan probably thought he had won — Jesus was dead! But precisely at that moment of “lowest humiliation”, God’s power was fully displayed; death was overcome, and Satan’s power was stripped away. How forcefully Paul puts it: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15).

The background of the word “triumphing” is the triumphal procession of a victorious Roman general returning to the city: the chariot in front, the captives behind, the whole city lining the streets. Paul is saying that the cross is Christ’s triumphal chariot. In the world’s eyes it was an instrument of execution; in God’s eyes it was the chariot of victory.

How did Jesus fight this battle? He fought it in a way that looked nothing like fighting. “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). What he spoke on the cross was not a curse but: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Brothers and sisters, this is the mystery of spiritual warfare: Satan tried to win by exalting himself; Jesus won by laying himself down. God’s victory is not suppressing the other side but turning it upside down. He did not pin the enemy to the ground; he made the enemy’s weapons entirely useless.

Jesus answered Satan’s pride with humility, and Satan was defeated so completely that he had nothing left to say. Why nothing left to say? Because Satan could no longer accuse a man who had never sinned yet was willing to die in the place of sinners; every accusation he had fell empty. The proclamation John heard in his vision was: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). The weapons that overcome the enemy are the blood of the Lamb and a testimony that lays down its life — and both are the fruit of humility.

The same principle still holds today. “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul learned this from a “thorn”. Three times he begged the Lord to take it away; the Lord did not remove it, but gave him something better: power displayed in weakness.

The prophet Zechariah said the same long before: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6). Brothers and sisters, 321 reminds us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. The reason we end up exhausted in the battle is often not that the enemy is too strong but that we are using the wrong weapons — we are fighting with our own might, ability, eloquence and face, so no wonder the fighting wears us out.

Scripture also gives us a living example. How mighty Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, was! He stood on his palace and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). Then God drove him from human society to live with the wild animals, until he lifted his eyes to heaven and his reason returned. His final testimony was: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37). God did not destroy him; God humbled him in order to save him. Brothers and sisters, God’s purpose in dealing with pride has never been to destroy people but to win them back.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Is the Strongest Weapon in Relationships
sections.html:
The third key point brings this truth back into our daily living.

We often want to deal with problems by “authority”. When people don’t submit, don’t listen, don’t cooperate, our most instinctive reaction is to pull rank, raise our voice and put our emotions on display. Parents say, “I’m your father!” Husbands say, “I’m the head of this house!” Co-workers say, “This should have been my call in the first place!” Words like these may bring temporary compliance, but they cannot buy a lasting relationship.

Brothers and sisters, remember these three sentences: power can make people yield; humility can make people turn. Power builds control; humility builds connection. Power changes behaviour; humility changes the heart.

The Lord Jesus spelled this out long ago: “But Jesus summoned them, and said, ‘You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many’” (Matthew 20:25–28).

“It shall not be so among you.” These few words are the watershed between the kingdom of God and the Worldly system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: the higher you are, the more people serve you. God’s system is turned upside down: the higher you are, the more people you serve. Jesus did not abolish authority; he redefined it: authority exists to serve, not to dominate.

So at the Last Supper he did something even his disciples tried to stop — he tied a towel around himself, took a basin of water and washed his disciples’ feet one by one, including Judas, who was about to betray him. Then he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

On the cross Jesus did not command people to repent; he died for sinners. He loved people through action and won them over through humility. That is why Paul could dare to say: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

Research on marriage and family gives us strong support here. The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington spent many years in his “Love Lab” filming and analysing how couples interact. He and his colleagues found that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but the presence of “contempt” in their interactions — the eye-rolling, the sneering, the looking-down-on-you attitude. What is contempt? Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship. Conversely, he also found that couples who are willing to accept each other’s influence, and willing to “repair” in the middle of conflict, have the most stable relationships. Being willing to be influenced is what humility looks like in concrete form.

Research on workplaces and teams says the same. A 2013 study by Bradley Owens, Michael Johnson and Terence Mitchell in the journal Organization Science found that humility shown by leaders — acknowledging their own limits, appreciating others’ strengths, being eager to learn — is positively associated with team learning and performance. Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, with her 1999 concept of “psychological safety”, likewise showed that only when those who lead are willing to admit they make mistakes will team members dare to speak the truth. A leader who never admits a mistake earns not respect but silence.

In his 2001 book “Good to Great”, the management scholar Jim Collins studied companies that went from good to great and found that their leaders shared one trait, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: deep personal humility combined with fierce professional will. Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research has brushed against the edge of this truth; how much more has the Lord we believe in lived it out with his whole life two thousand years ago.

A picture often comes to my mind. Two goats meet on a narrow log bridge that only one can cross at a time. If neither will back down, they lock horns and both fall into the water — both sides lose. But if one is willing to lie down and let the other step over it, both cross safely. The one that lay down seems to have lost, but in fact it saved two lives.

In families, churches and teams, when we face conflict, misunderstanding or opposition, if we are willing to lay ourselves down first — to listen first, understand first, give way first — we will discover that humility brings a transformation of the heart rather than grudging compliance in behaviour. James says: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Solomon says: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

Humility may look like a loss for a while, but its fruit lasts. It wins people’s trust, respect and love. Paul even said to the Corinthian believers who were suing one another: “Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). Brothers and sisters, in God’s ledger, no one who was willing to lose out has ever truly lost.

Scripture holds a beautiful example of this. Jacob had owed Esau a debt for twenty years — he had cheated him out of the birthright and the blessing and fled to Haran. Twenty years later, on his way back, he heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men, and he was terrified. What did he do? First he prayed, then he sent gifts ahead of him drove by drove, and finally he himself went on ahead of everyone, and “bowed himself to the ground seven times” (Genesis 33:3). The brother who had come with four hundred men, bent on settling scores, saw this, and the Bible says: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4). The force of four hundred men was never used; seven bows to the ground melted twenty years of hatred. Brothers and sisters, this is the power of humility.

This is God’s way: not to overawe people with force, but to move them with love.

Let’s connect this back to 321: 321 says “people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things”, and also that the order of service is “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. Many people turn the order upside down — they grab the ministry first, want relationships second, and only care about life last — and the result is that the ministry gets done but the people scatter. We must also remember the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If my relationship with God is right, I don’t need to prove myself in front of people; and only those who don’t need to prove themselves have room to humble themselves.

Then there is the precious 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in front of each “2”, we practise living a selfless life, and the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that fruit is not grown in a monastery; it is grown in relationships. The person who is hardest to get along with is the very garden God has given you to bear fruit in.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Living Humility Out as a Road
sections.html:
If we sum up today’s message in the language of 321, it becomes very clear.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, humbled himself and was obedient to death; that is the pattern I am to learn. The Bible is my standard — it is not my feelings, my face or my hurt that have the final say, but God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — humility is not a discipline I grit my teeth to keep up; it is fruit the Holy Spirit grows in me.

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: the scene of a conflict is often a battle over the throne — who is King here, me or Jesus? If I insist on winning, it is actually I who am sitting on the throne. Let Jesus receive all the glory: the final test of humility is this — when it’s all over, who has been lifted up, me or the Lord?

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system runs on power; God’s system runs on denying of self. Every time we choose humility, we lay one more brick of God’s system in our own family, small group and workplace.

Next, look at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. The most important thing in today’s lesson is the first — the change of mindset. I used to think that “winning” meant the other person backing down; now I know that “winning” means their heart being won back. I used to think humility meant losing out; now I know humility is a strategy. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry naturally changes.

321 also often reminds us of four shifts in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective — people see the cross as defeat, God sees it as victory; from the earthly to the heavenly — earth keeps score of who has the upper hand, heaven remembers who was willing to deny themselves; from the temporary to the eternal — how light a moment’s face is compared with eternal reward; from the worldly to the godly — no longer winning by the world’s methods, but by God’s.

And remember: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. In a conflict our focus easily wanders — one moment fixed on our own grievance, the next on the other person’s fault, the next blaming the circumstances. When the focus slips, the heart is thrown into turmoil; when the focus returns to Jesus, the heart is steadied. Solomon says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Finally, the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with a brother or sister who is also pursuing selflessness, supporting and reminding one another; go on to build a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children and passing life on; then move into a “5”, serving alongside spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team, establishing God’s system together. Brothers and sisters, it is hard for one person to stay humble for long, because pride loves to sprout in isolation; but when two people watch over each other and three generations pass life on to one another, humility can become a culture.

And all of this points to the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God — led by the Holy Spirit, corrected by the Bible, living out the life of Jesus, letting Jesus be King, and in the end letting Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to root them deep in our lives.

Practice 1: In Conflict, Be Still First

Don’t rush to react. Pray first, and let God remind you how to respond.

Information: First let the truth enter your mind — “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). Physiology tells us too that in strong emotion the brain’s amygdala reacts before anything else; the psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his 1995 book, called this “amygdala hijack”, and in that moment our judgement drops sharply. So “being still first” is not passive; it is so that the heart can come back before God.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you — in that conflict, what was I really protecting: the truth, or my face?

Conviction: Acknowledge from the heart that stillness is not losing; stillness is handing the first word to God. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

Implementation: This week, when someone touches a sore spot, first count silently to ten and pray one short sentence in your heart: “Lord, please be King.”

Evaluation: Before bed, think back: how many times today did I rush to answer back? How did those times turn out?

Correction: Identify the one situation, the one person, the one sentence that most easily makes you lose control, and pray over it in advance.

Repetition: Keep at it for forty days in a row, and stillness will turn from a struggle into an instinct.

Multiplication: Teach this practice to your children and your small-group members, and practise it alongside them.

Practice 2: Choose to Lay Down Your Rights

When you are “in the right, in authority and in a position to act”, practise stepping back and letting God speak.

Information: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Revelation: The Lord Jesus existed in the form of God, yet did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped. What he laid down were rights he truly possessed. Brothers and sisters, what we so often cannot lay down are merely rights we imagine we have.

Conviction: Believe that if I give way, God himself will step in; if I take matters into my own hands, God steps back.

Implementation: This week, pick one matter where “I’m clearly in the right” and deliberately don’t fight over it; write it down in your prayer journal and hand it to God.

Evaluation: A month from now, look back: what became of that matter?

Correction: If you find that you are taking revenge through a cold war or silence, that is not laying down your rights; it is fighting by other means, and you need to repent.

Repetition: Practise on small things, so that you can stand firm when big things come.

Multiplication: Tell others the testimony of how God acted after you laid down your rights.

Practice 3: Serve Others in Humility

When a relationship is tense, take the initiative to care for and help the other person, expressing love through action.

Information: “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2).

Revelation: At the Last Supper the Lord washed Judas’s feet. The very man he served was the one about to betray him.

Conviction: Believe that action melts a hard heart better than words.

Implementation: This week, for the person you least want to face, do one small, concrete thing — a glass of water, a word of greeting, a helping hand.

Evaluation: As I did it, was my heart willing, or did it carry a whiff of proving myself?

Correction: If your motives are impure, don’t stop serving; ask the Lord to cleanse your motives, and keep going.

Repetition: Keep doing it, until there is no bitterness left in your heart when you pray for that person.

Multiplication: Share it in your small group and invite a brother or sister to do this practice with you, and you will become each other’s “2”.

Practice 4: Meditate on the Cross of Jesus

Think about how he overcame pride with humility, and ask him to give you the same heart.

Information: Quietly read Philippians 2:5–11, slowly, one verse a day.

Revelation: Ask the Lord one question — Lord, how low did you go? And what am I still holding on to?

Conviction: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). This is not a suggestion; it is a command, and a promise too.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three minutes meditating on the cross, then bless one person who has wronged you.

Evaluation: After doing this for a while, have my feelings towards that person changed?

Correction: If your heart is still hard, tell the Lord honestly about that hard heart and ask him to give you a new one.

Repetition: Build meditation on the cross into your daily morning devotion, as a regular practice.

Multiplication: Gather your family and read a passage of Philippians 2 together at the dinner table.

A Gentle Reminder

Power can subdue people but cannot change them; humility looks weak, yet it can conquer the hardest heart. Jesus’ humility was not retreat; it was the strategy of victory.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s draw today’s message together.

God could destroy Satan by authority, but he chose to win by humility. Because true victory is not destroying the opponent but transforming the heart. The cross of Jesus is the height of humility, and the beginning of victory.

Let’s look once more at that spiritual law. Satan said “I will” five times, and he was brought down to Sheol; but in the Garden of Gethsemane Jesus said: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39) — and he was exalted to the highest place. Brothers and sisters, which kind of words are you speaking today?

How gentle is the invitation the Lord Jesus holds out to us: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Notice that the Lord did not say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me” — learn my ways. What he promises is not the thrill of victory, but rest for the soul. For only someone who no longer needs to prove himself is truly free.

Peter urges us in the same way: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6). “In due time” — the timetable for being lifted up is in God’s hands, not ours. Our part is simply to go low; the lifting up we leave to God.

So today, let us follow the Lord’s example, and in the face of pride’s challenge and conflict with others, choose humility and choose love.

I want to issue three calls to you. First, in your heart, let Jesus take the throne again — not me as King, but Jesus as King. Second, this week, take the first humble step towards one person — a phone call, an apology, a move to reach out. Third, give all the glory to Jesus — when a relationship is truly healed, remember that it was not your own skill but the Lord’s grace.

Then God’s glory will be revealed through us, pride will be put to shame, humility will triumph, and the showers of revival will surely fall upon this land.

keyVerses: who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:6–8)

Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. (Philippians 2:9–11)
declarations: Lord, I want to learn from you — to win not by pride but by humility.
Help me lay down my rights and lay down myself, and live out your gentleness and humility in every relationship.
May your humility become strength in me, so that I overcome pride with love and hardness with gentleness.
practices: Choose to lay down your rights
Meditate on the cross of Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you. You existed in the form of God, yet for our sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and were obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Lord, forgive us. So often we try to overpower people with authority, win them with arguments and control them with our emotions, yet refuse to take your way — going low, denying ourselves, moving people with love. Please cleanse us of every “I will” inside us that refuses to let go.

Holy Spirit, work in us today and give us the heart of Jesus. Let us be still first in conflict, give way when we are in the right, reach out in love in tense relationships, and meditate on your cross every morning.
May our families, our small groups and our church be knit together through humility; may pride find no foothold among us.
Be King, Lord, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Isaiah 14:13–14 records Satan’s five “I will”s. Looking back over this week, what has been the strongest “I will” in your heart? If you let Jesus be King in that matter, what would be different?

Philippians 2:6–8 says the Lord Jesus “emptied himself”. In the most tense relationship you have right now, which specific right is God asking you to “lay down”? How do you plan to take the first step this week?
l079.title: Humility Is a Strategy for Victory
l079.subtitle: Humility Is the Antidote to Pride (Part 2)
l079.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: The Three Seconds After the Blow Are the Real Pulpit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by taking you back to a very concrete scene.

It is a Wednesday evening, and the church’s co-workers’ meeting is under way. Just as it is about to wrap up, one of the co-workers suddenly says: “This was your fault in the first place.” The tone isn’t harsh, but the words are hard; there aren’t many people in the room, but everyone who matters happens to be there. You sit there with a smile still on your face, while inside you have already started gathering evidence — which day you sent the message, which time you reminded everyone, which task was never your responsibility at all. You don’t say a word, but you know full well that if the other person says one more thing, you will spread that whole pile of evidence out on the table.

Brothers and sisters, that moment is the truest moment of our lives. Because a person’s spiritual condition is seen not in how well he speaks from the pulpit but in what rises first in his heart in the three seconds after he has been wronged. The words from the pulpit are ones we have prepared; the reaction in those three seconds is what flows naturally out of our lives.

The most natural human reaction is an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. It is almost instinct. In secondary-school science we learned Newton’s third law of motion: between two bodies, action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction. Pride between people seems to obey the same law: you push me once, I’ll push you back once — and usually with a little interest added. You give me one cold word, I give you two; you step back one pace, I step back three. In the end both people are standing where they started, neither willing to move first, and the relationship simply freezes.

This is what the 321 vision keeps reminding us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Pride is never subdued by pride; it is only fed by it. Fire cannot put out fire; only water can.

Yet Jesus’ teaching runs completely against our instincts. He says: “whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). He wants us to answer pride with humility and overcome evil with good.

Notice that he isn’t asking us to shrink back in weakness, nor to pretend it doesn’t hurt. He wants us to learn his love, a love that goes beyond the world’s logic. Humility is not losing your dignity; it is choosing love. Humility is not retreat; it is victory.

The church father Augustine pointed out in The City of God that pride is the beginning of all sin. C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, likewise wrote that according to Christian teachers the essential vice, the utmost evil, is pride. If pride is the root of the disease, what is the cure? Not a cleverer argument, not a more elegant counter-attack, but humility.

This is the third talk in “Humility Is the Antidote to Pride”. In the first two we saw together that the root of pride is the self-centred life — leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place — whereas humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position: let man be man and let God be God. Today we face a more practical question: when someone else’s pride has already struck me in the face, what am I to do?

Brothers and sisters, the answer lies in three pictures: a left cheek turned, a cloak handed over, and an extra mile walked.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Fourth Way on the Mountain
sections.html:
To understand these words of Jesus, we first need to go and stand on that mountain.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew, also called Levi, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve disciples and formerly a tax collector in Capernaum. A man who had once collected taxes from his own people on behalf of Rome, despised by everyone, later became the one who recorded the charter of the kingdom of heaven — that alone is the finest footnote to grace. The Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christian readers. Matthew quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah God promised, the Son of David, the true King of Israel.

Matthew chapters 5 to 7 are the familiar Sermon on the Mount, the first of the five great discourses Matthew records; you could call it the constitution of the kingdom of heaven. In this discourse Jesus says six times over: “You have heard that it was said … but I tell you …” He was not abolishing the law. He said plainly: “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill” (Matthew 5:17). He was bringing the law back from an external code to the intention in God’s heart.

The passage we read today is the fifth of those six contrasts. The sixth, which follows straight after, is “love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44); and the conclusion of the whole section is: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). In other words, turning the other cheek is not an isolated rule; it is the road to becoming “like the Father”.

“An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth” comes from Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Many people think God was encouraging revenge, but the very opposite is true. In the ancient Near East, revenge had no upper limit. Genesis records Lamech arrogantly boasting: “If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times” (Genesis 4:24). A life for an eye, a whole clan for a tooth — that is the logic of humanity once it has left God. When God gave “an eye for an eye”, he was putting a ceiling on revenge: compensation could not exceed the damage. And this law was a judicial principle for judges to administer, not a personal licence for revenge.

But by Jesus’ day, this law, originally meant to restrain revenge, had been co-opted into a charm to justify it. People said: “Even the Bible says an eye for an eye — why should I put up with it?” And that is exactly where Jesus takes up the words: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil.”

The Greek word for “resist” is anthistēmi, meaning to stand opposite, to oppose head-on. Jesus is not telling us to take no stand against evil — James 4:7 says plainly, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you”, using the very same word. What Jesus forbids is resisting evil people by evil people’s methods; he forbids us to answer pride with pride. He wants us to change battlefields and change weapons.

There is one more thing we must keep in mind. Judea at that time lay under the iron heel of the Roman Empire. Taxes were heavy, soldiers were arrogant, the people were humiliated. Faced with this, the Jews of the day had roughly three options: the Zealots urged armed revolt, the Pharisees urged separating themselves by the law, and the Essenes simply withdrew into the wilderness — out of sight, out of mind. And on the mountain Jesus opened a fourth way — overcoming evil with humility and love.

Brothers and sisters, two thousand years have passed, and these four ways still lie before us. In the office, at home, in our chat groups, we are still choosing every day: Do I hit back? Do I use a spiritual label to wall myself off from people? Do I retreat into my shell and give them the cold shoulder? Or do I take the Lord’s fourth way?

sections.heading: 1. Jesus Answers Human Pride with Humility
sections.html:
1. The Text: A Saying Often Misunderstood

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

This saying is often misunderstood, as if Christians should let anyone push them around — not make a sound when struck, not seek help when harmed. In fact, what Jesus is teaching is not cowardice but spiritual responsiveness: do not answer pride in pride’s own way, but dissolve hatred with humility.

2. Exegesis: Why Specifically the “Right Cheek”?

Notice one detail: Jesus says the “right cheek”.

The vast majority of people are right-handed. If someone wants to strike the right cheek of the person facing him with his right hand, an open-handed blow from the front won’t reach it; he can only do it with a backhanded flick. In first-century Jewish society, a backhanded slap was not a fight but an insult — a declaration from master to servant, from superior to inferior: you are beneath me. The Mishnah, the compilation of Jewish oral law, records in its tractate on damages, Bava Kamma, that the compensation for an ordinary slap was two hundred zuz, while for a backhanded slap it was four hundred — double. Clearly, in the understanding of the time, it was not a wound to the body but a wound to one’s dignity.

So what Jesus is dealing with is exactly the kind of wound we find hardest to handle: not the wound of a fist, but the wound of losing face.

Then what does “turn the left cheek too” mean? If the other person wants to humiliate you with the back of his hand and you turn the other cheek towards him, he can only strike with an open palm — and an open-handed blow is what passes between equals. This turn looks like conceding defeat, but in fact it is a quiet and powerful declaration: you can strike me, but you cannot decide who I am; my identity in God is not in your hands.

This is not cowardice; this is handing sovereignty back to God.

We need to see this in balance too. Turning the left cheek does not mean forbidding every reasonable defence. When the Lord Jesus himself was on trial and an officer struck him with the palm of his hand, he still spoke up: “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” (John 18:23). He reasoned, but did not strike back; he pointed out the wrong, but did not curse. 1 Peter 2:23 describes it most vividly: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.”

Brothers and sisters, the key is not “whether I may speak” but “whether my heart is still bent on revenge”.

3. The Cross: We Struck the Right Cheek; He Turned the Left

There is a line in the lesson that shakes me every time I read it: we were the ones who struck the right cheek; the left cheek he turned to us of his own accord.

Let’s pull the camera all the way back to the beginning. God loved the world and placed the Garden of Eden in human hands: “subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth” (Genesis 1:28). What God gave humanity was authority, trust and relationship. And what did humanity do? It listened to the serpent — “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — and chose to leave its originally intended position and try to take God’s place.

A betrayal like that is far worse than “striking the right cheek”. The created struck the Creator; the beloved betrayed the One who loved.

Yet God did not retaliate. He sent his only, beloved Son Jesus into the very world that had struck his right cheek. The prophet Isaiah foretold the scene long before: “I gave my back to those who beat me, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair. I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). That was not passively taking blows; that was actively bearing them.

Jesus had the power to wipe out all human rebellion. In the Garden of Gethsemane he told Peter plainly: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53). A Roman legion was six thousand men; twelve legions of angels — what a force that would be! But he did not ask. He had the right to take revenge, yet he chose to lay it down. As he hung on the tree, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Paul condensed the whole of this into one of Scripture’s greatest passages: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

The word “emptied himself” is kenoō in Greek, meaning to pour out, to make oneself nothing. This is exactly what the 321 vision calls selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing, not self-annihilation; selflessness is emptying ourselves so that God’s fullness can fill us. Only an empty cup can hold living water.

Brothers and sisters, if Jesus had not “turned the left cheek”, we could never have been restored to relationship with God. Salvation is not God giving up on justice; it is God causing justice and mercy to meet at the cross. He did not strike back; he reached out his hands. He did not condemn us; he died for our sins.

4. Illustration and Science: The Ninety-Second Lesson

The Harvard-trained neuroanatomist Jill Bolte Taylor, in her book My Stroke of Insight, shares a very valuable observation: when an emotion is triggered, the chemicals involved flood into the bloodstream and are then flushed out again, and the whole physiological process takes only about ninety seconds. If we are still angry after ninety seconds, it is usually not because the physical reaction hasn’t finished but because we have chosen to let that thought keep looping in our minds. The psychologist Daniel Goleman, in his 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, also used the term “amygdala hijack” for the state in which emotion seizes us in an instant and we have struck back before we’ve had time to think.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a very practical lesson: in the moment you are struck, don’t respond yet. Breathe first, pray first, and move your focus off the other person’s face and onto the face of Jesus.

The 321 vision puts it well: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When my focus is on myself, what I see is my grievance; when my focus is on others, what I see is hatred; when my focus is on my circumstances, what I see is despair. Only when my focus is on Jesus do I see the Lord who turned his left cheek for me, and only then can my heart soften.

Remember too: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. When we rely on the brain, the more we think, the angrier we get, and the more we tally things up, the more unfair it all seems; when we rely on the heart, the Holy Spirit can work in those ninety seconds. Rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled. For out of the heart flows the wellspring of life.

5. Applying 321: Let Jesus Be King, Starting in Those Three Seconds

The first of the Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. However Jesus faced humiliation, that is how I face humiliation. He did not strike back, so I will not strike back.

The first of the Two Core Values is: let Jesus be King. The most concrete moment to let Jesus be King is those three seconds — when my “self” leaps up to administer justice, I say to the Lord: Lord, this seat is yours, not mine. I step down; you step up.

This is where the fivefold change begins: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and when relationships change, ministry will bear real fruit. Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — the fivefold change begins with the mindset.

The mindset to change today is this: being struck does not mean I have failed; not striking back when I am struck is how I win.

sections.heading: 2. Defusing Conflict with Humility, Overcoming Pride
sections.html:
1. “Why Should I Have to Put Up with This?”

When we are misunderstood, hurt or wronged, the natural reaction is: “Why should I have to put up with this?”

Brothers and sisters, listen to the subject of that sentence — “I”. Why should I; I did nothing wrong; I was only doing it for everyone’s good; I’ve served for so many years. However many times “I” appears in a sentence shows how big the “self” is. This is the response of pride.

But Jesus teaches us: overcome pride with humility.

Letting go of the attitude “I’m right, I deserve respect” and choosing to respond with forgiveness and gentleness not only sets us free, but also gives the other person’s heart a chance to be moved.

Notice the words “sets us free”. Many people think forgiveness lets the other person off the hook, but in fact the first person forgiveness releases is yourself. The psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College in the United States and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science in 2001 which found that when participants recalled a grudge and nursed unforgiveness, their blood pressure, heart rate, facial muscle tension and skin conductance all rose markedly; and when, in their imagination, they chose empathy and forgiveness, these stress responses dropped significantly.

In other words, unforgiveness is a punishment you pay for yourself. You think you’ve locked the other person in prison, but in fact you’re the one bringing him his meals every day.

Proverbs said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). A gentle answer is not powerless; it is the only power that can put the fire out.

2. Coat and Cloak: Don’t Let Things Get in the Way of People

Scripture says: “If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also” (Matthew 5:40).

This was a startling thing to say at the time. The “coat” is chitōn in Greek, the tunic worn next to the skin; the “cloak” is himation, the outer robe, which the poor wore to cover themselves by day and used as a blanket at night. The law of Moses specially protected this cloak: “If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:26–27).

In other words, the cloak was expressly safeguarded by law; no one could hold on to it. And Jesus says: let him have even this.

What does that mean? It means — don’t let possessions and entitlements become stumbling blocks in relationships. I clearly have the right, I could clearly sue, I clearly have a case; but for love’s sake I can choose not to use that right.

Paul said the same thing to the church: “Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7).

Brothers and sisters, if we quarrel over face or profit, the relationship will break; if we lay down the “self” for love’s sake, we gain back real connection.

The 321 vision says: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. The order is life first, then relationships, then ministry. How many families have seen brothers stop speaking to each other for good over a plot of land, a sum of money, or a word of apology never spoken. The things stayed; the people left.

John Gottman, the marriage researcher at the University of Washington, spent many years observing how couples interact and identified the “Four Horsemen” of relationships — criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling — of which he considers “contempt” the strongest predictor of divorce. What is contempt? Contempt is pride putting on a facial expression and walking out the door: that cold laugh, that roll of the eyes, that “What would you know?”

So to save a relationship, the first thing is not to prove who’s right but to wipe the contempt off our own faces.

3. The Extra Mile: The Distance at Which Love Gains Influence

“Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.” (Matthew 5:41)

The Greek word for “compel” is angareuō. It comes from the courier conscription system of the Persian Empire and later became a legal privilege of the Roman army: a soldier could press any civilian of an occupied territory into carrying his pack for one Roman mile. A Roman mile was a thousand paces, about 1,478 metres today.

Picture the scene: a Jewish youth walking along the road, and a Roman soldier dumps dozens of kilos of equipment onto his back. How he must have hated it! But he had no choice but to carry it, and when exactly one mile was up, he would throw it down hard on the ground and walk off without a backward glance.

Jesus says instead: when you’ve finished that mile, say — I’ll walk another mile with you.

No one compels you to walk that mile. On the first mile you are a slave; on the second, a free man. The first mile is law; the second is grace. The first mile is duty; the second is love. Between the first mile and the second, sovereignty comes back into your hands: he is no longer compelling you; you are choosing to love him.

There is a man in Scripture who was “compelled” with the very same word. “As they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name, and they compelled him to go with them, that he might carry his cross” (Matthew 27:32). That “compelled” is angareuō in the original. Simon was only a traveller passing by, forced to carry the cross of a condemned man. But Mark’s Gospel records a detail: he was “the father of Alexander and Rufus” (Mark 15:21). Later, in Romans 16:13, Paul sends greetings: “Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.” Many commentators believe this is the same Rufus and his family.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The mile he was compelled to walk became the mile that brought his whole family to salvation.

Going the extra mile means laying down our own will and thinking of others. This “extra mile” is often the distance at which love gains influence and a relationship is won back.

The social psychologist Robert Cialdini, in his book Influence, points out that “reciprocity” is one of the most universal rules of behaviour in human society: when people receive kindness, they naturally feel a pressure to return it. What does that mean in relationships? It means the extra mile you walk leaves a place in the other person’s heart. Of course, we don’t go the extra mile to manipulate anyone; we go the extra mile because the Lord went countless extra miles for us. But God is often pleased to use such a mile to soften a hardened heart.

Dr Martin Luther King Jr. wrote these famous words in Strength to Love: “Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.”

4. Applying 321: The 920 Practice and Relationships Where Both Win

The 920 practice in the 321 vision fits right here. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in front of them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice: almost every one of these nine graces can only be grown amid the friction of relationships. Without people who try your patience, you can’t grow patience; without people who make you want to explode, you can’t grow gentleness; without people who make you want to hit back, you can’t grow self-control.

So the person who strikes your right cheek is not only your difficulty; he is also a field God has given you.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When I stop answering him in his own way, the cycle is broken right here with me. Breaking that cycle takes one person who is willing to stoop down first. Brothers and sisters, may we be the ones who stoop down first.

sections.heading: 3. David’s Humility: The Overcomer Who Would Not Grab Power
sections.html:
1. The One Hunted Was Not a Sinner but a Righteous Man

David’s life is a living testimony of “turning the left cheek”.

He was hunted by Saul not because he had done anything wrong, but because he was successful and praised. The women came out singing: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). From that day on, “Saul watched David” with a jealous eye (1 Samuel 18:9).

Brothers and sisters, how true to human nature this is. Sometimes we come under attack not because we did something wrong, but because we did something right. It’s like being “struck on the right cheek” — wronged, envied.

Suffering that comes from our own mistakes is somewhat easier to accept; suffering that comes from our faithfulness is especially hard to bear. David hid in the wilderness for about ten years — living in caves, feigning madness, taking refuge in enemy territory — and through those ten years he faced just one question every day: God, what on earth have I done wrong?

2. The Knife in the Cave

At last the opportunity came. Saul, pursuing David with three thousand chosen men, went into a cave to relieve himself — and David and his men were hiding in the depths of that very cave (1 Samuel 24:1–3).

His men immediately said: “Behold, the day of which Yahweh said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you’” (1 Samuel 24:4). Now the time had come!

How reasonable it sounded. The timing, the place, the mood of the men — even “God’s promise” — everything lined up. Many of life’s great falls happen not when the temptation is obvious, but when the temptation looks very spiritual.

David quietly cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. But Scripture records: “Afterward, David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt” (1 Samuel 24:5).

Notice that what he cut was only a piece of cloth, not a life. Yet even cutting a piece of cloth troubled his conscience — that is a sensitive heart. Brothers and sisters, spiritual sensitivity doesn’t wait for a great wrong before it takes alarm; it feels the sting even over the corner of a robe.

Then he said to his men: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:6).
