“Anointed” in Hebrew is mashiach — the very word “Messiah”. What David meant was: Saul’s position was given by God; removing him is God’s prerogative, not mine. He chose humility and chose to leave the judgement to God.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride, on the other hand, is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and trying to take God’s place. In that cave David held to his originally intended position.

3. God Himself Vindicated Him

David came out of the cave, called out to Saul from a distance and held up the piece of robe in his hand. And what happened? Saul wept aloud and said to David: “You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you” (1 Samuel 24:17).

A piece of robe not used to kill was more powerful than a sword.

More precious still, David didn’t hold back just once. In 1 Samuel 26 the same opportunity came again; his officer Abishai said, “Now therefore please let me strike him with the spear to the earth at one stroke, and I will not strike him the second time.” And David still said: “Don’t destroy him; for who can stretch out his hand against Yahweh’s anointed, and be guiltless?” (1 Samuel 26:8–9).

Restraint once may be good manners; restraint twice is real life.

In the end God himself vindicated David, raised him up as king and made him the most glorious king in Israel’s history. Paul says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

“Give place to God’s wrath” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “rather give way”, but literally it is “leave room for the wrath”. It means: you step back first, so that God has room to come in and work. The reason we so often don’t see God’s vindication is that we keep occupying that place ourselves.

4. The Way Up Is the Way Down

This reminds us: true authority is not won by fighting for it, but received through humility.

Jesus says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). Peter also says: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Notice those three words: “in due time”. God’s lifting up runs on God’s timetable. Waiting is the truest test of humility.

Psychology has a famous study: the “marshmallow experiment” carried out by the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Researchers placed a marshmallow in front of a child and said: if you can wait until I come back before eating it, you can have two. Follow-up studies found that the children who had been better able to wait generally showed better self-control and better ability to cope with frustration as adolescents. In recent years some scholars have also pointed out that a family’s socio-economic background and how trustworthy the child’s environment is are equally important factors — if a child learns early on that adults’ promises are often broken, of course he won’t want to wait.

Brothers and sisters, that second half is actually the more precious reminder. Whether we can wait depends on whether we trust the One who made the promise. David could wait in that cave because he knew the God who had anointed him, who never breaks his word.

So David sings in the Psalms: “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this: he will make your righteousness shine out like light, and your justice as the noon day sun. Rest in Yahweh, and wait patiently for him” (Psalm 37:5–7).

God’s way of lifting us up is not self-promotion but self-humbling. Humility is not a sign of weakness; it is the starting point from which God means to exalt you.

5. Applying 321: Spiritual Companions in 235

Through David’s ten years in the wilderness, God did not let him walk alone. God provided Jonathan for him. “Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:3). When David was at his lowest, “Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose, and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16).

This is the 235 relationship of 321: first find someone selfless and become each other’s “2” — spiritual companions; then build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, when we are misunderstood, what we need most is not a crowd who will help us curse people, but a Jonathan who strengthens our hand in God. Ask God for a Jonathan of your own, and ask him to make you a Jonathan for someone else.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
When we set today’s message back into the 321 framework, it becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he turned his left cheek, so I turn mine too. The Bible is my standard — not my emotions, not how others see me, but the Lord’s word decides how I respond. The Holy Spirit is my guide — in those ninety seconds it is the Holy Spirit who is in charge of my heart, not my hot temper.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — I no longer act as judge in my own case; let Jesus receive all the glory — whether I am praised or misunderstood, in the end all the glory goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A community full of revenge builds a human system; only a community that forgives one another and bears with one another is God’s system.

The core lesson is this: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And every picture we’ve looked at today — turning the left cheek, handing over the cloak, walking the extra mile — is one and the same thing: laying down the “self”. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is fullness without limit.

Our perspective must shift too: from the human perspective to God’s perspective — people see that I’ve lost out, God sees that I’ve become like him; from the earthly perspective to the heavenly — earth argues over who was right and who was wrong, heaven remembers who loved whom; from the temporary perspective to the eternal — the cloak is temporary, the soul is eternal; from the worldly perspective to the godly — the world says you’ve only won if you’ve won, God says you only gain by giving up.

The Path of Serving is the same road: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. Turning the left cheek looks like a single movement, but in fact it is the whole road from Spirit to Understanding to Life to Service to God.

And the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry. If our lives lack humility, our relationships will keep breaking; and if our relationships keep breaking, however big our ministry grows, it is a house built on sand.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared four practices for us. Let’s follow the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — and put them into effect one by one.

Practice 1: The Right-Cheek Practice

When someone misunderstands or criticises you, don’t rush to defend yourself; bless them first.

Information: Copy Matthew 5:39 onto a card and put it where you will see it every day.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you — who struck your “right cheek” most recently? In that moment, what was really stung in your heart: the facts, or your face?

Conviction: Say to the Lord, “You are right”, not merely “It would be better to do it this way.” Conviction means handing over sovereignty.

Implementation: This week, whenever someone points out your fault, first count silently for ninety seconds, then open your mouth and speak one word of blessing over them.

Evaluation: Before bed, ask yourself: did I replay that conversation in my head today?

Correction: If you did, turn your focus back to Jesus and look at the face that was struck for you.

Repetition: Keep at it until “bless first” becomes your natural response.

Multiplication: Teach this practice to your family and your small-group members.

Practice 2: The Left-Cheek Practice

When you are treated unfairly, choose to lay down your rights and ask God for the strength to love.

Information: Read Matthew 5:40 and 1 Corinthians 6:7.

Revelation: Ask God — what is the “cloak” I’m clutching and won’t let go of right now? A sum of money? An apology? A word of vindication?

Conviction: Acknowledge that before God, relationships matter more than things, and people matter more than tasks.

Implementation: Choose one matter you have every right to fight over but decide not to, and concretely let it go.

Evaluation: After letting it go, does my heart feel lighter, or am I still counting my losses?

Correction: If you’re still counting, count them out one by one to God, and then entrust them to him.

Repetition: Every time something similar comes up, make the same choice.

Multiplication: When someone one day asks you why you didn’t fight, tell them the Lord’s words.

Practice 3: The Extra-Mile Practice

In your relationships, give a little more, understand a little more, forgive a little more.

Information: Read Matthew 5:41, and remember those extra 1,478 metres.

Revelation: Ask God to show you one person — the one with whom you only want to finish the “first mile” and then turn away.

Conviction: Believe that the second mile is not wasted; it is the distance at which love gains influence.

Implementation: This week, do something for that person that they haven’t asked for and that you have no obligation to do.

Evaluation: As I did it, was my heart willing, or was I forcing myself?

Correction: If you were forcing yourself, first ask the Lord to renew your heart, then do it a second time.

Repetition: Let “one more mile” become a habit of your daily living, not an occasional good deed.

Multiplication: Take a brother or sister with you and walk that second mile together.

Practice 4: Turn Your Eyes to Jesus

Meditate on his humility and forgiveness on the cross, and ask that his heart would become your heart.

Information: Read Philippians 2:5–8, Luke 23:34 and 1 Peter 2:23.

Revelation: In stillness, look at that scene — as he was being nailed to the cross, whom did he pray for?

Conviction: Acknowledge that none of my grievances comes to even a ten-thousandth of what he suffered.

Implementation: Every morning, spend three minutes bringing before the Lord the person most likely to sting you that day.

Evaluation: This week, has my focus been more on Jesus, or on myself, on others, on my circumstances?

Correction: Turn your focus back — however many times a day you need to, it’s never too many.

Repetition: Let “turning my eyes to Jesus” become the first thing I do every time I’m hurt.

Multiplication: Share your experience, so that others may be comforted too.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Humility is not weakness but strength under restraint; it is not indulgence but choosing to respond in the way of love.

These two sentences matter a great deal, and we need to distinguish them clearly.

Strength under restraint means I have power in my hands, but I choose not to use it. Not striking back when you have no power is called helplessness; not striking back when you do have the power — that is humility. Jesus had twelve legions of angels at his command; that is why his not striking back carries weight.

Choosing the way of love means that humility does not equal doing nothing. In the face of real harm, the boundaries that should be set must still be set, the police who should be called must still be called, and those who need protecting must still be protected. The Lord Jesus has never told anyone who is being abused to stay in danger. Humility deals with the revenge in my own heart; it does not cancel out practical wisdom in the real world.

When you are willing to turn the left cheek, you overcome not only your enemy but also yourself.

And to be honest, the hardest one to overcome has never been the person who struck you; it is the “I” inside you that refuses to let go.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, what we have seen today is a different kind of King.

Jesus chose to overcome pride with humility. He did not passively take the blows; he actively loved. One who passively takes blows is a victim; one who actively loves is an overcomer. The same lowly posture — but with a different heart inside it, the outcome is completely different.

His “turning the left cheek” is the starting point of salvation; his “going the extra mile” is the road of revival.

From heaven to the manger was one mile; from the manger to the cross, another mile; from the cross to the door of your heart and mine, yet another mile. All the way he came, and not a single step of it was compelled.

When we follow his heart, we will discover that humility is not losing but gaining; not falling back but being lifted up by God.

So this morning I want to extend an invitation to you. Picture a face in your heart: the person who misunderstood you, the person who hurt you, the person who still hasn’t apologised to you to this day. Then say to the Lord: Lord, I hand the right to judge back to you. You are King; you are in charge of this. I am willing to turn the left cheek; I am willing to walk the extra mile.

Let us dissolve hatred and rebuild relationships through humility, overcome in love, and be lifted up in humility.

May Jesus be King in our families, King in our church, King in every moment when we are offended. May all the glory go to him.

keyVerses: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also. If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also. Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two. Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.” (Matthew 5:38–42)
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. (Matthew 23:12)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, I will no longer answer pride with pride; I will overcome the evil of the world with your humility.
When someone strikes my right cheek, give me a heart of love and patience, so that I put forgiveness in place of revenge and gentleness in place of hardness.
May your humility become my glory, so that I find freedom in letting go and victory in obedience.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. We were the ones who struck your right cheek; your left cheek you turned to us of your own accord. Had you not refused to strike back, we could not stand before you today.

Lord, forgive us — forgive us for talking about humility with our lips while keeping accounts in our hearts; forgive us for the sneers we never voiced, the counter-attacks wrapped up in spiritual language, the grievances we replay again and again.
Holy Spirit, work within us. When we are misunderstood, hold back our tongues; when we are wronged, hold up our hearts; when we have the power to take revenge, remind us that the seat belongs to you.
Give us the heart of David, so that we would rather wait for your timing than snatch our own justice; give us the heart of Christ, so that we can bless those who strike us.
May our families be healed through humility, may our church be united through humility, and may Satan find no breach among us.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 5:39 says: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” Share: what was the most recent experience that made you feel “struck on the right cheek”? What was the first reaction that rose in your heart at the time? If you could do it again, what would you do?

1 Samuel 24:6 says: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed.” Share: is there something right now that you are holding in your hand, ready to “stretch out your hand” at any moment? Are you willing to hand it over to God? What is the “second mile” you will walk this week?
l080.title: Turn the Other Cheek, Go the Extra Mile
l080.subtitle: Humility Is the Antidote to Pride (Part 3)
l080.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: He Plainly “Could” — Yet He Chose “Not To”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let’s go back first to one particular night. It is late, after the Passover meal, in the Garden of Gethsemane at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and torchlight is flickering between the olive trees. Judas arrives leading a band of men — officers from the chief priests, soldiers carrying swords and clubs. The blood rushes to Simon Peter’s head; he draws his sword and with one stroke cuts off the right ear of the high priest’s servant. In that moment Peter thinks he is protecting his Lord.

But Jesus stops him. And he says words no one could ever forget: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the weight of that sentence. In the Roman army a “legion” numbered roughly five to six thousand men. Twelve legions is more than seventy thousand of heaven’s host. On the very night he was bound, led away and spat upon, he held in his hand the authority to summon seventy thousand angels. It was not that he lacked the power; he had the power and did not use it. It was not that it was taken from him; he laid it down himself.

That is what the Bible calls humility.

The world often equates humility with weakness. The nineteenth-century philosopher Nietzsche, in his writings, called the humility, compassion and submission that Christianity teaches a “slave morality” — chains the weak use to bind the strong. To this day many people carry the same thought hidden in their hearts: fight whenever you can, because if you don’t fight you lose; win whenever you can, because giving way means you’re useless.

But brothers and sisters, true humility has never been powerlessness. It is strength under restraint — the love that willingly lays down its rights.

Have you ever watched a father six foot three tall, with powerful arms, holding a baby only seven days old? His hands tremble, every movement slows right down, he is careful even about how he breathes. His strength hasn’t diminished one bit, yet he gathers all of it in, simply so as not to hurt that tiny life in his arms. That isn’t weakness; it is restraint within love. True strength is never measured by how hard it can explode, but by how steadily it can be held.

That is what our Lord is like. He laid down his place in the glory of heaven and entered into human weakness; he laid down the right to be served and became a servant who serves others. His humility was not a passive retreat but an active obedience.

In my pastoral work I often meet a certain kind of brother. At work he is highly capable — his judgement is sound, his decisions quick, his staff respect him. But at home he treats his wife and children in exactly the same way: he demands, he corrects, he directs. One day, with red eyes, he said to me, “Pastor, out there I get everything right. Why is it that at home I get everything wrong?”

Brothers and sisters, his problem wasn’t ability; it was position. He had carried the position of “manager” into the home of a “husband”. He was sitting in a seat that wasn’t his, using rights he shouldn’t have used, and so every relationship had slipped out of place.

And these are exactly the three things today’s lesson wants to tell us. First, humility is not low self-esteem; it is making God our focus. Second, humility is laying down our rights and submitting to the will of God. Third, humility is returning to the place God has given us — that is, returning to our originally intended position.

In the 321 vision we say: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Today’s lesson sets out to open that sentence up, word by word.

May the Holy Spirit himself be our guide this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Joy Sent from Prison
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of this passage in Philippians 2, we first need to know the circumstances in which Paul wrote it.

The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. In the view of most evangelical scholars, the letter was written between AD 61 and 62, very probably in Rome. Paul was then a prisoner awaiting Caesar’s judgement. He says so plainly in the letter itself: he is “in chains”. He did not know whether tomorrow would bring life or death; he said that to live is Christ and to die is gain.

A man in chains wrote a letter brimming with joy. The word “joy” appears more than a dozen times in this letter. Brothers and sisters, this is the mystery of the Christian faith: true freedom lies not in our circumstances but within.

What kind of city was Philippi? Philippi lay in the province of Macedonia and was a Roman colony (colonia). In 42 BC, Antony and Octavian defeated the forces of Caesar’s assassins on the plain of Philippi, and afterwards settled discharged veterans there. The city enjoyed the “Italian right”, and its inhabitants prided themselves on their Roman citizenship. It was a city that cared intensely about “status” and “standing”. Roman society was a sharply tiered ladder — senators, equestrians, commoners, freedmen, slaves — layer upon layer, each with its own honour and shame. In a city like that, the pursuit of a whole lifetime was to climb one more rung.

The church at Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe. Acts 16 records how Paul met Lydia there, the seller of purple cloth, and how he and Silas were thrown into prison there, sang hymns of praise to God at midnight, the earth shook violently, and the jailer and his whole household came to faith. This church had the closest relationship with Paul of all, and time and again supplied him when he was in need.

Yet even such a good church had its troubles. We can tell from the letter that discord had arisen in the church. In 4:2 Paul names two sisters in particular, Euodia and Syntyche, urging them to be of one mind in the Lord. In a spiritual church, the commonest breach is not heresy but “contending” — contending over who is right, contending over face, contending over who matters more.

So at the very start of chapter 2 Paul urges them: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4)

Brothers and sisters, notice how Paul resolves the dispute. He doesn’t convene an arbitration hearing, doesn’t analyse who is right and who is wrong, doesn’t draw up new regulations. He does something far more fundamental — he lifts up Jesus Christ and says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

The verses that follow, 2:6–11, are regarded by many scholars as a hymn of the early church, known as the “Christ Hymn”. It falls into two halves: the first half is a “descent”, the second an “ascent”.

The staircase down has seven steps: he existed in the form of God; he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped; he emptied himself; he took the form of a servant; he was made in the likeness of men; he humbled himself and became obedient; he was obedient to the point of death, the death of the cross. Step by step he goes down, all the way to the bottom — not merely death, but death on a cross. In Roman society the cross was the punishment reserved for slaves and rebels, the most shameful of deaths; by law a Roman citizen could not be subjected to it. He went to the furthest end of glory’s opposite.

Then the text says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The one who descended to the lowest place was raised by God to the highest. The first word of this verse is “therefore” — one of the most important “therefores” in the whole Bible. Humility is not the end of the story; exaltation is. But the only road to exaltation is the road down.

This is where the key passage of our lesson stands. When we read today about “laying down rights and returning to our originally intended position”, we are not reading a piece of moral exhortation; we are reading of a road our Lord has already walked himself.

sections.heading: 1. Humility Is Not Low Self-Esteem, but Making God Our Focus
sections.html:
Many people misunderstand humility. They think humility means thinking little of yourself, putting yourself down; they think humility is that polite wave of the hand in front of others: “Oh no, not me, I’m hopeless, I can’t do anything.”

Brothers and sisters, that isn’t really humility. It is just another expression of being self-centred.

Have you noticed that someone who keeps saying “I can’t” is actually talking round and round one single word — and that word is “I”? The proud person says, “I’m the best”; the person with low self-esteem says, “I’m the worst.” What they say is opposite, but the subject of the sentence is exactly the same. Pride lifts the self too high; low self-esteem pushes the self too low; but both of them have their eyes fixed hard on themselves.

So true humility is not seeing yourself as low; it is not looking at yourself at all.

The Standard of Scripture: Think Soberly

Paul puts it with great precision: “For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3)

In the Greek this verse is a beautiful piece of wordplay. Paul uses four verbs from the same root in a row: do not “think too highly” (hyperphronein), but “think soberly” (sōphronein). This word sōphronein, “to think reasonably”, originally means “to be clear-headed, sound-minded, not confused”. In other words, the Bible’s definition of humility is not “underestimating” but “being sober”.

A truly humble person won’t say, “I can’t do anything,” because that isn’t true; nor will he say, “I can do everything,” because that is even less true. He will say, “This is a gift God has given me, and I will use it faithfully; that one isn’t mine, and I will learn to appreciate it in others.” He is sober, because he measures himself by what “God has apportioned to each” — the measuring rod isn’t in his hand; it’s in God’s.

The New Testament word for “humility” is tapeinophrosynē, literally “lowly-mindedness”. Interestingly, in the Greek culture of the day the word originally carried a negative sense: it described the base, contemptible mentality of a slave. It was the Christian faith that turned the word upside down, transforming it from a mark of shame into a mark of glory. How could it be turned around? Because the Son of God himself walked this road.

The Old Testament word for “humble” is anav. Scripture says, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth stopping to think about. Who was Moses? He was the man who dared to stand before Pharaoh of Egypt and say, “Let my people go”; the man who stretched out the staff in his hand over the Red Sea and the waters parted; the man who spent forty days and nights on Mount Sinai without food or drink, speaking with God face to face. And the Bible says that the humblest man on all the earth was him.

Clearly, humility is in no way a lack of strength. Humility is placing your strength in God’s hands, to be deployed as he directs.

The Root of Humility: the Fear of God

The focus of humility is not how strong or weak “I” am, but how great God is. When we truly know God’s glory and sovereignty, we naturally know our own place.

The prophet Isaiah is the finest example. In the year that King Uzziah died, he saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne, the train of his robe filling the temple, and the seraphim calling to one another, “Holy, holy, holy.” In that moment Isaiah cried out: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5)

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Isaiah was not humbled because people had humiliated him; he was humbled because he saw God.

So the root of humility is a heart that fears God. Job argued with God for more than thirty chapters and said many reasonable things; until God spoke to him out of the whirlwind and asked him where he was when God laid the foundations of the earth. Then Job put his hand over his mouth and said that he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye saw him; therefore he abhorred himself and repented in dust and ashes.

Seeing God, we see ourselves clearly. That is the shortest road to humility.

Humility is admitting one thing: I am not Lord; he is.

A Mirror and a Window

I often use this picture: low self-esteem and pride are both mirrors; humility is a window.

There are two kinds of mirror. One is the funfair mirror that makes you look tall and huge — that is pride. The other is the distorting mirror that makes you look squat and small — that is low self-esteem. But whichever mirror it is, the only person you ever see in it is yourself.

Humility isn’t swapping one mirror for another; humility is replacing the mirror with a window. A window doesn’t reflect you; a window lets you see the sky outside and lets the light come in. A humble person has eyes for God, for others, for needs, for the calling — he is simply no longer filled up with himself.

June Price Tangney, professor of psychology at George Mason University in the United States, in a study published in 2000 in the “Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology”, pointed out that the core of humility is not self-deprecation but several related qualities: an accurate assessment of one’s own abilities and limitations, openness to new ideas, the ability to see oneself as just one part of a much larger world, and a “relatively low self-focus” — in other words, a kind of “forgetting of the self”.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what the Bible says. On this point the best psychology in the world has walked right up to the Bible’s front door.

So why do people overestimate themselves? In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University published a famous series of experiments in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology”. They found that in tests of logical reasoning, grammar and sense of humour, the people who performed worst rated their own performance far above their actual scores. The phenomenon came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect”. The reason is simple: to know that you aren’t good at something, you need precisely the ability you lack.

So the more ignorant a person is, the more confident; the more knowledgeable, the more humble. C. S. Lewis, in “Mere Christianity”, called pride “the great sin”, and pointed out a piercing truth: almost everyone dislikes pride in others, yet hardly anyone sees it in themselves.

Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point

In the 321 vision we keep reminding ourselves of one sentence: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life; the mark of the new self is selflessness. And selflessness is not destroying yourself, not becoming a person without opinions, without worth, without a voice. Selflessness is moving aside the “self” that stands in front of the light, so that the boundlessness of Christ can flow out from within us. So selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul describes this experience most clearly of all: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to ask you to check one thing. When you say, “I can’t,” are you fearing God, or protecting yourself? When you say, “I can,” are you trusting God, or proving yourself?

Humility isn’t making “me” small; it is seeing God as great.

sections.heading: 2. Humility Is Laying Down Our Rights and Submitting to God’s Will
sections.html:
Now we come to the heart of this lesson.

Philippians 2:6–8 records Jesus’ path of humility: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

This passage has three key words worth opening up one by one.

The first word is “form”, in the Greek morphē. It refers not to outward appearance but to the form in which an inner, real essence shows itself. So “existing in the form of God” means: he was God from the beginning — not merely like God.

The second word is “grasped”, in the Greek harpagmos. Its verb means “to seize, to snatch, to clutch tightly”. Paul says he did not consider equality with God “a thing to be grasped”. That is: his equality with God was his already, not something he had snatched, so he had no need to cling to it for dear life. Brothers and sisters, a very deep spiritual principle is hidden here — the more truly someone possesses something, the less they need to clutch it; the more insecure someone is, the tighter they hold on.

The third word is “emptied”, in the Greek kenoō, meaning “to pour out, to empty”. He did not pour away his divinity; what he emptied out were his rights. He took that brimming cup of glory and poured it out with his own hands.

So Jesus’ humility was an active laying down of rights. His rights were not stripped from him; he was “willing to lay them down”.

The lesson lists four rights that he laid down. Let’s look at them one at a time.

First, He Laid Down the Right to Be God

He shared the same glory and honour as God the Father, yet he chose to become a man and to enter the limitations of a creature.

In his prayer just before he went into the Garden of Gethsemane he said to the Father, “Now, Father, glorify me with your own self with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” (John 17:5) “Before the world existed” — he is the one who comes before time itself. Yet this Lord who created time entered time; this Lord who upholds all things became a baby who had to learn to walk; this all-knowing Lord, Scripture says, grew in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and people.

Paul sums it up in one sentence: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

Brothers and sisters, it is like a great linguist who, in order to help a child who can’t yet talk understand his love, gladly lays aside his entire vocabulary and uses only the few syllables the child can grasp, saying them over and over again. Love is always willing to come down to the other’s height.

Second, He Laid Down the Right to Receive Glory

He was worthy of worship as King of kings, yet he was misunderstood, humiliated and crucified.

Isaiah prophesied it more than seven hundred years beforehand: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.” (Isaiah 53:3)

He worked so many miracles — he fed five thousand with five loaves and two fish, he raised Lazarus from the dead; yet the people of his home town said, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” The religious leaders said he cast out demons by the prince of demons. He deserved worship, and received ridicule; he deserved a crown, and received thorns.

Brothers and sisters, what we find hardest to let go of is often not money but “being affirmed”. We can do a great deal for the Lord, yet find it very hard to bear when no one knows what we’ve done. Jesus could bear it.

Third, He Laid Down the Right Over Life and Death

He had the power not to die, yet he willingly obeyed the Father’s will and died on the cross.

This isn’t our inference; he said it himself: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.” (John 10:18)

So the cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a triumph of the Roman authorities or the religious powers. He walked up to the cross himself. In the Garden of Gethsemane, his sweat falling to the ground like great drops of blood, he prayed: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39)

Brothers and sisters, notice that turning word — “nevertheless”. Perhaps the most powerful word in the whole Bible is that “nevertheless”. Before it are real emotions, a real struggle, a real burden; after it, complete obedience. Humility isn’t the absence of feeling; humility is feeling it and still obeying.

Fourth, He Laid Down the Right to Be Respected

He was despised, spat upon and crowned with thorns, and still he did not argue back or strike back.

Peter saw that scene with his own eyes, and later he wrote: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)

Isaiah’s prophecy is just as exact: “As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth.” (Isaiah 53:7)

Brothers and sisters, he didn’t answer back — not because he had nothing to say. Had he chosen to argue, no one could have out-argued him; had he chosen to judge, no one could have stood. He didn’t answer back because he had committed himself to the one who judges righteously.

This is the secret of humility: not “I can’t”, but “I entrust”.

This Is Humility: Not Losing, but Choosing to Lay Down

So humility is not loss but a choice to lay down; it is not weakness but a willing lowering of oneself in order to obey God. The power of humility comes from being willing to lay down the power of “I can” and let God reign.

Paul learned this lesson. In 1 Corinthians 9 he sets out very clearly that those who preach the gospel have a legitimate right to live by the gospel; yet he says, “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 9:12) He had the right, he knew he had the right, and he chose not to use it. Why? For the sake of the gospel, for the sake of people.

Brothers and sisters, let’s think about this: what do we mean by “strength under restraint”?

A fire hose under high pressure can knock a grown man off his feet. Yet the focus of a firefighter’s training is never how to make the water blast harder, but how to grip it, how to open and close it, how to aim it. A nuclear power station is the same: what really determines safety is not how much energy the fuel rods can release, but whether the control rods can be inserted in time. A system’s maturity lies not in its maximum output but in its brakes.

People are the same. A person’s true maturity isn’t measured by how far he can go, but by whether he can stop when it is time to stop.

In his 2001 book “Good to Great”, the management scholar Jim Collins led a research team that sifted through 1,435 large American companies and identified eleven that had truly leapt from good to great and then outperformed the market for fifteen years. They had not originally intended to study leaders at all, but the data kept pointing to the same conclusion. The leaders of these great companies — Collins called them “Level 5 leaders” — shared one feature: two apparently contradictory things held together — extreme personal humility combined with intense professional will. They gave the credit to others and to good fortune, and took the responsibility on themselves.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s management research has discovered it: the highest positions are kept for the lowliest posture.

In the 321 vision we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite line of attack is to stir up the “I can”, “I deserve it”, “why him and not me” within us. The moment we reach out to grab our rights, we fall into his trap. But when, like our Lord, we let go, Satan has nothing to take hold of.

For pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Is Returning to the Place God Has Given Us — Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
If “laying down our rights” is the action of humility, then “returning to our originally intended position” is its substance.

God has appointed every person a place. God is God, and man is man; the Father is the Father, and the Son is the Son; a leader is a leader, and a servant is a servant. From its very first chapter the whole Bible speaks of an ordered universe: light has its place, the waters have their place, sun, moon and stars each keep their seasons, birds and beasts each come “after their kind”. God says “after their kind” again and again. Order is not a restriction; order is grace.

“Originally intended position” is a biblical idea

“Originally intended position” is not a phrase we invented; the idea comes from the Bible itself. Describing the fallen angels, Jude writes: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6) Where the WEB says “first domain”, the Chinese Union Version uses the very word we render “originally intended position”.

Brothers and sisters, look closely at why the angels fell. Scripture doesn’t say it was because they committed adultery, or stole, or murdered. Scripture says they “didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place”.

So the most primitive shape of sin is leaving one’s place.

In Isaiah 14 the prophet uses the arrogance of the king of Babylon to point to a deeper fall behind it: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Five times “I will”, each one higher than the last. The final “I will” shows his hand — “I will make myself like the Most High!”

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? This is Philippians 2 played in reverse. Jesus “was” equal with God, yet did not grasp at it; this one “was not” equal with God, yet tried to seize it. One plainly had it and laid it down; the other plainly did not have it and tried to snatch it. That is the starkest contrast between humility and pride.

And Satan paved this same road into the Garden of Eden. He said one sentence to Eve, and that sentence still rings in our ears today: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

“Like God” — these two words are where every human tragedy begins. Man was not content to be man; he wanted to be God. Man was not content to be loved; he wanted to be in control. From that day on, man left his originally intended position.

So pride is “stepping out of position” — wanting to be God, wanting control, wanting to be above others. Humility is “stepping back into position” — acknowledging that God is Lord, and that I am only his servant, his vessel, his child.

Scripture says it with great economy: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) The next step after leaving your position is always a fall.

The Lord Himself Returned to the Servant’s Place

Though Jesus had the standing of God, he was willing to return to the place of a “servant”.

John 13 records that evening. Notice the order of the text — this order matters enormously: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:3–5)

Brothers and sisters, it was “knowing that all things were in his hands” that he then knelt down to wash feet.

In those days washing feet was work done by the lowest slave in the household. Rabbinic tradition even ruled that a Jewish slave could be exempted from washing feet; that task was left to Gentile slaves. That night the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest, and not one of them would pick up the basin. In the end, the one who picked up the basin was the Lord.

When he had finished, he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:14–15)

Brothers and sisters, remember this principle: only when a person is sure of who he is can he let go of his posture.

It was precisely because he knew who he was, where he came from and where he was going that he could pick up that towel. Turn it around: why do we so often find it impossible to let go? Because we aren’t sure. Unsure of our worth in God’s eyes, we have no choice but to fight for position before people; unsure that we are loved, we have no choice but to use our rights to prove we still matter.

So the deepest humility grows out of the deepest security; and the deepest security grows out of knowing God’s love.

When Each Keeps Their Place, the Glory Shows

The Lord reminds us that this principle must land in every real relationship.

In the family, a husband must not use his authority to press others down. The command Scripture gives husbands is not “keep your wife in line”, but “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25). The place of the head is not a place for pressing down; it is a place for giving yourself up.

A wife need not fight for control. This is not belittling her; it is a matter of place. The whole passage of household teaching rests on one prior sentence: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) Submission is not one-sided oppression; it is reverence flowing both ways.

A leader seeks not status but service. The Lord could not have put it more decisively: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:26–28)

It is the same in the church. Speaking of the members of the body, Paul says: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18) The eye cannot replace the hand, and the foot need not envy the eye. A body is healthy not because every member is the same, but because every member is in its place.

Brothers and sisters, let me give you two pictures to help us remember.

The first picture is an arched bridge. A stone arch bridge has no nails and no steel; it stands because each stone passes its load to the stone beside it. The bridge holds not because one stone is especially strong, but because every stone keeps its place. Let a single stone shift outward by an inch, and the whole arch comes down.

The second picture is the Dead Sea. In Israel the Jordan River flows from north to south and first runs into the Sea of Galilee. The Sea of Galilee has an inlet and an outlet, so its water is living: there are fish in it and fishing villages on its shores — it was there that the Lord called his disciples. The same river flows on south and empties into the Dead Sea. The surface of the Dead Sea lies about 430 metres below sea level, the lowest point on dry land on earth; but the Dead Sea has only an inlet and no outlet. Its water can only evaporate, so the salt grows ever more concentrated, nearly ten times as salty as ordinary seawater. Fish cannot live there, and nothing green will grow.

Brothers and sisters, the Dead Sea isn’t dead because it receives too little; it is dead because it only takes in and never gives out.

A person is just the same. A life that will only receive and never give up, that wants only its rights and will never pay out, will never be humble however low it sits — it will only grow salty and bitter. True lowliness is not the lowliness of the Dead Sea but the lowliness of the Sea of Galilee — low enough to receive the water from upstream, and low enough to be willing to hand it on downstream.

Humility is letting God return to the place that is his, and letting me return to the place that is mine.

In the 321 vision we put it even more plainly: let man be man and let God be God. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. When each of us acts according to our originally intended position, God’s order and glory are revealed.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is really the very heart of the 321 vision. Let’s set it out clearly.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The key passage of this lesson is all three foundations playing together. Jesus is my role model — he said, “I have given you an example”; humility is not a theory but a figure walking ahead of us. The Bible is my standard — our definition of humility doesn’t come from the world; it comes from Romans 12:3 and Philippians 2:6–8. The Holy Spirit is my guide — because laying down our rights is something we cannot keep up for a single day in our own strength: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, another way of saying “return to our originally intended position” is “let Jesus be King”. If I sit on the throne, he can only stand to one side; if I give up the throne, he reigns as King. And when he reigns, the glory naturally goes to him — “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9), and this passage ends (2:11) with “to the glory of God the Father”. The destination of the whole Christ Hymn is not Jesus’ exaltation but the glory of God the Father.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

An ordered system is made up of people who have returned to their originally intended position. Let one person step out of position and the system begins to tilt; let every person step back into position and the system stands firm. God’s system is held together not by organisational structure but by humility.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Eve reaching out to pick the fruit — that is the self-centred life. The king of Babylon with his five “I will”s — that is the self-centred life. The disciples arguing at the Last Supper about who was the greatest — that too is the self-centred life.

The mark of the new self is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

So we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan attacks with pride. If we respond with pride, pride provokes pride and both sides lose; if we respond with humility, humility draws out humility and both sides win.

The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective

The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Today’s lesson sets out to change one mindset — to exchange the old mindset that “humility equals weakness, equals being taken advantage of” for the new mindset that “humility is strength under restraint; it is returning to our originally intended position.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

So the order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If someone has not stepped back into position in his relationship with God, he will certainly step out of position in his relationship with others.

This is also a shift of perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s — man says that to let go is to lose; God says that to let go is to be lifted up. From the earthly to the heavenly — earthly positions are limited; heavenly rewards are limitless. From the temporary to the eternal — being misunderstood is only temporary; the Lord’s praise is eternal. From the worldly to the godly — the world’s ladder climbs upward; the ladder of God’s kingdom goes down.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

What is the 920 practice? Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice the last of the nine graces: self-control. What is self-control? It is strength gathered in — exactly what this lesson calls “plainly able, yet choosing not to”. Humility is not an inborn temperament; it is a fruit the Spirit bears.

What are 235 relationships? Becoming a “2” with a selfless person — that is a spiritual companion; establishing a “3” — that is spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” — that is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, notice this: all three kinds of relationship require humility. A self-centred person cannot find a true companion, because he wants allies, not fellow travellers. A self-centred person cannot be a spiritual parent, because what he wants is followers, not children. A self-centred person cannot build a team, because a team needs someone willing not to be the brightest star.

So humility isn’t just one lesson within 321; humility is the key to whether 321 can ever touch the ground.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson sets out four practices for us. We are going to take these four deeper through the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they don’t stop at being moved but genuinely walk into our daily living.

Practice 1: Lay Down the Right to Control

When things don’t go your way, practise not manipulating, and let God be Lord.

Information: first put the truth into your head. Memorise John 10:18 and Matthew 26:39. The Lord had the power to lay his life down and the power to take it again; the Lord said, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light so you can see the one thing you most often reach out to control — is it your child’s grades? Your spouse’s routine? A co-worker’s methods? Your own medical report? Write that thing down by name.

Conviction: admit before God that control is not love; control is distrust. Place that thing in God’s hands and say to him: the sovereignty over this belongs to you.

Implementation: set yourself a concrete “hands off” exercise this week. For example: this week you ask about your child’s homework only once and don’t follow up a second time; when a co-worker does things differently from you, as long as it doesn’t go against the truth, let him try it his own way once.

Evaluation: every evening ask yourself two questions — How many times did I reach out and grab today? How many times did I pray today?

Correction: when you find you’ve reached out again, don’t condemn yourself; step straight back into position. Spiritual maturity isn’t never falling again; it is getting back into position faster and faster after each fall.

Repetition: doing it once isn’t practice; doing it again and again is. Take forty days as one cycle and keep a record throughout.

Multiplication: share your experience with your “2”, and invite a brother or sister to walk these forty days with you.

Practice 2: Respect Other People’s Roles

At home, in church or at work, learn to respect the authority and order God has established.

Information: read Ephesians 5:21 and 1 Corinthians 12:18. Submitting to one another flows from the fear of Christ; the arrangement of the members is set by God, just as he desired.

Revelation: ask God to show you the person in a position over you that you least submit to at present. Not the person you dislike most, but the one you least submit to — the one you secretly think “has no business being there”.

Conviction: admit one thing — what you’re refusing to submit to isn’t really that person; it is God’s arrangement in putting him there.

Implementation: pray for that person for seven days this week, and find one opportunity to affirm to his face something he has done well.

Evaluation: when you said those words of affirmation, did you feel light inside, or awkward? The awkward place is exactly where God wants to work.

Correction: if you find you have talked about him behind his back, confess it to God, and stop.

Repetition: extend this exercise to a second person, then a third.

Multiplication: in your small group, lead the way in building a culture of “no judging behind backs”, so that humility becomes the very air the team breathes.

Practice 3: Serve Without Seeking a Return

Deliberately do some unseen acts of service, and train a heart that is “willing to lay down”.

Information: the Lord said, “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

Revelation: ask God to show you how much of what you do is done in order to be seen.

Conviction: believe one thing — the God who sees in secret is far more dependable than the people who applaud in public.

Implementation: this week, do three “unseen acts of service”. Arrive early at the meeting place to set out chairs; quietly clean up the kitchenette; give to or pray for a brother or sister without their knowing. When you’ve done them, tell no one.

Evaluation: when you keep quiet about it, is there a little itch inside you? That little itch is the “self” still there.

Correction: whenever that itch appears, turn it into a prayer: Lord, this was done for you.

Repetition: make “unseen service” a fixed weekly practice, with weight and frequency, like exercise.

Multiplication: when your children or your spiritual children ask you why you do it, tell them the story of the Lord washing feet.

Practice 4: Give Thanks Continually

Thank God for making you his servant, and let humility become a glory.

Information: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:18)

Revelation: the opposite of pride is not only humility but also gratitude. For of all I have, there is nothing I did not receive. Ask God to show you which things you have “received” that you’ve been treating as “earned”.

Conviction: truly believe that “I am his servant” is an honour, not a demotion. To be used by the King of kings is itself grace.

Implementation: every night before you sleep, write down three things you’re thankful for, specific down to the person, the event and the time. In 2003 the American psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published a study in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology”: participants assigned to record things they were grateful for each week, compared with those who recorded hassles or neutral events, rated their lives as a whole more positively, were more optimistic about the coming week, and reported fewer physical complaints.

Evaluation: after a week, read back through and see how many of your three things are about “things”, how many about “people” and how many about “God”.

Correction: if they are all about things, lift your gaze higher.

Repetition: forty days in a row, without a break.

Multiplication: at your family altar, lead the whole family in counting your blessings together, so that gratitude becomes the family culture.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, before we come to the close, please keep this reminder from the lesson in your heart:

Humility is not pressing yourself down; it is letting God be lifted up.

When you lay down the rights you think “I’m owed”, God himself prepares a greater glory for you.

This isn’t a bargain; it is God’s character. Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6). Notice the words “in due time” — the timetable for being lifted up is in his hands, not ours. Our part is to go low; his part is to lift up. Try to rush the timing, and you’ve stepped out of position again.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s gather this lesson up into three sentences.

Humility is not loss but return; not powerlessness but surrender; not being trampled on but being lifted up by God.

Jesus laid down his rights in heaven and gained the glory of all the earth. In the same way, when we are willing to lay down, God himself will raise us up and give us honour in his kingdom — for whoever humbles himself will be exalted. The Lord himself said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

So this morning I want to issue three calls to you.

The first call: turn from the mirror to the window. Stop spending your strength proving how good you are, and stop spending it proving how bad you are. Take your eyes off yourself and fix them on Jesus. Jesus is the focal point — not yourself, not other people, not your circumstances.

The second call: loosen that clenched hand. This morning the Holy Spirit may already have placed something on your heart — a position, an honour, a bit of justice you mean to win back, a person you are holding on to tightly. In your heart, open your hand and say to the Lord: Lord, this is yours, not mine.

The third call: return to your originally intended position. If you are a husband, return to the place of giving yourself up; if you are a wife, return to the place of mutual submission; if you are a parent, return to the place of shepherding; if you are a son or daughter, return to the place of honouring; if you are a leader, return to the place of serving; if you are a co-worker, return to the place of working alongside. And above every one of these places, you and I share just one originally intended position — we are servants, and he is Lord.

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

When we return to our originally intended position, God returns to his throne; and when God is on his throne, our homes, our churches and our workplaces will be filled with his glory, inch by inch.

May we live a life of humility all our days, just as he did — with the heart of a servant, glorifying the Father in heaven.

keyVerses: Philippians 2:5–8: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

Romans 12:3: “For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.”
John 13:15: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”
practices: Lay down the right to control
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that we have misunderstood humility all along. We thought humility meant being taken advantage of; we thought letting go meant losing; we thought only what we fought for and won was truly ours. Please forgive us.

Lord, we have seen you. You plainly could, yet you chose not to; you held the authority over twelve legions of angels, yet you willingly let yourself be bound; you knew that all things were in your hands, yet you knelt down to wash your disciples’ feet. Lord, before such a one as you we have nothing left to say; we can only worship.

Lord, I want to learn your ways — to lay down my own rights and return to the originally intended position you have set for me. No longer insisting on my own will, no longer fighting for control, but wanting only to obey your will.

Lord, by the power of the Holy Spirit, bear in us the fruit of self-control; give us wisdom when it is time to speak and rest when it is time to keep silent; make us faithful when it is time to reach out and at peace when it is time to let go.
Lord, be Lord in my life and receive the glory. May I live a life of humility all my days, just as you did — with the heart of a servant, glorifying the Father in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Philippians 2:6–8: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” Jesus laid down four rights: the right to be God, the right to receive glory, the right over life and death, and the right to be respected. Of these four, which is hardest for you to lay down right now? Name the specific situation, and ask the group to pray for you.

Jude 6: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” In your present relationships at home, at church or at work, is there a position where you have “stepped out of place”, or a position where you have been “absent”? What one concrete step will you take this week to return to your originally intended position?

l081.subtitle: Humility Is Not Weakness; It Is Strength Under Control

sections.heading: Introduction: The Lord of the Universe, Asleep in a Manger
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Before we open the Bible, let’s first grow quiet together and picture a scene in our hearts.

It is an utterly ordinary night. Outside the town of Bethlehem, in a borrowed shelter for animals, a baby is wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough. The inn has kept no room for him; this world’s first response to him is “no room”. And yet this baby lying in the manger is the one through whom all things were made, the King whom angels worship day and night without ceasing. The Lord of the universe has shrunk himself to the size of a baby.

Brothers and sisters, this is not just a heart-warming Christmas story. It is the greatest descent in the universe, and the deepest humility in all of history.

The lesson we enter today is titled “Laying Down the Right to Be God”, the first lesson in the series “Jesus’ Role Model”. The first of the Three Foundations of the 321 vision is “Jesus is my role model”. We often say we want to imitate Jesus, but to imitate him we must first see one thing clearly: what exactly did he lay down?

Astronomers tell us that the observable universe is roughly ninety-three billion light years across, while the earth we stand on is only a little over twelve thousand seven hundred kilometres in diameter. Set the earth in such a universe and it doesn’t even count as a speck of dust. And yet, brothers and sisters, the distance between man and God is immeasurably greater than the distance between man and the universe. For that is not a difference of size; it is the difference between creature and Creator, between the finite and the infinite.

Yet Jesus crossed it. He did not send an angel in his place, nor call to us from far off in heaven. He crossed that eternal chasm himself, became man and lived among us. The apostle John sums up the whole mystery in a single sentence: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)

Brothers and sisters, right at the start I want to ask you three questions, and these three questions are the three stretches of road this lesson will walk.

The first question: when you “have”, can you lay it down? When you have authority, resources, reputation, talent — can you still serve like a servant?

The second question: when you “can”, do you still rely on God? When you’ve done something so often that you could do it with your eyes shut, do you still pray first?

The third question: when you “know better than others”, do you still submit? When you can plainly see more clearly than your boss, understand more than your parents, are more mature than your leader — are you still willing to stay in your place and submit?

Some people draw near to God only when they “can’t”, call on God only when they “have nothing”, and learn humility only when they “have no standing”. But Jesus was not like that. He laid down when he “had”, relied when he “could”, and submitted while he held his “position”. That is the role model we are learning from today.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A City Obsessed with Status Receives a Letter About Going Down
sections.html:
To understand Philippians 2, we must first get to know the man who wrote the letter, the people who received it, and the city itself.

The writer was the apostle Paul, and when he wrote he was in prison. From the mention of “the whole palace guard” in Philippians 1:13 and “Caesar’s household” in 4:22, the great majority of evangelical scholars conclude that he was imprisoned in Rome, around AD 61. Notice this detail: a prisoner bound in chains wrote the most joyful letter in the New Testament; a man who had lost his freedom teaches us what it means to lay down our freedom gladly and willingly.

The recipients were the church at Philippi, founded by Paul on his second missionary journey around AD 49–50 and recorded in Acts 16 — the first time the gospel set foot on European soil. Its first members were a remarkable mix: Lydia, a merchant in purple cloth, of high social standing; a slave girl possessed by a spirit and exploited by others for profit, of the lowest standing of all; and a jailer of the Roman Empire, representing public authority. Three people of utterly different status became brothers and sisters in the same church. What would enable them to live together in harmony was certainly not human self-cultivation, but the humility of Christ.

Now look at the city. Philippi began as a small gold-mining town; in 356 BC it was enlarged by Philip II, king of Macedon, who named it after himself — that is where the name “Philippi” comes from. In 42 BC, Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar’s assassins Brutus and Cassius on the plain of Philippi. After the war Rome settled large numbers of veterans there, and Philippi became a Roman colony enjoying the “Italian right” — its residents held Roman citizenship and its legal privileges.

Brothers and sisters, this point is crucial. Philippi was a city that took pride in “status”. Acts 16:21 records that the men who accused Paul made a point of calling themselves “Romans” — their sense of superiority leaps off the page. The very air of the city was thick with one message: climb higher; make sure people see you’re above everyone else. And it was in such a city that Paul wrote a passage about “going down”. He did not tell them to give up their citizenship; he reminded them: “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).

Now look at the context. Philippians 2:5–11 is not a theological treatise appearing out of nowhere; it is the ground of an exhortation. Just before it Paul says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4) Why say this? Because there was friction in the church. By chapter 4 he even names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two co-workers at odds, and the whole church affected.

How does Paul deal with the problem? He doesn’t call a mediation meeting or draw up a set of rules. He does something far more fundamental — he sets Jesus Christ before their eyes. He says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). The way to resolve tension between people is not first to change others but first to change our mindset; not first to deal with the issue but first to return to Christ. This is exactly what the 321 vision says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, then ministry changes.

Many scholars call Philippians 2:6–11 the “Christ Hymn”; it was very likely sung in the worship of the early church. Its structure is very clear. Verses 6–8 are a staircase going all the way down — from the form of God, to emptying himself, to the form of a servant, to the likeness of men, to humbling himself, to obedience unto death, to death on a cross. Verses 9–11 go all the way up: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

Brothers and sisters, remember this shape: first down, then up. The world teaches us to climb up; the Bible teaches us to go down. The world says that when you reach the top you gain glory; the Bible says that when you go all the way down, God will lift you up. How clearly 1 Peter 5:6 puts it: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.”

Now let’s follow the lesson and walk down these three steps one at a time: laying down the right that comes with “having”, laying down the right that comes with “being able”, and laying down the right that comes with “position”.

sections.heading: 1. Laying Down the Right of “Having”: From Glory Down to Humanity
sections.html:
1. The Text: He Had It, Yet Did Not Grasp It

“who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6)

2. Light from the Original: “Form” and “Grasped”

The Greek word for “form” is morphē. It refers not to an outward shape but to “the form that displays the essence”; Greek has another word, schēma, for an external, changeable appearance. Paul uses morphē here, and the meaning is very clear — Jesus did not merely “look like God”; in his essence he was God. John 1:1 says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He was not later raised up to be God; he always was.

Interestingly, in verse 7 Paul says he took “the form of a servant”, and he uses the same word, morphē. This tells us he is truly God and he truly became a servant; his divinity was not pretended, and his servanthood was not an act.

The second key word is “grasped”, in the Greek harpagmos. Its root means “to plunder, to seize by force”; it can refer to a prize of war to be clutched at all costs. So the sentence means: Jesus did not regard “equality with God” as something he must grip tightly in his fist and let no one touch.

Brothers and sisters, here we meet the sharpest contrast in the whole Bible.

In Genesis 3:5 the serpent says to Eve: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Man was not God, yet wanted to be “like God”.

In Isaiah 14:13–14 the fallen one says: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” He was not the Most High, yet wanted to be “like the Most High”.

Do you see it? The way of Satan and Adam was: “not God, yet trying to seize God’s position.” The way of Jesus was: “God from the beginning, yet not clutching God’s rights.” One snatches upward; the other gives downward. This is exactly what the 321 vision puts its finger on: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

3. Emptying Himself Is Not Losing His Divinity but Laying Down the Right to Use It
