Verse 7 says he “emptied himself”. The Greek is ekenōsen, literally “poured out, emptied”.

We must interpret this very carefully here, so as not to go astray. What Jesus emptied himself of was not his divinity. On earth he still forgave sins, calmed storms and received worship; Colossians 2:9 says, “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.” What he emptied himself of was “the right to use his rights as God” — he willingly set aside the privilege of summoning heaven’s armies at any moment, of being spared all suffering, and gladly entered a body that knew hunger, weariness, tears and death.

He had the right to be God, yet chose the limitations of being human. He could have commanded angels to serve him, yet chose to serve people; he need not have suffered, yet chose to bear the agony of the cross for us. In the Garden of Gethsemane he said with his own lips: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53) It was not that he couldn’t; it was that he wouldn’t.

2 Corinthians 8:9 puts it in the most moving of sentences: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.”

4. An Illustration: What If You Had to Become a Snail?

The lesson offers a powerful comparison: if we had to turn from human beings into animals, we would all find it hard to accept; how unimaginable, then, is the humility of the God who created the universe being willing to become one of the creatures he made.

The British writer C. S. Lewis uses a similar picture in “Mere Christianity”: if you want to get some sense of what the Incarnation means, think how you would like to become a slug or a crab. Merely imagining it makes us squirm — because that is going down several levels.

But brothers and sisters, the gap between a human and a snail is still the gap between one creature and another. The gap between God and man is the gap between the infinite and the finite. Scientists estimate that the human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells (Bianconi et al., 2013, “Annals of Human Biology”), and the precise design of every one of those cells points to the Creator. And this Creator actually entered a body made of cells — a body that could hunger, thirst, tire and bleed.

Why would he do this? There is only one answer — for love. This is humility: not being forced down, but willingly coming down for love. Bowing your head because you are forced is called humiliation; only bowing it willingly is called humility. Many people in this world are pushed down by circumstances — that isn’t humility, it’s helplessness. Jesus had every right not to come down, yet chose to come down. That is humility.

5. A Generation Climbing Up, a Saviour Coming Down

Psychological research holds up a mirror to the face of our age. Jean M. Twenge and colleagues, in a study published in 2008 in the “Journal of Personality”, found that from 1979 to 2006 the scores of American college students on the Narcissistic Personality Inventory showed a marked upward trend. She later co-wrote, with W. Keith Campbell, the book “The Narcissism Epidemic”, arguing that contemporary culture constantly reinforces a sense of self that says “I’m the most important, I’m the most special.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the very air we breathe every day. Advertising tells us “you deserve it”, and social media keeps inviting us to show off our most glamorous side. The whole world’s gravity pulls upward, toward the self. Yet in that air the Bible points to a Saviour who went down and says: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.

What is the “having” in our own lives? It may be a little authority — you’re a manager, a parent, a small-group leader. It may be a few resources, some talent, a little time. Laying down the right of “having” doesn’t mean throwing these things away; it means no longer treating them as grounds for “I can be above others”, but as vessels through which “I can serve others”.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

The phrase “emptied himself” is the most perfect demonstration of selflessness. But brothers and sisters, be sure to remember: selflessness is not having nothing, not self-denial in the sense of self-rejection, not regarding yourself as worthless. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When Jesus emptied himself, he did not become any less God; rather, he let God’s love pour out to all humanity through a finite body. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is the fullness without limit.

And the outcome? Philippians 2:9 says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” Notice that “therefore”. He was not exalted first and then humbled; it was because he humbled himself that God exalted him. Laying down is not losing; laying down is where gaining begins.

sections.heading: 2. Laying Down the Right of “Being Able”: Relying on the Father in Everything
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Son Can Do Nothing of Himself

“Jesus therefore answered them, ‘Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.’” (John 5:19)

2. Background: Words Spoken Under the Threat of Death

These words were not spoken on a quiet hillside; they were spoken under enormous pressure. John 5 records that beside the Pool of Bethesda Jesus healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years — and that day was the Sabbath. So the Jews persecuted him. Jesus answered, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” (John 5:17) The moment those words were out, the situation escalated: verse 18 says the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. It was at that very moment that Jesus spoke verse 19. People were plainly out to kill him, and yet he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself.”

3. Exposition: Not a Lack of Ability, but the Nature of a Relationship

We must be very careful not to misread this as “the Son is inferior to the Father”. Orthodox evangelical faith holds to the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit are of one substance, equal in power and equal in glory. The “can’t” Jesus speaks of is, in the Greek, ou dynatai ... aph’ heautou — “cannot of himself”. This “cannot” is not a deficiency of ability but an unwillingness rooted in relationship — he is so completely one with the Father that he never would, and never will, take any independent action apart from the Father.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we can trace this theme through:

“I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

“I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things.” (John 8:28)

Brothers and sisters, did you notice? In all Jesus’ life, not one action, word or judgement was done “of himself”. He did not lean on his divinity to take shortcuts; he depended entirely on the Father’s guidance. The four Gospels record again and again that he withdrew into the wilderness to pray, rose before dawn to pray, prayed all night. He could work miracles, and still he prayed; he could teach, and still he first listened for the Father’s voice.

The lesson puts its finger on our sore spot in a single sentence: for us, we pray only when we “can’t”; once we “can”, it’s easy to rely on ourselves. But the role model Jesus gives us is this — even when he could, he chose to depend.

4. An Illustration: The Greatest Danger Isn’t Not Knowing How, but Thinking You Know

There is a very famous psychological finding here. In a study published in 1999 in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology”, Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University reported that in tests of grammar, logical reasoning and sense of humour, the people who performed worst were the most likely to overestimate their own ability and ranking — what came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect”. Their explanation: if a person lacks a certain skill, he also lacks the skill to recognise that he lacks it.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the lesson says: in spiritual service, in work, in decision-making, the greatest danger is not “not knowing how” but “thinking you know how”.

Picture a scene from everyday life. Someone who has just passed their driving test grips the wheel with both hands, keeps checking the mirror and slows down at every junction. And the old hand with twenty years behind the wheel? One hand on the wheel, chatting on the phone, wondering what’s for dinner. Which one is more likely to have an accident? Not the one who doesn’t know how — the one who knows it all too well.

The spiritual life is the same. A new believer reads the Bible like digging for treasure and prays like breathing; but someone who has served for years may preach from old notes, pray in the same old words and run Sunday by the same old routine. Inside they think, “I know this one,” and so God gets shown to a seat on the side.

The Lord Jesus could not have been more emphatic: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) And Proverbs says: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

5. True Humility Is Not Admitting Weakness but Admitting Need

This sentence from the lesson is worth memorising: true humility is not admitting weakness but admitting need. The humble, however experienced, still depend on God; the proud, however helpless, still want to rely on themselves.

Psychological research on humility points the same way. June Price Tangney of George Mason University, in a paper published in 2000 in the “Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology”, argued that humility is not self-deprecation but involves several components: an accurate assessment of one’s abilities and achievements, the ability to acknowledge one’s mistakes and limitations, openness to new ideas, and turning one’s attention away from the self toward the larger whole.

Brothers and sisters, notice that last one — turning one’s attention away from the self toward the larger whole. Isn’t that just what the 321 vision says? Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

The 321 vision has a saying that is the very key to this point: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Everything we do flows from the heart.

“Once I can, I rely on myself” — that is relying on the brain; “even when I can, I still depend” — that is relying on the heart. The third of the Three Foundations is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. The pattern of Jesus’ ministry on earth is precisely the pattern of a man wholly led by the Holy Spirit — Luke 4:1 says he “was led by the Spirit into the wilderness”, and Luke 4:14 says he “returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee”. He did not go it alone on the strength of his own divinity; what he modelled was a life obedient to the Holy Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, if you exchange the mindset “I can, so I do” for “even though I can, I will first ask God”, your life will be different.

sections.heading: 3. Laying Down the Right of “Position”: Submitting to Sinful People
sections.html:
1. The Text: He Went Down with Them

“And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.” (Luke 2:51)

2. Background: A Twelve-Year-Old Boy and Three Days of Searching

Luke 2:41–52 records the only event from Jesus’ childhood that is written down in any detail. Every year at Passover, Joseph and Mary went up to Jerusalem. The year Jesus was twelve, when the feast was over, they had travelled a day’s journey home before they discovered the boy was not among their relatives. They went back to Jerusalem and searched for three days, and finally found him in the temple.

At thirteen a Jewish boy became a “son of the commandment”, formally taking on responsibility for keeping the law; twelve was the age of preparation. How does Scripture describe the scene? “After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions. All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.” (Luke 2:46–47)

He was brilliant beyond others; even the most learned rabbis of the day were amazed. And when Mary, after three days of anguish, asked him why he had treated them like this, he answered: “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49) These are the first words Jesus speaks in the Bible, and his very first sentence declares his relationship with the Father. By human logic, he could well have stayed on in the temple to keep debating and teaching; after all, he was right — he of all people should be occupied with his Father’s affairs.

But the next verse says: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.”

3. Exposition: Submission That Lasted Eighteen Years

The Greek word for “subject to” is hypotassō, originally a military term meaning “to rank oneself under someone”; it is not a forced capitulation but a voluntary ordering. Even more noteworthy is the tense of the verb: Luke uses the imperfect with a participle, indicating a continuous, long-running state.

In other words, this was not a single concession but a long stretch of years. Luke 3:23 says that when Jesus began his ministry he was about thirty years old. From twelve to thirty — nearly eighteen years — the Bible is almost entirely blank: no miracles, no sermons, no crowds; only a carpenter’s workshop in Nazareth. Mark 6:3 records that later the people of his home town said, “Isn’t this the carpenter?”

Brothers and sisters, think about it: the Creator of the universe spent eighteen years measuring timber, planing timber, nailing timber, submitting to a foster father and a mother. And Luke 2:52 says: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.” The years of submission were not wasted years; they were years of growth.

There is a very deep truth here: the sinless Jesus submitted to sinful parents; the perfect Lord obeyed imperfect people. Joseph was only his legal father; and Mary, though highly favoured, was also someone who needed a Saviour — she herself sang: “My soul magnifies the Lord. My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47). In calling God “my Savior” she shows that she too was among those being saved.

Hebrews 5:8 says: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” He did not first learn to obey and then become the Son of God; he was the Son of God and still learned obedience.

4. An Illustration: When You Know More, Do You Still Submit?

The lesson asks a very sharp question: when we know more than our boss, more than our parents, more than our leaders, can we still humbly submit?

This is a real tension. A young co-worker fresh out of seminary, head full of new methods, watches the old pastor run meetings the same way he has for thirty years and thinks: this is wrong; it should be done like that. He may well be right. But as soon as he opens his mouth with an “I know better than you” tone, it is no longer a question of right and wrong; it is a question of pride and humility. The 321 vision puts it exactly: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

Management research confirms this truth too. In a study published in 2013 in “Organization Science”, Bradley P. Owens, Michael D. Johnson and Terence R. Mitchell found that leaders’ “expressed humility” — a willingness to acknowledge their own limitations, appreciate others’ strengths and stay open to new views — was positively related to their followers’ work engagement, job satisfaction and intention to stay. Of course, we are not humble because it works; we are humble because that is what Jesus is like.

Scripture’s teaching is consistent: “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1). “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (1 Peter 5:5)

Of course, we must also keep the Bible’s proportions: submitting to authority does not mean going along with sin. When human commands conflict with God’s commands, the apostles’ answer is clear: “We must obey God rather than men.” (Acts 5:29) Jesus submitted to Joseph and Mary, but he never once went along with sin. Laying down the right of “position” means laying down my pride and my own opinions — not laying down God’s standard.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Return to Our Originally Intended Position — Let Man Be Man and Let God Be God

The 321 vision says that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. In the temple Jesus first established his relationship with the Father — “I must be in my Father’s house”; then, carrying that settled identity, he went back to Nazareth to submit to people.

Brothers and sisters, this order matters enormously. Someone whose standing before God is insecure will always fight for standing before people; only someone who knows for certain who he is has the strength to take a place beneath others. Jesus didn’t need to “stay in the temple and debate” to prove he was the Son of God, because he already was.

The lesson says: don’t insist on “I know better than you”, but choose “I am still willing to submit”. This is exactly what 321 says — humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position; let man be man and let God be God. In the home at Nazareth, Jesus let Joseph be the father, let Mary be the mother, and let the heavenly Father be God. He took nobody’s place.

This is also the foundation of “235 relationships”. To become a spiritual companion — someone’s “2”; to establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; to form a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades — the first condition is this: am I willing to stand beneath others? Am I willing to give the credit away? Am I willing, when I am right, still to choose to submit? Without this step, relationships can never be established.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Three Layings-Down on the Road of Selflessness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set these three layings-down back into the framework of the 321 vision.

1. The Three Foundations Match the Three Layings-Down

Laying down the right of “having” matches “Jesus is my role model”: we no longer ask what others do; we ask what Jesus does. The world’s role models climb up; Jesus’ role model goes down.

Laying down the right of “being able” matches “the Holy Spirit is my guide”: being able doesn’t mean I’m right; being experienced doesn’t mean God wants me to do it this way.

Laying down the right of “position” matches “the Bible is my standard”: I submit not because that person deserves it but because God’s word says so; I lay down my opinion not because I’m wrong but because the Bible stands above my feelings.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King; Let Jesus Receive All the Glory

Brothers and sisters, what does “laying down the right to be God” mean? In the language of 321, it is “let Jesus be King”.

Inside each of us there is a little throne. If “self” sits on that throne, we will clutch our “having”, boast of our “being able” and fight for our “position”; if Jesus sits on that throne, we will naturally be able to lay them down. The question has never been “how much should I lay down?” but “who is on the throne?”

And the end of this road is already written in Philippians 2:11: “to the glory of God the Father.” All of Jesus’ descent comes in the end to glory. He himself said: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” (John 17:4) Brothers and sisters, someone who is willing to lay down does not lose glory; he puts glory back where it always belonged.

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

The Worldly system is a pyramid: those on top press down on those below. God’s system is turned upside down: those on top hold up those below. Jesus said: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) If someone won’t lay down “having, being able, position”, what he establishes will inevitably be a human system — resting on ability, seniority and rank. Only if someone is willing to lay them down can what he establishes be God’s system — resting on grace, on the Holy Spirit, on submitting to one another.

4. The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless: Humility Overcomes Pride, Selflessness Overcomes Satan

Isaiah 14 records five “I will”s — I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. This is the manifesto of pride, the self-centred life at its extreme.

Philippians 2, by contrast, records a whole chain of “laying down” — not considering equality with God a thing to be grasped, emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, humbling himself, becoming obedient, even to death. This is the road of humility, selflessness at its fullest.

These two roads met head-on in history. In the temptation in the wilderness Satan said to Jesus, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” (Matthew 4:9) It was a shortcut to glory without going to the cross, and Jesus refused it. He defeated the one who would not submit by submitting, and overcame the one so full of “self” by selflessness. This is what the 321 vision keeps stressing: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not a powerful Christian but a Christian with no “self”; because you cannot get a grip on someone who isn’t gripping anything.

5. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective

321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with mindset. Most people’s mindset is: to lay down is to lose. This lesson tells us otherwise: laying down is not losing; laying down is the beginning of finding freedom. Once this mindset changes, life begins to change; when life changes, the choices of daily living change; when daily living changes, relationships at home, at work and in the small group change; and when relationships change, ministry will bear real fruit. That’s why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Some people have served for years and built large ministries, yet their relationships are in chaos — and the reason is often that three things have not been laid down: having, being able, position.

Our perspective must shift too: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, Jesus being born in a manger was a failure; from God’s perspective, it was the beginning of salvation. Seen from earth, eighteen years as a carpenter were years buried in obscurity; seen from heaven, they were perfect obedience. Seen in the short term, laying down means losing out; seen from eternity, “God also highly exalted him.”

6. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice says: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, look at these fruits: patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, self-control — which of them doesn’t require us first to lay ourselves down? If you don’t lay down “I’m in the right”, you can’t be patient; if you don’t lay down “I’m too busy”, you can’t be kind; if you don’t lay down “I want it”, you can’t exercise self-control. All nine graces grow on the tree of selflessness. And 235 relationships — becoming someone’s “2” as a spiritual companion, establishing a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, forming a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of comrades — every level needs someone to bow their head first.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Turning Mindset into Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them out layer by layer.

Practice 1: Practise Laying Down in What You “Have”

When you have authority, position or resources, choose to serve humbly.

This week, write down three things you “have”, and for each one think of a way to serve someone with it. If you have a car, give an elderly member a lift to the meeting; if you have professional expertise, look over a document for a brother who needs help; if you have time, make a phone call to ask after someone.

Practice 2: Practise Depending in What You “Can Do”

Even when you know it well, pray first and seek God’s heart.

Pick the one thing you’re most practised and most confident at — leading a Bible study, giving a presentation, cooking a meal — and before you start, be still for three minutes and entrust it to God. The more familiar something is, the more you need to pray; because that is exactly where you’re most likely to forget God.

Practice 3: Practise Submitting in Your “Position”

Respect the authority God has established, and learn to experience blessing through submission.

Think of someone you “know more than” yet must submit to — perhaps a boss, a parent, a spouse, a co-worker. This week, over one thing you would normally have fought for, choose to say: “All right, I’ll do it your way.” Then notice what God does in your heart.

Taking These Three Practices Deeper Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Stage one, Information: write down what you heard today. Philippians 2:6–8, John 5:19, Luke 2:51 — three passages, three layings-down. Copy them into your notebook and put them up where you’ll see them.

Stage two, Revelation: ask God to turn the information into light. Information only reaches the head; revelation reaches the heart. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, which is the ‘having’, the ‘being able’ or the ‘position’ that I cling to most?” Let the Holy Spirit point out that specific name, that specific thing.

Stage three, Conviction: acknowledge from the heart that God is right. Not “I know I ought to lay it down”, but “I believe laying it down is better than holding on.” Conviction is the surrender of the will, not merely the agreement of the mind.

Stage four, Implementation: do at least one this week. Don’t try all three at once — just one, but really do it. Implementation is the bridge by which a mindset enters daily living.

Stage five, Evaluation: each evening spend three minutes looking back — where did I grab hold again today? Seeing it honestly is the beginning of progress.

Stage six, Correction: once you see it, adjust. If today you grabbed the top spot in front of your family, go and apologise tomorrow; if today you charged through in your own strength, tomorrow pray first and then move. Correction is not remorse; it is turning around.

Stage seven, Repetition: doing it once won’t change a person; doing it again and again will. Jesus submitted again and again for eighteen years — how can we hope for a three-day crash course?

Stage eight, Multiplication: bring someone along with you. This week, share what you’ve learned through the practice with a brother or sister, or invite a companion to do these three practices with you. The 321 vision says that life is multiplied — when you lay down, others get to see what laying down looks like.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Laying Down Is Not Losing
sections.html:
Laying down is not losing; laying down is the beginning of finding freedom. When you are willing to lay down the right to “be God”, you become more like “the Son of God” — Jesus Christ.

Why does laying down bring freedom? Because the one who grips is not free. Hold on to face, and face ties you up; hold on to position, and position ties you up; hold on to “I’m right”, and that “right” ties you up. A clenched fist can catch nothing; only an open hand can receive.

The Lord Jesus said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Brothers and sisters, rest is not having nothing to do; rest is selflessness — having no “self” left to fight for.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that manger where we began.

When Jesus laid down the right to be God, he did not lose his honour; rather, he revealed the glory of his love. He entered the world in the form of humility, so that through him we might gain life and gain salvation.

He teaches us that humility is not weakness, but being able and still willing to obey; not being forced to lay down, but choosing to lay down for love.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: what if Jesus had insisted on his right to be God? He would still be God, still seated on the throne; the angels would still worship him; he would not have lost a thing. The ones who would have lost are us — we would have stayed in our sin for ever, separated from God for ever, with no way home for ever. He laid down, so that we could gain. That is the gospel.

So today, through this lesson, God asks us a question: what are you still clutching in your hand?

Perhaps it’s a title, and you can’t bear to hand over the baton. Perhaps it’s an “I know this better than anyone”, and you won’t listen to others. Perhaps it’s control in a relationship, and it has to be done your way. Perhaps it’s an old wound you’re gripping tightly, refusing to forgive. Brothers and sisters, not one of those things can be carried into eternity. But every time you let go for love, heaven writes it down.

The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. This morning I want to invite you to do something very simple and very deep — open your hand, and in your heart say to the Lord: “Lord, this seat is yours, not mine. I come down; you go up.”

When we learn humility like this from Jesus, we too are walking the road of selflessness, living a life that truly glorifies God.

Today, may you serve people where you “have”, depend on God where you “can”, and willingly submit where you hold a “position”. May Jesus reign as King in your home, reign as King in your work, reign as King in your heart. All the glory to him.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)
declarations: Lord, you existed in the form of God, yet you did not insist on your equality with the Father, but emptied yourself and took the form of a servant.
Help me to learn your ways: not proud when I have, not self-reliant when I can, not self-exalting when I hold a position.
Help me to depend on you in everything and obey your will.
May your humility become my glory; may your likeness become my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
practices: Practise laying down in what you “have”
Practise depending in what you “can do”
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you.

Lord Jesus, this morning we have seen your humility. You existed in the form of God, yet willingly emptied yourself; you could have commanded angels, yet chose to serve sinners; you could have stayed in the temple to teach, yet chose to go back to Nazareth and submit. Lord, before you we have nothing to say; we can only bow our heads and worship.

Lord, we confess that we are often proud when we have, self-reliant when we can, and self-exalting when we hold a position. We cling to things that will surely pass away, and let go of you. Please forgive us.

Holy Spirit, shine your light on us now and point out the one thing we are gripping tightly in our hands. Give us the strength to let go today. Give us the mind of Christ, so that we gladly go low for love — not forced, but willing.
Lord, we give our families to you, our work to you, our service to you. Reign as King among us, and receive all the glory.
We ask this in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
discussion: Philippians 2:6–7: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” Share: in your life right now, which “having”, “being able” or “position” is hardest for you to lay down? Why is it hard?

Luke 2:51: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them.” Share: has there been a time when you plainly felt you were right, yet chose to submit? How did God later bless you through it? If something like that is happening now, how do you plan to respond?
l082.title: Laying Down the Right to Be God
l082.subtitle: Jesus Our Role Model (Part 1)
l082.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Glory — Something to Pursue, or Something to Lay Down?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin by asking you a question: if an opportunity were placed in front of you right now — a chance for the whole world to see you, to praise you, to remember your name — would you reach out and take it?

We live in an age that longs to be seen. On social media every post is waiting for a heart; every video is counting its views. Some people airbrush their lives into flawless perfection for the sake of a few more likes; some are so afraid of being overlooked that they no longer dare to be quiet, even when quiet is what they need. In 2009 the psychologists Jean Twenge and W. Keith Campbell published The Narcissism Epidemic, in which they pointed out that, according to cross-generational statistical analysis, the average score of American college students on the Narcissistic Personality Inventory (NPI) has been rising steadily since the 1980s. This finding is not a scolding of any one generation. It is a reminder of one thing: deep in the human heart there is a hunger — to be seen, to be affirmed, to be lifted up.

That hunger is not in itself a sin. God made us to live in being loved and being accepted. The question is this: to whom do we bring that hunger? Do we lift our hearts up and wait for the Father’s acceptance, or do we lay our hearts open and wait for the applause of the crowd?

In the eyes of the world, glory is something you pursue; but in the eyes of Jesus, glory is something you lay down.

That sentence is the key to today’s lesson. Jesus is the King of kings and Lord of lords; all honour and authority are his. The angels of heaven worship him, and the worlds were made through him. If anyone ever had “the right to glory”, it was he. And yet he chose to come into the world in the form of a servant. He did not exalt himself; he chose to humble himself. He did not grasp at glory; he let the glory go to God the Father.

This is the most profound example he has left us: the true meaning of glory lies not in being honoured by people, but in being willing to serve in humility.

I remember an old preacher who served a small rural church for more than thirty years. He never published a book, never spoke from a conference platform, and no one ever threw him a celebration. When he died, some fifty people sat in the small hall of the funeral home, most of them children he had raised in the faith, now middle-aged. At the memorial someone said, “Pastor never once made us remember his title — but he made us remember Jesus for the rest of our lives.” In that moment I suddenly understood: there is a kind of glory you can only receive after you have laid it down.

There is a line in the message of Kingdom 321 that cuts to the heart: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. And what is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Brothers and sisters, today we are going to look together at how Jesus “laid down the right to glory”. What he laid down is the very thing we most want to hold on to; and what he received is the very thing we can never grasp, however hard we try.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Book of Joy Sent from a Prison
sections.html:
To grasp how much weight the phrase “laying down the right to glory” carries, we first need to stand where Philippians was written.

The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 60 and 62, during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome. A prisoner in chains wrote a letter that the church through the ages has called “the Epistle of Joy” — just four short chapters, in which the word “joy” comes up again and again. That in itself is a miracle, because joy does not come from circumstances; joy comes from relationship.

The letter was sent to the church in Philippi. Philippi was a city of Macedonia, and after the Roman civil war of 42 BC it was made a Roman “colony” (colonia). Acts 16:12 calls it “a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony.” Many of the people living there were retired Roman soldiers and their descendants; they held Roman citizenship and were exempt from some taxes. You can imagine the air in that city: rigid ranks, status above everything, pride in being Roman. What a person in Philippi cared about most was: who am I, where do I rank, on which tier is my name written?

The Philippian church was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). This church loved Paul dearly and supplied his needs again and again. But even this good church had a thorn in it. Chapter 4, verse 2 urges two women co-workers, Euodia and Syntyche, “to think the same way in the Lord” — clearly there was friction between them. And in chapter 2, verse 3 Paul names the root of the problem directly: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? That great “Christ Hymn” of Philippians 2 — the highest passage on Christ in all the ages — was not a theological treatise Paul wrote at his desk. It was a prescription written to heal a church of the disease of competing for glory. When people in the church were comparing who was higher, arguing over who was bigger and grabbing the credit, Paul did not begin with management theory or mediation techniques. He did only one thing: he lifted Christ up and said, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.”

This is one of the most basic principles of the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When relationships go wrong, we don’t start by repairing the relationship; we start by coming back to Christ and letting our life be changed. When the life is changed, the relationship changes as a matter of course.

There is one more piece of background worth mentioning. Many scholars believe that Philippians 2:6–11 was originally a hymn of the early church, which Paul quoted. The hymn has a very clear structure, shaped like a giant “V”: it comes all the way down from the highest glory — down to human likeness, down to the form of a servant, down to death on a cross; and then it rises all the way up from the lowest point — God highly exalts him, every knee bows, every tongue confesses, and the glory goes to God the Father.

That “V” is the devotional map of the whole Bible. Satan took the opposite road. He said, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God!” (Isaiah 14:13) — and he fell. Jesus took the road of humbling himself, and he was exalted to the highest place.

Selflessness overcomes Satan; humility overcomes pride. This is not a slogan; it is the law by which the universe runs.

Notice one more key word as well. Verse 6 says that Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” The Greek word behind “a thing to be grasped” is harpagmos, meaning “a prize of war to be clutched and never let go.” This goes straight to the question of “rights”: Jesus truly did possess that right. The glory was his all along; it was not something he had seized. But he did not treat it as a trophy to be gripped tight in his hand.

Brothers and sisters, there is a vital distinction here: laying down a right and having no right are two different things. A man with no money cannot be called generous; a man with no standing cannot be called humble. True humility is having a right and not using it, having glory and not displaying it. Jesus’ humbling of himself is glorious precisely because he was worthy of it all along.

sections.heading: 1. Jesus Laid Down the Right to Glory and Chose a Lowly Form
sections.html:
1. “Emptied himself” — the decision to pour himself out

Philippians 2:7 says: “but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.”

“Emptied himself” is the Greek ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from the verb kenoō, meaning “to empty, to make empty.” For this reason the verse has given its name in theology to the doctrine of kenosis.

We need to make one thing clear first, so as not to be misunderstood: when Jesus “emptied himself,” he did not empty himself of his deity. He did not stop being God; he remained fully God. What he emptied himself of was the way his glory, equal with God’s, was put on display — his right to use the honours of his divinity. Colossians 2:9 says, “For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily.” He lacked nothing. He simply no longer insisted on being seen.

Paul uses two very carefully chosen words here. The “form” in “the form of a servant” is the Greek μορφή (morphē), meaning an outward form that truly matches the inner nature; while the “likeness” in “being made in the likeness of men” is ὁμοίωμα (homoiōma), meaning outward resemblance. In other words, when he became a servant, he was not putting on a show or playing a role; he truly, genuinely became a servant. He really did come down among us.

And the word for “servant” here is the Greek δοῦλος (doulos) — not a “helper,” not an “employee,” but a “slave”: the very bottom of Roman society, with no status, no rights, no name. A Roman citizen in Philippi reading these words would have felt his heart skip a beat: the Lord of the whole universe took the form of a slave.

2. From the manger to the donkey’s colt — every step turning away from glory

When Jesus came to earth, he did not arrive with the pomp of the Son of God. He had no escort of heavenly hosts — though he could easily have asked for one. In Matthew 26:53 he says so himself: “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” He could have; but he did not ask.

He was born in a manger. Luke 2:7: “She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.”

He grew up in a carpenter’s home. Mark 6:3 records what the people of his hometown said: “Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James, Joses, Judah, and Simon?”

He had no striking appearance. Isaiah 53:2 had prophesied it long before: “He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.”

When people wanted to set him up as king, he slipped away. John 6:15 says: “Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.” Brothers and sisters, picture that scene: five loaves and two fish have just fed five thousand people, the crowd’s excitement has boiled over, the crown has all but been carried up to him — and he turns, goes up the mountain, and prays alone.

When he entered Jerusalem in glory, he did not ride a warhorse. Matthew 21:5 quotes the prophet: “Behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” In the ancient Near East, a king returning in triumph rode a warhorse; those who rode donkeys came seeking peace. He was the King, yet he chose a young colt that no one had ever ridden.

At every step, from his birth through his ministry, Jesus deliberately turned away from glory. He did not seek applause or crave position; he longed only to accomplish the Father’s will. In John 4:34 he says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.”

3. The lesson of the moon

Brothers and sisters, I want to use a picture from the sky.

We often speak of the bright, clear moon and of moonlight like water. But astronomy tells us a plain fact: the moon gives off no light of its own at all. The albedo of the moon’s surface — how much light it reflects — is only about 12 per cent; in other words, it reflects back only a small fraction of the sunlight that falls on it and absorbs the rest. Put another way, the moon is one of the poorer reflectors in the whole solar system; its surface is about as dark as an asphalt road.

But look up at a full moon — it lights up the whole night.

Why? Because although it has no light of its own, it is in the right position, facing the sun.

This is the example Jesus gives us, and it is the secret of a lifetime of service. We don’t need to shine by ourselves; we only need to stand in the right place and turn our faces towards the true Light. The moon never argues, “This light is mine.” It simply reflects, quietly. And precisely because it doesn’t contend, for countless ages people have looked up in the dark and seen light.

Turn it around: when is the moon at its darkest? Not when it is furthest from the sun, but when it moves between the earth and the sun and puts itself out in front — that is called a solar eclipse. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when we push ourselves to the front and block God’s light, we not only fail to shine; we create darkness.

4. The road of lifting up the Father

Jesus did not choose the road of “being lifted up by people”; he chose the road of “lifting up the Father.”

In John 5:41 he says: “I don’t receive glory from men.”

In John 8:50 he says: “But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges.”

In John 7:18 he states the principle like an exceedingly sharp blade: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.”

He laid down the right to glory so that God’s glory could be fully revealed in him. John 1:14 says: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” How wonderful — at the very moment he hid his glory, people saw the true glory.

His life reminds us that true honour lies not in being seen by people, but in God seeing our hearts.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: from the self-centred life to selflessness

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

What is the self-centred life? It is making myself the centre of everything — I must gain everything, I must be seen in everything. When Adam and Eve ate that fruit in the Garden of Eden, it was so that they would “be like God, knowing good and evil” — wanting to take God’s place. That is where the self-centred life begins.

What is selflessness? Selflessness is not having nothing; it is not denying yourself into nothingness, and still less is it an inferiority complex. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Galatians 2:20 puts it most precisely: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Look at Jesus emptying himself: he poured himself out, and God exalted him to the highest place. Emptying does not mean becoming zero; it means making room for the fullness of God to fill. If a cup is full, nothing more can be poured into it. If you are clutching your own glory tightly in your hand, God has no way to place his glory in your hand — because your hand is already full.

This is the first step of the fivefold change: a change of mindset. When our mindset about “glory” changes — from “I must get it” to “I must lay it down” — our life begins to change; when our life changes, our daily living changes; when our daily living changes, our relationships change; when our relationships change, our ministry changes.

Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Jesus walked this road first.

sections.heading: 2. Laying Down the Glory of Titles and Status, Recovering a Servant’s Heart
sections.html:
1. Whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all

In Jesus’ teaching, the road to “greatness” is a road that goes down.

Mark 9:35 records that the disciples had been arguing on the road about who was the greatest. How did Jesus respond? “He sat down, and called the twelve; and he said to them, ‘If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all.’”

By Mark 10, James and John come asking for the seats at his right and left, and the other ten are indignant with them. Jesus says it again, even more plainly: “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.” (Mark 10:43–44)

Notice two words here. “Servant” is the Greek διάκονος (diakonos), originally “a waiter who serves at table,” which later became the root of the church’s word “deacon.” “Bondservant” is the Greek δοῦλος (doulos) we met earlier — a slave. Jesus is saying: if you want to be great, go and carry the plates; if you want to be first, go and be a slave.

And then he speaks the sentence that sums it all up: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)

Brothers and sisters, on the very road where the disciples were arguing about rank, Jesus was walking towards the cross. It is one of the most glaring contrasts in the Bible: the Lord was going down, while the disciples were climbing up.

2. Today’s trap: turning service into status, and an office into an identity

Yet many who serve today have fallen into another trap — turning service into status, and an office into an identity.

Ordination was originally the church’s affirmation of, and commission to, those who serve. Laying on hands, sending out, recognising gifts — this is biblical order, and in itself it is beautiful. But when ordination becomes a status symbol, it strays from God’s heart. Many no longer long to serve the Lord; they long for titles and applause. That attitude turns “ministry” into a “race for status,” and lets glory slip from God’s hand into human applause.

Jesus diagnosed this disease long ago. Matthew 23:8–12: “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers. Call no man on the earth your father, for one is your Father, he who is in heaven. Neither be called masters, for one is your master, the Christ. But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

The word “Rabbi,” Hebrew רַבִּי (rabbi), literally means “my great one,” “my lord.” Jesus is not forbidding us to address our teachers respectfully; he is dismantling a structure — one that assigns seats by forms of address and sets a person’s worth by titles. He wants the church to have only one identity: brothers and sisters; and only one who is great: Christ.

3. Paul’s example: not a title, but a mission

Paul was an apostle, but he never treated “apostle” as a title.

Notice the wording of Ephesians 1:1: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God.” He does not write “His Excellency the Apostle Paul”; he ties “apostle” to “the will of God” — in the Chinese Union Version “by the will of God” even stands first — describing himself in terms of a trust he has been given. What he stresses is not a title but a mission; not how high his standing is, but obedience to a calling.

And in Romans 11:13 he says: “For I speak to you who are Gentiles. Since then as I am an apostle to Gentiles, I glorify my ministry.” (The word “glorify” is exactly the Greek doxazō, “to give glory.”) He did take his office seriously — but look at the purpose in what follows. He goes straight on to say it is so that he “may provoke to jealousy those who are my flesh, and may save some of them.”

Do you see it clearly? Paul wanted people to respect his office, not for the sake of status, but so that the body of Christ might be built up and the true gospel spread. He valued his office for the sake of its fruit; he made nothing of his title for his own sake.

In 1 Corinthians 4:7 he nails this mindset down: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?”

Brothers and sisters, there is not one thing about us that we could boast of which we did not receive. Our gifts were received, our health was received, our opportunities were received — even our faith was received. A person who goes around showing off a present someone else gave him is a comical sight.

4. An office is a function, not an identity

Ephesians 4:11–12 says: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.”

Notice that word “for.” The fivefold ministry exists for one clear purpose: the perfecting of the saints. An office is a function, not an identity; a title is a tool, not a glory.

Think of a hospital: surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, cleaners — each has a place. If the anaesthetist thinks he is a cut above the cleaners, infections in the operating theatre will cost lives. The parts of the body do not compete over who is higher; they work together. In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul makes it utterly plain: the members of the body that seem to be weaker are all the more indispensable.

When a church ranks its people by the height of their titles, it has lost the heart of Jesus, who “took the form of a servant.” Jesus did not call himself “Jesus, the Son of God.” The name he most often used for himself was “the Son of Man.” He said only: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve.” (Mark 10:45)

5. Two true illustrations

The first illustration comes from music. Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750) is one of the greatest composers in history. He had a lifelong habit: at the top of his scores he wrote “J.J.” — the Latin Jesu Juva, “Jesus, help me”; and at the end he wrote “S.D.G.” — Soli Deo Gloria, “to God alone be the glory.” Three hundred years later, concert halls around the world are still playing his music. A man who handed the credit to God found that God carried his name all the way to our day.

The second illustration comes from the study of leadership. In Good to Great, published in 2001, Jim Collins studied companies that leapt from mediocrity to excellence and sustained it for fifteen years or more. He found that their leaders shared a common trait, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: these people combined “personal humility” with “professional will.” When things went well, they gave the credit to others and to good luck; when things went wrong, they took the responsibility themselves. This is not a religious book; it is business research — yet it confirms a heavenly law: lasting influence belongs to those who don’t grab the credit.

There is an even more direct study. In 2013 the scholars Bradley Owens, Michael Johnson and Terence Mitchell published research in the journal Organization Science showing that the humility leaders express is positively correlated with their staff’s engagement at work, their willingness to learn, and team performance. Humility is not weakness; humility works.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: let man be man, and let God be God

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

The pride of titles is, at heart, “leaving our originally intended position.” God gives me a position so that I may serve in it; but I take that position and make it my worth. It is like a man who is handed a key to open a door, but hangs the key round his neck as a pendant and shows it off to everyone — while the door stays shut.

The 321 vision also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This plays out in the church every day. One co-worker stresses his experience; another stresses her gifting. One person contends, the other goes on the defensive; and by the end the ministry is still standing, but life has died and the relationship is broken. Turn it around: when one person is willing to bow first, the other’s heart softens; when one person is willing to say first, “I didn’t handle that well,” the air in the whole team relaxes.

This is the very foundation of 235 relationships. With one selfless person you become a “2” — spiritual companions; then you go on to build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and in the end you become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. But note: all of this rests on selflessness. Two self-centred people can never become a “2”; they will only become two competitors. If spiritual parents are self-centred, what they produce is spiritual competitors, not spiritual children.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: 3. The True Meaning of Glory: Not Raising Ourselves Up, but Raising God Up
sections.html:
1. “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing”

Jesus chose to hide himself, not because he lacked power, but because he knew that true glory comes from being lifted up by the Father.

In John 8:54 he says: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God.”

Glory that comes from ourselves will fade away; glory that comes from God endures for ever.

The Hebrew word for “glory” is כָּבוֹד (kabod), whose root meaning is “weight, heaviness.” A person of glory is a person of “weight.” The Greek is δόξα (doxa), originally meaning “opinion, reputation”; in the Septuagint it was used to translate kabod, and so took on the sense of “radiance made visible.”

Put together, these two words give us a beautiful picture: true glory is a matter of “weight,” not of “volume.” People of weight don’t need to be loud; it is people without weight who need to keep proving themselves.

And God speaks with absolute finality. Isaiah 42:8: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.”

Brothers and sisters, think about this quietly: if God will not share his glory even with engraved idols, what makes us think we can keep his glory for ourselves and come to no harm?

2. Looking impressive is not the same as glory

In the same way, if our service in the church is for the sake of letting people see our performance and our ability, then everything we do, however impressive it looks, does not count as glory in God’s eyes.

The Lord Jesus speaks very solemnly in Matthew 6:1: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.”

Notice that he did not say, “Don’t do good works.” He said, don’t do them “to be seen by them.” In the same Sermon on the Mount he also said, in Matthew 5:16: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Do these two verses contradict each other? Not in the least. The only difference is in the last phrase: to whom does the glory go? Done before people with the glory going to God, it is light; done before people with the glory going to ourselves, it is a performance. The very same good deed can be worship, or it can be a show — the difference lies in which way the motive points.

John 12:43 writes the epitaph of a group of people who failed. It says that many of the rulers believed in Jesus but, because of the Pharisees, did not dare to confess it, “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.”

Brothers and sisters, this verse is worth reading every morning. It was not that they did not believe; it was that they “loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” Their faith was not the problem; their order of priorities was.

3. The spotlight effect: far fewer people are watching you than you think

Here I want to quote a finding from psychology that I find very helpful.

In 2000 the social psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky published a series of experiments in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in which they described the “spotlight effect.” They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, and then asked them to guess how many people had noticed what they were wearing. The participants’ estimates were roughly double the actual number.

In other words, we always assume the whole world is watching us, when in fact hardly anyone is. For the sake of a spotlight that doesn’t exist, we have spent most of our lives nervous, comparing and performing.

This finding confirms the wisdom of Scripture from the other side. Brothers and sisters, human eyes are so unreliable, so fleeting, so easily distracted — and yet we have lived for them for decades. But there is One whose eyes never leave you. Hebrews 4:13 says: “There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account.”

Living under human eyes is exhausting, because you never know whether they actually saw. Living under God’s eyes is rest, because he has never once missed anything.

4. The offering that seems so small

Only when we are willing, like Jesus, to lay down, to humble ourselves and to serve, does the offering that seems so small become true glory.

Mark 12 records that the Lord Jesus sat opposite the treasury and saw a poor widow put in two small coins. He called his disciples and said, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury.” (Mark 12:43) In man’s accounts, she gave the least; in God’s accounts, she gave the most.

John 13 records the most profound scene of all. It was before the Passover, and the Lord knew that the hour had come for him to leave this world. He “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:4–5)

Brothers and sisters, how many pairs of feet did he wash that night? Twelve. Including the pair that would shortly walk out into the night to betray him.

Then he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” (John 13:14)

In those days, washing feet was work for the lowest slave in the household. And the one doing it was the Ruler of the universe. At the start of that passage John adds a particular word of explanation — verse 3 says: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God.”

See the cause and effect clearly: precisely because he knew who he was, where he had come from and where he was going, he was able to bend down.

Brothers and sisters, what an important lesson this is. People who cannot bend down are often not so much too proud as too unsure. Someone who doesn’t know who they are in God has to prove themselves by their position; only someone who knows they are God’s beloved child has the freedom to wash other people’s feet.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

The Two Core Values of 321 are exactly what this lesson is about: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

What does it mean to “let Jesus be King”? It means that on the throne of my life only one person sits. I don’t sit there, and neither does anyone else. Every place where I still want to be seen is a place where I still want to sit on the throne.

What does it mean to “let Jesus receive all the glory”? Notice that word “all.” Not giving most of the glory to him and keeping a little bit for myself. The double negative in Psalm 115:1 really cuts to the heart: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.”

The psalmist says “not to us” twice. Why twice? Because if he said it only once, our hands would still reach out.

The 321 vision says: our perspective must shift — from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective. Applause is human, earthly, temporary and worldly; God’s acceptance is divine, heavenly, eternal and godly.

2 Corinthians 4:7 says: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” A clay jar is worth nothing; its value lies in what it holds. When people see glory shining out of a clay jar, no one praises the jar.

John the Baptist distilled all of this into one short sentence — John 3:30: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Downward Road That Leads to the Highest Heaven
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s gather up what we have seen today in the language of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Today’s lesson is titled “Jesus’ Model.” Philippians 2:5 says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” Notice that Paul does not say, “Imitate Christ’s behaviour”; he says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” Behaviour can be copied; the mind must be renewed. A role model is not there to make us perform humility, but to make us ask the Lord to give us his heart.

The Bible is my standard. What is glory? The world has its own definition, and the church sometimes quietly borrows the world’s definition. Only the Bible can set the standard for us. John 8:54, John 12:43, Psalm 115:1, Isaiah 42:8 — these verses are our measuring rod. When my feelings say, “I ought to be seen,” and the Bible says, “Not to us,” which one will I listen to?

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Laying down glory cannot be done by willpower. The more you grit your teeth and tell yourself, “I will be humble,” the more you will secretly check whether anyone has noticed your humility. That is relying on the brain and ourselves. The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Humility is not something squeezed out by suppression; humility is fruit borne by the Holy Spirit. Galatians 5:22–23 lists the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit, and “gentleness” is among them.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. There is only one throne. If he is not the one sitting on it, then I am. Every time I feel put out because my name wasn’t mentioned, a little “me” is quietly climbing onto the throne.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the acceptance test for a whole lifetime of service. When the job is done, whom do people remember? This is not a rebuke; it is a reminder — because it is so easy, without our even noticing, to slip into our own pockets what should have gone to him.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, this point matters especially. A church that ranks people by title is building “man’s system” — a pyramid, where the higher you go the fewer there are and the bigger they are. What Jesus wants to establish is “God’s system” — a body, where every member is indispensable and there is only one Head, Christ.

In man’s system, people climb upwards; in God’s system, people serve downwards. In man’s system, power presses down from the top; in God’s system, life flows down from the top.

The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless

Self-centred people end up worn out by their service, because they have to keep defending their position. Selfless people end up joyful in their service, because they have no position to defend.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When I no longer need to prove myself, I am free. When I am no longer afraid of being overlooked, I am able to love people well.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite attack is to whisper to you in the middle of your service, “Did anyone see that?” That one question has destroyed more ministry than any persecution.

The fivefold change

Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

A change of mindset: from “glory is something to fight for” to “glory is something to give to God.”

A change of life: no longer controlled by applause, with a new steadiness in the heart.

A change of daily living: beginning to do good things no one knows about.

A change of relationships: beginning to thank God sincerely for other people’s success.

A change of ministry: no longer comparing whose ministry is bigger, only asking whether God’s will has been done.

The order cannot be reversed. Many people try to start with ministry, and the result is that the ministry grows ever bigger while the life grows ever emptier. The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The 920 practice

920: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life; and we let the fruit of the Spirit, the “9”, grow in that relationship in all nine of its expressions.

Start today. Whom will you meet today? Your spouse, your children, your colleagues, your co-workers, the brother who always jumps in to speak first, the sister who never remembers your name — every one of them is your “2.” Laying yourself down before them is the truest worship you can offer today.

235 relationships

True spiritual companions are two people who have laid themselves down. True spiritual parents are those who entrust their children to God rather than tying them to their own side. A true fivefold-ministry team is a group of people who work together and don’t compete over who is higher.

Brothers and sisters, if two people on a team both want to be the head, that is not a team; that is a tug of war.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Learning to Let Go through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice One: Examine your motives for serving

Ask yourself: am I doing this to glorify God, or to be seen by people?

Information: first put the Scripture into your heart. Matthew 6:1: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.”

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. You can’t do this step yourself, because when it comes to motives, we can’t see ourselves clearly. Psalm 139:23–24 is the best prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.”

Conviction: admit that “loving men’s praise more than God’s praise” is a sin, not a personality trait.

Implementation: this week, before each time you serve, be still for ten seconds and say, “Lord, this is for you.”

Evaluation: every night before bed ask yourself: was there anything today that, once I’d done it, I especially wanted someone to know about?

Correction: hand that thing over to God, and deliberately don’t mention it.

Repetition: one week isn’t enough; do it for a whole season. A change of mindset takes time.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion and ask each other this question.

Practice Two: The discipline of hidden service

Deliberately do good things no one knows about, which only your Father knows.

Information: Matthew 6:3–4: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.”

There is a detail here that is often overlooked: the Lord Jesus says, “don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” — not even your own other hand should know. In other words, the hardest audience to guard against is not other people; it is the video recorder inside our own hearts that keeps replaying the scene.

Revelation and Conviction: you must believe that the “Father who sees in secret” is real. That takes faith. Hebrews 11:6 says: “Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.”

Implementation: this week, do one good deed that will never be discovered. Give an extra offering anonymously; tidy up after someone without saying so; pray for the person who hurt you without telling anyone.

Evaluation and Correction: if, once you’ve done it, you badly want to tell someone — congratulations, you’ve found a place that really needs dealing with. Bring it before the Lord.

Repetition and Multiplication: make “good deeds in secret” the normal pattern of your daily living, and do them together with your children.

There is an interesting confirmation of this. In 2008 the psychologists Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published research in the journal Science showing that people who spent money on others felt happier afterwards than people who spent the same money on themselves. When God made us, he wrote “giving brings joy” into our design.

Practice Three: Get rid of the pride of titles

Learn to call brothers and sisters by their names, rather than honouring them only by their titles.

Information: Matthew 23:8: “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.”

In How to Win Friends and Influence People, published in 1936, Dale Carnegie wrote a line that has been widely quoted: a person’s name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language. A name stands for the person himself; a title stands only for his function. And this is how God treats us too — Isaiah 43:1 says: “I have called you by your name. You are mine.” He does not call us by our titles; he calls us by our names.

Implementation: this week, make a point of remembering the names of three brothers and sisters and calling them by name — especially the people nobody usually notices: the ones who sweep the floor, who direct the parking, who work in the kitchen.

Evaluation and Correction: if you find you can remember the names of people with titles but not the names of people without them, that is the place that needs dealing with.

Repetition and Multiplication: let your small group become a place where people are called by name.

Practice Four: Learn to appreciate others

See the value of other people’s service, rather than comparing who is more highly regarded.

Information: Romans 12:10: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor preferring one another.” Philippians 2:3: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.”

Revelation: comparison is a thief. In 1954 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward “social comparison theory,” pointing out that people naturally evaluate themselves by comparing themselves with others. It is a human instinct — and precisely Satan’s handiest weapon, because as long as I keep comparing, I will never be satisfied and never be thankful.

Implementation: this week, praise three people’s service specifically and face to face, and mention the details. Not “You’re great,” but “That material you prepared for us last week saved me two hours.”

Evaluation and Correction: when you hear someone else being praised and your heart sinks, don’t scold yourself — treat it as an alarm clock. That is exactly the place that needs letting go.

Repetition and Multiplication: make “appreciating others” a regular part of your small-group meetings.

A Gentle Reminder

Laying down glory is not giving up your worth; rather, it is letting God himself lift you up in his presence.

When you no longer crave being seen by people, God can be seen in you.

1 Peter 5:6: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.”

Notice those words: “in due time.” The timetable is in his hands, not ours. Our responsibility is to humble ourselves; God’s responsibility is to lift us up. If we rush to do God’s job for him, God will simply let us bear the consequences ourselves. Proverbs 16:18 says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.”

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: Letting the Unseen Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s come back once more to that “V.”
