Jesus did not choose the road of “being exalted”; he chose the road of “humbling himself to serve.” He laid down the right to glory to teach us that true glory lies not in being seen by people, but in letting people see God through our lives.

But please don’t forget the second half of that “V.” Philippians 2:9 says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.”

The word “Therefore” is the hinge of the whole passage. Because he humbled himself, “therefore” God exalted him to the highest place. Humbling is not the end of the story; humbling is the road.

And where does that road end? Verse 11: “every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

So the whole purpose of salvation, the end point of all cosmic history, comes down to one sentence: let Jesus be King, and let the glory go to God.

This is the call we receive today.

When we are willing, as he was, to take the form of a servant, our lives too will reflect the glory of heaven — a glory that belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, finally I want to speak to three kinds of people.

If today you are in a position where you are seen — on the platform, among the leaders, surrounded by praise — this lesson is your protection. May you, like Bach, write at the end of every piece of work: to God alone be the glory.

If today you are in a position where no one sees you — in the kitchen, in the sound booth, in intercession no one knows about — this lesson is your comfort. Your Father sees in secret, and he has never missed a single time.

If today you are hurting because you have not been seen — someone took the credit for your work, someone forgot to thank you — this lesson is your healing. Hand that grievance over to the One who “seeks and judges” (John 8:50). He will vindicate you, and the way he vindicates you is far more beautiful than anything you could win for yourself.

Let us rise together and walk that downward road. Because that downward road is the only road that leads to the highest heaven.

keyVerses: Philippians 2:5–11

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”
declarations: Lord, you possessed the glory of all things, yet you were willing to empty yourself and become a servant to serve the world. Teach me to let go of my grip on position and glory, and to live solely for the glory of your name. May I be faithful in hiddenness and joyful in lowliness, and may my whole life become a vessel that glorifies you.
practices: Get rid of the pride of titles
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we bow down before you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. You had the right to glory, yet you laid it down; you were worthy of all honour, yet you chose the manger, chose the donkey’s colt, chose the towel and the basin, chose the cross. Lord, we bow down and worship you.

Forgive us. Forgive us for treating service as status and office as identity; forgive us for loving men’s praise more than your glory; forgive us for being unwilling to be faithful in secret while working hard to perform in front of people.

Give us the mind of Christ Jesus. Holy Spirit, search our motives and shine your light on the pride hidden within us. Help us this week to practise in earnest: examining our motives, hiding our good deeds, getting rid of the pride of titles, and learning to appreciate others.
Lord, we are willing to let you be King; we are willing to let you receive all the glory. Use our small lives to become vessels that reflect your glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the God of peace himself sanctify us completely. May the grace of the Lord be with us all always. Amen.
discussion: Philippians 2:5–7 says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” In your present daily living or ministry, what is one “right” you know you have but are willing to lay down for the Lord’s sake? What would laying it down look like in practice?

John 12:43 says that many of the rulers believed in Jesus but did not dare to confess it, “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” Think back to something recently where you cared a great deal about what others thought. What were you really longing for in that situation? If you brought that longing before the Father, how would he respond to you?
l083.title: Laying Down the Right to Glory
l083.subtitle: Jesus Our Role Model (Part 2)
l083.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: What Is Printed on Your Business Card?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to answer a question that is very simple, yet not easy to answer: suppose someone handed you a blank business card right now and asked you to print just one line on it — “the identity you most want people to know you by.” What would you print?

Some would print a job title: manager, teacher, doctor, engineer. Some would print a place of service: small-group leader, deacon, co-worker, pastor. Others would print a relationship: so-and-so’s father, so-and-so’s mother. That little card is really a mirror. It shows what our hearts value most, and it shows where we have placed our own worth.

In Jesus’ day the Roman Empire had a grand ceremony that drew the eyes of the whole city, called the “triumph.” When a general came home from a great victory, the Senate would allow him to wear a laurel wreath and stand in a four-horse triumphal chariot, riding through streets packed with people. Banners, spoils of war, captives, flowers — and all along the route the people shouted his name. It was the highest glory a man could receive in his lifetime. The church father Tertullian records in his Apology that at such a moment a man stood in the chariot behind the general, and he had only one task: amid the roaring waves of acclaim, to lean close to the general’s ear and keep reminding him, “Look behind you, and remember that you are only a man.”

Brothers and sisters, that is the most honest reminder humanity has ever devised — and also the one most easily drowned out by cheering. The higher a man stands, the less he can hear those words; the louder the applause, the less he can hear the voice of God.

And in that very same era, under that very same sky, another King entered a city. He had no triumphal chariot, only a donkey’s colt no one had ever ridden; he had no spoils of war, only twelve disciples still arguing about who was greatest; he had no laurel wreath — and a few days later he wore a crown of thorns. He was worthy of all glory, yet of his own accord he laid down the right to glory.

In the eyes of the world, glory means position, fame and power; but in the eyes of Jesus, true glory lies in humbling oneself and serving. He did not grasp at the glory of being called “King”; instead he served people in the posture of a servant. He did not demand that people exalt his name; he let the glory of God the Father be revealed through him.

Jesus’ example reminds us that serving is not lifting ourselves up but laying ourselves down; true honour lies not in what people call us, but in whether God is pleased with our hearts.

So in today’s lesson we are going to look together at three things: first, an office is not a title — glory belongs to God, not to man; second, our true identity in the Lord is a fivefold identification that runs from glory down to lowliness; third, when we lay down our freedom, we gain a far greater freedom.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The City That Loved Face the Most Receives the Letter That Cared for Face the Least
sections.html:
The author of Philippians is the apostle Paul. When he wrote this letter he was not in a spacious study but in prison. Based on church tradition and on clues within the letter itself — Paul mentions “the whole palace guard” and “those who are of Caesar’s household” (Philippians 1:13; 4:22) — most evangelical scholars believe the letter was written during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome, around AD 60 to 62.

The church that received it, in Philippi, was the first church in Europe, planted on Paul’s second missionary journey. Acts 16 records that wonderful story. At Troas Paul saw a vision of a man of Macedonia begging him, “Come over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9). Obeying the leading of the Holy Spirit, he crossed the sea, and by the river outside Philippi he met Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. Then he cast a spirit out of a slave girl, and for that he was beaten with rods and thrown into prison. At midnight in the cell he sang hymns of praise to God, the earth shook violently, and the jailer and his whole household came to the Lord. This church began with a businesswoman, a demon-possessed slave girl and a jailer — three people from completely different social classes, who became one family in Christ.

When we get to know the city of Philippi, we can understand the weight of this letter even better. In 42 BC a great battle that decided the fate of Rome broke out on the plain of Philippi. After the war, Octavian settled large numbers of retired soldiers there, making Philippi a Roman “colony.” Many of its residents held Roman citizenship, with tax exemptions and legal privileges. Though they lived in Macedonia, they dressed the Roman way, governed the Roman way, and held being Roman as their highest pride. Acts 16:21 records their accusation against Paul: they “advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.” One short sentence lays bare the whole city’s sense of identity.

More importantly, the first-century Mediterranean world was a classic “honour and shame” society. A person’s worth was not something he decided for himself; it was set by public opinion. Titles, the order of seating, how others addressed you, where you sat at a banquet — none of these were small matters; they were declarations of status. In such a culture, a “slave” was the person with the least honour, and the “cross” was the most shameful punishment of all. The Roman statesman Cicero even said that the very word “cross” should be kept far away not only from the bodies of Roman citizens, but from their thoughts, their eyes and their ears.

It was to just such a city, the city that loved face the most, that Paul wrote the letter that cared for face the least. He was not discussing abstract theology; he was dealing with a very concrete problem: there was discord in the church. In Philippians 4:2 Paul names Euodia and Syntyche and urges them “to think the same way in the Lord”; 1:15 says that some were preaching Christ out of envy and strife. So, just before today’s key passage, Paul first says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:3–4)

Then he sets a hymn before their eyes. Philippians 2:6–11 has been called the “Christ Hymn” by the church through the ages, and many scholars believe it was originally sung in the worship of the early church. Paul quotes it not to help the Philippians understand a little more Christology, but to get them living like this Christ. That is why the first sentence of the passage is a command: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: Jesus’ humbling of himself is not a story for us to admire; it is a set of footsteps for us to walk in. He laid down the right to glory so that we would learn to lay it down too.

sections.heading: 3. An Office Is Not a Title — Glory Belongs to God, Not to Man
sections.html:
1. The true meaning of “emptied himself”: not losing, but laying down a right

Our key passage says: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7)

There are three key words here, worth chewing on slowly.

The first is “form,” in the original Greek morphē. It refers to the true outward form that flows from one’s essential nature, not a disguise thrown on over the top. So “existing in the form of God” means he was God all along — fully and completely God. In the same way, “taking the form of a servant” was not playacting; he truly and really became a servant.

The second is “a thing to be grasped,” in the original harpagmos, meaning “a prize of war clutched and never let go.” Jesus’ equality with God was his from the beginning, not something he had seized; but he did not treat that equal standing as something he had to grip tightly and never release.

The third is “emptied himself,” in the original ekenōsen, literally “poured himself out.” This word is often misunderstood, so we need to be clear: when Jesus emptied himself, he did not empty himself of his deity; he did not stop being God for a while. Orthodox faith has always held that the incarnation is deity plus humanity, not deity minus something. What he poured out was “the right to glory” — he laid down the display of the honour, privilege and radiance that were rightfully his. He was willing to be wrapped in cloths in a manger, willing to sweat in a carpenter’s workshop, willing to have people point at him and say, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?”

So remember this sentence: emptying himself was not losing himself; emptying himself was laying down a right.

Jesus came into the world in the form of a servant, yet he came bearing God’s power and mission. He did not parade the title “Messiah”; again and again he told those he had healed not to spread the news. Nor did he demand that his disciples call him “Master”; instead, at the Last Supper he took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist and washed his disciples’ feet, one by one. When he had finished he said: “You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:13–15)

Brothers and sisters, notice Jesus’ logic. He did not say, “I’m not really the Lord, so I wash feet.” He said, “I really am the Lord, so I wash feet.” True authority is not for being served; it is for serving others.

2. An office is a function, not a rank

Yet many churches today have fallen into “the myth of titles.” The “offices” God gives were meant to build up the body of Christ, but they are often misused as “status symbols.”

Ephesians could not put it more clearly: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Look at the structure of this passage. What God gives are “gifts” and “offices,” and their purpose is “the perfecting of the saints, the work of serving, the building up of the body of Christ.” From beginning to end, an office is a verb, not a noun; a job, not a rank; it exists so that others may be built up, not so that I may be exalted.

Once an “office” is treated as a “title,” people begin to turn glory away from God and towards themselves. What was “I have been sent to serve” becomes “I am a person of standing”; what was “Lord, use me” becomes “People, notice me.” The distance between the two is only a single step — yet it is the distance between heaven and earth.

3. Can an office sin?

Here is a question worth quietly pondering: can an office sin?

The office of “pastor” was established by God to shepherd the flock. The office itself cannot sin; it is “people” who sin. But when people treat “pastor” as a status, a rank, a social position, then when a particular pastor falls, people wrongly conclude that “the office of pastor” has lost its dignity. And the result? The world no longer respects the church, nor does it respect God’s calling.

Hold this sentence in your heart: when people exalt titles, they lose their reverence for the office.

In many Western countries, people no longer see the pastor as anything sacred; some even regard it as just another job. That is precisely because people have humanised and secularised the spiritual office, forgetting that all of it was established for the glory of God.

God declared his position long ago: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” (Isaiah 42:8) Brothers and sisters, God does not compete with man for glory, because glory never belonged to man in the first place; but neither will God ever hand his glory over to man, because that would destroy man.

4. The lesson of the moon, and Level 5 Leadership

Let’s look up at the moon. The moon is the brightest body in the night sky, and poets in every age and land have written its praises. But we all know a basic astronomical fact: the moon gives off no light of its own. Its albedo is only about 12 per cent — that is, it reflects back just over a tenth of the sunlight that falls on it — and yet that is enough to light up the whole night.

The moon’s glory lies entirely in facing the sun; the moon’s greatest danger would be to think the light was its own. Brothers and sisters, every one of us who serves is a moon. When someone says, “You preached so well,” “Your singing was so moving,” “Your small group is so full of life” — that is the most dangerous moment, because it is so easy to mistake reflected light for light of our own. And the moment the moon turns its back on the sun, it becomes the biggest patch of darkness in the dark.

In the field of management there is a similar finding. In his research study Good to Great, Jim Collins analysed decades of corporate data and identified eleven companies that made the leap from good to great. The research team had expected to find a group of dazzling, self-promoting celebrity CEOs — and were astonished at what they found instead. The leaders who took these companies to lasting greatness almost all shared one trait: they were profoundly modest, disliked talking about themselves, gave the credit to others and to luck, and shouldered the responsibility themselves. Collins called them “Level 5 leaders.” A principle that management science took decades and mountains of research to discover, the Bible wrote down two thousand years ago: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

5. Applying 321: return to our originally intended position and let God be God

The 321 vision tells us that the root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and the root of every problem is pride. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. What the serpent said in the Garden of Eden was: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — that is leaving our originally intended position.

And what is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

“The myth of titles,” when you get to the bottom of it, is leaving our originally intended position. It is sitting in the “servant’s” seat as though it were the “master’s” seat, treating the “messenger” as the “one who gives the message,” mistaking the “reflector of light” for the “source of light.” And Jesus did exactly the opposite: he already held the highest position of all, yet he willingly went down to the lowest place, so that God the Father might receive all the glory in him.

The first of the Three Foundations says: Jesus is my role model. Brothers and sisters, today’s first lesson is this — like Jesus, treat your office as the work of serving, not as a badge of status; treat applause as reflected moonlight, and send all of it back to the sun.

sections.heading: 4. Our True Identity in the Lord — a Fivefold Identification from Glory Down to Lowliness
sections.html:
If we are not to take titles as our glory, then how should we see ourselves? The Bible gives us five identities in the Lord, and every one of them points towards “humility” and “surrender.” These five identities are not five options; they are one road — a road that goes lower the further you walk, yet grows brighter the further you walk.

First: brothers and sisters (Matthew 23:8)

The Lord Jesus says: “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.” (Matthew 23:8)

The background to this saying is pointed. Just two verses earlier Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees “love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues, the salutations in the marketplaces, and to be called ‘Rabbi, Rabbi’ by men” (Matthew 23:6–7). “Rabbi” originally meant “my honoured one, my master.” Jesus is not forbidding the distinction between teacher and student; he wants to tear down the ladder of rank that is stacked up out of forms of address.

So he goes on: “But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:11–12)

In Christ we share one Father; we are one family, equal with one another and loving one another. “All of you are brothers” — this is the foundation of the spiritual family, reminding us never to rank one another by our place of service or by how many years we have been believers.

California’s redwoods are the tallest trees on earth; the tallest of them stands more than 115 metres high — over thirty storeys. The remarkable thing is that trees this tall have very shallow roots, usually only two to four metres deep. Why don’t they fall over? Because redwoods never grow alone. They grow in groves and forests, and underground their roots intertwine and lock together, forming an invisible net. When the wind comes, every tree is held up by the whole forest.

In 1995 the psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary put forward their well-known theory of “the need to belong.” Reviewing a large body of research, they concluded that forming stable, caring bonds with others is a basic and universal human psychological need, strong enough to affect our emotions, our health and even our lifespan. When God made man he said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” Human beings were never made for isolation.

321’s “235 relationships” say exactly this: join with a selfless person to form a “2,” becoming spiritual companions; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, when we call one another “brother” and “sister,” we are reaching our roots out towards one another, so that the whole forest stands together.

Second: servants (Matthew 20:26–28)

Jesus says: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:26–28)

The occasion of these words is also telling. The mother of Zebedee’s sons came with her two sons and asked Jesus to let one sit at his right and the other at his left. When the other ten disciples heard, they were indignant — not because the two shouldn’t have asked, but because they themselves hadn’t asked first. Brothers and sisters, the old self is still arranging the seating even in the presence of Jesus.

Jesus uses two words. “Servant” is diakonos in the original, someone who waits at table, passing dishes and always on call; it later became the word for “deacon.” “Bondservant” is doulos, someone who belongs entirely to his master. Jesus’ meaning is clear: in the kingdom of God, the way up is the way down.

Those who serve the Lord are not there to be served but to serve others. The higher the position, the heavier the responsibility; the more honoured the standing, the more we need to learn to bend down.

In 1970 Robert Greenleaf, a former executive at AT&T, published a short essay, “The Servant as Leader,” putting forward a view that was quite counter-intuitive at the time: the best leaders are those who first resolve to be servants, and the test of such a leader is whether those he leads grow as a result — healthier, freer, more capable of serving others themselves. That essay went on to shape half a century of leadership studies. But, brothers and sisters, this is no new idea. It is the example Jesus set two thousand years ago — and he did not only say it, he did it: he gave his life as a ransom for many.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A true servant sees people before results, and cares about relationships before outcomes. For in the kingdom of God, ministry was never the goal — people are.

Third: slaves (Romans 6:22)

Paul says: “But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.” (Romans 6:22) The word for “servants” here is doulos — slaves.

Notice the two movements in this verse: “being made free from sin,” and then “having become servants of God.” In Paul’s mind there is no third way; a person is either a slave of sin or a slave of God. The idea of “being nobody’s slave” is really an illusion.

We have been bought back by the precious blood of Jesus. “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) We no longer belong to ourselves; we belong to him. A slave has no rights of his own, only his master’s will.

The Old Testament has a beautiful picture of this. Under the law, a Hebrew servant served for six years and in the seventh could go free. But “if the servant shall plainly say, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children. I will not go out free;’ then his master shall bring him to God, and shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.” (Exodus 21:5–6) That pierced ear was a lifelong mark, declaring to everyone: I could have gone, but because of love I chose to stay.

Brothers and sisters, true freedom is not having no master; it is choosing the right master. True obedience is not forced; it is willing. The psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, who developed “self-determination theory,” made an important discovery: when people do something because they embrace its value and have internalised it as part of themselves, their motivation, engagement and perseverance far outstrip those of people driven by outside pressure or lured by rewards. In other words, the strongest force is not compulsion but willingness.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. That is just what Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The moment we hand ourselves over is the moment we truly find ourselves.

Fourth: prisoners (Ephesians 3:1)

Paul calls himself “the prisoner of Christ Jesus”: “For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles.” (Ephesians 3:1) And in Ephesians 4:1 he says again: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”

Pay attention to Paul’s choice of words. He does not say, “I am Rome’s prisoner”; he says, “I am the prisoner of Christ Jesus.” The very same chain means something completely different depending on how you look at it. In Roman eyes it was an instrument of punishment; in Paul’s eyes it was an office. He had not been locked up by Caesar; he had been sent into prison by Christ.

He gave up his freedom for the gospel, yet he counted his chains an honour, because he knew that a body shut up in prison could still release the mighty power of God. He says: “Now I desire to have you know, brothers, that the things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the Good News, so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ.” (Philippians 1:12–13) And again: “I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained.” (2 Timothy 2:9)

In 1660, in England, a preacher who had started out as a tinker, John Bunyan, was thrown into Bedford jail for refusing to stop preaching the gospel, and was held there, all told, for twelve years. In prison he had no pulpit, no congregation, no title — only a pen. Released in 1672, he was imprisoned again for preaching in 1675, and it is generally held that The Pilgrim’s Progress was written during that second, shorter spell in prison. After its publication in 1678 the book was translated into more than a hundred languages, and for over three hundred years it has led countless people onto the road to heaven. Brothers and sisters, they could lock up Bunyan’s body, but they could not lock up the word of God.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Paul’s prison and Bunyan’s cell tell us one thing: even when humble people are restricted, they can still glorify God. For our freedom has never been in the hands of our circumstances; it is in the hands of the Lord.

Fifth: condemned prisoners (1 Corinthians 4:9)

Paul says: “For, I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men.” (1 Corinthians 4:9)

The verse just before is full of Paul’s heartache: some in the Corinthian church thought they were already filled, already rich, already reigning as kings (1 Corinthians 4:8). They were splitting into factions in the church, comparing whose leader was more spiritual. Paul answers them with a stunning picture: do you think you’re sitting in the stands, reigning as kings? We apostles are the condemned prisoners marched into the middle of the arena, saved for the final act.

“Spectacle” is theatron in the original — the theatre. “Sentenced to death” is epithanatios, describing those already condemned and awaiting execution. In the Roman arena such people were sent out last on the programme, and the whole crowd knew they would not walk out alive.

Paul says: that is us. We no longer belong to the world, we no longer live for ourselves, and we are ready at any moment to lay down our lives for the Lord. He puts it without the slightest ambiguity: “I die daily.” (1 Corinthians 15:31)

That is how Stephen finished his life. As he was being stoned to death, Scripture records: “But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and said, ‘Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!’” (Acts 7:55–56) Brothers and sisters, elsewhere the Bible says Jesus is “seated on the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1); only here does it say he is “standing at the right hand of God.” The Lord stood up — for a condemned prisoner who, in the world’s eyes, was as lowly as dust, the King of heaven rose to his feet.

An identity like this is utterly lowly in human eyes, yet utterly glorious in God’s eyes.

The ladder of five identities

Brothers and sisters, put these five identities together: brothers and sisters, servants, slaves, prisoners, condemned prisoners. From the first to the fifth is a gradual road of humility. The further along you go, the more you lay down self; the more you lay down self, the more you are able to live out the glory of Christ.

On the world’s ladder, people climb up rung by rung, and at the top there is nothing left but themselves; on heaven’s ladder, people step down rung by rung, and at the bottom there is nothing left but Christ.

And this is the very road the Lord Jesus himself walked. He went from the form of God to the form of a servant; from the form of a servant to the likeness of men; from the likeness of men to death; and from death to death on a cross. Five steps, each one lower than the last. And then Scripture says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” (Philippians 2:9)

Notice that word — “Therefore.” Exaltation is not won by striving; exaltation is the result of humbling.

sections.heading: 5. Lay Down Your Freedom and Gain a Greater Freedom
sections.html:
1. A ladder that seems to go backwards

In the world’s eyes, those five identities seem to become ever lowlier and ever less free: brothers and sisters are at least equals; servants must take orders; slaves do not even own their own bodies; prisoners lose their movement; condemned prisoners lose even their lives. It is a downward ladder, each step narrower than the last.

But in the Lord it is exactly the opposite. The more we lay down worldly freedom, the more we experience heavenly freedom.

Only when we lay down our own control can we be led by the Holy Spirit; only when we lay down our own face can we serve sincerely; only when we lay down our own glory can the glory of Christ be seen.

True freedom is not “I do whatever I want”; it is “I let the Lord do whatever he wants.”

2. What the Bible says about freedom

The Bible has never defined freedom as having no constraints. The Lord Jesus says: “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36) True freedom is a release of identity — being redeemed out from under the power of sin.

Paul says: “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.” (Galatians 5:1) But he immediately goes on: “For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.” (Galatians 5:13)

Peter puts it even more directly: “as free, and not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.” (1 Peter 2:16)

Brothers and sisters, do you see? In the Bible, “freedom” and “serving” have never been opposites. The purpose of being set free is to be free to love and free to serve. A person bound by his own face is not free; a person who cannot be at peace without others’ approval is not free; a person who must be addressed by a certain title in order to feel valuable may look impressive, but is in fact the most tightly bound of all.

3. More choice, less freedom

People today assume that freedom means the more options the better. But psychological research has given us a surprising answer. In 2000 Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford University carried out what became a very famous experiment in an upmarket supermarket. At a tasting stand they sometimes set out twenty-four kinds of jam and sometimes only six. The twenty-four jams drew more people to stop — but in the end only about 3 per cent actually bought any; the six jams drew fewer people, yet about 30 per cent of them got out their money and bought.

Four times the options, yet the purchase rate fell to a tenth. The researchers called this “choice overload.” Unlimited options, it turns out, don’t make people freer; they only make people more anxious, slower to decide and less satisfied with what they decide.

That is a portrait of many people’s lives. Anything is possible, and so nothing is certain; they grab at everything, and so they can hold on to nothing. But when someone says to the Lord, “I want only your will,” they are set free from endless comparing, calculating and worrying over gain and loss. Brothers and sisters, the real lightness of life does not come from having more options; it comes from having only one Master.

4. The kite and its string; pressure and life

Think of a kite. A kite is held by a string. The string looks like a restriction, but it is the very reason the kite can fly. The headwind can lift it high only because the string is holding it from below. If the string snaps, the kite does not gain its freedom; it begins to fall.

Here is an example even closer to home. Standing at sea level, every square centimetre of our bodies bears about a kilogram of atmospheric pressure; added up, the weight pressing on an adult’s whole body comes to well over ten tonnes. Yet we feel nothing, and we are not crushed. Why? Because there is an equal pressure inside us, pushing out from within against the pressure outside.

Brothers and sisters, what a beautiful spiritual picture this is. The pressure outside cannot crush us — not because the outside pressure is small, but because Christ is within. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Only a person filled with Christ on the inside can bear being humbled on the outside. Conversely, a person who is empty inside has no choice but to grab desperately at titles, applause and other people’s approval on the outside to hold himself up.

5. Nothing to boast of

When we see clearly who we are in the Lord, we discover that all the glory belongs to him, and we have nothing to boast of.

Paul asks it pointedly: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Our gifts were received, our opportunities were received, even our breath was received. If all of it was received, what is there to boast about?

That is why Paul places his conclusion at the summit of Romans: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

Of him — he is the beginning; through him — he is the way; to him — he is the end. From start to finish it is all him. Where in the middle is there any room for our names?

321 says: we must shift from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Titles are earthly and temporary; the fruit of an office is heavenly and eternal. Human applause will fade, but the Lord’s “Well done, good and faithful servant” will never change.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he laid down the right to glory, and we lay it down in the same way. The Bible is my standard — we do not measure our worth by human standards, but by the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — only the Holy Spirit can make a person willing, from the heart, to go low, because the flesh only ever climbs upwards.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — there is only one King, and I return to my originally intended position as a servant; let Jesus receive all the glory — not most of it, all of it.

The Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: the higher up you are, the more people serve you. God’s system is turned upside down: the higher up you are, the more people you serve. Jesus is at the very top, yet he washed feet at the very bottom — that is God’s system.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred people must be seen, must be addressed properly, must be lifted up; selfless people ask only one thing — that people would see Jesus. Selflessness is not reducing yourself to zero; it is placing yourself into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan once said, “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14). His weapon is pride; but pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Only humility inspiring humility can bring about a win for both. When one person in a family bends down first, the air in the whole home changes; when one co-worker lays down the argument first, the whole team is healed.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first thing we ask for today is a change of mindset — from “a title is glory” to “an office is a trust.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and only when relationships change does ministry change. The order cannot be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Nor can the priority of relationships be reversed: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Much of people’s pain comes from putting “things” first — and so the more they do, the drier they become.

The 920 practice says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” The person beside you today — your spouse, your child, your colleague, the hardest-to-get-along-with brother in your small group — is God’s lesson for you to practise the “0.” Live out selflessness before them, and let the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in you: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

The Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First we are led by the Holy Spirit, and only then do we truly understand; with understanding we live out life; with life we can serve; and at the end of serving, all the glory goes to God. Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end this road runs in only one direction — not me going up, but him going up. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four concrete practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice One: Change the way you address people

Learn to call one another “brother” and “sister,” as a reminder of our equality and unity.

Information: first read Matthew 23:8–12 three times and memorise the words “all of you are brothers.” Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show you which form of address your heart cares about most. Conviction: confess before the Lord — my worth is not given by what others call me; it is settled by the precious blood of Jesus. Implementation: this week, change how you address at least three people, calling them “brother” or “sister.” Evaluation: each night ask yourself, did someone’s title change the way I spoke to them today? Correction: if so, tell the Lord you are sorry in prayer, and adjust next time. Repetition: make it a month-long habit, not a one-day inspiration. Multiplication: bring this practice into your small group and invite everyone to do it together.

Practice Two: Cultivate a servant’s attitude

Take the initiative to serve, and whether the task is great or small, do it as for the Lord.

Information: memorise Colossians 3:23 — “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” Revelation: let the Holy Spirit point out the hidden thoughts in your heart that say, “I shouldn’t have to do this sort of thing.” Conviction: believe that in God’s eyes no act of service is small, because the measure is not the size of the task but the direction of the heart. Implementation: every day, deliberately do one act of service that no one will know about and no one will thank you for — wash a stack of dishes, put away the chairs, quietly pray for someone. Evaluation: afterwards, is your heart sweet or resentful? Correction: if there is resentment, ask the Lord to exchange the heart that works “for men” for a heart that works “for the Lord.” Repetition: forty days in a row. Multiplication: bring a brother or sister to do it with you.

Practice Three: Willingly lay down your rights

At home, at church or at work, take the initiative to lay down the argument and lay down control.

Information: read Philippians 2:5–8 again and again, and especially remember the words “but emptied himself.” Revelation: ask the Lord to show you which right you are least willing to lay down — the right to have the last word? The right to receive an apology? Or the right to arrange other people’s lives? Conviction: acknowledge that Jesus laid down rights far greater than these. Implementation: this week, choose a conversation you would normally have fought to the bitter end, and stop of your own accord — listen to the end first, then respond; or simply swallow that “I told you so.” Evaluation: after laying it down, is the relationship closer or more distant? Correction: if you have substituted suppression for humility, ask the Lord to give you genuine gentleness. Repetition: treat every conflict as a chance to practise. Multiplication: share as a testimony what God did after you laid down your right.

Practice Four: Reflect on your identity

Meditate on “I am a slave of Christ,” and seek his will in everything.

Information: memorise Galatians 2:20 and Romans 6:22. Revelation: in the stillness of your early-morning devotion, ask the Holy Spirit to engrave this identity on the tablet of your heart. Conviction: say to the Lord, I was bought with a price; I am not my own. Implementation: every morning, let the first words you say on rising be to the Lord: “Today I am your servant; please send me.” Evaluation: at the end of the day, look back — how many of today’s decisions did I first ask my Master about? Correction: hand back to him the places where you went your own way. Repetition: let this sentence become the first thought each time you open your eyes. Multiplication: teach your children and your disciples to begin their day this way too.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that business card we began with.

True honour is not being called “Pastor So-and-so” or “Leader So-and-so”; it is that when people see you, they can see the likeness of Jesus. The more we lay down human glory, the more God can receive his glory in us.

Jesus laid down the right to glory and took the form of a servant, teaching us that the highest glory of serving is the willingness to humble ourselves. He was not raised up by a title; rather, he revealed true honour through the cross.

The Roman general needed someone behind him whispering, “Remember that you are only a man,” because he could so easily forget who he was. But our Lord needed no one to remind him; from the beginning he knew who he was — and precisely because he knew who he was, he dared to bend down and wash feet. Brothers and sisters, only those who truly know who they are before God are unafraid to humble themselves.

So today, let us also learn his likeness — lay down human glory, live out a servant’s heart, and let God receive all the glory in our lives.

Let us make this declaration of faith together:

Lord, you laid down the right to glory and took the form of a servant, becoming our example of serving. Help me to lay down the praise and position people give, and in my serving to seek your pleasure alone. Let me be your servant willingly, a blessing to my brothers and sisters, glorifying your name all my life.

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:5–8)
practices: Change the way you address people
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we bow down before you. Thank you for sending your only beloved Son, who, existing in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant and was made in the likeness of men, becoming obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross.

Lord, we confess that we often do the very opposite. We spend our whole lives striving for the things you spent your whole life laying down. We care more about what people call us than about how you see us; we are more afraid of being overlooked than of offending you. Forgive us.
Holy Spirit, change our mindset this very day, and let us see that an office is a trust, not a badge; serving is grace, not seniority; applause is moonlight, not our own light.

Help us, at home, at church and at work, to be willing to be brothers and sisters, servants and slaves — even willing to be prisoners for the Lord, people who die daily for the Lord. Give us a gentle and humble heart, so that whatever position we are in, when people see us they see Jesus.
May all glory, praise and dominion be to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, forever and ever. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Take a quiet moment to think: what do you most care about being called? Which need inside you does that form of address satisfy? “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Share with your small group which “right to glory” you are willing to lay down, starting this week.

Of the five identities — brothers and sisters, servants, slaves, prisoners and condemned prisoners — which one have you reached so far? Which is the hardest for you to step into? “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7) Pray for one another, asking the Lord for strength to take that step.

sections.heading: Introduction: An Age in Which Everyone Wants to Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we are going to reflect together on a lesson that looks very small, yet takes a whole lifetime to learn: learning to hide ourselves, so that Jesus is seen.

We live in an age unlike any before it. One mobile phone is a television station; one account is a stage. That in itself is not a bad thing, and God uses these tools to spread the gospel too. But, brothers and sisters, this age has quietly planted a mindset in our hearts: being seen means you have value, and not being seen is as good as not existing.

There was a sister who had served on the worship team for three years. One Sunday she wasn’t on the platform at all; she was down on the floor setting out chairs and looking after the children. After the service she sat in her car and suddenly felt like crying. She said, “I was doing exactly the same thing — for the Lord. But nobody saw it, and I feel as if today was wasted.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had a moment like that? You did something good that nobody knew about, and your heart felt a little empty; you were overlooked once, and your heart felt a little sour. That little emptiness, that little sourness, is a very honest signal. It is telling us that inside our service there still lives an “I” that badly wants to be seen.

And our Lord Jesus, with his whole life, walked a path that ran in exactly the opposite direction.

He was the King of kings, yet he chose to be born in a manger, to grow up in Nazareth, and to spend thirty years as an unknown carpenter. With a single word he could still the wind and the waves, yet again and again he charged those he had healed, “Tell no one.” When the crowds wanted to make him king, he withdrew alone to the mountain. He had every “right to glory”, and time after time he laid it down.

That is the theme of this lesson: laying down the right to glory.

In the vision of Kingdom 321 we often say that the old self is self-centred and the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. And the side of pride that is hardest to detect hides inside our service — I am still serving God; I would just like to be seen by people a little while I’m at it.

The lesson puts it beautifully: true glory does not lie in being seen, but in letting Jesus be seen.

Today we will follow the lesson’s four key points and learn step by step: first, Jesus chose a way of serving that was “hidden” rather than “famous”; second, what people see should not be me, but Jesus; third, submarine service — being seen by God is better than being seen by people; fourth, facing ourselves honestly — on whom, in the end, is my focus?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Light of the Sermon on the Mount, and the Hiddenness in Mark
sections.html: Before we come to the key points, let’s set out the background clearly. Once you understand the background, the weight of these words is completely different.

sections.heading: 1. The Author, Audience and Times of Matthew’s Gospel
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). In those days a tax collector held a job his own people despised. Yet the Lord Jesus said to him, “Follow me,” and he got up and followed him. The man least likely to be used by God went on to write the first book of the New Testament; and throughout that whole book, when he mentions himself, he honestly labels himself “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). Brothers and sisters, that in itself is a silent sermon: a person changed by the Lord is no longer in a hurry to put a crown on his own name.

Matthew is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish believers. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily, explaining again and again that “this was to fulfil what the prophet said”, in order to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah the Jews had awaited for so many years.

sections.heading: 2. The Sermon on the Mount: The Charter of a Brand-New Kingdom
sections.html:
Our theme passage comes from Matthew 5 and belongs to the “Sermon on the Mount” (Matthew 5–7), the charter of the Kingdom of Heaven proclaimed by the Lord Jesus. He begins with the Beatitudes, turning our whole set of values upside down — blessed are the poor in spirit, blessed are those who mourn, blessed are the gentle. Straight after that he says, “You are the salt of the earth … You are the light of the world.”

Notice the order: first comes the “life” of the Beatitudes, and only then the “influence” of salt and light. This is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. We don’t start by working out how to shine; we first let our life be renewed by the Lord, and the light shines out naturally.

There is one more very important thing. In the very same discourse, right at the start of chapter 6, the Lord Jesus says, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

Matthew 5:16 tells us to let our light “shine before men”, yet 6:1 says, don’t do it “before men”. Do these two sayings contradict each other? Not at all. The difference is not whether we are seen, but who receives the glory once we have been seen. The conclusion of 5:16 is “glorify your Father who is in heaven”; the motive in 6:1 is “to be seen by them”. The very same good deed can be a lampstand, or it can be a stage.

“To be seen by them” in the original Greek is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι (pros to theathēnai). The verb’s root, θεάομαι (theaomai), means “to look at, to watch as a spectator”, and the English word theatre comes from this very root. The Lord Jesus’ point is a sharp one: don’t turn good works into a performance. No wonder he goes on to use the word “hypocrites” — in Greek ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs), which originally meant “an actor wearing a mask on the stage”.

sections.heading: 3. The “Messianic Secret” in Mark’s Gospel
sections.html:
Several of this lesson’s other passages come from Mark. Scholars point to a distinctive feature of this book which they call the “Messianic secret” — Jesus repeatedly forbids people to make him known.

After cleansing the man with leprosy he says, “See you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them” (Mark 1:44). After healing the deaf man with the speech impediment, “He commanded them that they should tell no one, but the more he commanded them, so much the more widely they proclaimed it” (Mark 7:36).

Why? Because the Messiah the Jews of that day had in mind was a political liberator who would overthrow Rome. Had Jesus allowed the crowds to exalt him on their own understanding, the way of the cross would have been drowned in human enthusiasm. He had to walk the whole way of the cross first; only then would people truly understand who he was.

Mark 1:45 records the result: once his fame spread, “Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places.” Brothers and sisters, fame never comes free.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Chose a Way of Serving That Was “Hidden”, Not “Famous”
sections.html:
Right at the outset the lesson points to a surprising fact: in the Gospels, Jesus often avoided the crowds and refused to be exalted by people.

Scripture: Three Deliberate Withdrawals

The first was after a healing. “Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, ‘I want to. Be made clean.’ When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was made clean. He strictly warned him, and immediately sent him out, and said to him, ‘See you say nothing to anybody’” (Mark 1:41–44).

The second was after a busy day. “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The evening before, “all the city was gathered together at the door” — the most “successful” night of his ministry. The next morning, before it was light, he did not go out to receive applause; he withdrew to the wilderness to meet with the Father.

The third was when the applause was loudest. After feeding the five thousand with five loaves and two fish, “Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). Notice the words “by force”. This is the hardest kind of pressure to refuse — not pressure to sin, but pressure to be king.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: He Is the Servant Who “Will Not Strive, Nor Shout”

Why did Jesus act this way? Matthew gives us the best explanation. Matthew 12:15–19 records: “Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all, and commanded them that they should not make him known: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, ‘Behold, my servant whom I have chosen; my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations. He will not strive, nor shout; neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets.’”

“They should not make him known” is not polite modesty; it is the portrait of the Servant that the prophet foretold some seven hundred years earlier. True authority has no need to strive; he is so great that he does not need to prove himself.

The lesson is spot on: Jesus would not let people make miracles the foundation of their faith, nor let fame replace the way of the cross. What he sought was not for people to praise him, “How great you are,” but for people to turn and say, “How great God is!”

The God Who Hides Himself

This disposition is not Jesus’ alone; it is the disposition of the triune God. Isaiah 45:15 says, “Most certainly you are a God who has hidden yourself, God of Israel, the Savior.”

The word for “who has hidden yourself” in Hebrew is מִסְתַּתֵּר (mistatter), from the root סָתַר (satar, to hide). It is in the reflexive form, meaning “to make oneself hidden”. God is not hidden by anyone else; he chooses to hide himself.

And notice the context of this verse. Isaiah 45 is about Cyrus, king of Persia. More than a hundred years before Cyrus was born, God called him by name: “I have called you by your name” (Isaiah 45:4). All his life Cyrus never came to know this God — the text says, “though you have not known me” — and yet God used him to set the exiled Judeans free to return home. Brothers and sisters, this is the God who hides himself: he works behind the scenes of history, leaving no signature and no photograph, yet moving the course of the whole world.

He does not need to be publicised; he only needs to be revealed.

An Example from Life: The Invisible Light

There is a beautiful scientific fact here. Light itself is actually invisible. Look side-on at a beam of sunlight in a vacuum and you will see no beam at all; the reason we can see the shaft of light from a cinema projector is that dust in the air scatters it. In other words, the presence of light is made known through the things it illuminates. Light never shines for its own sake.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the Lord Jesus meant by “You are the light of the world”. When a Christian truly shines, what people remember is not the light, but the path it lit up.

Applying 321: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position; Humility Is Returning to It

The 321 vision says that pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Jesus’ withdrawal in John 6:15 is the perfect demonstration. The crowd wanted to give him a throne — a premature, cheap throne that bypassed the cross. Had he accepted it, he would have left the position the Father had appointed for him. Withdrawing to the mountain was returning to that position — letting the Father be the Father and the Son be the Son.

Our temptations today are often variations on that same temptation: someone wants to set a crown on your head, and it is not the crown the Father means to give you. Brothers and sisters, learn to withdraw to the mountain.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: What People See Should Not Be Me, but Jesus
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point brings us back to the theme passage.

Scripture: A Lampstand Is Not a Stage

“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:14–16)

This passage is often misread as “Christians should be bold about putting themselves forward”. Look carefully at three details.

First, the Lord says, “You are the light of the world,” not “You must find a way to become light.” This is identity. John 8:12 says, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” Our light is moonlight, borrowed from him.

Second, the picture the Lord uses is a “stand”, a lampstand. A lampstand’s job is to hold the lamp up high so that its light reaches further. The lampstand itself never gives off light, and nobody walks into a room and compliments the lampstand. Brothers and sisters, we are the lampstand, not the lamp.

Third, the passage concludes, “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” If good works don’t carry people’s eyes to the Father in heaven, they are only a handsome performance.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: The Witness of the Early Disciples

When Peter healed the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate, everyone was amazed. Peter immediately moved the focus away from himself: “By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all” (Acts 3:16).

In this one short verse, “his name” appears twice. Peter did not say, “Our faith is so great.” He said, “By faith in his name.”

Now look at Acts 4:13: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” What amazed the council was not their education, not their eloquence, but this — “these two men had been with Jesus.”

That is the highest praise there is. When people look at you, what they recognise is the fragrance of Jesus. Second Corinthians 2:14 says, “Now thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place.” What is the nature of a fragrance? You can smell it, but you can’t grasp it; it lingers on a person, but it isn’t that person’s own.

An Example from Scripture: He Must Increase, but I Must Decrease

John the Baptist understood this better than anyone in the whole Bible. When his disciples came to him, jealous, and said, “Everyone is coming to him,” John’s reply became the motto of servants of God in every generation since:

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

In the original, “increase” is αὐξάνω (auxanō, to grow) and “decrease” is ἐλαττόω (elattoō, to lessen, to become smaller). This is a continuing action in progress — not a one-off decision, but a lifetime of letting yourself become smaller.

And the Lord Jesus’ verdict on him was this: “Among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer” (Matthew 11:11). Brothers and sisters, do you see the wonderful contrast? All his life he worked at becoming smaller, and the Lord said no one was greater than he.

Psychology: We Want to Be Seen More Than We Think

Psychology has a thoroughly documented phenomenon called the “self-serving bias”. In a classic 1975 review, Dale Miller and Michael Ross showed that people tend to credit their successes to themselves and blame their failures on circumstances. A 1981 study by the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson in Acta Psychologica was even more direct: among the American drivers surveyed, about 93 per cent believed their driving skill was above the median. Mathematically, that is impossible.

Brothers and sisters, this is not meant to condemn us; it is meant to make us honest. If we overrate ourselves even behind the steering wheel, how much more in the pulpit, or when we are being praised? The Bible’s diagnosis came earlier and goes deeper: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9)

sections.heading: Applying 321: Jesus Is the Focal Point
sections.html:
What the 321 Vision Says: Jesus Is the Focal Point — Not Ourselves, Not Others, Not Our Circumstances.

The lesson’s words are worth memorising: if Jesus is the focal point of our service, we can be used by God; if the focal point is ourselves, then even if we are lifted up, we will soon fall. True “fame” is not people remembering my name, but people coming to know the name of Jesus through me.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Submarine Service — Being Seen by God Is Better Than Being Seen by People
sections.html:
The lesson uses a vivid picture: Jesus calls us to be “submarines”, not “aircraft carriers”.

A Picture: The Aircraft Carrier and the Submarine

In human eyes an aircraft carrier is dazzling. It is like a floating city; wherever it goes, every satellite in the world can see it. A submarine is the exact opposite: it moves silently through the deep sea, giving off no light and making no sound, straining even to keep its own position hidden. It puts its greatest effort not into being seen, but into not being seen.

But, brothers and sisters, though the submarine is unseen, at the decisive moment it can exert enormous influence. What an aircraft carrier fears most is often the very submarine it cannot find.

The lesson draws a crucial conclusion: spiritual life is not measured by exposure, but by depth.

Science Bears It Out: What Can Be Seen Is Only Ever a Small Part

The natural world preaches this truth everywhere. Sea ice has a density of about 920 kilograms per cubic metre, and seawater about 1,025, so the part of a floating iceberg that shows above the surface is only about a tenth of its volume. What really decides how stable it is and how big it is lies in the nine-tenths below the water.

Plants are the same. In a study published in 1937, the American botanist H. J. Dittmer measured the root system of a single rye plant and found that the roots alone ran to some six hundred and twenty kilometres, and with the root hairs added the total length came to more than ten thousand kilometres. Above ground you see a grass a few dozen centimetres tall; below ground, out of sight, are more than ten thousand kilometres of lifelines.

Brothers and sisters, where will you put your effort? Into the tenth that shows above the waves, or the nine-tenths in the deep?

Scripture: The Father Who Sees in Secret

The Lord Jesus’ teaching could not be clearer: “But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6).

The Greek for “in secret” is κρυπτός (kryptos), meaning “hidden, concealed”; the English word cryptography comes from it. The Father is right there in that hidden place: he is not waiting for you in the applause; he is waiting for you behind the closed door.

In the same chapter the Lord speaks of three things — giving, prayer and fasting — and all three times he closes with the same pattern of words (Matthew 6:4, 6:6, 6:18). Three repetitions mark the Lord’s emphasis.

And his verdict on the other kind of person is this: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). In the original, this phrase is commercial language, meaning “the receipt has been issued; the account is settled in full.” Brothers and sisters, this is a very solemn word: the moment human applause breaks out, the account in heaven is closed. Do you want to collect now, or collect then?

The lesson says it well: this is the spiritual order of glory — it isn’t that people see you first; it is that God sees you first.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: Every Servant of God Has Taken the Lesson of “Hiddenness”

The lesson mentions Moses, John the Baptist, Elijah and Paul, and it is a very accurate observation. Almost everyone God has used mightily was first prepared in hiddenness.

Moses spent forty years in Pharaoh’s palace; at forty he struck out in his own strength, and ended up fleeing into the wilderness. Acts 7:30 says, “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.” Forty years of shepherding: God was wearing away a prince’s “self”.

Before Elijah’s great victory on Mount Carmel, God first said to him, “Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan” (1 Kings 17:3). He had to be hidden by the brook before he could stand on the mountain.

And John the Baptist? “The child was growing and becoming strong in spirit, and was in the desert until the day of his public appearance to Israel” (Luke 1:80). The wilderness was his seminary.

Nor did Paul, after he came to faith, rush off to hold evangelistic rallies; rather, “I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus” (Galatians 1:17).

And our Lord himself spent thirty of his thirty-three and a half years in Nazareth. “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them … And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:51–52). Thirty years hidden, three and a half years of ministry — that ratio deserves our quiet meditation.

The Witness of History: A Prayer Meeting No One Saw

On 13 August 1727, in a little village in eastern Germany called Herrnhut, “the Lord’s watch”, a group of Moravian Brethren believers who had fled from Bohemia experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit during a communion service. After that revival they held no great evangelistic rallies. They did just one very unremarkable thing: they divided into shifts and prayed in turn, twenty-four hours a day, without a break. That prayer went on for more than a hundred years, and the missionaries later sent out from this little village reached the West Indies, Greenland and Africa. A group of people whose names nobody remembers prayed in secret for a hundred years and changed the history of modern missions.

The New Testament has a man like this too. Colossians 4:12 says, “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.” The Greek for “striving” is ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnizomai), a word from the arena, for wrestling and combat. Where no one could see, he wrestled for his brothers and sisters.

Applying 321: Hidden in Christ

The lesson is exactly right: “hiding ourselves” is not running away from the community; it is choosing to hide ourselves in Christ. Colossians 3:3 says, “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” This is precisely what 321 calls selflessness.

Note this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Brothers and sisters, put a drop of water on a table and it soon dries up; put a drop of water into the ocean and it will never dry up. Being hidden is not disappearing; it is entering into the infinite.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Facing Ourselves Honestly — On Whom, in the End, Is My Focus?
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth key point turns the blade towards ourselves. In a generation where anyone can become a “celebrity”, we need all the more to examine ourselves: who, in the end, is the focus of my service?

Three Honest Questions

The lesson gives us three questions. Answer them quietly in your heart; there’s no need to say them aloud, because God already knows.

First, when people mention my service, is it my name they remember, or the name of Jesus?

Second, when someone else is praised, do I feel jealous or resentful inside?

Third, when others speak of what Jesus has done through me, am I quick to add, “Actually, I also …”?

The third question cuts deepest. That little “Actually, I also …” is often said lightly, naturally, wrapped in spiritual packaging, yet it gives away the real longing at the bottom of the heart: I want to be seen too.

Scripture: The Most Dangerous Kind of Piety

The Lord Jesus’ severest criticism of the Pharisees was not that they lacked piety, but that their piety was put on for people to see. “But they do all their works to be seen by men. They make their phylacteries broad, enlarge the fringes of their garments” (Matthew 23:5).

Notice that what they wore were “phylacteries”, boxes holding Scripture, and that in itself was not wrong (Deuteronomy 6:8). What was wrong was the motive — turning God’s word into an ornament for themselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most dangerous kind of sin, because it wears the robe of piety. The lesson asks very honestly whether we are truly “hidden in Christ”, or are still wrapping the “self” in a spiritual robe.

Psychology: The Spotlight Effect

In 2000, Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky of Cornell University in the United States published a famous series of experiments and named the “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on a very embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room full of people, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed. On average the participants guessed about half; in reality only about a quarter had.

The conclusion: we grossly overestimate how much attention other people pay to us. We always feel that a spotlight is following us around overhead, when in fact most people are busy looking at the one over their own heads. Brothers and sisters, this is very liberating news: the image you are working so hard to protect is not being watched by nearly as many people as you think. You can let it go.

Another study points us in an even more beautiful direction. Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia in Canada, Michael Norton of Harvard University and their colleagues published research in the journal Science in 2008 which found that people who spent money on others were happier than people who spent the same money on themselves. The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Famous Words

The evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with saying that a man’s character is what he is in the dark. And Paul puts it even more plainly: “For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends” (2 Corinthians 10:18).

Applying 321: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

If this kind of self-examination rests only on our own effort, it soon turns into another form of law, and can even become a new pride — “I understand humility better than other people do.”

The 321 vision reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Self-examination is not dissecting ourselves; it is opening our heart and letting the Holy Spirit shine his light in.

That is why David prayed like this: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). He did not say, “I will search myself.” He said, “Search me.”
