Only true humility can let people see nothing but Jesus. And true humility is not something I manufacture; it is something the Holy Spirit works out within me.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting Jesus Be Seen Is Letting Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson is the very heart of the 321 vision in a single sentence: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Philippians 2:6–8 says, “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” “Emptied himself” in Greek is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to pour out, to make oneself empty”. His glory was not snatched from him; he emptied himself. This is what “laying down the right to glory” means.

The Bible is my standard. We don’t judge by feelings whether “this counts as pride”; we let God’s word take the measure. Matthew 6:1 is a measuring rule, and John 3:30 is a measuring rule too.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Hiding ourselves is not suppressing ourselves. Suppression is forcing the self down by effort, and sooner or later it springs back; the work of the Holy Spirit is to make us genuinely no longer crave that position inside.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. There can be only one lead actor on a stage. When I step back one pace, he comes forward one more; if I don’t step back, I block him from view.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Isaiah 42:8 says, “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” Glory is not something we can grab, nor something we should try to.

Establish God’s system. The Worldly system is a pyramid: the higher you go, the fewer people there are and the more visible they become. God’s system is a body, and its most vital organs are often hidden deepest inside. First Corinthians 12:22 says, “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” The heart never goes up on stage, yet it never stops for a moment.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The heart the lesson describes, the one in a hurry to add “Actually, I also …”, is the self-centred life of the old self. And “letting Jesus be seen” is the selflessness of the new self.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan fell precisely because he wanted to raise his own seat higher. Isaiah 14:13–14 records his thoughts: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” Those five “I will”s are the template for all pride.

Our Lord walked in exactly the opposite direction: from heaven to the manger, and from the manger to the cross. Pride climbs upwards; humility goes downwards. But God’s law is this: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a team, as soon as one person starts grabbing the credit, everyone else immediately turns defensive and starts keeping score, and the ministry grinds to a halt; on the other hand, as soon as one person gives the credit away, the whole atmosphere of the team relaxes.

The Fivefold Change and the Shift of Perspective

What this lesson brings is exactly the fivefold change that 321 speaks of: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Where is the change of mindset here? From “I only have value when I’m seen” to “Being seen by God gives me value.”

It is also a shift of perspective: from man’s view to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the Worldly to the godly. Human applause is temporary; God’s reward is eternal.

And remember the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people turn it upside down and rush into ministry first; the ministry grows big, but the life inside grows empty. The Lord Jesus lived in Nazareth for thirty years before he came out to minister for three and a half.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. We practise living out a selfless (0) life, so that in that person the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit are borne — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that not one of these nine graces is called “fame”. And what is the nature of fruit? Fruit isn’t for the tree to eat. An apple tree never eats its own apples.

235 relationships: become a “2” with someone who lives selflessly, build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — and become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. What is the greatest joy of spiritual parents? That their children surpass them. A true spiritual father is overjoyed when, one day, people talk about his son without needing to mention his own name at all.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking It Through with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives four practices for daily living. We will use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work each one out in practice.

Practice 1: Serving in Secret

Deliberately do some acts of service that nobody knows about — visiting, giving, interceding — without seeking anything in return.

Information: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3).

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to show you that serving in secret isn’t losing out; it is banking the account in heaven.

Conviction: Settle it truly in your heart — the Father sees in secret, and that is enough.

Implementation: This week, do one good deed that nobody at all will know about; when it’s done, don’t post about it and don’t share it in your small group.

Evaluation: Afterwards, ask yourself: did I feel a little let down because nobody knew? That little disappointment is exactly the place the Lord wants to heal.

Correction: If you do feel let down, hand it over in prayer and say to the Lord, “This one was for you.”

Repetition: Once a week, for a whole year.

Multiplication: Don’t go teaching others how to do it; live it out, so that people are drawn to it.

Practice 2: Redirecting the Glory

When people praise you, turn at once to the Lord and say, “All of this is his grace.”

Information: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Revelation: Praise is like a ball: as soon as you catch it, pass it straight on; hold it too long and it sticks.

Conviction: I am a channel, not a reservoir.

Implementation: Prepare a sentence of your own, such as “Thank you — this really is the Lord’s grace.” Neither pretending nor taking the credit.

Evaluation: Watch for two extremes — accepting every word of it, or protesting too much. Sometimes protesting too much is a way of fishing for more praise.

Correction: Name the people who really deserve the credit, including the ones behind the scenes.

Repetition: Treat every compliment as another round of practice.

Multiplication: When you praise others, point the glory to God as well — “I can see God at work in you.”

Practice 3: The Focus Check

Ask yourself one question every day: today, did I make people see more of me, or more of Jesus?

Information: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Revelation: At the end of the day, let the Holy Spirit replay the day’s footage.

Conviction: Believe that this self-examination is not self-reproach; it is being loved.

Implementation: Every night, for one minute before you sleep, quietly ask this question.

Evaluation: Once a week, look back: in which situations am I most likely to turn the camera on myself?

Correction: For the situation where you stumble most easily, make a decision in advance.

Repetition: Let it become a bedtime habit, as natural as brushing your teeth.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion, become each other’s “2”, and ask each other this question every week.

Practice 4: Submarine Prayer

Pray for hidden service, asking God to let his glory be revealed in the hidden places.

Information: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6).

Revelation: See the members of the church whom no one sees — the ones setting out chairs, the ones washing cups, the mother at home praying for her children with tears.

Conviction: Believe that God sees them, every single one, without missing anyone.

Implementation: This week, pray for three “hidden” co-workers, and send each of them a short message to tell them, “I prayed for you.”

Evaluation: Do I only pray for the people on the platform?

Correction: Widen your intercession list to include people who will never be named.

Repetition: Once a week.

Multiplication: Lead your small group to pray together for the unseen, so that everyone’s eyes are turned towards them.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: True Glory Is the Radiance Hidden in Christ
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the lesson’s gentle reminder: “being seen by God” is worth more than “being seen by people”. When you are willing to be hidden in Jesus, in his own time he will let his glory shine through you. Don’t be in a hurry to be seen.

Jesus laid down the right to glory and chose to be a hidden servant. He did not pursue fame, yet he has influenced all of humanity; he did not pursue applause, yet he has brought the nations to bow before his name. Philippians 2:9–11 says, “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

Look at the order: first he emptied himself, then the Father exalted him. He did not fight for a single inch for himself, yet the Father gave him the name above every name.

First Peter 5:6 says, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” The timetable is in God’s hands, not ours; all we have to do is humble ourselves, and wait.

So today I want to issue a call to you, brothers and sisters.

First, hand over the microphone. The microphone you have been gripping all this time — today, pass it to Jesus.

Second, turn the camera around. Stop pointing it at yourself and focus it on the Lord who is worthy of the glory.

Third, be willing to go down into the deep. If God has not yet let you be seen, don’t be anxious: he is thickening your steel hull, so that you can dive deeper and travel further.

True glory is not the brilliance of being seen, but the radiance hidden in Christ. When we choose to be “hidden”, God’s glory can shine brightly on the earth through us.

This morning, let us declare together: Lord, I want to be a submarine in your hand — not asking to be seen, only asking to be used by you.

keyVerses: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:14–16)
“Most certainly you are a God who has hidden yourself, God of Israel, the Savior.” (Isaiah 45:15)
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you.

You existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. You had every right to glory, and time after time you laid it down. Lord, when we see you, we see what true greatness is.

Lord, forgive us. So often, while we serve you, we quietly keep a seat for ourselves; with our lips we say, “Glory to the Lord,” yet in our hearts we hope someone will remember our name. Cleanse our motives with your precious blood.

Holy Spirit, be our guide, so that deep within we truly no longer crave that position — not by suppressing it, but by being filled and satisfied with you. Teach us to serve in secret and to pray in the hidden place.
Lord, we are willing to be the lampstand and not the lamp; to be a submarine and not an aircraft carrier; to be the moon, reflecting your light.
Make our whole lives vessels through which Jesus is seen and God the Father is glorified.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: The Lord Jesus repeatedly charged people “that they should not make him known” (Matthew 12:16), and when the crowds wanted to make him king, he even “withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). In your present service or work, is there an “opportunity to be lifted up” from which you need to learn to step back? What is hardest for you about stepping back?

Question 2: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6). Share a time when you “served in secret”: nobody saw it at the time — what did you honestly feel inside? If you believe the Father truly sees in secret, what is one thing nobody will know about that you are willing to do this week?
l085.title: Let Jesus Be Seen
l085.subtitle: Jesus Our Role Model: Laying Down the Right to Glory
l085.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: A Generation Longing to Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Today we are going to learn together a lesson that seems to run completely against the current — learning to hide ourselves, even while God is using us greatly.

We live in a generation full of stages and spotlights. One mobile phone is a film studio; one account is a stage. Day and night the algorithm whispers the same sentence in our ear: you only exist if you’re seen; you only have value if you’re liked.

But, brothers and sisters, psychology gives us a very interesting reminder. In 2000, a team led by Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University, with Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Medvec, published experiments in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology that named the famous “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to guess: how many people noticed your shirt? The participants guessed about half; when the others were actually asked, only about a quarter had noticed.

The conclusion is blunt: we always assume we are standing under a spotlight, when in fact the light was never even switched on. We overestimate how much people are watching us, and underestimate how much God is watching us. We spend our whole lives performing for a crowd that isn’t actually looking at us, and forget the Father who sees in secret, who has never for one moment taken his eyes off us.

The life of the Lord Jesus followed a path that ran in exactly the opposite direction. He was the King of kings, yet he was born in a manger and spent thirty quiet years in a carpenter’s workshop in Nazareth; with a single word he could still the wind and the waves, yet again and again he charged those he had healed, “Tell no one”; when the crowds came to make him king by force, he withdrew alone to the mountain to pray.

The lesson puts it beautifully: he did miracles without seeking applause, and served people without seeking a name; what he let people see was not himself, but the glory of God the Father. True glory is glory hidden in humility.

How, then, can we keep hiding ourselves even while God is using us greatly? The Bible gives us a most precious principle, which this lesson calls “the three movements of hiddenness”.

Step one: be hidden in the body of Christ, and learn to serve as a team.

Step two: help others to be more successful than yourself.

Step three: lay down status and authority.

Finally, we will see that the hidden life actually brings out a deeper glory.

Brothers and sisters, these three movements are not three techniques; they are a downhill road — a downhill road the Lord Jesus himself walked first. Philippians 2 says that he “emptied himself”. The Greek behind “emptied himself” is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to pour oneself out”. Emptying is not becoming zero; emptying is making room, so that God’s glory can come and dwell. This is exactly what 321 says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; selflessness is not having nothing — it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out.

Brothers and sisters, in the kingdom of God the road down is the road up.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Letters and the Testimony of a Forerunner
sections.html: Before we unfold the four key points, let’s set out the background of the theme passages clearly. Once the background is clear, the weight of these words is completely different.

sections.heading: 1. John 3:30: The Forerunner’s Last Word
sections.html:
“He must increase, but I must decrease” was not a fine phrase spoken when things were going well; it was spoken as his following was draining away.

John 3 records that the Lord Jesus and his disciples were baptising in the Judean countryside, while John the Baptist was baptising at Aenon near Salim. John’s disciples came to him with obvious resentment: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). In today’s words: Teacher, everyone has gone over to his side, and there’s hardly anyone left here.

John’s reply is one of the most beautiful declarations of humility in the whole Bible. First he says, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3:27). Then he uses a wedding as a picture: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full” (John 3:29).

And then John speaks that sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

“Increase” in the original is αὐξάνειν (auxanein), meaning “to grow, to grow larger”; “decrease” is ἐλαττοῦσθαι (elattousthai), meaning “to become smaller, to diminish”. John means this: the direction of my whole life is to let my own shadow grow shorter and shorter, and his light grow longer and longer.

sections.heading: 2. Colossians 3:3: A Life Hidden in God
sections.html:
Colossians is one of the apostle Paul’s “Prison Epistles”, generally thought to have been written between AD 60 and 62, while Paul was a prisoner in Rome. The Colossian church was not founded by Paul personally; it was planted through Epaphras’ preaching of the gospel (Colossians 1:7). At the time the church faced a blended heresy: the rules of Jewish legalism, the mysticism of angel worship, and the asceticism that treated the body harshly. They had one thing in common — all of them exalted “my experience, my knowledge, my spiritual discipline”. Paul’s answer was to turn people’s eyes back to Christ.

In chapter 3 Paul states the turning point of the whole letter: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

The word “hidden” is κρύπτω (kryptō), here in the perfect passive, κέκρυπται, meaning “has been hidden, and remains hidden there”. Notice that the Bible does not tell us to “go and hide ourselves”; the Bible says we “have already been hidden”. Hiddenness is not a goal I must strive to achieve; hiddenness is a position I have already received. I don’t need to prove myself, because my life is already in the safest place there is — in Christ, in God.

And the very next verse says, “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). Hidden first, revealed later. Hidden in God today, revealed in glory one day. Brothers and sisters, this is the logic of hiddenness.

sections.heading: 3. Philippians 2:5–8: A Church in Conflict, and a Hymn to Christ
sections.html:
Philippians is also a Prison Epistle. Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16), and the church he loved most dearly. Yet in this lovable church there was an unlovely problem — conflict. In chapter 4 Paul names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). That is why chapter 2 opens with, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3).

Then he stops reasoning and hangs up a picture instead — Philippians 2:5–11, known as the “Christ hymn”. The Son of God comes down all the way from the highest throne: he empties himself, takes the form of a servant, is made in the likeness of men, humbles himself, becomes obedient, to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Seven steps, all the way down. And the result? “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). The one who went down, God himself lifted up.

sections.heading: 4. Ephesians 4:15–16: The Picture of the Body
sections.html:
The passage for this lesson’s first key point comes from Ephesians, another Prison Epistle. Ephesians 4:11–16 is the fullest passage in the whole Bible on serving in the church: the fivefold ministry God has given — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers — is “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). Notice the order: the fivefold ministry is not there to do ministry for its own sake, but to perfect the saints; and perfecting the saints is not for the saints’ own sake, but to build up the body of Christ. The end of the whole chain is not any one person; it is Christ. “Perfecting” in the original is καταρτισμός (katartismos); its root is used in Matthew 4:21 for James and John “mending their nets”, and in medicine it meant “setting a broken bone”.

Now let’s walk step by step into the three movements of hiddenness.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Hidden in the Body of Christ — Learning to Serve as a Team
sections.html:
Scripture: The Whole Body Fitted Together by Him

The lesson says: Jesus is the head of the church, and we are members of his body.

“But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:15–16)

There are two key words here. “Knit together” in the original is συμβιβάζω (symbibazō), “to join, to bind closely together”; “joint” in the original is ἁφή (haphē), a joint or point of connection. Paul is saying that the strength of the body does not lie in one especially large muscle, but in every joint being connected in the right place.

Brothers and sisters, the joints are the least noticeable part of the body; no one ever praises their own knee joint. But let one joint go wrong and the whole person can’t move. The most important service in the church is often this kind of “joint” service — unseen by anyone, yet carrying the weight of the whole body.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: No Member Can Be Glorified on Its Own

The lesson is quite right: every member of the body has its function, but none can be glorified on its own. In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul explains this even more thoroughly:

“The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

“No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22)

“When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26)

The lesson puts it very realistically: the eye can’t do without the hand, nor the hand without the foot; if one member sticks out too far, the whole body loses its balance.

An Illustration: Thirty-Seven Trillion Cells and a Symphony Orchestra

Science gives us an astonishing picture. In 2013, Eva Bianconi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy published a study in the Annals of Human Biology estimating that an adult human body is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells. And of those thirty-seven trillion cells, not one has its own name; not one gives interviews, makes the headlines or runs a fan page. Each does its own job, working quietly; and the sum of them all is a living, thinking, loving “you”. Brothers and sisters, the body of Christ is just like that.

Or think of a symphony orchestra. What the audience usually remembers is the leader of the first violins and the conductor, but what really makes a symphony is the sections that never have a solo from beginning to end — the second violins, the violas, the double basses, the timpani. The conductor Leonard Bernstein is generally credited with saying that the hardest player to find in an orchestra is the one willing to play second violin. Without the second violins there is no harmony; a solo is beautiful, but on its own it can never become a symphony.

The lesson says that true team service lets people see no individual, only Jesus. In such service nobody is more important than anybody else, because the focus is not on “who is more impressive”, but on “whether Jesus can reveal his glory through us”.

Applying 321: Let Jesus Be King, and Establish God’s System

The Two Core Values of Kingdom 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

The word “system” is precisely the picture of a body. In a system there are no stars, only members; no ranking of high and low, only the question of whether you are joined up or not. If the focus of my service is “letting me be seen”, then the one reigning as king in my heart is actually me; if the focus of my service is “letting the body of Christ be built up”, then Jesus truly reigns as King in my heart.

321 also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. Focus on yourself and you’ll angle for credit; focus on others and you’ll compare; focus on your circumstances and you’ll complain. Only when Jesus is the focal point can we truly work together.

So this lesson’s first practice is very down to earth: in serving, say “we” more and “I” less. Don’t underestimate a pronoun — language shapes the mind, and the mind shapes the life. As we grow used to saying “we”, the self-centred old self steps back, little by little.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Second Step of Hiddenness — Helping Others to Be More Successful Than Yourself
sections.html:
Scripture: Greater Works Than These

“Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.” (John 14:12)

Brothers and sisters, just think how astonishing this sentence is. What a teacher fears most is a student who surpasses him; a master craftsman will often keep one trick back. Yet the Lord Jesus not only keeps nothing back — he declares with his own lips: you will do greater works than I. The lesson says it well: this sentence reveals the core of Jesus’ service — making others greater than himself.

“Greater” here does not mean that the disciples are greater than the Lord; it refers to the scope and fruitfulness of the work. While Jesus was on earth he worked mainly within a small patch of Palestine; but when the Holy Spirit came, the gospel spread “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

The Lord Jesus even said something more startling still: “Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you” (John 16:7). My leaving is to your advantage. Brothers and sisters, could you say that? We are often afraid that if we’re not there, things won’t get done; the Lord Jesus said, I am leaving the stage so that you can step onto it.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: Moses and Joshua, Elijah and Elisha

The lesson gives two pairs of role models.

Moses trained Joshua. God said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him” (Numbers 27:18). And he said, “You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey” (Numbers 27:20).

The Hebrew word behind “authority” here is הוֹד (hod), meaning majesty, splendour, and the verse literally says to put “some of your hod” on him. God did not tell Moses to produce a separate portion of honour for Joshua; God said: give him some of yours. Brothers and sisters, what a lesson that is — true succession means cutting off a piece of yourself.

Elijah brought Elisha to maturity. What did Elisha ask for? “Elisha said, ‘Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me’” (2 Kings 2:9). Elijah did not get angry; he only said, “You have asked a hard thing” (2 Kings 2:10).

The lesson says that their successors accomplished greater works than they did, yet they were neither jealous nor competitive; instead they rejoiced that their spiritual sons were being used by God.

The opposite example is Saul. He heard the women singing, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). His response was this: “Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, ‘They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?’” (1 Samuel 18:8)

Brothers and sisters, it is the same song: had Moses heard it, he would have rejoiced for Joshua; Saul heard it and flew into a rage. The difference is not in the song; it is in the heart.

An Illustration: Level 5 Leaders and a Spiritual Parent’s Heart

Management studies offer a powerful confirmation. In Good to Great, published in 2001, Jim Collins screened more than 1,400 companies that had appeared on the Fortune 500 and identified eleven that had truly leapt from good to great. Then he asked: what did the chief executives of these companies have in common?

The answer surprised everyone. They were not celebrity leaders but what Collins called “Level 5 leaders” — people who combined “extreme personal humility” with “intense professional will”. Collins also observed a pattern he called “the window and the mirror”: when things went well, these leaders looked out of the window and gave the credit to others; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took full responsibility. Celebrity CEOs did exactly the opposite.

This fits the Bible’s principle astonishingly well. Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

The lesson uses the warmest of words: a spiritual “parent’s heart”. What parent anywhere is jealous because their children have done better than they have? A parent’s heart says: I can go unseen, as long as you are brought to maturity. Paul said to Timothy, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). There are four generations in that verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Spiritual productivity does not lie in how much I have done, but in how much I have entrusted to others.

Applying 321: The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

Kingdom 321 has a very precious practice called “the 920 practice”. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; in our dealings with them we practise living out a selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Notice that not one of the nine graces is for ourselves; a fruit tree does not eat its own fruit. Building others up is exactly what the 920 practice looks like in concrete terms.

Then there are “235 relationships”. Becoming a “2” with someone who lives selflessly means having a spiritual companion; building “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” means a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. See how beautiful this order is: first companions, then parents and children, and only last of all a team. Without a spiritual parent’s heart you will never bring forth spiritual children; and without spiritual children, a fivefold-ministry team is only an organisational chart.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. So this lesson’s second practice is to take the initiative in encouraging and supporting the development of other people’s gifts. This is not politeness; it is sowing seed. When we stop seeking our own success and help others succeed, we are truly hidden in the glory of Christ.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Third Step of Hiddenness — Laying Down Status and Authority
sections.html:
Scripture: All Authority Has Been Given to Me — Therefore, You Go

The lesson says that Jesus rose from the dead and overcame the power of sin and death; he could have stayed on earth and reigned as king, but he chose to “lay it down”.

“Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, ‘All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’” (Matthew 28:18–19)

Brothers and sisters, notice the key words in this passage: “therefore, you” — the Chinese Union Version, following many Greek manuscripts, reads “Therefore you go”.

By human logic the sentence ought to run: since all authority has been given to me, therefore I will go. But what the Lord Jesus says is: therefore, you go. He holds the authority in his hand, yet hands the action over to his disciples. He did not carry on taking first place himself; he raised up many more people to complete the mission.

And he goes on: “teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). He withdrew to where he cannot be seen, yet he is present in a deeper way — no longer limited to one body and one place, but through the Holy Spirit present with thousands upon thousands of disciples at once.

Brothers and sisters, this is the mystery of “laying down”: he takes one step back, and the kingdom takes a great step forward.

Scripture Interprets Scripture: The Authority of the Gentiles, and the Authority of God’s Kingdom

The Lord Jesus had made this principle plain long before. When James and John asked to sit at his right and left, the Lord said:

“You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all. For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:42–45)

“Servant” in the original is διάκονος (diakonos), originally “one who waits at table”; “bondservant” is δοῦλος (doulos), a heavier word still, meaning “slave”. The Lord Jesus is not telling us to give up influence; he is turning the direction of influence upside down. In the world, authority grabs upwards; in God’s kingdom, authority flows downwards.

On the night he was betrayed he prayed, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). When he said this, the cross had not yet happened and the church had not yet been founded. How could he say the work was accomplished? Because his measure of success was never “how much have I completed?” but “have I walked my stretch of the road according to the Father’s will?”

An Illustration: Laying Down Is Not Retiring — It Is an Upgrade

The lesson has a superb sentence here: some people think “laying down” means “retiring”, but in God’s kingdom “laying down” means “transforming”.

We lay down the identity of “leader” and support others in the role of “servant”; we lay down the power of “control” and bless others with the heart of a “parent”. Laying down is not losing; it is an upgrade.

There is a very beautiful picture of this in the living world. In 1997, the forest ecologist Suzanne Simard of the University of British Columbia in Canada published research in the journal Nature showing that the trees in a forest are linked to one another through underground mycorrhizal networks, through which they can pass carbon, nitrogen and water to neighbouring trees; the oldest, largest trees send nutrients through this unseen network to the seedlings in their shade.

A great tree stands there, apparently doing nothing but occupying a spot. But below ground it is sending its own nourishment out, little by little, so that other trees can grow. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a picture of spiritual parents?

The Greatest Test of a Spiritual Leader

The lesson says that this is the greatest test of a spiritual leader — whether you are willing to lay it down and let someone else be lifted up. Hold a position long enough and it grows into your flesh: at first it’s “I am doing this ministry”; gradually it becomes “this ministry is mine”; and a while later it becomes “it can’t be done without me”.

The way 321 puts it is more direct still: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The lesson says that when church leaders are willing to lay down authority, the whole church can avoid power struggles and division, and instead build a culture of humility and love, filled with the glory of Jesus. If a leader is willing to let go first, while he is still needed, the whole church will learn a lesson that a hundred classes could never teach.

Applying 321: Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan

321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan fell precisely because he would not stay in his originally intended position. He said, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God!” (Isaiah 14:13). He left his position and wanted to take God’s place.

The Lord Jesus walked exactly the opposite road: he existed in the form of God, yet willingly took the form of a servant. That is why Satan cannot overcome Jesus — every one of Satan’s weapons is designed for self-centred people. He can lure you with fame, wound you with humiliation, provoke you with comparison; but in a selfless person these hooks have nothing to catch on. The Lord Jesus said, “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Laying down status and authority is not making ourselves worthless; it is putting ourselves back in our originally intended position. 321 says it well: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

So this lesson’s third practice is to learn to step back and let the younger generation take up the work of service. Stepping back is not leaving; stepping back is changing places — from the front of the stage to behind it, from holding power to interceding, from teaching to walking alongside.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Hidden Life Brings Out a Deeper Glory
sections.html:
God Raises Up Others Where We Lay Things Down

The lesson says that when we choose to hide ourselves, God is freer to use us. Where we lay things down he can raise up others, and at the moment we step back he can let his kingdom spread.

This is a spiritual law. God said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’” (Judges 7:2). From thirty-two thousand down to three hundred: God was not weakening Gideon; he was removing everything that might take a share of the glory.

Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). A clay jar was the cheapest container of the day — it chipped, it cracked, nobody looked at it twice; but precisely because it was so plain, people noticed the treasure inside. So often we spend our whole lives trying to polish the jar so that people will admire the jar; but God says, what I want is for people to see the treasure inside.

Applause for Being Seen by People, Reward for Being Seen by God

The lesson offers a very powerful contrast: service seen by people brings brief applause; service seen by God brings eternal reward.

The Lord Jesus made this very clear in the Sermon on the Mount: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

“But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

Notice how the Lord Jesus says “in secret” again and again. Our Father in heaven is not a God who needs us to switch on the light before he can see. Hebrews says, “For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them” (Hebrews 6:10). People forget; the meeting minutes leave things out; your name gets missed off the year-end thank-you list — but God does not forget.

321 says: turn from the human, earthly, temporary, Worldly perspective to God’s heavenly, eternal, godly perspective. Applause is earthly and temporary; reward is heavenly and eternal. Brothers and sisters, which one do we want?

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal Seen through the Three Movements of Hiddenness
sections.html:
Let’s set the message of the whole lesson inside the 321 framework and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. The three movements of hiddenness are not a method devised by some spiritual elder; they are the road the Lord Jesus himself walked first: he was hidden in the flesh for thirty years, he equipped his disciples to do greater works, and he laid down his earthly position and ascended to return to the Father.

The Bible is my standard. Every step we have looked at today has clear scriptural grounding: Ephesians 4:15–16, John 14:12, Matthew 28:18–20, Colossians 3:3. We don’t decide by feelings whether to step back; we act according to the standard of the Bible.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to let go, whom to hand over to, how to let go — all of it needs the Holy Spirit’s guidance. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. If we calculate with our brains, we will never find the “right moment” to step back; if we obey from the heart, the Holy Spirit will tell us clearly.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. When I say “we” more in the team, I am letting Jesus be King; when I rejoice that someone else is being used, I am letting Jesus be King; when I loosen my grip while I am still needed, I am letting Jesus be King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The word “all” is very strict. Not ninety per cent to the Lord and ten per cent kept back for myself — all of it. Paul says, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

Establish God’s system. The fruit the three movements of hiddenness are meant to bear is a body that depends not on stars, but on Christ as its head. A system can be passed on; a star cannot.

The Fivefold Change

321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This order cannot be reversed.

The mindset this lesson sets out to change is very clear: from “I only have value when I’m seen” to “There is only value in letting Jesus be seen”; from “success is how much I have completed” to “success is how many people I have brought to maturity”; from “laying down means losing” to “laying down is an upgrade”.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives four practices for daily living. 321 has “the eight stages of changing our mindset”: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to put the four practices solidly into effect.

Practice 1: Practise team spirit — in serving, say “we” more and “I” less

Information: Remember Ephesians 4:16 — “being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part.”

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light so that I see my true place in the body, and also see the situations in which the “I” is especially likely to pop out.

Conviction: Acknowledge a fact — no member can be glorified on its own.

Implementation: This week, every time you share, report or give thanks, deliberately change “I did” to “we did it together”, and name at least one co-worker.

Evaluation: Every night, take three quiet minutes to ask yourself: how many times did I say “I” today? Was there a time I said it so people would know it was me who did it?

Correction: If you find you’ve taken the credit, add a line the next day: “Actually, Brother So-and-so did that first.”

Repetition: Keep it up for forty days; habits of speech only change through repetition.

Multiplication: Bring this practice into your small group, invite the members to do it with you, and remind one another.

Practice 2: The blessing of building others up — take the initiative to encourage and support the development of other people’s gifts

Information: Remember John 14:12 — “he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord to give me a spiritual parent’s heart, and to show me which brother or sister around me God wants me to build up.

Conviction: Believe that other people’s success does not reduce my worth; God’s grace is not a pie with only so many slices.

Implementation: Write down three names. Pray for them every day this month, and do one concrete thing: introduce an opportunity to serve, give a book, offer a sincere word of praise face to face, or give up your own place to them.

Evaluation: When they are praised, is my first reaction inside joy, or a sour feeling? Facing it honestly is where growth begins.

Correction: If you find jealousy there, confess it at once and speak a blessing over them out loud; blessing them aloud is the most effective way of dealing with jealousy.

Repetition: Refresh the list every quarter, and keep going.

Multiplication: Teach those you are building up to go and build up the next person. That is the four-generation succession of 2 Timothy 2:2.

Practice 3: The practice of laying down position — learn to step back and let the younger generation take up the work of service

Information: Remember Matthew 28:18–19 — the authority is in the Lord’s hands; the action is handed to the disciples.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to shine his light: which position in my hands am I gripping too tightly, a position I should already have handed over?

Conviction: Believe that laying down is not retiring but transforming; not losing, but an upgrade.

Implementation: This quarter, pick out the ministry you do most comfortably and hand it over completely to a younger co-worker: hand over the responsibility, the resources and the platform — and don’t take it back when they do it less than perfectly.

Evaluation: Once I’ve handed it over, how many times can I not resist stepping in? Have I ever said, “I used to do it better”?

Correction: If you find yourself taking control back, let go once again, and say to their face, “I believe in you. Go for it.”

Repetition: Hand over one thing each quarter. After a few years you will find your own hands empty — and God’s kingdom full.

Multiplication: Let those who take over one day hand the position on to the next person in the same way.

Practice 4: A heart for quiet service — faithfully completing what the Lord has entrusted, in places where no one sees

Information: Remember Matthew 6:3–4 — “so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let me truly know the Father who sees in secret, and to be deeply convinced that his eyes never doze.

Conviction: Believe that being seen by God is better than being seen by people.

Implementation: This week, deliberately do three good deeds nobody knows about — a phone call to pray for someone, a quiet gift, a cleaning job no one sees. When you’ve done them, tell no one; tell only your Father in heaven.

Evaluation: Afterwards, is there a little itch inside to have it known? That little itch is the evidence that the self-centred life has not yet stepped down.

Correction: Every time the itch appears, turn it into a prayer: “Lord, this was done for you. Please accept it.”

Repetition: Let hidden service become a long-term habit of your daily living.

Multiplication: Once you have tasted the joy of serving in secret, you will naturally bring others along to do it with you — and it won’t need any publicity.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the lesson’s closing words.

Jesus did not seek a stage of glory; he chose to hide himself and give the glory to the Father. With his life he tells us that the people God truly uses are not those who exalt themselves, but those who know how to hide themselves.

Luke’s Gospel records that on the day of his resurrection the Lord walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus. When they sat down to eat, “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him, then he vanished out of their sight” (Luke 24:31). Look at the order: they recognised him, and then he vanished. The Lord Jesus never came to leave his own image behind, but to set people’s hearts alight. Those two disciples said afterwards, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us?” (Luke 24:32). This morning the Lord comes among us in just the same way.

So — will we make a decision?

First, in the team, I am willing to be the joint that connects, not the member that sticks out.

Second, among people, I am willing to be a spiritual parent and rejoice in other people’s success.

Third, in my position, I am willing to loosen my grip while I am still needed, and let the younger generation rise up.

Fourth, in secret, I am willing to be faithful, because my Father in heaven sees in secret.

When we are willing to be hidden, God’s glory will surely shine within us, so that what people see is no longer us, but the glorious Jesus Christ.

May every one of us become that kind of person — not asking to be seen, only asking that Jesus be seen; not seeking glory, only seeking that the glory go to the Lord.

Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
“For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Colossians 3:3)

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)
declarations: The lesson’s gentle reminder puts it like this: God does not look at how many people see you; he looks at how many people you are willing to let see Jesus. Hiding yourself is not losing your worth; it is letting your worth be fully used by God. Brothers and sisters, these two sentences are worth copying out and sticking up above your desk.

We often misunderstand this, thinking that being hidden means being buried, and being quiet means having no influence. But the Lord Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). When the grain falls into the ground, it is hidden; yet what grows up after the hiding is much fruit. If you will not be buried, you will only ever be a single grain.
Let us read the lesson’s declaration of faith together, from the heart:

Lord, I am willing to learn your way: even while you are using me, to keep hiding myself. Let me serve humbly in the team, find joy and contentment in building others up, and experience true freedom in laying down position. May my whole life give glory to you alone.
The lesson ends by saying: not asking to be seen, only asking that Jesus be seen; not seeking glory, only seeking that the glory go to the Lord.
This is exactly the cry of the psalmist: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake” (Psalm 115:1).
practices: Practise team spirit — in serving, say “we” more and “I” less
The blessing of building others up — encourage and support the development of other people’s gifts
The practice of laying down position — learn to step back and let the younger generation take up the service
A heart for quiet service — faithfully complete the Lord’s charge where no one sees
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. This morning you have shone the light of your example into our hearts. We confess that inside us there is an “I” that badly wants to be seen: we crave applause, we fear being overlooked, and our hearts turn sour when others are praised. Lord, have mercy on us and forgive us.

Give us the heart of spiritual parents, so that we truly rejoice when others are used. Give us the courage to let go, willing to hand our place to the next generation while we are still needed. Give us the joy of serving in secret, so that we can be faithful all our lives without needing anyone’s applause.
Lord, let our lives be hidden with Christ in you. Let our shadows grow shorter and shorter, and your light longer and longer.

May our families, small groups and churches no longer fight over positions, but only build one another up; may there be no more stars, only members; may we no longer exalt anyone’s name, but exalt the name of Jesus alone.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). In your present service or work, what is one thing you hope will “be seen”? If you handed it over to God completely — letting him increase and you decrease — what would you find hardest to let go of?

“Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father” (John 14:12). Name one specific person God has placed beside you whom you need to build up. What one concrete thing do you plan to do for them this month?
