When we measure our lives by the world’s standard, we have already quietly changed kings.

sections.heading: 5. A Warning Bell for the Church: The Danger of Sliding from God’s Rule to Human Rule
sections.html:
Jesus said: “on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the possessive in this verse: “my” church. The foundation of the church is Jesus himself, and the ownership belongs to Jesus himself — it belongs to no one else. Paul put it even more plainly to the elders of Ephesus: “Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.” (Acts 20:28) The church was bought with precious blood, and the buyer is Jesus. Colossians 1:18 says: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” — preeminence “in all things,” not in some things.

The early church let the Holy Spirit reign: in everything they prayed, sought and obeyed. There is a deeply moving detail in Acts. The Jerusalem Council had to deal with the problem of the Gentile believers — the thorniest issue of the day and the one most likely to split the church. The decision they finally wrote down began like this: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you” (Acts 15:28). Look at the order — “the Holy Spirit, and to us”: the Holy Spirit first, ourselves second. That one sentence is the loveliest mark of a church under God’s rule.

But as time went on, people gradually came to govern the church by human methods. Structures, rules, power and titles slowly took the place of the Holy Spirit’s leading. “God’s rule” became “human rule,” and believers leaned on organisation, tradition and influence, losing their sensitivity to God’s voice and their reverence for it.

In fact, this danger had already appeared in New Testament times. The apostle John wrote these grieved words: “I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say.” (3 John 9) “Loves to be first” is the Greek philoprōteuō, literally “to love being first.” Brothers and sisters, this word appears only once in the whole New Testament, and it is used to describe a leader in the church. The most dangerous disease in a church is not a lack of gifts; it is the love of being first.

Let me use an illustration from the body. In our hearts there is a very small cluster of tissue called the sinoatrial node. It is the heart’s natural pacemaker, normally firing about sixty to a hundred electrical signals a minute, and the whole heart muscle contracts together in time with that one signal. It is tiny, yet it is the only one giving the orders. What happens if many stray pacemaker points spring up in the atria, each demanding its own contraction? That is atrial fibrillation. From the outside, the heart looks busier than usual and beats faster, but the amount of blood it actually pumps drops sharply.

Brothers and sisters, that is a church that has lost God’s rule. It isn’t that there’s no activity — there’s too much; it isn’t that no one is working — too many people are giving their own orders. On the surface the calendar is full; inside, the blood supply is failing. A church’s health doesn’t lie in how many programmes it runs, but in whether it has only one pacemaker.

Here the 321 vision gives us a very practical measuring rod: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When a church runs into trouble, it is almost always because that order has been turned upside down. Once ministry is put first, people become tools for getting ministry done, and relationships start to strain; once relationships strain, life is drained; once life is drained, ministry is left with nothing but technique and emotion. Turn it the right way round and put life first, and ministry doesn’t shrink — it gains roots, strength and joy.

The 321 vision also says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. How many church conflicts have been over a budget, a venue or a position? In the end the job got done, but the people scattered. Brothers and sisters, pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. One person insists on his rights, another insists on hers, and in the end both are right — and the church is the loser.

Yet in these last days God is calling his people back to the starting point — back to the government of “God’s rule,” letting the Holy Spirit reign once more. Church history has borne witness to this again and again: every true revival has had at its heart not a new strategy but the same old thing — God’s people letting God be King again. On 13 August 1727, at a gathering in Herrnhut, the Spirit of God was poured out on the Moravian Brethren, and this band of refugees, who until then had been endlessly quarrelling with one another, began a round-the-clock relay of watchful prayer that went on for a hundred years. Revival did not begin with a meeting but with repentance; not with a strategy, but on our knees.

When the church is no longer built for people and glorified for people, but exists for Jesus and is glorified for Jesus, God’s glory will once again be revealed among his people.

This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. It is also the Goal of 321: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, the difference between God’s system and man’s system is not whether there is organisation, but who sits in the middle. Man’s system is centred on man and uses structures to protect people’s positions; God’s system is centred on Jesus and uses order to serve God’s will.

John the Baptist left us a short but weighty sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) His disciples had come to complain that everyone was going off to follow Jesus. John didn’t say a word in his own defence; he said he was only the friend of the bridegroom, and that hearing the bridegroom’s voice filled him with joy. Brothers and sisters, being able to rejoice when someone else increases is the surest evidence that God’s rule is reigning.

sections.heading: 6. Our Personal Response: Letting Jesus Be King Again
sections.html:
Having spoken of creation, of history and of the church, the message now comes back to you and me.

The lesson text says: “laying down our rights” does not mean abandoning our responsibilities; it means acknowledging that God is wiser than we are. That needs to be made clear. Laying down our sovereignty doesn’t mean being passive, it doesn’t mean lying flat and giving up, and it doesn’t mean refusing to make decisions. Quite the opposite — those who hand their sovereignty to God act with greater courage, because they know the outcome is not in their own hands.

“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) Notice: the verse does not say “don’t use your own understanding,” but “don’t lean on your own understanding.” God still wants you to use your mind; he simply won’t let you treat your mind as God.

In daily life we often slip into living under “human rule” without even noticing — wanting to control outcomes, wanting to manipulate others, wanting the final say. Brothers and sisters, let’s do a small check-up.

Have you ever chosen a path for your child that was really a dream you never finished yourself? That is wanting to control outcomes.

Have you ever hidden a hook in something you said, so the other person would answer the way you wanted? That is wanting to manipulate others.

Have you ever said out loud, “Let’s pray and seek God together,” when in your heart you’d already decided and were only waiting for everyone else to agree? That is wanting the final say.

In 1966 the psychologist Julian Rotter put forward the theory of “locus of control,” distinguishing an “internal” from an “external” locus: people with an internal locus believe outcomes are in their own hands; people with an external locus believe outcomes depend on luck or on others. Research shows that those leaning towards an internal locus are generally more proactive and more successful. But brothers and sisters, the Christian life has a third kind, one this scale cannot measure — not handing sovereignty to myself, nor to fate, but to a Lord with a name, who loved me and gave himself up for me. That isn’t an external locus of control; that is trust. Trust doesn’t mean you stop putting in effort; it means you know whose hands you are working in.

The heart of “human rule” is “for myself”; the heart of “God’s rule” is “for God.” When we lay down our self-centredness, Jesus’ sovereignty can be restored in our lives.

To know whether this road can really be walked, we have the most reliable role model there is. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus fell to the ground, his sweat like great drops of blood falling on the ground, and his prayer was: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

Brothers and sisters, notice the shape of this prayer. Jesus didn’t pretend he didn’t want the cup taken away — he really did say, “remove this cup.” True obedience isn’t having no opinion; it is having an opinion and still placing it under the will of God. So you don’t have to pretend you aren’t struggling; you only have to say that “nevertheless” after the struggle. Between “my will” and “your will” stands only one word: “nevertheless.” That one “nevertheless” is the place where human rule is handed back to God’s rule.

Once that turning point comes, the formula of life changes: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

This is what the 321 vision calls “selflessness.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness doesn’t mean there is no me; it means “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” You have not disappeared; you have been filled by a greater Person. Think of a glove: an empty glove can do nothing at all, but once a hand fills it, it can do everything the hand can do. The glove hasn’t lost itself; the glove has found itself.

And what does Jesus promise on this road? “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that rest does not come from taking the yoke off; it comes from changing yokes. The yoke of human rule you carry alone; the yoke of God’s rule you carry together with the Lord.

The gentle reminder in our lesson puts it beautifully: “human rule” pursues control and ends in anxiety; “God’s rule” pursues entrusting and ends in peace. Humility is not losing strength; it is letting strength return to its proper source — God.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Brothers and sisters, look at which way the verbs run in these two verses: humbling yourself is what you do; exalting is what God does. Our greatest mistake is trying to snatch God’s work and do it ourselves — and when we exalt ourselves, God resists us.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s message within the framework of 321 and see it all clearly at once.

The Three Foundations. First, Jesus is my role model — in Gethsemane he said, “not my will, but yours, be done,” the perfect demonstration of returning from human rule to God’s rule. Second, the Bible is my standard — the content of God’s rule is not some vague feeling but what God has said; that tree in Eden was a boundary precisely because God had spoken. Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide — “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28): God’s rule is not a distant government but the Holy Spirit’s present leading in your heart and mine.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — this is the very theme of this lesson: from “I am king” back to “he is King.” Let Jesus receive all the glory — the word “all” cuts deepest, because we so often keep a little bit back for ourselves.

The Goal. Establish God’s system. The most fundamental difference between God’s system and the Worldly system is who sits on the throne. When Israel said “like all the nations,” that was the Worldly system.

From the self-centred life to selflessness. The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life; the root of the problem is pride. The five “I will”s of Isaiah 14, that one bite of fruit in Genesis 3, that one sentence “like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 — at heart they are exactly the same. And there is only one remedy: selflessness. Selflessness is not the passivity of self-negation; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan cannot get a grip on a person who has nothing for him to grab. If you have no seat to defend, he has no leverage to threaten you with; if you don’t care who gets the glory, he has no bait to lure you with.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Be transformed” is the Greek metamorphoō, “to change form” — the thorough change of a caterpillar into a butterfly, not a change of clothes. When the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry at last bears real fruit.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s subject, God’s rule, begins with our relationship with God. If you have not let him be King in your relationship with God, the other three layers will all be out of place: your relationship with yourself turns into self-condemnation or self-inflation, your relationship with others turns into competition and control, and your relationship with things turns into anxiety and performance.

A change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. “Human rule” is the human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective; “God’s rule” is the divine, heavenly, eternal, godly perspective. Look at the same matter from different perspectives and you reach completely different conclusions.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — so that the Holy Spirit bears his fruit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice that these nine graces have one thing in common — every one of them requires you to lay down a right of some kind. Patience lays down the right to have it now; gentleness lays down the right to hit back; self-control lays down the right to indulge. So the fruit of the Spirit turns out to be the fruit God’s rule bears in a person.

The 235 relationships. Become a “2” with selfless people — spiritual companions who remind each other who is King; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing on the life that lets Jesus be King; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together. Brothers and sisters, it is hard to hold on to God’s rule alone, because we cannot see our own pride; but a “2” can help you see it.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — that is Spirit; the Bible is my standard — that is Understanding; Jesus is my role model — that is Life; let Jesus be King — that is Service; let Jesus receive all the glory — that is God. Today’s lesson is really the whole road, from “Spirit” all the way to “God.”

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Brothers and sisters, human rule is the product of the brain — calculating, comparing, scheming; God’s rule is the surrender of the heart — trusting, entrusting, resting.

sections.heading: 8. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing the word is where the real work lies. Our lesson gives us four practices; let’s take them one at a time.

Practice 1: A Prayer Entrusting My Rights

Each morning in your prayer time, declare: “Lord, today I hand the sovereignty of my life over to you.”

Notice the words “each morning.” Handing over sovereignty has an expiry date, just as manna couldn’t be kept until the next day. What we handed over yesterday, we quietly take back again this morning. So this isn’t a one-off ritual; it is a daily practice. I suggest, brothers and sisters, that you say this sentence as soon as you open your eyes, before you reach for your phone. Whoever’s voice you hear first in a day is most likely whoever will govern that day.

In the Twelve Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous, the third step reads: “Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.” Even people in the world know that some bondages are only broken when sovereignty is handed over — how much more we who have the true and living God.

Practice 2: Obedience in Decision-Making

Before every decision, first ask: “Is this what I want, or what God wants?”

Ask this question before you decide, not after. We are very good at finding spiritual reasons for decisions we’ve already made, so the order matters enormously. You can add two follow-up questions: will this decision still count five years from now, in the light of eternity? And if the spiritual companion I respect most found out about this decision, would I feel the need to explain myself?

Note too that “what God wants” is not something we guess by feeling. The Bible is my standard. Where the Bible speaks plainly, there is no need to ask again; where the Bible does not speak plainly, seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance within its principles, and have it confirmed in community.

Practice 3: God’s Rule in the Family

In family prayer, let God’s word be the final standard, rather than emotions or habit.

Brothers and sisters, the family is the first place God’s rule is lost and the place it most needs to be won back. At home we are most prone to let two things be king: one is emotion — whoever shouts loudest wins; the other is habit — this is just how our family has always done it. Neither of these is the word of God.

Here is one concrete suggestion: in family prayer, read a short passage of Scripture first, and only then discuss things. When opinions differ, the question isn’t “who’s right?” but “what does God’s word say?” The most powerful lesson a parent can teach is not “do as I say,” but saying in front of the children: “I was going to do it that way, but God’s word says this, so Dad has changed his mind.”

Practice 4: Obedience in the Church

In serving, seek not position and control, but room for the Holy Spirit to move freely.

The temptations of serving are subtle: we may not covet a title, but we very often covet “being needed.” When something can’t get done without me, there’s a secret satisfaction in my heart. Brothers and sisters, that too is grabbing for power.

The practice is simple: hand over to someone else the area of service you do most easily, and resist the urge to correct the way they do it; and when your own proposal isn’t adopted, go home and pray a blessing over the brother who suggested something different. These little things are the church’s Gethsemane.

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

The 321 vision teaches that changing our mindset goes through eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Let’s place today’s practices within these eight stages.

Stage one, Information. You have received the information today: human rule began in Eden, Israel’s tragedy is in 1 Samuel 8, and the way out for each of us is in Gethsemane. Please write these things down.

Stage two, Revelation. For information to become revelation, the Holy Spirit must open your eyes. Ask the Lord in prayer: “Lord, please show me the one thing in my life I have not yet handed over.” Usually your heart already knows what that one thing is.

Stage three, Conviction. For revelation to become conviction, you must say yes. Conviction isn’t saying, “That’s a good teaching”; it is saying, “That teaching governs me.” Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that we don’t know; it’s that we won’t submit.

Stage four, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, take up at least one of the four practices. Don’t try all four at once — that usually doesn’t last three days. Begin with “a prayer entrusting my rights,” because it is the source of the other three.

Stage five, Evaluation. Set a regular time each week to look back: in what matter did I take sovereignty back? What triggered it? Usually it is one of three situations — things getting out of control, losing face, or falling behind schedule.

Stage six, Correction. When you see it, change it — and make the change specific. Not “I’ll be more humble,” but “at the next meeting, I’ll wait until three other people have spoken before I say anything.” God’s rule is restored in specific, small things.

Stage seven, Repetition. Doing it once isn’t practice; doing it again and again is. Brokenness isn’t a one-time operation; it is a lifelong lesson. Going straight back to stage one after a failure is itself a victory.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once you have tasted the sweetness of God’s rule, take someone along with you. Find your “2,” share these four practices with them, and ask each other once a week: “This week, who has been King in your life?” This is how 235 relationships begin, and how God’s system is established.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, from Eden until today, humanity has kept wrestling between “human rule” and “God’s rule.”

Adam reached out his hand in the garden, wanting to be his own god; Israel opened its mouth at Ramah, wanting a king like the nations; Diotrephes loved to be first in the church, wanting to be number one; and you and I, on every ordinary morning, are quietly deciding as well: who will be King today?

But Jesus’ example has already shown us clearly — true freedom is letting God be King.

In The Great Divorce, C. S. Lewis wrote what is widely seen as one of his sharpest and tenderest insights: in the end there are only two kinds of people — those who say to God, “Thy will be done,” and those to whom God says, “Thy will be done.” Brothers and sisters, this morning, which kind of person will you be?

When we lay down our sovereignty and hand over control, we are not losing; on the contrary, we gain a more abundant life. This is not a spiritual slogan; it is a spiritual fact. When your hand is clenched, all it can hold is what fits inside your fist; when your hand is open, it can receive as much as the sky is wide.

Let us turn from “human rule” back to “God’s rule,” from “relying on ourselves” back to “letting God reign,” so that Jesus truly reigns as King within us and receives the glory.

One day this proclamation will ring out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15) Brothers and sisters, since that day is certain to come, why not begin this very morning? Hand the kingdom over to him, give the throne back to him, give the glory to him.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.’” (1 Samuel 8:7)
Echoing verse: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to lay down my own rights and let you be King of my life and my family. I will no longer lean on my own understanding, but will seek your will in all things. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
(This declaration echoes the prayer the Lord Jesus taught: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Matthew 6:10)
prayer: Each morning in your prayer time, declare: “Lord, today I hand the sovereignty of my life over to you.”

Notice the words “each morning.” Handing over sovereignty has an expiry date, just as manna couldn’t be kept until the next day. What we handed over yesterday, we quietly take back again this morning. So this isn’t a one-off ritual; it is a daily practice. I suggest, brothers and sisters, that you say this sentence as soon as you open your eyes, before you reach for your phone. Whoever’s voice you hear first in a day is most likely whoever will govern that day.

In the Twelve Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous, the third step reads: “Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.” Even people in the world know that some bondages are only broken when sovereignty is handed over — how much more we who have the true and living God.

Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. You are the Lord who created heaven and earth, the King who rules over history, and the Saviour who loved us and gave himself up for us.

Lord, please forgive us. So often we call you Lord with our lips while making ourselves king in our hearts; so often we ask you to bless our plans but won’t let you change them. Like the Israelites, we say, “like all the nations”; like Adam, we reach out for a seat that doesn’t belong to us.
Lord, this morning we want to learn your prayer in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours, be done.
May your Holy Spirit show me the corner of my life I have not yet handed over, and give me the courage to give the key back to you.
Make our families take your word as their standard, not emotion and habit; let our serving give the Holy Spirit room to move freely, seeking neither position nor control.
Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
May Jesus reign as King within us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Samuel 8:7: “Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.’” The Israelites wanted a king “like all the nations.” In your life right now, is there some matter where your heart is also saying “like all the nations”? Please name it specifically, and share how you plan to hand it back to God.

Luke 22:42: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” In this prayer Jesus first honestly spoke his own will, and then placed it under the Father’s will. Is there something recently that is still stuck at “my will,” where you just can’t bring yourself to say that “nevertheless”? Please share with your group, and pray for one another.
l090.title: From Human Rule Back to God’s Rule
l090.subtitle: The Heart of Humility Is Letting God Be King Again
l090.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: One Line Out of Place, Fifty Million in the Dark
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

On the afternoon of 14 August 2003, North America suffered the largest blackout in its history. Some fifty million people across the north-eastern United States and the Canadian province of Ontario lost their power in the sweltering heat of high summer. New York’s subway trains stopped dead in pitch-black tunnels, lifts stuck halfway between floors, every traffic light in the city went out at once, and the crossroads dissolved into chaos.

The joint US–Canadian task force that investigated afterwards found that the starting point of this enormous disaster was almost unbelievably small. A high-voltage transmission line in Ohio, carrying too heavy a load, heated up and sagged until it touched a tree that had not been trimmed in time; and at that very moment the alarm system in the control centre failed, so no one noticed in time. One line left the place where it was meant to be, and within a few hours the whole grid went down like a row of dominoes.

Brothers and sisters, this is what “disorder” looks like. Disorder seldom begins with something big. Disorder almost always begins with something small — with “one little thing that is not where it is meant to be.”

Over the last few lessons we have been learning about humility together: true humility is laying down our rights. In today’s lesson the Bible takes us one layer deeper: true humility is not only laying down our rights; it is returning to our originally intended position.

Laying down our rights is being willing to stop insisting on “what I deserve”; returning to our originally intended position is being willing to go back to “the place God has appointed for me.”

Laying down our rights is loosening our grip on what is ours; returning to our originally intended position is setting our feet back inside the square God has marked out for us.

When someone leaves the place God has prepared for them, confusion and disorder follow; but when we return to the position God has given us, life runs once again in the order of blessing.

So please take these two sentences to heart today:

The first step of humility is laying down the rights of “self”;

the deeper level of humility is returning to the order of God.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with three questions.

Why is it that in some families everyone works so hard and everyone loves one another so much, and yet they keep quarrelling until they are utterly worn out?

Why is it that in some churches everyone is so gifted and so zealous, and yet in the end they go from “co-workers” to “combatants”?

Why is it that some people have been believers for years, never miss a meeting and pray a great deal, and yet their lives carry a restlessness and weariness they cannot put into words?

Very often the problem is not too little love or too few gifts; the problem is being in the wrong place. The hand is working very hard — but it is trying to do the eye’s job. The foot is doing its best — but it wants the head’s seat. The harder we try, the greater the chaos; the more effort we put in, the more we get hurt.

Today we will look together at four things: God is a God of order; there is a God-appointed order in our relationships; there are consequences to leaving our originally intended position; and — humility is willingly returning to God’s order.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, One Key Word
1. Jude: What Is Our “Originally Intended Position”?
sections.html:
The author of the letter of Jude is generally held by evangelical scholars to be Jude, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. He calls himself “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James” (Jude 1). He did not call himself “the Lord’s brother”; he called himself only “the Lord’s servant” — and that in itself is a declaration of returning to his originally intended position.

Jude wrote this short letter because something had gone wrong in the church: “For there are certain men who crept in secretly, even those who were long ago written about for this condemnation: ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into indecency, and denying our only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 4).

Then, in a single breath, Jude gives three examples from history as a warning: the people who did not believe after the Exodus, the angels who did not keep their proper place, and Sodom and Gomorrah (Jude 5–7). The middle one of the three is our key text today:

“Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

The Greek word behind “first domain” — which the Chinese Union Version renders as “their proper position” — is archē, meaning “beginning, origin, the office of rule, the sphere of authority entrusted to someone.” The Greek word for “dwelling place” is oikētērion, “a residence, the place where one is meant to live.”

Notice this: what those angels lost was not power, not intelligence, not splendour; what they lost was their “place.” They did not fall because they did some unimaginably monstrous deed; their fall consisted precisely in this — they left the bounds that God had set for them.

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the Bible’s most profound definitions of sin: the essence of sin is often not “doing something bad” but “standing in the wrong place.”

sections.heading: 2. 1 Corinthians 14: A Chaotic Meeting and a God of Peace
sections.html:
First Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul, generally dated around AD 55, from Ephesus (in 1 Corinthians 16:8 Paul says he will stay on in Ephesus until Pentecost).

Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, sitting at the narrow neck of the Greek peninsula. It had thriving shipping and booming trade — and it was also crowded with idols and morally corrupt. This church had a peculiar feature: its gifts were extraordinarily rich, but its order was extraordinarily chaotic. When they met, everyone scrambled to speak in tongues, everyone scrambled to prophesy, and even their love feasts split into factions. Paul could only say with grief, “you come together not for the better but for the worse” (1 Corinthians 11:17).

It was in that very situation that Paul spoke a defining sentence: “for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:33). And at the end of the chapter he draws his conclusion: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

The Greek word for “order” is taxis, originally a military term for an army’s ranks, formation and posts. The strength of an elite unit lies not in its numbers but in everyone being at their post.

Brothers and sisters, God never proves his presence through chaos. Where God is, there is order; and where there is order, the glory of God shines out.

sections.heading: 3. Romans 12: The First Fruit of a Renewed Mind
sections.html:
Romans 12 is the hinge on which the whole letter turns from doctrine to daily living. Paul first says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). Then he says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

And then the first fruit of a renewed mind appears. It is not power, not gifts, not achievement; it is this — seeing your own place accurately:

“For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

The Greek behind “think reasonably” is sōphroneō, meaning “to be clear-headed, to be of sound mind” — neither inflating nor belittling oneself. Straight away Paul illustrates it with the body and its members: “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Romans 12:4–5).

See the sequence clearly: the mind is renewed, then we see our true place, then we function normally among the members. This is exactly the fivefold change that 321 speaks of — change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

So today’s lesson is not just teaching a principle; it aims to renew one of our most fundamental mindsets: my place is given by God, and my greatest blessing is to stay faithfully in it.

sections.heading: 1. God Is a God of Order — His Glory Displayed in Order
sections.html:
The very first sentence of the Bible proclaims a God of order: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).

The second verse describes the state of things before creation was shaped: “The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). The Hebrew behind “formless and empty” is tohu wabohu, meaning “desolate, shapeless, an utter void.” Notice: God’s work of creation is precisely turning chaos into order and emptiness into abundance.

Then, day after day, everything proceeds in perfect order:

“God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). “God called the light ‘day’, and the darkness he called ‘night’. There was evening and there was morning, the first day” (Genesis 1:5).

On the second day God made the expanse and divided the waters below it from the waters above it; on the third day God made the dry land appear, and the earth brought forth grass, plants and fruit-bearing trees; on the fourth day God made the lights in the sky to mark day and night, seasons, days and years; on the fifth day the waters teemed with living creatures and birds flew above the earth; on the sixth day God made the beasts and livestock of the land, and last of all made man in his own image.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the order?

First light, then the separation of day and night; first the sky and the waters, then the birds and the fish; first the land and the plants were prepared, and only then was man created to live among them. God always prepares the “container” first and then puts in the “contents”; he prepares the “home” first and then brings in “those who will live there.” God never places a person somewhere that has not yet been made ready.

That is why Scripture says, “Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). The very act of “putting him” there means placing man in a particular position. From the very beginning, human dignity has been bound up with “place.”

Now lift your eyes to the sky. The average distance between the earth and the sun is about 149.6 million kilometres — a distance scientists call one “astronomical unit.” The earth’s axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and so we have spring, summer, autumn and winter. The moon is on average about 384,000 kilometres from the earth, and its gravity pulls on the tides of the oceans day and night. In the seventeenth century Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) discovered the three laws of planetary motion; and in 1687 Isaac Newton published “Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy,” in which, by universal gravitation, he wrote the motion of all the heavenly bodies into a few lines of equations.

What these great scientists actually did was just one thing: they described the order God had established. No wonder the psalmist says, “The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1).

Order is not only in the heavens; it is inside our bodies too. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to three scientists — Jeffrey C. Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael W. Young — for discovering the molecular mechanisms that control the biological clock, our circadian rhythm. It turns out that even the tiniest cells in our bodies run to a twenty-four-hour rhythm. When people turn day and night upside down for long stretches and go against that rhythm, their bodies begin to break down.

Brothers and sisters, from the farthest star to the smallest cell, all creation is singing the same song: this God is a God of order.

The apostle Paul says, “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:17). “Held together” carries the sense in the original of “joined together, kept bound as one.” The universe does not hold itself up; it is upheld by him.

In Book 19 of “The City of God,” the church father Augustine gave a famous definition of peace: the peace of all things is the tranquillity of order. In other words, without order there is no true peace. If a home has no order, however large the house, it will have no rest; if a heart has no order, however great its achievements, it will have no peace.

Order is the display of God’s glory. When all things move in their own places, harmony, stability and beauty naturally shine forth. In the same way, when a person’s life is within God’s order, they experience peace and blessing; when it leaves that order, life falls into confusion and brokenness.

From the perspective of 321, this is the second of the Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. What is a standard? A standard is the line God has painted on the running track of our lives. The white lines on a sports field are not there to restrict the athletes; they are what make the race a race. Without those lines, however fast you run, it does not count. God’s word is the same. His standard is not a railing that blocks us but a track that carries us.

sections.heading: 2. The Order of Relationships — Honouring Our Originally Intended Position within Our Roles
sections.html:
God has established order not only in the universe but also in relationships. Every person has a role and a place given by God.

Ephesians 5:21 is the overarching principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” Notice that before Paul speaks of any particular role, he speaks first of “subjecting yourselves to one another.” So the order the Bible speaks of is never the strong crushing the weak; it is every person, in the fear of Christ, returning to their own place.

Paul then works this principle out in three sets of relationships: husbands and wives, children and parents, servants and masters (Ephesians 5:22–6:9). Let us look first at the two within the family.

The first is husband and wife. “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully: God’s command to husbands is weightier than his command to wives. Wives are to submit; husbands are to deny themselves. What does it mean to deny yourself? It means giving yourself away; it means dying for her. When a husband is ready every day to lay down his life for his wife, her submission is not hard at all.

The second is children and parents. “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1). “‘Honor your father and mother,’ which is the first commandment with a promise: ‘that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth’” (Ephesians 6:2–3).

The parent–child relationship also has another side: the parents. “You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).

Parents have the role of discipline and guidance, but they must not abuse their authority or wound their children with anger; children are to honour and obey their parents, learning to fear God through submission. This is not a matter of higher and lower status; it is the order of love.

Someone may ask: if we are to submit to one another, why do we still need an order? Paul puts it very clearly elsewhere: “But I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3). Brothers and sisters, notice that last phrase — the head of Christ is God. The Son shares equal honour and glory, equal nature and authority with the Father, yet the Son willingly stands in the place of submission. So “submission” never means “inferiority.” In the triune God we see the most perfect order, and we also see the most perfect love.

When every person stands in their originally intended position, the family is full of peace and blessing; but when someone leaves their place, the family falls into confusion and conflict.

Psychological research offers corroborating evidence here too. Salvador Minuchin (1921–2017), the founder of structural family therapy, pointed out in his 1974 book “Families and Family Therapy” that healthy families have clear “subsystems” and “boundaries” — the couple is one subsystem, the parent–child relationship is another. When the boundaries blur — for instance, when a child is drawn in to fill a spouse’s place and carry emotional responsibilities that do not belong to them (what psychologists call “parentification”) — the whole family system stops functioning. Another pioneer of family systems theory, Murray Bowen (1913–1990), also observed that when the relationship between two people becomes tense, they very easily pull in a third person to form a “triangle”; in the short term this eases the tension, but in the long term it locks the problem in place.

Brothers and sisters, this research is not meant to replace the Bible; it confirms from another angle what the Bible said long ago: when we leave our originally intended position, relationships get hurt.

The workplace is the same. In 1970 three scholars — Rizzo, House and Lirtzman — published their scales for “role conflict” and “role ambiguity,” and a great body of organisational behaviour research since then has shown again and again that when people are unclear about the scope of their responsibilities, or are asked to play conflicting roles at the same time, their work stress, emotional exhaustion and intention to quit all rise markedly. What wears people out most is often not having too much to do, but not knowing where they stand.

And of all role models, the most beautiful is Jesus himself.

He is the Lord who created all things, yet he submitted to his earthly parents: “And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart” (Luke 2:51). For thirty years he quietly lived as a carpenter’s son.

All his life he also submitted to the Father: “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30).

Jesus did not rise above the order; he stood in the right place and fulfilled God’s will through submission.

There was another man who understood this. The centurion of Capernaum said to Jesus, “Just say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and tell another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and tell my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matthew 8:8–9). When Jesus heard this he marvelled and said, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel” (Matthew 8:10).

Brothers and sisters, where did this centurion’s faith come from? It came from understanding “the order of authority.” Only a person who knows he is under authority can truly recognise who is in authority. So remember this: those who understand submission have the greatest faith; those who understand how to stand in their originally intended position are best able to see God at work.

From the perspective of 321, this is exactly the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. It is also the 235 practice of relationships — becoming “2” spiritual companions with selfless people, establishing “3” relationships of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and going on to become “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Every relationship is a place; every place is a trust from God.

sections.heading: 3. The Consequences of Leaving Our Originally Intended Position — Pride Brings Confusion and Downfall
sections.html:
Many of the Bible’s tragedies have to do with “leaving one’s originally intended position.”

The first, and the earliest, happened in heaven.

“How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:12–15).

This passage was originally a lament over the king of Babylon, but the church through the ages has consistently held that it reveals the truth about the fallen one who stood behind him.

Two things need saying here first, so that we don’t use the wrong names. First, “Lucifer” is not a name found in the original text of the Bible. The Hebrew is helel, meaning “shining one, morning star”; the Latin Vulgate translated it as Lucifer, which is where the name comes from, while the Chinese Union Version simply translates the meaning: “bright star, son of the morning.” Second, the Bible never calls him an “archangel”; in the New Testament the title “archangel” appears only twice: Jude 9 names Michael, and 1 Thessalonians 4:16 gives no name — neither refers to him. He was originally one of the most highly honoured of created beings, but his honour did not give him the right to leave his originally intended position.

Count how many times this passage says “I will” — I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. Five “I will”s in all.

Brothers and sisters, these five “I will”s are the anatomy of pride. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place. He did not reject God; he wanted to “be” God.

And the result? “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.” He wanted to go up, and went down; he wanted to rise, and fell. This is what Jude speaks of: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6).

The second example took place in the wilderness. Korah and his followers, discontented with Moses’ leadership, gathered against Moses and Aaron and said, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?” (Numbers 16:3).

What is striking is that Korah himself was a Levite, a descendant of Kohath, who already held an extremely honourable office — drawing near to God, serving at the tabernacle, carrying the holy furnishings of the sanctuary. Moses said to him, “Is it a small thing to you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do the service of Yahweh’s tabernacle, and to stand before the congregation to minister to them; and that he has brought you near, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? Do you seek the priesthood also?” (Numbers 16:9–10).

“Is it a small thing?” Brothers and sisters, that question deserves for every one of us to grow quiet and think about it. Korah’s problem was not that he had no place; it was that he looked down on the place God had given him. His hands already held enormous grace, but his eyes were fixed on someone else’s office.

The result: the earth “swallowed them up with their households, all of Korah’s men, and all their goods” (Numbers 16:32). And another two hundred and fifty men who had offered incense were consumed by fire (Numbers 16:35).

The third example took place in the palace. King Uzziah of Judah was a capable and good king; the Bible says, “He did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes” (2 Chronicles 26:4). But afterwards? “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against Yahweh his God; for he went into Yahweh’s temple to burn incense on the altar of incense” (2 Chronicles 26:16). The priest Azariah, with eighty courageous priests, tried to stop him, but he flew into a rage — and at that very moment “the leprosy broke out on his forehead” (2 Chronicles 26:19). From then until the day he died, he was cut off from the house of God.

Brothers and sisters, Uzziah was a king, but a king is not a priest. His failure was not a lack of devotion — he was going in to burn incense and worship! His failure was this: he did something that looked spiritual from the wrong place.

Then there is King Saul. He could not wait for Samuel to come, so he offered the burnt offering himself (1 Samuel 13:8–9). Samuel’s answer to him became one of the heaviest sentences in the Bible: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim” (1 Samuel 15:22–23).

String these examples together and we see the same trajectory: dissatisfied with the place God has given → reaching out to grab a place that is not ours → confusion → destruction.

In fact, humanity’s first fall happened in just this way. The serpent said to the woman, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). “Like God” — that was the first birth of the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

And what does a society that has left God’s order look like? The book of Judges gives us a cold conclusion: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). With no king, everyone does what is right in his own eyes; and when everyone does what is right in his own eyes, no one has peace.

Let me illustrate with a modern picture. Every day the cells in our bodies are dividing and renewing, each at its own post: heart muscle cells only contract, nerve cells only transmit, skin cells only cover. But there is one kind of cell that is different. The World Health Organization describes cancer as abnormal cells growing uncontrollably, going beyond their usual boundaries and invading other parts of the body.

Brothers and sisters, notice this — cancer cells are not an enemy invading from outside; cancer cells were originally our own cells. What makes them deadly is not that they are bad, but that they have left their originally intended position, crossed their boundaries and stopped submitting to the regulation of the body as a whole.

It is the same in our relationships, in our families and in the church. What hurts most is often not persecution from outside, but someone inside who has left their originally intended position.

That is why 321 puts it so precisely: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. One person leaving their place forces another to leave theirs; one person returning to their place encourages another to return too.

Brothers and sisters, remember this: God establishes order not to restrict us but to protect us.

Order lets love be expressed safely, lets authority operate rightly, and lets life be built up in unity. Just as railway tracks are not there to restrict the train but to let it run at full speed — a train without tracks is not called free; it is called derailed.

sections.heading: 4. Humility Is Returning to Order — Willingly Standing in the Place God Has Given
sections.html:
Having come this far, we can understand one thing: humility is not putting ourselves down; it is recognising our own place.

“For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

Notice that Paul is using the language of a balance. “Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” — don’t overestimate; “to think reasonably” — don’t underestimate either. Some people think humility means constantly saying, “I can’t, I’m not worthy, I’m useless.” But that isn’t humility; it is just another way of talking about yourself all the time. True humility is taking our eyes off ourselves, letting them rest on the place God has appointed, and saying, “Lord, this is what you have given me; here I will be faithful.”

In Book 3 of “Mere Christianity,” in the chapter “The Great Sin,” the British scholar C. S. Lewis says that pride leads to every other vice; it is “the complete anti-God state of mind.” Why? Because the essence of pride is leaving one’s place, and leaving one’s place means pushing God out of his.

Paul goes on to use the body as an illustration: “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Romans 12:4–5).

In 1 Corinthians he puts it in more detail: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired” (1 Corinthians 12:18). “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

The lesson text puts it so well: if the hand wants to see in place of the eye, if the foot fights to become the head, the whole body stops functioning normally.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever thought about it? If a hand really grew an eye, that would not be called a gift; it would be called a deformity. The glory of a member lies not in being able to do another member’s job, but in doing its own job as well as it possibly can, and gladly staying joined to the other members.

That is why Ephesians says, “But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:15–16). “Every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part” — these few words are the secret of a healthy church.

I often think of a symphony orchestra. The most eye-catching moment in a performance may be the concertmaster’s violin solo; but what truly gives the music its depth are the second violins, violas and double basses who spend their whole lives playing the inner parts. There is a widely told story — its source is hard to trace — that the conductor Leonard Bernstein was once asked which was the hardest instrument in the orchestra, and he answered, “Second fiddle.” For playing beautifully is not hard; what is hard is being willing to play in harmony, without stealing the first violins’ limelight.

Brothers and sisters, how many “second violins” are there in the church? The one who arrives an hour early on Sunday morning to unlock the doors and set out the chairs; the one who prays quietly when no one is watching; the one washing dishes in the kitchen. On heaven’s score, not one of their notes is missing.

The apostle Peter says, “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

The picture of “clothing yourselves with humility” — the Chinese Union Version has “girding yourselves with humility,” like tying on a servant’s apron — may well be the scene Peter could never forget for the rest of his life: the Lord Jesus tying a towel around his waist and kneeling down to wash his feet. That night the disciples were arguing about who was the greatest; and the Lord who created the universe chose to kneel at their feet.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

Put this passage side by side with Isaiah 14. The one who said, “I will make myself like the Most High,” was brought down to Sheol; this One “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,” but emptied himself, humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death.

And then the Bible says, “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–11).

Brothers and sisters, this is the law of the kingdom of heaven: those who grab for position fall; those who return to their originally intended position are lifted up.

So a humble life is one that is willing to pray like this: “Lord, let me rest quietly in the place you have given me, do what you want me to do, and accomplish your will.”

From the perspective of 321, this is exactly the practice of selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When I stop fighting for a place that is not mine, I gain the infinite God right in my own place. Jesus is the focal point — not myself, not other people, not my circumstances — and that is the simplest definition of returning to our originally intended position.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Returning to Our Originally Intended Position Is Letting Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s place what we have seen today within the framework of 321, and it will become even clearer.

The Three Foundations are three declarations about place. Jesus is my role model — he submitted to his heavenly Father and to his earthly parents; with his whole life he demonstrated what it means to return to our originally intended position. The Bible is my standard — a standard is the boundary line God has drawn around my place; I don’t find my place by feelings, I find it by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — every day it is the Holy Spirit who brings me back to where I ought to stand and reminds me: you stepped out of place there; step back.

The Two Core Values are the core of order. To let Jesus be King is to acknowledge that there is only one on the throne; I do not sit in that seat, and I do not let any person or thing sit in it either. To let Jesus receive all the glory is to send every bit of credit back to where it was always meant to go — if glory stops at me, it has been intercepted; when glory goes to Jesus, it flows freely.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. What is a system? A system is a group of people, each in their place, joined to one another. A pile of bricks is not a house, and a pile of talented people is not a system; only when they are built up in order do they become God’s temple.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred people spend their whole lives asking, “Where is my seat? Why him and not me?” Selfless people ask only one thing: “Lord, where do you want me to stand?”

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Satan fell in the first place by leaving his position, and what he fears most is seeing someone who willingly returns to theirs; for he has no way at all to deal with a person who is content in their originally intended position and gives the glory to the Lord.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today’s lesson begins with mindset — my place is given by God, not won by my own fighting. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes. So the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. How many ministries have broken apart not because someone did the wrong thing, but because someone stood in the wrong place!

The shift of perspective happens here too: from man’s perspective to God’s — man sees places as high or low, God sees places as a trust; from the earthly to the heavenly — on earth we compare who is in front, heaven looks at who is where they ought to be; from the temporary to the eternal — the seat you win today will belong to someone else tomorrow, and only God’s trust endures for ever; from the worldly to the godly — worldly positions exist to be seen by others, godly positions exist so that God may be seen.

The 920 practice fits right here too. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” At home, my spouse is my 2 and my children are my 2; in church, my co-workers are my 2; at work, my boss and colleagues are my 2. When I live out the selfless “0” before every “2,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Have you noticed? Every one of these nine graces can only grow when I am standing in my own place. The first things a person who oversteps loses are peace and gentleness.

The same is true of 235 relationships. “2” is becoming spiritual companions with selfless people — companions are companions because neither one grabs the other’s place. “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children — parents have their place and children have theirs; parents who overstep crush their children, and children who overstep block the passing on of the heritage. “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers (Ephesians 4:11): five offices, five places, each doing its own part, and so the body grows.

Finally, the Path of Serving is also a path back to our originally intended position: Spirit — letting the Holy Spirit guide; Understanding — taking the Bible as our standard; Life — taking Jesus as our role model; Service — letting Jesus be King; God — letting Jesus receive all the glory. From beginning to end there is only one direction: putting God back in God’s place, and putting me back in mine.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, if truth stops at our ears, it becomes knowledge; only when truth reaches our feet does it become life. The following four practices are this lesson’s assignments. Please put them into practice one by one.

sections.heading: 1. Reflecting on My Place
sections.html:
Think about your roles in your family, your workplace and your church. Have you overstepped or neglected your originally intended position?

Take a pen and paper and write down every place you currently occupy: whose spouse I am, whose parent, whose child, whose colleague, whose co-worker in ministry. Then beside each role ask two questions: in this place, have I reached out to do things that are not mine to do (overstepping my originally intended position)? In this place, have I dumped onto others the things I ought to do (neglecting my originally intended position)?

Overstepping hurts people, and so does leaving a place empty. What God wants is not the person who does the most, but the person who stands most exactly where they belong.

sections.heading: 2. Practising Submission
sections.html:
When those in authority give instructions or suggestions, don’t rush to argue; first seek God’s heart.

This week, when you hear an opinion you disagree with — from your husband, your parents, your manager, your pastor — please be quiet for three seconds first and say in your heart, “Lord, what do you want me to learn from this?”

The Bible says, “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God” (Romans 13:1). I submit to human authority because I submit to the God who established that authority. Of course, if an authority asks us to go against God’s word, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29); but apart from that, submission is our safest place.

sections.heading: 3. Restoring Order
sections.html:
In a relationship conflict, don’t ask who is right and who is wrong; ask, “Am I standing in my own place?”

This is a question that can change marriages, change families and change churches. Because the question “Who is right and who is wrong?” pushes both people into the judge’s seat — and there is only one Judge. When both people sit on the judgment seat, no one in the home is left standing in the place of love.

The next time conflict comes, swap the question: don’t ask, “Where is he wrong?” Ask, “Where should I be standing?” You will find that the moment you return to your place, the other person’s heart softens too. Humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

sections.heading: 4. A Prayer of Reverence
sections.html:
Pray every day: “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.”

This prayer has a scriptural foundation: “You shall observe to do therefore as Yahweh your God has commanded you. You shall not turn away to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32). The prophet also says, “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it’” (Isaiah 30:21).

Brothers and sisters, God’s voice often comes not from in front of us but from behind us; for he is the Shepherd, and he watches over us and guides us from behind. Offer this prayer every morning, and your day will have its track.

Walking the Practice Through: The Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Real change is not a one-off feeling of being moved; it is a road that can be walked to the end. 321 divides the changing of our mindset into eight stages, so let’s walk through them with today’s lesson.

Stage one, Information: I now know — God is a God of order, and I have an originally intended position that God has given me.

Stage two, Revelation: the Holy Spirit has let me see — that long-running conflict in my home was not because someone wasn’t good enough, but because someone was not in their place; that inexpressible restlessness in my heart was because I had been doing God’s work and sitting in his seat.

Stage three, Conviction: I agree from my heart — the order God has established is good; it is there to protect me, not to restrict me.

Stage four, Implementation: I begin to act — this week, in one specific relationship, I return to my place. Wives, stop making decisions on your husband’s behalf; husbands, begin to deny yourselves for your wives; children, phone home; co-workers, stop going over the head of the brother in charge to meddle.

Stage five, Evaluation: be quiet for five minutes every evening and ask yourself — did I leave my place today? At what moment? Why? Was it fear? Was it impatience? Or did I want to be seen?

Stage six, Correction: find the real root, confess it to God, and where necessary apologise to the person. “I just overstepped you — I’m sorry.” That one sentence often carries more power than ten sermons.

Stage seven, Repetition: don’t expect to get it right the first time. Returning to our originally intended position is a lifelong practice; when you fall, stand back up in your place. The Holy Spirit will bring us back to that line again and again.

Stage eight, Multiplication: once you have tasted the peace that is found in order, go and bring someone else along. Share this lesson with your “2” and walk these eight stages together. One person who returns to their originally intended position makes the people around them want to return to theirs too.

A Gentle Reminder

Order is not bondage; it is blessing.

Freedom outside of order is the beginning of destruction; submission within order is the starting point of glory.

A kite flies high not because it has broken free of its string, but because it has a string. Once the string snaps, the kite does not fly higher; it crashes faster.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we began with a sagging power line and saw how an entire city can be plunged into darkness; and we began with the first day of creation and saw how God turns chaos into order.

When people return to their originally intended position, God’s order is restored, relationships are healed and lives are built up.

True humility is not bowing our heads; it is returning to God’s order.

So this morning I want to invite you to grow quiet and let the Holy Spirit ask you a question: Lord, is there a place you gave me that I have left? Is there a place you did not give me that I am clinging to?

Perhaps it is that chair at home — you have sat in the place that belongs to your husband, or you have left the place that belongs to a father. Perhaps it is that office in the church — in your heart you have always looked down on the service God gave you, with your eyes fixed on the person up on the platform. Perhaps it is the throne in your heart — with your mouth you say Jesus is Lord, but in reality it has always been you who makes the decisions.

Come back. Come back to that place. There you will find God’s protection, God’s provision and the peace God has prepared for you.

May we all learn from Jesus, our role model, standing in the right place, submitting to God’s will, and letting his glory fill our lives once again.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the ultimate meaning of returning to our originally intended position.

keyVerses: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6)
“Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1 Corinthians 14:40)

“For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3)
declarations: Lord, you are the God of order;
all that you have established is good.
Grant me a humble heart,
to return willingly to the place you have prepared for me,
never overstepping, never exalting myself;
may you reign in my life and be glorified.
practices: Reflecting on my place: write down all your roles and check each one for overstepping or leaving it empty.
Practising submission: when you hear an opinion you disagree with, be quiet for three seconds and pray before you respond.
Restoring order: in conflict, don’t ask “Who is right and who is wrong?” — ask only “Am I standing in my own place?”
A prayer of reverence: say every day, “Lord, let me walk in your order, turning neither to the left nor to the right.”
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
You are the God of order, not a God of confusion. From the farthest star to the smallest cell in our bodies, everything moves along the course you have set.

Lord, forgive us. So often we are not content with the place you have given us; our eyes are fixed on other people’s offices, and our hands reach for authority that does not belong to us. So often, too, we neglect our own originally intended position and push onto others the responsibilities that are ours to carry. Have mercy on us, we pray.

We ask that the Holy Spirit would guide us and bring us back each day to the place you have appointed. Let us return to the order of love in our families, to our originally intended position of faithfulness in our workplaces, and in the church let each joint do its own part, as we bow quietly before you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly emptied yourself and became obedient to the point of death. Give us that same mind, we pray. Let us never overstep, never exalt ourselves, and turn neither to the left nor to the right.
May you reign in our lives, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6). In your family, workplace or church right now, is there a place God has given you where you are unwilling to stand? What makes you unwilling?

“For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). Please share a time when you “overstepped” or “left your place empty.” How did God later bring you back to your originally intended position? What did that experience teach you?
l091.title: Return to Our Originally Intended Position
l091.subtitle: Order
l091.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Universe Doesn’t Need You on Night Shift
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Let me begin with a very ordinary, homely question: when you opened your eyes this morning, what was the first thought that surfaced in your heart?

My guess is that, for many of us, that first thought was not thanksgiving but a list. The children’s grades, a parent’s test results, the case that’s stuck at work, the bills, the knots in our relationships — one after another they queue up beside the bed, waiting for you. The sun isn’t even up, and your shoulders are already aching. Deep in our hearts lies an assumption we rarely say out loud: if I don’t hold all this up, it will all collapse.

But listen to a fact. In the hours you slept last night, your heart did not take the night off. At seventy beats a minute it beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day, and you have never once given it an order. Right now the earth beneath our feet is racing around the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second, without a hair’s breadth of error, and nobody is working the night shift to push it.
