In 2013 a study published in the journal Science by Lulu Xie and colleagues at the University of Rochester in the United States found something more: while we sleep, the brain’s glymphatic system speeds up the clearing away of the metabolic waste that has built up during the day. God even cleans out your brain for you while you sleep.

The psalmist put this into poetry long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain. It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.” (Psalm 127:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, the universe doesn’t need you on night shift. God is never late, and he never drops anything. So why are we still so tired?

The introduction to this lesson gives us a very simple yet very profound sentence: “Let God be God, and let man be man.” Our greatest pride is wanting to “replace God”. We think we can help God do things faster and better; we think he is too slow, too quiet, too inactive. With one breath we cry, “Lord, I trust you,” and with the next we slot his work into our own diary.

This kind of replacing usually wears two faces.

The first face is “replacing God in the doing” — I’m going to produce the result for God. If the sick person isn’t healed, I blame myself; if my child doesn’t turn back, I double the pressure; if the promise hasn’t yet come true, I come up with a clever plan to help God get it done early.

The second face is “replacing God in the glory” — I’m going to take the applause on God’s behalf. The thing succeeds, people praise me, and my lips say, “Thank the Lord,” while my heart quietly makes a note: that was my gift, my hard work.

These two faces actually grow from one root: pride.

The Bible has a very short and very sharp verse that cuts straight to the heart of this: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6) Where our English Bible has “first domain”, the Chinese Union Version reads “proper position” — the very word this lesson keeps returning to. The Greek word is ἀρχή (archē), which means “beginning”, and also “office” or “position of authority”. The angels did not fall because they lacked ability, but because they refused to stay in the place God had assigned them. Sin has never been only doing the wrong thing; it is standing in the wrong place.

The core message of Kingdom 321 Online Fellowship puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

In this lesson we will follow the text along four steps: recognising our position — I am human, not God; learning to let go — let God be God; seeing the danger of replacing God — the example of Abraham; and giving the glory to God — not grabbing what belongs to God.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, bring us back to the place where we ought to stand.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Source, the Means and the End of All Things
sections.html:
The theme passage of this lesson comes from the close of Romans 11. To understand these four verses, we first need to stand where they were written.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. From the clues in the letter — he commends Phoebe, “a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae” (Romans 16:1), and mentions “Gaius, my host and host of the whole assembly” (Romans 16:23), and Cenchreae was the port of Corinth — scholars generally conclude that the letter was written around AD 56–57, in Corinth, towards the end of Paul’s third missionary journey. At the time he was preparing to take the churches’ gift to Jerusalem, and then to travel by way of Rome to Spain (Romans 15:24–26).

The church in Rome that received the letter had not been founded by Paul, and it was a mixture of Jewish and Gentile believers. In AD 49 Claudius had ordered the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2); a few years later they began to return, only to find that the church was now mostly Gentile. And so a question arose: could the Gentile believers now think themselves superior?

Romans 9 to 11 is Paul’s answer to that question. He works his way through God’s election, Israel’s stumbling and the grace given to the Gentiles, and finally gives the Gentile believers a stern warning: “Don’t be conceited, but fear.” (Romans 11:20) For the branches cannot boast over the root; the wild olive shoot that was grafted in draws its richness from that root.

At this point Paul’s pen suddenly stops. He no longer argues; he worships. Romans 11:33–36 is one of the most magnificent doxologies in the New Testament. The three questions he fires off in a row are all drawn from the Old Testament: the first two come from Isaiah 40:13, and the third echoes Job 41:11. These three questions press right on the deepest root of the sickness in the human heart: we always assume we can serve as God’s adviser, that we can give God ideas, and even that God owes us something.

Then Paul writes the verse that sums everything up: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things.”

Here the Greek uses three prepositions, like three pillars holding up an entire temple: ἐξ (of him) — God is the source of all things; διά (through him) — God is the sustainer of all things; εἰς (to him) — God is the destination of all things. He is the beginning, he is the way, and he is the end.

If all things are “of him”, then my gifts, my health, my family and my service are all received. If all things are “through him”, then there is not a single moment when I am holding myself up — not even the breath I am drawing now. If all things are “to him”, then none of the fruit or the glory should stop with me.

Genesis 1:26 says that God made humankind to have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky and all the earth. What we were given is “stewardship”, not “ownership”. A steward may use all of his master’s resources, but he may not sit in his master’s chair. “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2) A steward’s duty is to be faithful, not to be almighty.

The last line of this doxology is the conclusion of the whole Bible, and the destination of this lesson: “To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”

This is exactly the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. To let Jesus be King is to live out “of him and through him”; to let Jesus receive all the glory is to give back what is “to him”.

Now let us follow the text and walk back to our own originally intended position.

sections.heading: 3. Recognising Our Position: I Am Human, Not God
sections.html:
1. The position we most easily confuse

Right at the start the text points out a mistake we often make without noticing: “taking over” God’s place.

The example it gives is very true to life: we pray for someone who is sick. If they are not healed, we blame ourselves and suspect our faith is not strong enough; if they recover, we easily become smug and think, “My prayers are powerful.”

Listen carefully to what these two reactions have in common: whether it is self-blame or self-congratulation, the focus is on “me”. The first is the pride of discouragement, the second the pride of success; they are two sides of the same coin.

But the authority to heal belongs to God, not to us. Our responsibility is to pray and to trust; the outcome rests in God’s will. We are responsible for obeying; God is responsible for accomplishing. If the sick person gets well, God receives the glory; if they do not, we still hold on to our faith.

The text draws this boundary in a single, crystal-clear sentence: “I am human; I pray. You are God; you heal.”

This is the humility of standing in our originally intended position.

2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: even the Son of God stayed in his place

There is a sentence worth remembering for the rest of our lives. The one who said it was not a weak disciple but the Lord Jesus himself:

“Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19)

Think about it: even the Son of God made flesh deliberately lived on earth in a place of obedience to the Father. Before he died he said, “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). If even Jesus did not grab the Father’s place, what right do we have?

The Lord also said, “Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’” (Luke 17:10) “Unworthy servants” doesn’t mean we have no value; it means we claim no credit and seek no reward.

Paul says as well: “Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3) “To think more highly” is the Greek ὑπερφρονεῖν (hyperphronein), literally “to over-think” — to let your thoughts spill over into a space that doesn’t belong to you.

3. The boundary of responsibility: the backpack and the boulder

In Galatians, Paul uses two verses that seem to contradict each other to mark out the boundaries of our position.

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:2)

“For each man will bear his own burden.” (Galatians 6:5)

The second verse says each person carries his own; the first says we are to carry one another’s. Is that a contradiction? No. In English both verses say “burden”, but the original uses two different words. The “burden” of verse 5 is φορτίον (phortion), the pack a soldier carries on his back — each person’s own share of responsibility, a load he can manage. The “burdens” of verse 2 are βάρος (baros), a crushing boulder — a disaster no one can carry alone.

Our pain often comes from getting these two the wrong way round: we toss onto God the backpack we ought to carry ourselves, and then snatch up the boulder that only God can lift, and carry it until our spine is bent out of shape.

Psychology offers corroborating evidence here. In 1966, in Psychological Monographs, the American psychologist Julian B. Rotter introduced the idea of the “locus of control”. Research since then has broadly found that a healthy state of mind is neither to take everything on ourselves nor to blame everything on our circumstances, but to discern accurately what lies within our control and what does not. In their 1992 book “Boundaries”, the clinical psychologists Henry Cloud and John Townsend also observe that many Christians are worn out not because they love too much, but because they have drawn their boundaries in the wrong place.

The sixteenth-century French surgeon Ambroise Paré is called the father of modern surgery. He is generally credited with a saying that is still repeated today: “I dressed him, and God healed him.” The beauty of that sentence lies in its division of labour: dressing the wound is my job, and I give it everything I have; healing is God’s job, and I entrust it to him completely. Brothers and sisters, do today’s dressing well, and then leave the healing to God.

4. The hardest test of all: at home

The text then carries this principle into the closest place of all: the family.

We often want to “change other people” — to change our husband, our wife, our children. We draw up a list of their problems, remind them again and again, raise our voice, even put pressure on them with spiritual language. The result is that the relationship grows tighter and tighter, and the person does not change.

But the only one who can truly change a human heart is the Spirit of God. Our responsibility is to change ourselves and to love to the end.

The text says something I really love: “Give the hard part to Jesus, and do the easy part ourselves — that is the dividing line between humility and wisdom.”

Changing other people is hard; changing ourselves is hard too, but that is the part God has handed to us. In his 1961 book “On Becoming a Person”, the American psychologist Carl Rogers wrote: “The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.” The idea of “differentiation of self” put forward by the family-therapy pioneer Murray Bowen points to the same thing: the less a person is pulled along by the other’s emotions in a close relationship, the healthier the relationship becomes.

You don’t have to control someone in order to love them; it is when you let go of control that love truly begins.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision: The Priority of Relationships
sections.html:
The 321 vision speaks of “the priority of relationships”: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The chaos in our homes often comes from getting the order upside down. We deal with “things” first — whose turn it is to wash up, who came home late again; then we deal with “people” — how could you do that? — and we never first become quiet before God. Returning to our originally intended position means setting the order straight: first with God — this home today is yours; then with ourselves — please change this controlling heart of mine first; then with others — I am going to love him, not manage him; and only last of all, things.

The 321 vision also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. Manage your child as an item on your to-do list, and you will lose the person he is.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, ask yourself honestly: in my daily living, which matter have I been sitting on God’s seat over all this time?

sections.heading: 4. Learning to Let Go: Let God Be God
sections.html:
1. The root of anxiety is gripping too tightly

The text says that the reason we grow anxious, troubled and disappointed is often that we “grip too tightly”. When money runs short, we worry about what tomorrow will bring; when the future is unclear, we try to find our own way. Yet provision is God’s responsibility; obedience is ours.

Brothers and sisters, notice this word: “grip”. The essence of anxiety is not caring, but gripping. Caring is love; gripping is control. A father caring about his son’s future is love; wanting to decide every step for his son and hold every outcome in his hand — that is gripping.

The Lord Jesus put it very bluntly: “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” (Matthew 6:27) What have we gained in exchange for our worrying? Sleepless nights, stomach aches, quarrels with our family — everything except one extra moment of life.

“To be anxious” in New Testament Greek is μεριμνάω (merimnaō), from the same root as “to divide” (μερίζω). The true face of anxiety is a heart torn in two: half of it here eating breakfast, half of it inside tomorrow’s disaster; half of it worshipping, half of it calculating.

2. The theme promise: seek his Kingdom first

The text quotes that familiar verse: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33)

Notice the word “first”. The Lord did not say “seek only” his Kingdom, nor did he say those other things don’t matter; he is speaking about order. Food and clothing do matter, but they may not take first place.

The context of this verse is Matthew 6:25–34. The Lord first speaks of the birds of the sky: “See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns” — and the heavenly Father feeds them. Then he speaks of the lilies of the field. Finally he draws his conclusion: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.” (Matthew 6:34) God wants us to focus on trusting, not to be anxious about outcomes.

Notice, though: the birds neither sow nor reap, but they aren’t lying about either. Every morning they go out as usual to find food. God’s provision never cancels our duty; it only cancels our anxiety. You are to work, but you don’t have to be afraid; you are to do your best, but you don’t have to guarantee the outcome on God’s behalf.

3. Two actions: casting off and being still

Peter uses a very vivid word: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:6–7)

“Casting” is the Greek ἐπιρίπτω (epiriptō), meaning “to throw forcefully upon”. The same word appears in Luke 19:35, where the disciples “threw” their cloaks on the colt. It is a decisive action, done once and done fully — lifting the load off your own shoulders and flinging it onto someone else’s back.

Notice Peter’s order: first “humble yourselves”, then “cast”. For the person who will not come down low cannot cast off his worries. Beneath worry there is often an unspoken sentence: “Only I can deal with this.” That is pride, not a sense of responsibility.

David models another action: “Yahweh, my heart isn’t arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.” (Psalm 131:1–2)

What a beautiful picture. A baby not yet weaned lies in its mother’s arms wanting something; a weaned child lies in her arms wanting simply its mother. Brothers and sisters, as you lie in God’s arms today, are you wanting something, or wanting God?

4. Psychology as a witness: white bears and stress

In a classic experiment published in 1987 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Daniel M. Wegner and his colleagues asked participants “not to think about a white bear”. The result was that the participants not only kept thinking of white bears while they were suppressing the thought, but once the restriction was lifted, they thought of them even more often than people who had never been asked to suppress the thought at all.

Here is a reminder: gritting your teeth and telling yourself “Don’t worry” usually doesn’t work; the harder you try, the more you worry. The Bible doesn’t tell us to press our worries down by willpower, but to “cast” them away onto a God who cares for us. “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7) Not suppressing, but handing over.

Brothers and sisters, this is the first of the changes the 321 vision speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life. How you see a matter affects you more than the matter itself.

5. An illustration from life: struggling in the water

Any swimming coach will tell you that when people sink in the water, it is usually not because they can’t swim but because they are too tense. The human body is very close to water in density; with the lungs full of air and the body relaxed and lying flat, most people will float. But the moment you panic, thrash your arms and legs and let all your breath out, you go under.

The water hasn’t changed; you have. Faith is the same. The hands that hold you up have been there all along; it is our struggling that drags us down. Letting go doesn’t mean not moving; it means not flailing. It doesn’t mean not trying; it means not overstepping.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: rely on the heart and not the brain

The 321 vision has a very down-to-earth reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23).

“Relying on the brain and ourselves” means moving God’s seat into our own heads, rehearsing every worst-case scenario over and over and preparing a plan for each one. It is exhausting, and most of the disasters we rehearse never happen. “Relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit” doesn’t mean not thinking; it means surrendering before we think: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

The 321 vision also speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. If you weighed the thing you are anxious about today on the scales of eternity, how heavy would it still be?

If we let God be God, life becomes light and free, no longer weighed down.

sections.heading: 5. The Danger of Replacing God: The Example of Abraham
sections.html:
1. Ten years of waiting, and one clever plan

The text says that Abraham’s story is the deepest warning of all.

Let’s lay out the timeline. Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4); after he had lived in Canaan for ten years, Sarai gave Hagar to him, and he was eighty-five (Genesis 16:3); and when Isaac was born, he was a hundred (Genesis 21:5).

In other words, they very nearly made it. Only fifteen years to go.

This is how the Bible records it: “Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, ‘See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.’ Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” (Genesis 16:1–2)

Notice Sarai’s wording. “I will obtain children by her” is the Hebrew אִבָּנֶה (’ibbaneh), literally “I may be built”; the root “to build” (בנה, banah) is related to “son” (בֵּן, ben) and “house” (בַּיִת, bayit). What Sarai wanted was not just a child, but a life that had been built up. Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of us: we rush ahead, not because we don’t believe there is a God, but because we are afraid our own lives won’t get built, and so we start building God’s house for him.

And please pay close attention to another sentence: “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” It carries an ominous echo — in Genesis 3:17 God says to Adam, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice …” When a human voice replaces God’s voice, the ending goes wrong. Sarai acted with good intentions, Abram acted out of compliance, and neither of them was a bad person. Replacing God is very often done by good people.

2. The result: human methods produce human problems

The text asks the right question: what was the result?

Ishmael, born through “human methods”, brought conflict and division. God said of this child: “He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him.” (Genesis 16:12) As soon as Hagar conceived, she looked down on her mistress; Sarai mistreated her; Hagar ran away; and from then on the household had no peace (Genesis 16:4–6). By Genesis 21:10 Sarah is saying, “Cast out this servant and her son!” Abraham’s good intentions brewed long-lasting bitter fruit.

Later Paul, interpreting Scripture by Scripture, spelled out the spiritual principle in this event: “For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman. However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise.” (Galatians 4:22–23)

“According to the flesh” and “through promise” — these are the two roads. What is born of the flesh has to be kept going by more and more of the flesh; what is born of promise, God himself takes responsibility for to the end. Any result forced through by human methods will have to be propped up afterwards by still more human methods: obedience gained through pressure needs ever greater pressure to keep it in place. It is a road that grows more exhausting the further you go.

3. Human good intentions are not necessarily God’s intention

The text puts it with great insight: human good intentions are not necessarily God’s intention; wanting to help God is really replacing God. Pride doesn’t always shout out loud; sometimes it comes wrapped in the kindness of “I just want to help you”.

“‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.’” (Isaiah 55:8–9) He does not need our help; what he wants is our trust and obedience.

So it was with Saul as well. At Gilgal he waited seven days for Samuel; unable to wait any longer, he offered the burnt offering himself, and the moment Samuel arrived he said, “You have done foolishly.” (1 Samuel 13:13) He was only a little early. The greatest failures in the spiritual life are often not doing bad things, but grabbing God’s timing in doing the right thing.

4. Psychology as a witness: the action bias

This urge — “I can’t wait any longer; I have to do something” — is what psychology calls the “action bias”.

A study by Michael Bar-Eli and colleagues, published in 2007 in the Journal of Economic Psychology, analysed 286 penalty kicks in top-level football matches. Goalkeepers dived left or right more than 94 per cent of the time and stayed in the centre only about 6 per cent of the time; yet nearly 30 per cent of the kicks actually went down the middle, and goalkeepers who stayed put had the highest save rate. So why do goalkeepers still dive? Because conceding a goal while standing still feels more embarrassing than diving the wrong way. People would rather do the wrong thing than look as if they did nothing.

Brothers and sisters, that was Abram’s psychology exactly. Waiting ten years looked like doing nothing; taking Hagar at least looked like “moving God’s plan forward”.

Our hearts are by nature wired to grab hold of something; and faith is precisely the work the Holy Spirit does within us that runs against that nature.

5. The turning point: letting go on Mount Moriah

Thank the Lord, the story didn’t stop with Hagar. The text says that later, when God commanded Abraham to offer up Isaac, he learned to let go completely. This time he no longer used his own methods, but simply listened to God’s voice.

Notice what happened in between. Between Genesis 16:16 and 17:1, the Bible is silent for thirteen years. For those thirteen years he held the son he had produced by his own methods, yet he could not hear God’s voice — what a costly lesson.

Then, on Mount Moriah, the man who had once come up with plans on God’s behalf had the son he had received by faith asked of him by God. This time he offered no ideas; he simply rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey and walked for three days. As a result he not only experienced the provision of “Yahweh Will Provide”, but also received God’s blessing and trust.

“Abraham called the name of that place ‘Yahweh Will Provide’. As it is said to this day, ‘On Yahweh’s mountain, it will be provided.’” (Genesis 22:14)

“Yahweh Will Provide” is the Hebrew יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (YHWH yir’eh), which translated literally means “Yahweh will see”. God’s provision begins with God’s seeing. When Abraham reached the mountain, God had long since placed the ram in the thicket (Genesis 22:13) — that ram was not created at the moment he raised the knife; it was just that Abraham had not seen it before. Brothers and sisters, the provision you need today may already be on the mountain; you simply haven’t got there yet.

This is how Paul assesses Abraham’s final faith: “Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.” (Romans 4:20–21) Look at the order in this sentence: grew strong through faith, gave glory to God, and was fully assured. The final outlet of faith is giving glory to God — which is exactly our fourth key point.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan

The 321 vision says that pride is the root of the problem, and the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The Hagar episode was a product of the self-centred life: my calculations, my methods, my timetable. Mount Moriah was the practice of selflessness: “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (see Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When Abraham laid Isaac down on the mountain, what he received back was not only Isaac but the promise, “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring” (Genesis 22:18). Those who let go do not lose; those who let go gain God.

Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” Brothers and sisters, if God’s work is done in man’s way, it will certainly lack God’s supply — and we will try to make up the shortfall with more and more human methods, until we are utterly spent.

sections.heading: 6. Giving the Glory to God: Don’t Grab What Belongs to God
sections.html:
1. Another kind of replacing: keeping the applause for ourselves

The text reminds us that we may replace God not only in the “doing” but also in the “glory”. The first grabs God’s work; the second grabs God’s name. And the second is often more hidden, because it doesn’t need a hand to move — only a thought in the heart.

The text gives an example that makes us smile, yet stings: ask Sunday-school children, “Who parted the Red Sea?” and most will answer, “Moses.” But in fact it was God who parted the sea; Moses was only the vessel who stretched out the staff. The Bible says: “Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.” (Exodus 14:21)

Look at the structure of that verse: Moses stretched out his hand; Yahweh sent the wind. Moses was responsible for a one-second gesture; Yahweh was responsible for a whole night’s mighty work. And before that, Moses had already made it plain: “Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.” (Exodus 14:14)

The children get it wrong because they only see the person standing at the front. Brothers and sisters, so do we — and sometimes that person is us.

2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: the planter and the waterer are nothing

Paul also says: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6)

The background of this verse is the factional quarrelling in the Corinthian church. Some said, “I follow Paul”; others said, “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul’s answer was to move everyone’s position down a notch: “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7)

“Is not anything” isn’t self-deprecation; it is accuracy. From the moment a seed sprouts to the moment it bears fruit, no farmer can produce the mystery of “growth” in between; all we can do is put the seed in the ground and pour on the water. All we can do is our duty; the result always lies in what God does.

Paul shuts every human mouth with a question: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Brothers and sisters, think about it honestly: your mind, your health, the mentor you happened to meet, the door that happened to open — which of these did you earn yourself?

3. A sobering example: Moses strikes the rock

Grabbing God’s glory can carry a heavy price.

Numbers 20 records that at Kadesh the Israelites quarrelled because there was no water. God told Moses to take his staff and to speak to the rock so that it would give out water. But what Moses said was: “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10)

The Chinese Union Version reads “Must I bring water …”, but in the Hebrew the verb is first person plural — “Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” With a single sentence Moses turned God’s act into “our” act. Then, instead of speaking to the rock, he struck it twice with his staff. The water still came out, but God said to Moses: “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.” (Numbers 20:12)

Forty years of patience, brought down by one sentence.

Brothers and sisters, the fact that God made the water flow does not mean he approved of that “we … for you”. Fruitfulness in ministry does not mean God agrees with our taking the credit for it.

4. Three pictures from the New Testament

The New Testament gives us three vivid pictures of “giving the glory”.

The first is a negative one. In Caesarea, Herod put on his royal robes and addressed the people, and they shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” The result: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

The second is a positive one. In Lystra, Paul and Barnabas healed a man who had been lame from birth, and the crowds wanted to offer sacrifices to them as gods. At once they tore their clothes and shouted: “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you.” (Acts 14:15)

The third concerns an angel. In a vision John fell down to worship the angel who was speaking to him, and the angel said, “Look! Don’t do it! … Worship God.” (Revelation 19:10)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The apostles, even the angels, refuse to give an inch on this one thing: I too am human, I too am a servant, and the glory must not stop with me.

So however fruitful your service may be, however much people praise you — remember: we are human, not God. That God uses us is grace, but the glory must go to him.

The text also reminds us of the other side: don’t turn a prophet into a god, because prophets can be wrong too; don’t make an idol of God’s servants, because the power comes from God. Lifting a person up onto God’s seat harms him; being lifted up by others and not coming down harms yourself. “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

5. Witnesses from psychology and nature

When it comes to assigning credit, the human heart has a built-in bias. In a 1975 review published in Psychological Bulletin, the American psychologists Dale T. Miller and Michael Ross pointed out that people commonly display a “self-serving bias”: they attribute success to their own ability and effort, and failure to circumstances, luck or other people.

This is exactly the pair of reactions the text described at the start. Our hearts automatically pull credit inwards and push blame outwards; that is why we need, every day, to send the glory back on purpose.

Nature gives us a beautiful picture. The moon lights up the earth, but the moon itself gives off no light; it only reflects the light of the sun, and very inefficiently at that — the moon’s albedo is only about 12 per cent, and nearly nine-tenths of the sunlight that falls on it is absorbed. Yet that tenth or so reflected back is enough to light up an entire wilderness.

Brothers and sisters, we are the moon. We have no light of our own. What we can do is not shine, but not block the light; not manufacture glory, but reflect it. “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7)

The English writer C. S. Lewis wrote in “Mere Christianity” that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. Humility is not putting yourself down; humility is knowing exactly where you stand.

6. Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus receive all the glory

The text closes with Romans 11:36, which is also the theme verse of this lesson: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” This is the second of the Two Core Values of the 321 vision: let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, God’s glory never belonged to us in the first place. If we take it, we can’t keep it; it will only crush us. How many gifted servants in history fell not in suffering but in applause.

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) These words of John the Baptist are the freest declaration of everyone who has returned to their originally intended position.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Whole Picture of Returning to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
1. The Three Foundations

The first foundation is “Jesus is my role model”. The most complete return to an originally intended position in the whole Bible is the Son of God willingly taking the position of a servant: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8) He was worthy all along, yet did not grasp; we were never worthy, yet we grip for dear life.

The second foundation is “the Bible is my standard”. Abram’s mistake was not a lack of love, but replacing “what agrees with God’s word” with “what seems reasonable”. Without a standard higher than our feelings, our good intentions will become our masters.

The third foundation is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) Those who are led walk behind; those who want to replace God walk in front.

2. The Two Core Values and the Goal

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus be King answers the question “Who makes the decisions?” — that is the first three points of this lesson: I don’t decide the outcome, I don’t decide the timing, I don’t act on God’s behalf. Letting Jesus receive all the glory answers the question “Who gets the credit?” — that is the fourth point: I don’t sign my own name.

The Goal is to establish God’s system — an order in which “God is on the throne and people are in their originally intended position”. When a husband in a family no longer plays god to his wife, and a wife no longer plays god to the children — that home begins to have the taste of heaven.

3. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The 321 vision says that the old self is self-centred and the new self is selfless, and that the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. The Bible records Satan’s fall in a string of five “I will”s: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Humanity’s fall was a rerun of the same sentence: “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Leaving our originally intended position is the prototype of sin throughout the whole Bible.

And the road of the new self is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not wiping yourself out; selflessness is giving up your seat. That is why selflessness is never a loss, but entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — because the one who has come to live within is the infinite God.

4. The cycles of humility and pride

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

This is easiest to test at home. The husband says, “You just don’t understand,” and the wife immediately fires back, “No, you’re the one who doesn’t understand” — that is pride provoking pride, and both sides lose. But if one of them says first, “What I just said was wrong of me,” the other will usually soften too — that is humility inspiring humility, and both sides win. The person who has returned to their originally intended position is the one who softens first — not because they are in the wrong, but because they don’t need to win; their worth is in Christ.

5. The fivefold change and the Path of Serving

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

The mindset of this lesson comes down to one sentence: I am human, not God. Once this mindset truly reaches the heart, life changes — no longer strung tight; daily living changes — you can sleep; relationships change — you no longer control your family; ministry changes — fruitful service no longer puffs you up, and fruitless service no longer crushes you.

The 321 vision also speaks of the Path of Serving: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). The end of that path is exactly the end of this lesson.

At the same time, remember the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. How many people, in order to “do things for God”, have sacrificed their relationship with God and their relationships with their families — and that is the greatest price of replacing God.

6. The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice of the 321 vision says that every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living a selfless (0) life before them, we will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Look especially at four of them: patience — not grabbing God’s timing; kindness — not changing people by pressure; gentleness — having power yet not using it; self-control — knowing what is not yours to touch. All four are the fruit of returning to our originally intended position.

Remember too: fruit is “borne”, not “made”. “I am the vine. You are the branches. … apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) The originally intended position of a branch is to stay connected.

The 235 relationships of the 321 vision say: with selfless people, become a “2”, spiritual companions; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Only people who have returned to their originally intended position can build relationships like these — because they don’t need others to depend on them; together everyone depends on Christ.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Turning Mindset into Habit
sections.html:
The text gives us four concrete practices. The 321 vision says there are eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s look first at the four practices, and then use the eight stages to walk them into life.

Practice 1: Entrusting in prayer

How: after every prayer, declare, “Lord, I hand this over to you; its fulfilment is up to you.”

Going deeper: add one concrete action at the end of your prayer — hand the matter over out loud, and then stop going over it again and again. Peter says to “cast” it on God; that is an action, not a feeling. You could keep an “entrusting notebook”: write down the matter and the date, then turn the page. Look back three months later and you’ll be amazed how many things God has already dealt with — things you once lost sleep over.

Practice 2: Changing myself

How: when you want to change someone else, first ask the Lord to change your own heart.

Going deeper: set yourself a house rule — “one reminder costs one prayer”. Every time you want to open your mouth to correct someone in your family, pray for them once first. After you have prayed, what you want to say will come out softer, and your timing will be better. Remember the text’s dividing line: changing their heart is hard — give it to Jesus; giving them a smile at dinner tonight is easy — we do that.

Practice 3: Waiting in faith

How: while you have not yet seen the promise fulfilled, choose trust rather than agitation.

Going deeper: waiting is not empty; waiting has content. Find a verse for the thing you are waiting for, copy it out and read it every morning. While you wait, make no major decisions, take no shortcuts and don’t force things through by manipulation — these three “don’ts” are what faith looks like in practice.

Practice 4: Giving the glory to the Lord

How: when someone praises you, say in your heart, “Lord, this is your doing.”

Going deeper: besides saying it in your heart, learn to say it with your mouth too. You don’t need to deny the praise; just add, “Thank you — this really is God’s grace.” Then, in your prayers that day, give the glory for that specific thing back to God by name.

Walking the whole way with the eight stages

Stage 1, Information: this morning’s devotion is the information. You now know: “I am human, not God.”

Stage 2, Revelation: information is still in the head; revelation reaches the heart. Be quiet for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to point out one specific matter — the matter in which I am sitting on God’s seat right now. When it has a name and a setting, that is revelation.

Stage 3, Conviction: not just admitting “That’s right,” but surrendering: “I will live this way.” The mark of conviction is that you are willing to pay a price.

Stage 4, Implementation: choose one practice and do it for seven days first. Don’t do all four at once; one at a time, and it only counts if you actually do it.

Stage 5, Evaluation: every evening ask yourself three questions — Where did I overstep today? What did I truly hand over? Was there any praise I quietly kept for myself?

Stage 6, Correction: not self-blame, but adjustment. Self-blame goes back to self; correction goes back to Christ. When you find you’ve gone wrong, confess it at once and give the seat back at once.

Stage 7, Repetition: arrange these four practices over four weeks — week one, entrusting; week two, changing yourself; week three, waiting; week four, giving glory — and then go round once more.

Stage 8, Multiplication: pass on what you’ve learned to your “2”. Find a brother or sister, teach them today’s lesson, and hold each other accountable. When you begin to feed others, what you have received truly becomes your own.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call: Letting God Be Lord Is the Greatest Humility
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the text leaves us a few beautifully concise reminders. Please keep them in your heart:

Wanting to help God is really taking his place; wanting to control the outcome is really usurping his sovereignty. Letting go is not failure but trust; letting God be Lord is the greatest humility.

Replacing God is pride at its most extreme; letting God be God is humility at its most complete.

True faith is not doing things for God, but letting God work within me.

The greatest weariness of our lives comes not from having too much to do, but from sitting in the wrong seat. Sitting in God’s seat is the most exhausting job in the world, because our shoulders simply cannot bear that seat.

So this morning the Lord issues us a call, gentle yet firm: come down, return to your originally intended position.

Returning to our originally intended position is not being demoted; it is being set free. A steward doesn’t have to lose sleep over the stock in the storehouse, because the storehouse belongs to the master. “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10)

Returning to our originally intended position doesn’t mean doing nothing, either. Quite the opposite: those who have returned to their position act with greater precision. What is theirs to do, they give their all to; what is not theirs to do, they waste no strength on. With one hand they dress the wound; with the other they entrust it.

When we return to our originally intended position and acknowledge that he is Lord and I am only a vessel, God will display his glory through our obedience.

Brothers and sisters, let us together let Jesus be King — let him reign as King over my family, my work, my future and my service; and let us give all the glory to him, keeping none of it in our hands.

For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.

keyVerses: Romans 11:33–36

“Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?’ ‘Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?’ For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”
practices: Giving the glory to the Lord
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we come before you this morning.
Lord, I am willing to return to my originally intended position — to let you be God, and to be your servant.
I confess that when I so often want to help you, I really want to replace you; I so often speak of trust while my hands grip tightly. Forgive me all my pride wrapped up in good intentions.

I lay down my anxiety and my control. I will no longer use my own methods to help you finish things; I want only to trust and obey your leading. Right now I place in your hands the person and the matter that weigh on me. You are God; you are responsible for accomplishing it. I am human; I need only obey.
Holy Spirit, remind me every day: give the hard part to Jesus, and do the easy part myself. When I am praised, help me to turn and point to you; when I see no fruit, help me still to stand.
All glory, honour and power be yours, for ever and ever.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Genesis 16:2 says: “Sarai said to Abram, ‘See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.’ Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” In your life right now, is there something you are using “human methods” to help God finish early? Has it brought you peace, or more unrest?

1 Corinthians 3:6 says: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” Think of something recent that you did well and were praised for. Say specifically: which part was your “planting and watering”, and which part could only be God’s “giving the increase”? How will you give that glory back to God this week?
l092.title: Return to Our Originally Intended Position
l092.subtitle: Do Not Take God’s Place
l092.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Pride Is Being Out of Position; Humility Is Returning to Position
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. First, let me ask you to picture a scene with me.

A symphony orchestra walks onto the stage, and more than a hundred musicians take their places. The bows of the first violins are already raised, the double basses lean against shoulders, the French horns rest quietly in their players’ hands, and the timpanist stands guard over two drums that, by the look of it, will be struck only a few times all evening. Suddenly someone asks: since the violin sounds so beautiful, why not have all hundred of them play the violin? The answer is simple — then what is on stage would no longer be an orchestra, but a hundred violins. The volume would go up, but the music would vanish.

The church is the same. God never intended to make a hundred identical copies of you.

In church we often say, “Christ is the head, and we are the body.” Say it long enough and it can turn into a pleasant but empty slogan. In fact it is not an abstract metaphor but a truth about our “originally intended position”. Paul says: “He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” (Ephesians 1:22–23) And again: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18) There is only one head, but there are thousands upon thousands of members.

So true humility is not only knowing “I am not God”; it also means knowing “I am not the head”.

That sentence is worth growing quiet over this morning and chewing on slowly. Many Christians acknowledged long ago that they are not God — that is the starting point of faith, and it isn’t hard. What is hard is acknowledging “I am not the head” in the church, in the small group, in the family, in the serving team. I am not the one who sets the direction; I am not the one who must always be heard; I am not the one they cannot do without.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever met a scene like this in church? Over some small matter two people each think their own way is better; back and forth it goes, the tone grows harder and harder, and in the end the job gets done but the relationship is ruined. Or at home, a husband and wife argue over some trivial thing, and before long they are no longer really arguing about that thing at all, but about “who has the final say”.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In the words of today’s lesson, it comes down to this: pride is being out of position; humility is returning to position.

“Offside” is a term from the football pitch. However fast a player runs, however skilful he is, if he is standing in the wrong place, the goal doesn’t count. The spiritual world has its offside too. However many gifts a person has, however great their zeal, if they stand in the wrong place, that service will hardly endure before God.

In this lesson we will learn together to “return to our originally intended position”. The text takes us down this road through three key points: first, we are different, and that is why we belong together; second, no one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best; third, let Jesus be the head, and let me be just a member.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, personally put each one of us back in the place God has arranged for us.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter to a Divided Church
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of 1 Corinthians 12, we first need to know the author, the date, the recipients and the situation of this letter.

The author is the apostle Paul. He states who he is at the very start of the letter: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:1–2). It was written around the spring of AD 55, while Paul was on his third missionary journey and living in Ephesus. He leaves a clue at the end of the letter: “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost” (1 Corinthians 16:8). In other words, this letter was written with tears by a pastor far from home, for a church he had planted with his own hands, which was now splitting apart.

The recipients were the church in Corinth. The city of Corinth sat on the isthmus in southern Greece, with the port of Cenchreae to the east and the port of Lechaeum to the west — the throat linking central Greece and the Peloponnese. In 146 BC the Roman general Mummius destroyed the city; in 44 BC Julius Caesar ordered it rebuilt as a Roman colony, and it later became the capital of the province of Achaia. The rebuilt Corinth flourished rapidly. Merchants and travellers crowded in, and the population was a mixture — Roman veterans, Greeks, Jews, slaves and freedmen from the East all lived in one city. There was much wealth, and there were many idols; in the city stood the temple of Apollo, whose remains survive, and on the acropolis a temple to the goddess of love. Corinth’s licentiousness was famous throughout the world, so much so that Greek gained a verb, “to Corinthianise”, meaning to live a debauched life.

A city like this produced a church like this: gifts, but no character; excitement, but no order; spiritual displays, but no spiritual life.

In the letter Paul deals with their problems one by one: factions and divisions (chapter 1), pride and boasting (chapter 4), sexual immorality (chapter 5), suing one another (chapter 6), confusion about marriage (chapter 7), food offered to idols (chapters 8–10), disorder in their gatherings and at the Lord’s Supper (chapter 11), and disorder over spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14).

And all these problems had one single root. Paul points to it at the very beginning: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” (1 Corinthians 1:12) And again: “For you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” (1 Corinthians 3:3)

Jealousy and strife. Put plainly, it is the self-centred life. Everyone wanted to stand at the front; everyone thought their own way was the right one.

So when he reaches chapter 12, Paul writes out his prescription. He doesn’t begin with rules; he begins with “the body”. He says: “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12) And then: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.” (1 Corinthians 12:13)

In its day this verse was earth-shattering. In the Roman world a high racial wall stood between Jews and Greeks, and a deep class divide lay between slave and free. Yet Paul says: in the body of Christ, you all drink of the same Spirit.

There is a piece of history here worth mentioning. Using “the body” as a picture of a community was nothing new in the Greco-Roman world. The Roman historian Livy records that in 494 BC, when the common people of Rome withdrew to the Sacred Mount, the senator Menenius Agrippa told them a fable about “the belly and the limbs”, urging the commoners not to complain about the nobility but each to keep to his station. That used the image of the body to maintain the class system. Paul turns the image completely on its head: far from telling the lesser members to keep quiet, he says, “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary” (1 Corinthians 12:22), and that God gives “more abundant honor to the inferior part” (1 Corinthians 12:24).

Brothers and sisters, this is the gospel. The Worldly system uses “the body” to keep the little people down; God’s system uses “the body” to lift the little people up.

Notice too the overall flow of chapters 12 to 14: chapter 12 speaks of the diversity of gifts and the unity of the body; chapter 13 speaks of love as the most excellent way; chapter 14 speaks of how to use gifts in an orderly way in the gathering. The love chapter in the middle is not a wedding poem but a healing medicine placed right in the middle of their rivalry over gifts. Paul’s logic is this: however many gifts you have, without love they count for nothing; and the first concrete form love takes is each person returning to their own originally intended position.

The verses we read today, 1 Corinthians 12:17 and 21, fall right in the middle of this flow.

sections.heading: 1. We Are Different, and That Is Why We Belong Together
sections.html:
Paul says: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?” (1 Corinthians 12:17)

It is a question asked with a smile, yet it reveals a serious spiritual fact: God’s design is unity in diversity.

Look at the context. Paul first says: “For the body is not one member, but many.” (1 Corinthians 12:14) Then he describes two opposite emotions. The first is inferiority: “If the foot would say, ‘Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,’ it is not therefore not part of the body.” (1 Corinthians 12:15) The second is superiority, which is what verses 17 and 21 deal with. The person who feels inferior says, “I’m no use”; the person who feels superior says, “You’re no use.” Both sentences deny the very same thing — God’s arrangement.

So in between, Paul sets down a sentence that steadies everything like an anchor: “But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” (1 Corinthians 12:18)

Key word: set

The word “set” is the Greek etheto, the aorist middle of the verb tithēmi, meaning “to place, to establish, to appoint”. It is a completed action, and its subject is God himself. In other words, your place in the body was not drawn by lot, was not assigned by the pastor, and was not won by your own striving — God personally “put” you there.

Add to that the phrase “just as he desired”. The Greek is kathōs ēthelēsen, “as he willed”. Your position comes from God’s heart, not from human ratings.

Brothers and sisters, if this sentence sinks into your heart, you no longer need to envy anyone else’s position, starting today.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: dividing is the first act of creation

From the very beginning God is a God who “divides”. Genesis 1 records that when God said, “Let there be light,” he “divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4); he made the expanse and “divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse” (Genesis 1:7); and he made the dry land appear and gathered the waters into one place. Dividing is not the beginning of chaos; dividing is the beginning of order. Chaos is chaos precisely because everything is churned together.

The New Testament follows the same logic. Paul says: “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us.” (Romans 12:4–6) Peter says: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” (1 Peter 4:10) The word for “various” is the Greek poikilos, which originally means “multicoloured, richly patterned”. God’s grace is not one colour; it is a full spectrum.

That is why Paul says: “Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. There are various kinds of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all.” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6) Three times “various kinds”, three times “the same”. Diversity and unity have never been enemies; they are the fingerprints the triune God has left on the church.

Illustration: thirty-seven trillion cells, one blueprint

Let’s look at our own bodies. In 2013 Eva Bianconi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy published a study in the Annals of Human Biology estimating that an adult human body contains about thirty-seven trillion cells. Thirty-seven trillion is an unimaginable number.

But what is truly astonishing is not the quantity; it is this: almost every one of those thirty-seven trillion cells carries exactly the same set of DNA. One blueprint, growing into completely different functions — the light-sensing cells of the retina capture light, red blood cells carry oxygen, neurons transmit signals at over a hundred metres a second, and bone cells silently bear the weight of the whole body.

One blueprint, different callings. That is a picture of the church: we read the same Bible, we receive the same Holy Spirit, yet we are placed in completely different positions.

Back to the orchestra. In a performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, the timpanist may strike only a few dozen times all evening, and the triangle player may sound just a handful of notes. But take those few notes away and the music is missing a piece. The conductor won’t say to the triangle player, “You’ve got too little to do — switch to the violin.” Because he knows those few notes are exactly what he wants.

Research: the cleverest team is often not the strongest team

In 1981 the British researcher Meredith Belbin published his research on team roles from Henley Management College. He did something very interesting: he put together a team of the people with the highest intelligence-test scores, called it the “Apollo team”, and had it compete in a management simulation against other ordinary teams. The result was unexpected — the Apollo team often came last. The reason was that everyone was too good at analysing and too eager to lead, so the whole team spent its time debating; no one was willing to carry things out, and no one took responsibility for pulling things together.

From this Belbin coined a well-known saying: nobody is perfect, but a team can be.

Brothers and sisters, this is a modern footnote to what Paul said more than nineteen hundred years ago. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?

Applying the 321 Vision: difference is a blessing, not a threat

The text puts it well: if we want to change others so they become like us, we are in fact denying God’s creation.

That one stings. We rarely admit that we are “remodelling other people”, but think about it: when I say in my heart, “Why is he so slow?”, “Why does she go on so much?”, “Why does this person never do things the normal way?”, what I am really saying is: why aren’t you me?

That is the self-centred life. Self-centred people measure the whole world with themselves as the ruler; selfless people look at everyone through God’s heart. The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having no self; it is no longer making yourself the centre, the standard and the end point. Jesus is the focal point — not myself, not others, not my circumstances.

Paul has a sentence worth reading once a day: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

If you preach better than others, you received it; if you cook better than others, you received it; if you are more patient than others, you received that too. Since it is all received, none of it can be used for comparison.

The first of the 321 vision’s fivefold changes is “mindset”. Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. The mindset to change today is this: difference is not conflict; difference is richness.

Returning to our originally intended position means respecting God’s arrangement, appreciating other people’s differences, and accepting our own uniqueness.

sections.heading: 2. No One Is the Best, Everyone Else Is Better Than Me, and Together We Are at Our Best
sections.html:
Paul reminds us: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

This is an attitude of spiritual humility — no member is dispensable. Everyone matters, but no one matters most.

Notice how precise Paul’s examples are. He doesn’t say “the foot can’t tell the eye”; he says “the eye can’t tell the hand” and “the head can’t tell the feet”. He deliberately has the higher speak to the lower. Because the damage done by pride always flows downhill. In church it is rarely the new believer who looks down on the senior co-worker; it is usually the senior one who looks down on the newcomer. It is rarely the one who cooks who looks down on the one who preaches; it is usually the one on the platform who looks down on the one in the kitchen.

Key word: necessary

Next Paul says something that almost goes against common sense: “No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22)

“Necessary” is the Greek anankaia, meaning “essential, indispensable, impossible to do without”. Paul doesn’t say the weaker members are “of some use too”; he says they are “much rather necessary”.

And he presses further: “Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant propriety; whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part, that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another.” (1 Corinthians 12:23–25)

The word “composed” is the Greek sunekerasen, carrying the sense of “blending, mixing”, as one blends colours or seasonings. God didn’t just pile the members together any old how; like a master chef, he blended them. And the way God blends them is to give, on purpose, double honour to the one who is lacking.

So the result is: “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26)

If you have ever been woken in the middle of the night by a toothache, you understand this verse. One tooth, less than a ten-thousandth of your body’s volume, can keep the whole person awake all night. The body never says, “It’s only one tooth — just put up with it.”

Illustration: glands the size of a grain of rice that govern the whole body

The human body has a pair of often-overlooked organs — the parathyroid glands, usually four of them, attached to the back of the thyroid. Each is only the size of a grain of rice; all four together weigh less than 0.2 grams. In the whole body they are so small you would hardly know they were there.

But the parathyroid hormone they secrete governs the level of calcium in the blood of the whole body. Medicine has long known that if these four little things are accidentally removed during thyroid surgery, the patient develops low blood calcium and spasms in the hands and feet, and in severe cases it can be life-threatening.

“Those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” Brothers and sisters, God has placed a design like this in your body so that you can understand his heart for the church. The older saint who comes half an hour early every week to open up, set out chairs and boil water; the sister who prays for the meeting in a corner and never goes up front — they are the church’s parathyroid glands. Normally you don’t notice them; once they are gone, the whole body starts to go into spasm.

Research: the more people there are, the less effort each gives

But “together” does not mean “lots of people”. A warning is needed here.

In 1913 the French agricultural engineer Maximilien Ringelmann ran a rope-pulling experiment, something like a tug-of-war. He found that a person pulling alone gives 100 per cent of their strength; when two pull together, each gives on average only about 93 per cent; when eight pull together, each gives on average only about half. Later, in 1974, Alan Ingham and other researchers repeated the experiment and confirmed that this was not just poor coordination but a drop in motivation — with more people around, I put in a little less effort. Psychology calls this “social loafing”.

This is the exact opposite of “together”. People gathered in one place do not automatically become a body; people gathered together who each hide themselves only become a heap.

So what kind of team truly multiplies its strength? From 2012 to 2015 Google carried out an internal study called “Project Aristotle”, analysing more than 180 teams to discover the secret of high-performing teams. The conclusion surprised them: the key was not who was on the team or how many clever people it had, but a quality called “psychological safety” — a concept introduced in 1999 by Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, meaning that members dare to speak up, dare to admit mistakes and dare to reveal what they don’t know, without fear of being humiliated or punished.

Brothers and sisters, does that sound familiar? A church that dares to admit weakness is a strong church. And what makes people dare to admit weakness is exactly this: no one is the best, everyone else is better than me, and together we are at our best.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: each counting others better than himself

The text’s motto is really a plain-speech version of Philippians: “Doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” (Philippians 2:3)

“Counting others better than himself” is neither self-deception nor talking yourself down as worthless. The Greek hēgeomai means “to weigh, to judge, to regard”: in your thinking you deliberately put the other person first. It is a choice of the will, not an emotion.

The Bible gives a sad example. Samuel said to Saul: “Though you were little in your own sight, weren’t you made the head of the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17) Saul was once so small he hid among the baggage, but later he grew so big he would not listen to God’s word. Once people see themselves as big, they can no longer hold the position God gave them.

The Lord Jesus takes this principle all the way: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:26–28)

Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying something like this: I can do things you cannot, you can do things I cannot; together we can do great things. That is another way of saying the text’s motto.

Applying the 321 Vision: pride provokes pride, humility inspires humility

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Have you noticed that almost every conflict in church starts like this? One barbed remark gets an even more barbed reply; one disrespectful look gets an even colder look back. That is pride provoking pride. In the end there is no right or wrong, only winning and losing — and both sides lose.

The other way round, a simple “I didn’t think this through properly” will often be met with “No, I was too hasty as well.” That is humility inspiring humility.

That is why the 321 vision has the 920 practice: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Paul says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice that not one of these nine graces can be borne by a person on their own. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. God places different people around you precisely so that you can bear fruit.

In our service we must remember: each person’s gifts and calling are given by God. They are not capital for comparison but tools for serving. When each of us does our own part, the glory goes to Jesus, not to people.

sections.heading: 3. Let Jesus Be the Head, and Let Me Be Just a Member
sections.html:
Having come this far, we arrive at the heart of the lesson. The first two key points were horizontal — my relationships with my brothers and sisters; the third is vertical — my relationship with Christ. If the horizontal is to be level, the vertical must first be upright.

The text goes straight to the point: the core of pride is wanting to “take the place of the head”. Wanting to control, direct and dominate others is in fact usurping the sovereignty of Christ.

The Bible defines this very clearly: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

Key words: head and preeminence

“Head” is the Greek kephalē. In Paul’s usage the word carries two layers of meaning at once: first, “source” — life comes from him; second, “ruler” — authority goes out from him. So “Christ is the head of the church” doesn’t only mean that he governs us; it means our life comes from him. Cut off from him, we don’t just become weaker — we cannot live at all. The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

“Have the preeminence” is the Greek prōteuōn, a word that appears only once in the whole New Testament, right here in Colossians 1:18. Paul seems to have chosen a rare word on purpose, to say something utterly unique: only one has the preeminence in all things.

Notice the words “in all things”. It isn’t that he has first place in church but not at the office; it isn’t that he has first place on Sunday and someone else takes over on Monday. It is in all things.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: who was it that did not keep their position?

The first pride to appear in the Bible was not in a human being but in an angel. The prophet Isaiah records that chilling monologue: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Five “I will”s. Five times out of position.

Jude sums it up with one precise word: “Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day.” (Jude 6)

“First domain” — in the Chinese Union Version, “proper position” — is the Greek archē, whose basic meaning is “beginning, the original office and rank”. The angel did not fall for committing some monstrous crime, but for “not keeping its position”. Its original place was that of a worshipper, yet it wanted to sit on the throne of the one who is worshipped.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the 321 vision means: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing power and wanting to replace God. The essence of Satan is not some evil innovation, but a confusion of position.

And Christ took the completely opposite road: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Satan said, “I will make myself like the Most High”; Christ “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped”. Satan wanted to go up; Christ was willing to come down. “Emptied himself” is the Greek ekenōsen, literally “poured himself out until empty”.

So humility is not putting yourself down; humility is returning to your originally intended position.
