discussion: Think back honestly over this week: was there something you told yourself “I can’t do,” when really it was “I won’t”? When you read Matthew 5:44, “But I tell you, love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,” who is the first person who comes to mind? Are you willing to pray for him or her once today?

Right now, which person or which situation is God’s “humility classroom” for you? Set it against Romans 5:3–4, “Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope,” and talk it over: what does God want to produce in you? Which one thing will you practise concretely this week?
l096.title: Humility Is Not Hard
l096.subtitle: Which Is Easier — Humility or Pride? (Part 2)
l096.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Humility Is Not a One-Day Decision but an Everyday Choice
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

Let me begin with a scene. One Sunday afternoon, halfway through a church workers’ meeting, two brothers who had served for many years reached a standoff over a very small matter. One said, “I’ve run this process for eight years, and it’s always been done this way.” The other said, “But times have changed — young people simply can’t get in.” Both of them actually had a point, but by the end there was no truth left on the table, only “I have to win.” When the meeting broke up, each felt he had been wronged, and that week neither of them slept well.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed something? The vast majority of conflicts in our lives do not happen between “truth” and “heresy,” but between “what I want” and “what you want.” It is not a battle between good and evil; it is a wrestling match between me and you. And the thing that turns small matters into big ones, and differences into hostility — the Bible has a name for it: pride.

We have all heard many sermons telling us to “be humble.” So why, after all these years of hearing, is our temper still the same? Why can we sing “I want to be humble” in church with tears in our eyes, then get home and be quarrelling with our spouse within three minutes? The reason is simple: humility has stayed at the level of “ideas” and never come down to “practice.”

The lesson’s introduction puts it well: humility is not a character trait formed in a single day, but a practice of life that requires “choosing every day.” God does not demand that we be perfect all at once; what he gives us is a lifetime of opportunities to keep practising. There is enormous grace in that sentence. God did not say, “Today you must instantly become a perfectly humble person, and if you can’t, I’ll cut you.” What God says is, “Today, are you willing to choose once more?”

And where has God set up the training ground? Not in a monastery, not deep in the mountains, but in our dealings with people, in family life, in serving at church. Your dinner table at home is the training ground; your office is the training ground; that table at the church workers’ meeting is the training ground. Every time you are willing to lay yourself down and choose to return to your originally intended position, your life becomes a little more like Jesus.

In today’s lesson we will learn three practices of humility so concrete that you can use them by lunchtime today: “I will listen to you,” “I will take care of you,” and “It’s all my fault.”

These three sentences are so short that a child can say them, yet so hard that most adults never manage to say them in a lifetime. Why so hard? Because each one requires laying down a right. To say “I will listen to you,” you must lay down the right to “be right.” To say “I will take care of you,” you must lay down the right to “be served.” To say “It’s all my fault,” you must lay down the right to “shift the blame.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision stresses again and again: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Today’s three practices are three acts of laying down our rights, three returns to our originally intended position.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Letter from Prison to a City of Honour
sections.html:
To understand Philippians 2:3–4, we first need to know who wrote this letter, to whom, and in what circumstances.

Author and Date

The author of this letter is the apostle Paul. He signs it himself: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ; To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and servants” (Philippians 1:1).

When Paul wrote this letter, he was in prison. He says, “Now I desire to have you know, brothers, that the things which happened to me have turned out rather to the progress of the Good News, so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ” (Philippians 1:12–13). Evangelical scholars generally hold that the letter was written during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome, around AD 60–62.

Notice this picture: a man with chains on his hands is teaching a group of free people what it means to count “others better than himself.” This is no armchair theory. Paul is not talking about humility in easy times; he is talking about humility in a situation where he has lost all control.

The Church and the City

Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). At the time the city was a Roman colony; Luke specifically records: “and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony” (Acts 16:12).

A “Roman colony” meant that the city enjoyed Roman citizenship, and many retired Roman soldiers lived there. It was a city that prized status, rank and honour above all. In a culture like that, a person’s worth was set by “comparison”: Are you a citizen? How high is your position? Which seat do you take at the banquet?

So when Paul says, “doing nothing … through conceit,” he is not teaching an abstract principle; he is dismantling the values of an entire city.

Context: 2:3 Is Not an Isolated Sentence

The verses just before Philippians 2:3–4 read: “If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion, make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind” (Philippians 2:1–2).

The verses after are the loftiest Christological hymn in the New Testament: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Paul’s logic runs like this: the church must be united (2:1–2); the key to unity is humility (2:3–4); the model of humility is Jesus (2:5–8); and the outcome of humility is glory to God (2:9–11).

This is exactly the order of the 321 vision: Jesus is my role model, so I learn from his ways; the Bible is my standard, so I act according to it; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so I have the power to act. And the final destination is “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11) — let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

There is one more piece of background that is often overlooked. The church in Philippi had a specific problem: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). Two sisters were at odds. One very practical reason Paul wrote the whole of Philippians about joy, unity and humility was the rift between those two sisters.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us great comfort: the loftiest Christology in the Bible was written to resolve the most ordinary relational problem in a church. God cares so much about that small rift in your home or your small group that he is willing to set before you the mystery of his Son’s humbling.

sections.heading: 3. “I Will Listen to You” — Laying Down the Right to “Be Right”
sections.html:
1. The Scripture

“doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3)

2. A Light from the Original

“Rivalry” in the Greek is eritheia, originally meaning “competing for selfish gain,” “forming factions, jockeying for one’s own position.” “Conceit” is kenodoxia, made up of kenos (empty) and doxa (glory) — literally “empty glory”: it looks dazzling, but it’s hollow inside.

“Humility” here is tapeinophrosynē, formed from tapeinos (low) and phrēn (thought, mind) — literally “a mind brought low.” Take special note: before Paul wrote, this word was almost a term of contempt in Greek culture, carrying a whiff of “base, servile.” It was the Christian faith that turned this word into a virtue. Why? Because the Son of God himself brought himself low.

The word “counting” in “counting others better than himself” is hēgeomai, a word for “reaching a judgement after deliberation” — not a feeling, but a decision. Brothers and sisters, this matters a great deal: counting others better than yourself is not a self-hypnotising emotion but a choice of the will. You don’t first have to “feel” that the other person is better than you; you only have to “decide” to regard them that way.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Root of Quarrels Is Not Truth but “I Want to Win”

The text puts its finger right on it: people quarrel, more often than not, not over a question of truth but because “I want to win.” The Bible fully agrees with this diagnosis.

James asks even more bluntly: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1) The source of the fighting is not in the other person; it is in the craving to win inside me.

Proverbs describes the one who “doesn’t listen”: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). And again: “A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion” (Proverbs 18:2). Brothers and sisters, put these two verses together and you have a portrait: a person whose head is full of nothing but finishing what he has to say.

And God’s command to us is: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Three actions, and the order cannot be reversed: first listen, then speak, and only last does emotion get its turn. Most of our breaches come from turning that order around — first getting angry, then speaking, and only at the end grudgingly listening a little.

The text puts it precisely: “I will listen to you” is not blind agreement; it is acknowledging two things — that others may see what I haven’t seen, and that God can speak to me through others.

4. God Will Speak to You Through the Very Person You Look Down On

The text points out a phenomenon that cuts to the heart: we are willing to listen to “people of standing” and “people more forceful than we are,” but we find it hard to listen to the quiet, unremarkable ones.

The Bible has one example that pulls no punches. The prophet Balaam is riding his donkey; three times the donkey turns aside, and three times Balaam beats her. Then comes the strangest conversation in the Bible: “Yahweh opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, ‘What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?’” (Numbers 22:28)

This is what the text means: God once used a donkey to rebuke the prophet Balaam, and he may likewise remind us through children, co-workers, spouses, even people who seem “not to know any better.”

The opposite model is the boy Samuel. Eli taught him: “It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, Yahweh; for your servant hears’” (1 Samuel 3:9). And later Samuel really did answer this way: “Speak; for your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10).

“Speak; for your servant hears” — these five words are the spiritual prototype of “I will listen to you.” Notice the order: first comes the identity of “servant,” and only then the posture of “hearing.” If a person refuses to be a servant, he will certainly not hear.

5. An Illustration from Life: The Rules Rewritten by an Air Disaster

On 27 March 1977, at Tenerife airport in Spain’s Canary Islands, two Boeing 747 airliners collided on the runway, killing 583 people — the deadliest accident in the history of civil aviation.

The investigation report noted that the captain was one of the airline’s most senior and most respected flight instructors. The first officer had doubts and did speak up, but in that cockpit culture of “the captain has the final word,” his doubts were never truly heard.

This tragedy became a watershed in aviation history. Afterwards the global airline industry vigorously promoted “Crew Resource Management,” whose core comes down to one thing: however junior your rank, you have a duty to speak up; however senior your rank, you have a duty to listen.

Brothers and sisters, this is the real-world version of “I will listen to you.” The church is not a cockpit, but the principle is the same: when only one person in a team is allowed to speak, the team begins to fly in a dangerous direction.

6. Confirmation from Psychology

The medical world has a well-known observational study. Beckman & Frankel (1984), publishing in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that physicians interrupted patients on average about eighteen seconds after the patients began describing their concerns. Fifteen years later, a study by Marvel et al. (1999) in the Journal of the American Medical Association put the figure at twenty-three seconds.

The humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers and Richard Farson introduced the concept of “Active Listening” in 1957, pointing out that true listening is not merely hearing the words but hearing the feelings and intentions beneath them. They stressed in particular that listening is hard because it requires the listener to set aside his own position for a while — and that is exactly where the cost lies.

Another reminder comes from marriage research. The longitudinal study of couples’ interaction conducted by Gottman & Levenson (1992) at the University of Washington showed that what predicts a marriage heading for breakdown is not the number of quarrels but the manner of interaction; and of these, “contempt” is the most destructive.

What is contempt? It is when, as I listen to you, I have already decided in my heart that “what you’re saying isn’t worth hearing.” Brothers and sisters, this is pride in its most everyday, most unobtrusive form.

7. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. When I insist on “being right,” what right am I seizing? I’m seizing “the right to pronounce right and wrong.” And that right belonged to God all along.

I sit in God’s seat and announce who is right and who is wrong; and the moment I sit there, I can’t hear people, and I can’t hear God. This is the self-centred life.

“I will listen to you” is stepping down from that seat and returning to man’s originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The 321 vision also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice, rely on the brain and you’ll fret. Arguing is “relying on the brain” taken to its extreme: as I listen, I’m already drafting my rebuttal in my head. Listening is “relying on the heart”: I first receive you as a person, and then deal with your words.

Brothers and sisters, remember the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. “I will listen to you” looks like just a small speaking habit, but it is really a change of mindset — from “I want to win” to “I want to understand.” Change the mindset, and relationships change with it.

sections.heading: 4. “I Will Take Care of You” — Laying Down the Right to “Be Served”
sections.html:
1. The Scripture

“each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4)

2. A Light from the Original

The verb “looking to” in this verse is skopeō, from the same root as the English “scope” (as in telescope, or field of view), meaning “to fix one’s gaze on, to keep one’s attention on.” It is not “a glance”; it is “a steady look.”

Notice that Paul does not say, “Don’t look to your own things”; he says, “not just looking to his own things.” The Christian faith has never required us to abolish our own needs; it requires us to widen our field of view. You don’t have to switch your lens off, but you do have to learn to turn it.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Model the Lord Himself Set

The text says it very well: “You should take care of me” is self-centred thinking; “I will take care of you” is the act of humility.

The basis for this lies in the Lord Jesus’ own declaration: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

The context of this verse is vitally important. The mother of James and John had come asking Jesus to let her two sons sit in his kingdom, one at his right and one at his left. When the other ten disciples heard, they were indignant. You see — even those who had followed the Lord for three years were still thinking about seats. Jesus didn’t scold them; he said just one thing, and it turned the whole value system upside down: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant” (Matthew 20:26–27).

In the world’s system, the higher your seat, the more you are served; in God’s system, the higher your seat, the more you serve. This is exactly what the 321 vision means by “establish God’s system” — not painting the world’s pyramid in church colours, but turning the whole pyramid upside down.

And the Lord didn’t only say it; he did it. John’s Gospel records that he “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him” (John 13:4–5).

In first-century Palestine, washing feet was the job of the lowest servant in the house. That night, the Lord of the universe crouched on the floor, holding twelve pairs of dusty feet — including the feet of the man who was about to betray him.

When he had finished, he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

Another verse the text quotes is the continuation of this very passage: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34). And right after, the Lord says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Brothers and sisters, notice what badge the Lord Jesus gives. He did not say everyone would recognise us as his disciples because of our large attendance; he did not say it would be because our songs are beautiful and our preaching brilliant. What he said was: because you love one another.

4. Caring Is Not Meddling

The text has a sentence with a fine sense of proportion: “I will take care of you” is not meddling in other people’s business; it is actively noticing others’ needs, caring about their mood, being considerate of their feelings, helping them in their weakness.

Where does that sense of proportion lie? Meddling is “I’ll make the decision for you” — that is climbing back into God’s seat. Caring is “I’ll walk a stretch of the way with you” — that is standing in man’s originally intended position. Meddling suffocates people; caring lets them breathe.

The principle Paul gives is: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). What we bear are “burdens” — the things he cannot carry alone; not shouldering for him the responsibilities that are his own to carry.

5. An Illustration from Life: That Pot of Soup

I know a sister whose husband had an operation and was in hospital; she was rushing back and forth alone between the hospital and home. Someone in her small group posted a long message in the group chat, encouraging her to be strong and to trust. She said she read it and was grateful, but also felt empty inside.

Then a sister who normally said very little posted nothing at all. She simply placed a thermos flask at her door at seven every morning, with a pot of hot soup inside — fourteen days in a row.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual words are precious, but sometimes a pot of hot soup is the most solid theology there is. “I will take care of you” is usually not a grand plan, but an action concrete enough to be left on a doorstep.

6. Confirmation from Science and Psychology

Dunn, Aknin & Norton, in a study published in the journal Science in 2008, found that people who spent money on others reported greater happiness than those who spent the same money on themselves. This result appeared across surveys, field follow-ups and randomised experiments.

And the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which since 1938 has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years — its current director, Robert Waldinger, points out that the study’s most consistent finding is this: good relationships predict a person’s happiness and health in later life better than wealth and fame do.

The Lord Jesus stated this principle long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). These are words of the Lord passed on by Paul himself.

7. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision has a very precious practice called “the 920 practice”: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out a selfless (“0”) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (“9”) of its expressions.

The nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit are: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that not one of these nine graces can be borne behind closed doors on your own. Love needs someone to love; patience needs someone who provokes you; kindness needs someone in need; gentleness needs someone weaker than you. God puts your “2” beside you not to annoy you, but to make you complete.

The text says: if everyone chooses “I will take care of you,” the church will become a truly loving family. This is exactly what 321 calls the “235 relationships” — become a “2” with someone who is selfless, spiritual companions who support each other; build the “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together.

And the order of all this is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A church that puts ministry ahead of relationships will end up with very handsome reports and very weary people.

sections.heading: 5. “It’s All My Fault” — Laying Down the Right to “Shift the Blame”
sections.html:
1. The First Recorded Blame-Shifting in Human History

The text points out that humanity’s first reaction after sinning was to shift the blame. The Bible demonstrates this to the full as early as chapter 3.

“God said, ‘Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?’ The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’ Yahweh God said to the woman, ‘What have you done?’ The woman said, ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate.’” (Genesis 3:11–13)

Brothers and sisters, read Adam’s sentence slowly. He doesn’t just say “the woman”; he says “the woman whom you gave to be with me.” That one sentence shifts the blame onto two parties at once: first onto his wife, then onto God — you’re the one who gave her to me.

Eve is no better: “The serpent deceived me.”

The text is right: this is pride’s reaction — unwilling to admit, refusing to face it.

2. The One Who Is the Exact Opposite of the First Adam

But Jesus is completely different. He never sinned, yet he was crucified for our sins; he bore our responsibility — and this is humility at its height.

The prophet foretold it long ago: “All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

Peter says it even more directly: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds” (1 Peter 2:24).

Brothers and sisters, set these two pictures side by side:

The first Adam: sinned, and said, “It wasn’t me.”

The last Adam: without sin, and said, “Count it all against me.”

The distance between those two sentences is the distance between pride and humility — and the distance between death and life.

3. “It’s All My Fault” Does Not Mean Blurring Right and Wrong

Here the text adds a very important footnote: the humble do not blame themselves indiscriminately; rather, they are willing to take responsibility for the relationship.

This distinction is crucial. There is a kind of “self-blame” that is not humility at all, but another form of self-centredness — I take the responsibility for the whole world onto myself, because secretly I believe the whole world revolves around me. That is not selflessness; it is another version of the self-centred life.

The true “it’s all my fault” asks the questions the text raises: when someone else does wrong, do I also have some responsibility to bear? Did I fail to remind them? Did I fail to pray? Did I fail to keep watch?

The Bible has a special phrase for this kind of shouldering: “standing in the gap.” God says: “I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I would not destroy it; but I found no one” (Ezekiel 22:30).

Daniel was that man standing in the gap. He was so godly that even his enemies could find no fault in him, yet when he prayed he said: “we have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even turning aside from your precepts and from your ordinances” (Daniel 9:5). Notice that word — “we.” He could easily have said “they,” but he said “we.”

Nehemiah prayed the same way: “Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned” (Nehemiah 1:6).

Brothers and sisters, this is the breadth of heart of a spiritual firstborn: not pointing fingers from on high, but walking into the crowd and changing “they” to “we.”

4. The Lord Jesus’ Diagnosis of “Blaming”

The Lord says: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

And the way God gives is: “Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective” (James 5:16).

Notice the cause and effect in this verse: confession brings healing. The text says exactly the same — blaming cannot repair a relationship; only humility can win back a heart.

And before God this path is even more certain: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

5. Confirmation from Psychology and Management Science

On apologies, an experiment by Lewicki, Polin & Lount (2016), published in Negotiation and Conflict Management Research, showed that whether an apology is accepted depends on which components it contains; and of all the components, “acknowledgement of responsibility” is the single most decisive one.

In other words, the experimental data tell us something we have long known but don’t want to do: what really repairs a relationship is not “I’m sorry if I made you uncomfortable,” but “I was wrong in this, and I take responsibility.”

Brothers and sisters, “it’s all my fault” is the most direct and most powerful attempt at repair.

6. A Picture from Physics

Physics has a very simple principle: the lower an object’s centre of gravity, the more stable it is. That’s why a roly-poly toy has a heavy base: you can push it over, but it won’t stay down; push it, and it wobbles a little and stands right back up.

Brothers and sisters, humility is lowering the centre of gravity of our lives. Someone whose centre of gravity rests on “I must be right” and “I must save face” has a high centre of gravity, and one gust of wind knocks him over. Someone willing to say “it’s all my fault” has a low centre of gravity: when others push him, he wobbles a little and stands right back up.

The Bible said it long ago: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). And again: “The fear of Yahweh teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility” (Proverbs 15:33).

7. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Have you tried this experiment at home? You raise your voice by one decibel, the other person raises theirs by two; you take a step back, and quite often the other person softens too. This isn’t a psychological technique; it is a spiritual law.

The sentence “It’s all my fault” cuts the chain of conflict right through the middle. As long as one person is willing to cut first, the fire goes out.

And the Bible promises: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Peter quotes the same sentence too, and adds: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when you are proud, your opponent is not your spouse, not your co-worker — it is God himself. When I say “it’s all my fault,” I am not only bowing my head to a person; I am walking back from opposing God into God’s grace.

This is what 321 means by: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: 6. Three Roots: The Root System of a Humble Life
sections.html:
At the very end, the text gives a lovely little reminder: humility is not merely saying “I was wrong” with our lips, but being truly willing in our hearts to “learn from Jesus.” Listening to others is learning gentleness; caring for others is learning to serve; admitting fault is learning to take responsibility. These three practices are the three roots of a humble life.

“Learn from Jesus” comes straight from the Lord’s own invitation: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

Botany tells us that the root systems of many trees spread far wider than their canopies, and most of the absorption takes place in the finest root hairs. In other words, what sustains a great tree is not its few thick roots but the countless thousands of root hairs so fine they are almost invisible.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same. What holds you up is not those few brilliant moments of serving up front, but choosing, again and again where no one sees, “I will listen to you,” “I will take care of you,” “It’s all my fault.”

These three roots correspond to three kinds of learning:

Listening to others, learning gentleness — this is the lowering of the “mind.”

Caring for others, learning to serve — this is the lowering of the “hands and feet.”

Admitting fault, learning responsibility — this is the lowering of “face.”

Mind, hands and feet, face — lower these three, and your centre of gravity holds firm.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Not one of today’s three practices was dreamt up by man. The Lord first showed the heart of “your servant hears,” first knelt down to wash feet, first bore our responsibility on the cross. We are simply following in his footsteps.

The Bible is my standard. When I feel I’m not in the wrong, the standard is not my feelings; it is Philippians 2:3–4. Feelings can deceive me; the standard won’t.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, to be honest: by willpower alone, these three sentences will never come out of our mouths. It is the Holy Spirit within us — reminding, pouring out, empowering — who enables us, at the very moment our temper flares, to swallow our words and say something else instead.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. In every conflict there is only one throne. Either I am King, or Jesus is King. “I must be right” is me reigning as King; “I will listen to you” is letting Jesus reign as King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The summit of Philippians 2 is: “to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11). Our humility is not so that people will praise our good character, but so that people will see Jesus.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. The Worldly system says: whoever is loudest wins; whoever ranks highest gets served; whoever is best at shifting blame stays safe. God’s system is the exact opposite: whoever is willing to listen gains; whoever is willing to serve is great; whoever is willing to shoulder responsibility is healed.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

These three practices take aim at exactly three strongholds of the self-centred life:

“I must be right” is self-centredness in our opinions;

“I want to be served” is self-centredness in our needs;

“Shifting the blame” is self-centredness in our image.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, when “I” give up my seat, Christ lives in me. What I give up is not my life; it is my limitation.

Four Shifts of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s: man’s perspective asks “Who’s right?”; God’s perspective asks “Who can be built up?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: earth looks at whose seat is highest; heaven looks at whose knees are bent.

From the temporary to the eternal: win an argument, and three days later no one remembers; admit a fault once, and you may save a thirty-year relationship.

From the worldly to the godly: the world says, “Don’t let anyone walk all over you”; God says, “each counting others better than himself.”

The Priority of Relationships

The 321 vision says: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

This has very practical meaning for today’s three practices. If you have not first been heard and comforted before God, you will hardly have the strength to listen to others. If you have not first received God’s care for you, your caring for others will soon run dry. If you are not first sure that you are fully accepted in Christ, you will never be able to say “It’s all my fault” — because your worth is still staked on “I am right.”

Brothers and sisters, that is why the power for humility does not come from gritting our teeth; it comes from grace. Only a person who knows he has been loved to the uttermost can afford to lose.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Turning Three Sentences into Habits
sections.html:
The text gives four concrete practices. Let’s look at them one by one, and deepen them using the 321 vision’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice One: The Practice of Listening

At least once today, deliberately hear someone out to the end — without interrupting, without defending yourself.

Make it this concrete: today, choose one person and let them finish what they have to say, and in the meantime do only one thing — nod. When they’ve finished, first restate it once: “Do you mean that …?” Once you’re sure you’ve got it right, then give your view.

Practice Two: The Practice of Caring

Take the initiative to greet and help a brother or sister you seldom interact with.

Please don’t pick the easiest one. Look down your small-group list and find the person you haven’t spoken to for three months. “I’ve been thinking of you these past few days — how have you been?” is enough.

Practice Three: The Practice of Admitting Fault

When conflict arises, first ask yourself: “What responsibility can I take for this?”

Notice how cleverly this question is designed. It doesn’t ask, “Was I wrong?” — that question is far too easy to answer with “No.” It asks, “What responsibility can I take?” — a question that always has an answer.

Practice Four: The Practice of Prayer

Pray every day: “Lord, please make me someone who hears, who sees, and who is willing to take responsibility.”

Who hears — matching “I will listen to you”; who sees — matching “I will take care of you”; willing to take responsibility — matching “It’s all my fault.” One prayer wraps up all three practices.

Deepening It Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Stage one, Information. Today you have already received the information: what the three practices of humility are, what the Bible says, what the original language means. Information is the doorway, but if you stop at information, you’ve only understood one more lesson.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. What is revelation? It is God pointing to one specific scene in your life and saying, “Right here.” Perhaps even now a face has surfaced in your heart, a phone call you never returned, an apology you never spoke. That is revelation.

Stage three, Conviction. Conviction is when your heart truly yields and you stop defending yourself. This stage often comes with tears, because we finally admit: the problem really is with me.

Stage four, Implementation. Do it today; don’t wait until it “feels right.” Feelings never put themselves right; action leads feelings. At dinner tonight, let your family finish what they’re saying; before you leave work today, send that greeting; before bed tonight, say that sentence: “I was wrong in this.”

Stage five, Evaluation. In the evening, spend three minutes before God looking back: Did I listen today? Did I care? Did I take responsibility? Which time did I manage it? Which time did it come blurting out again?

Stage six, Correction. When you find you’ve interrupted someone again, don’t condemn yourself; just come back to the Lord and say, “Lord, tomorrow I’ll try again.” The Bible says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Stage seven, Repetition. This is the most crucial and the least romantic stage. There are no shortcuts to character, only repetitions. The text is right: humility is not a one-time decision but an everyday choice. Repeat an action long enough, and it turns from “practice” into “nature.”

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once these three sentences have become your nature, pass them on to your “2,” pass them on to your spiritual children. The goal of the 321 vision is to establish God’s system, and a system is not held up by one person; it is multiplied through life, generation after generation.

Brothers and sisters, remember: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry finally bears real fruit. This is the fivefold change, and not one step can be skipped.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, what we’ve learned today comes down to just three sentences:

I will listen to you. I will take care of you. It’s all my fault.

The text concludes: humility is not a one-time decision but an everyday choice. When we practise “listening, caring and taking responsibility” in daily life, we no longer live in the bondage of pride, but live out the gentle and humble life of Christ.

Notice that word “bondage.” Pride really is a kind of bondage. The proud are not free — they cannot admit fault, because admitting fault hurts too much; they cannot ask for help, because asking for help is too humiliating; they cannot listen properly to others, because they must keep proving themselves. They have locked themselves up.

It is generally held that the Church Father Augustine was once asked what the most important lesson of the Christian faith was, and he answered: first, humility; second, humility; third, humility. And the twentieth-century apologist C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, called pride “the great sin,” describing it as “the complete anti-God state of mind,” because the essence of pride is putting oneself in God’s place.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. And there is only one solution — let Jesus be King.

The text’s final sentence puts it superbly: practising humility every day is letting Jesus overcome in us every day.

That sentence is worth thinking about once more. We don’t practise humility to make ourselves better people so we can collect a certificate. We practise humility so that the King has somewhere to sit. Every inch of my seat I vacate is an inch by which Jesus’ kingdom expands within me.

So this morning I want to issue you a call.

Not a call to resolve, “From now on I’m going to be a humble person” — resolutions like that rarely last three days. I want to call you to do one small thing: today, just today, find one opportunity to say one of these three sentences.

Just once.

Because God does not require us to be perfect all at once; what he gives us is a lifetime of opportunities to keep practising. And a lifetime is made up of one “today” after another.

May the gentle and humble heart of the Lord Jesus reign as King in you and me today, and may all the glory go to him.

Lord, today I am willing to practise humility.
When I want to insist on my own way, teach me to say, “I will listen to you.”

May I learn, day by day through practice, to be like you,
let humility become the habit of my life,
and bring glory to you for ever.

Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You existed in the form of God, yet emptied yourself and took the form of a servant; you are Lord, yet you knelt down to wash your disciples’ feet; you never sinned, yet you bore all our responsibility. Lord, you are our role model of humility.

Lord, we confess that inside us there is a very big “I.” We like to be right, we like to be served, we like to push responsibility away. We use these things to protect ourselves, but in the end we lock ourselves up and push the people around us further away. Please forgive us.

Lord, today we are willing to practise. When I want to insist on my own way, remind me to say, “I will listen to you.” When I want to be served, remind me to say, “I will take care of you.” When I want to shift the blame, give me courage to say, “It’s all my fault.”
