discussion: Question one: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). Of the three practices — “I will listen to you,” “I will take care of you” and “It’s all my fault” — which sentence is hardest for you to say? Behind that sentence, what kind of right are you clinging to?

Question two: “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’” (Genesis 3:12) Think back to your most recent conflict. Apart from the other person’s responsibility, what responsibility can you take for it? This week, to whom will you say that sentence, and how?
l097.title: Practising Humility Daily
l097.subtitle: Three Practices That Turn Humility from a Principle into Daily Living (Part 1)
l097.partTitle: Unit 6 · The Key to Selflessness — Humility

sections.heading: Introduction: Humility Is Not a Theory but a Lifelong Practice
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This early morning, let us come before the Lord together and keep learning a lesson we will never finish learning in this life — practising humility every day.

An elderly preacher, after more than forty years of ministry, was once asked, “What lesson have you been slowest to learn in your whole life?” He thought for a long time, and answered with a single word: “Humility.” Preaching, he said, gets more polished the more you do it; you memorise more and more Scripture; the congregation comes to respect you more and more — but that “I” in your heart swells more easily the longer you serve. “I thought I had nailed the ‘I’ to the cross long ago,” he said. “I never expected that it was often only dozing — and the moment someone bumps into it, it leaps to its feet.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had that experience? You thought you were already very humble — until someone corrected you in public. You thought you had already denied yourself — until someone took the credit for your work. You thought you had already become gentle — until the person closest to you at home spoke to you in the very tone you can least stand. In that instant a voice inside you stood straight up and said, “I’m not wrong!” “Who does he think he is?” “I know more than he does!”

The thing that stood straight up is the self-centred life.

The 321 vision tells us that the root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and that the most visible shape it takes is pride. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. And what is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both sides overcome. That is why we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

In the last lesson we learned several practices of humility. Today we will go on to three more: “I will change myself to fit in with you,” “I am really nothing special,” and “I don’t understand anything.”

Please notice that none of these three sentences is a theory; each is a “choice.” They are not three slogans but three acts of “laying down a right.” The first lays down the right to “make others change.” The second lays down the right to “be seen.” The third lays down the right to “think I already understand.”

Humility is not a theory; it is a practice of life that has to be exercised again and again. In our everyday dealings with people and in our ministry, God gives us countless opportunities to learn humility. Sometimes those opportunities are hidden in conflict; sometimes they are hidden in success. When conflict comes, God is asking us, “Are you willing to change yourself first?” When success comes, God is asking us, “Where are you going to put this glory?” And when we think we understand, God is asking us, “Are you still willing to learn?”

Through “being willing to change,” “seeing our own limits” and “acknowledging that everything is grace,” God leads us step by step into a selfless life. These three choices look simple, yet they are a vital key to becoming more and more like Jesus and being used more and more by God.

Brothers and sisters, in this morning’s devotion we have not come to hear a talk about humility; we have come to make three decisions. May the Lord himself, this early morning, engrave these three sentences on the tablets of our hearts.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Servant’s Apron Tied Around the Waist
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from 1 Peter chapter 5. To grasp the weight of this passage, we first need to know the man who wrote the letter and the situation he wrote it in.

The author of 1 Peter is the apostle Peter. He introduces himself in the very first line: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). All five of these places are in Asia Minor, roughly today’s Turkey. The recipients are called people “living as foreigners”; the original word is παρεπίδημος (parepidēmos), meaning “resident aliens.” They had no citizenship on earth, no one to back them up, no voice.

The letter was written around AD 62 to 64, on the eve of the emperor Nero’s persecution of the church. It speaks again and again of “the fiery trial” (1 Peter 4:12) and of being “insulted for the name of Christ” (1 Peter 4:14). In other words, Peter was writing to a group of Christians who were being bullied, misunderstood and pushed to the margins.

Notice how much that situation matters. When people are being bullied, what is the most natural reaction? Self-defence, hitting back, puffing ourselves up, straining to prove “I’m not wrong” and “I’m not worth less than you.” Yet the first thing Peter says to these suffering people is not “You must fight for your rights” but — “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another” (1 Peter 5:5).

“Clothe yourselves with humility” — this “clothe yourselves” in the original is ἐγκομβόομαι (enkomboomai), a very rare word that appears only this once in the whole New Testament. Its root, ἐγκόμβωμα, refers to the apron a slave tied over his outer garment while working, fastened at the waist with a knotted cord. In other words, Peter means: put humility on like a servant’s apron, tie it tight, knot it, and let it become the most obvious mark you wear.

Brothers and sisters, why would Peter choose this word? Because he could never forget that scene for the rest of his life.

“…arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him” (John 13:4–5). That night the Lord of the universe tied on a towel, knelt on the floor and washed his disciples’ feet one by one. When it came to Peter’s turn, Peter pulled back his feet and said, “You will never wash my feet!” (John 13:8). The young Peter thought he was honouring the Lord; in fact it was the pride that refuses to let the Lord serve him.

Thirty years passed. The disciple who had pulled back his feet had become the old apostle who fed the Lord’s flock. When he took up his pen, he used the picture of that very apron: children, put on humility, tie it at your waist, just as the Lord did that night.

Then Peter quotes the Old Testament: “for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). The line comes from Proverbs 3:34: “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.” James 4:6 quotes the same words. “Resists” in the original is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: pride is not just a flaw; pride lines up Almighty God on the opposite side from us. What a fearful thing that is. Conversely, humility is not just a virtue; humility places us beneath the stream of grace. Water flows to the lowest place, and so does grace.

Then comes verse 6: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” There is a vital order here: first humbled, then exalted; first we go low, then we are lifted up. And “in due time” — the timetable is in God’s hands, not ours. The humble don’t need to fight for a high place, because the one who lifts them up is God.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very foundation of today’s three practices. When I say, “I will change myself to fit in with you,” I hand back to God the right to “make demands of others.” When I say, “I am really nothing special,” I hand back to God the right to “be seen.” When I say, “I don’t understand anything,” I hand back to God the right to “think I already understand.” Three times I hand it back; three times I tie on the apron.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: I Will Change Myself to Fit In with You — Laying Down the Right to “Make Others Change”
sections.html: “To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.” (1 Corinthians 9:22)

sections.heading: 1. Conflict Comes Not from Bad People but from Differences
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the greatest tension between people often comes not from “badness” but from “difference.” Different personalities, different styles, different values, different habits — and so conflict arises and misunderstandings pile up.

One person works fast, another works carefully; one says exactly what he thinks, another always considers other people’s feelings first; one likes plans written out clearly, another likes to figure things out along the way. Neither of them is a bad person, both of them love the Lord, yet after three months of serving together they’ve started sighing at each other.

It’s the same at home. Should the toothpaste be squeezed from the middle or from the end? Should the air conditioning be set to twenty-four degrees or twenty-seven? Should we leave half an hour early or cut it fine? Not one of these involves sin, yet grinding against each other day after day, day after day, grinds out a temper.

So we start to pray. And how do we pray? We often ask God, “Lord, change him!” We even wrap it up to sound very spiritual: “Lord, shine your light on him and let him see his own problem.” But God gently asks a question back in our hearts: “Are you willing to change yourself first?”

Brothers and sisters, that question is where humility begins.

sections.heading: 2. Paul’s Role Model: A Free Man Willingly Becomes Everyone’s Servant
sections.html:
That sentence in 1 Corinthians 9:22 was not a passing burst of emotion on Paul’s part; it is the conclusion of the whole chapter.

In this chapter Paul is talking about “rights.” In one breath he lists how many legitimate rights he has: the right to eat and drink, the right to take along a believing wife, the right to make his living from the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14). Then he says something startling: “But I have used none of these things” (1 Corinthians 9:15).

Next he states the heart of it: “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more” (1 Corinthians 9:19). Notice the words “brought myself.” The verb in the original is in the active voice — he was not forced; he chose it himself. Paul was a free man; no one could compel him to adjust himself. Precisely because he was free, his adjusting was true humility.

Then he goes on, layer by layer: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews”; “to those who are under the law, as under the law”; “to those who are without law, as without law”; and finally the gentlest line of all: “To the weak I became as weak” (1 Corinthians 9:20–22).

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: from strong to weak, coming to rest at last on “weak.” Paul was no chameleon; he never changed the content of the gospel. What he changed was his own posture, his own routine, his own diet, his own way of expressing himself. He clearly added a disclaimer: “not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). In other words: what I adjust is the method, not the standard; what I soften is my posture, not the truth.

Why did he do this? He says it plainly: “that I may by all means save some.” “Now I do this for the sake of the Good News” (1 Corinthians 9:23).

He did not demand that people accommodate him; he took the initiative to adjust himself, so that through him people could come to know Jesus more easily.

sections.heading: 3. An Everyday Illustration: The Plug Adapter and the Long Robe
sections.html:
I often think of a very down-to-earth comparison. When we travel abroad, what do we dread most? Bringing our appliances and finding they won’t fit the sockets. You can stand by the wall fuming, “Why are the sockets in this country so strange!” You can insist, quite sure you’re in the right, “My plug is the standard one!” But however right you are, the power simply won’t come. Unless — you’ve brought an adapter.

Brothers and sisters, humility is that adapter. It doesn’t change the nature of the current; it only changes the shape of the contact. The power of the gospel is that current, and not one bit of it may be reduced; but without a connector willing to change its shape, the current cannot get into the other person’s life. Will you be that adapter?

Church history has a famous example. When James Hudson Taylor (1832–1905) went to China as a missionary, Western missionaries generally wore Western suits and lived in the foreign concessions. Taylor did something that shocked his own countrymen: he put on a Chinese long robe and grew his hair long into a queue. Many Westerners mocked him for “lowering himself,” thinking he had thrown away a Westerner’s dignity. But he said he would rather the Chinese see not a foreigner but simply a man bringing the gospel. The China Inland Mission he later founded carried the gospel into inland provinces that many at the time could not reach.

Brothers and sisters, what Hudson Taylor changed was not the gospel but his own coat. What he laid down was not the truth but the right to “make others fit in with me.”

sections.heading: 4. Psychology Confirms It: Relationships Go the Distance When People Are Willing to Be Influenced
sections.html:
Psychological research also confirms the wisdom of Scripture from another angle.

The marriage researcher John Gottman of the University of Washington and his colleagues followed the interactions of newly married couples over a long period. In their study published in 1998 in the Journal of Marriage and the Family, they found a strikingly consistent pattern: husbands who were willing to “accept influence” from their wives had markedly more stable marriages, while exchanges that opened harshly, with blame from the very first sentence, were one of the key predictors of a marriage breaking down.

In other words, what decides how far a relationship can go is not who is more in the right, but who is more willing to be influenced by the other and to adjust first.

This is exactly what James says: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19); and exactly what Proverbs says: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

Brothers and sisters, psychology is only standing outside the door applauding the Bible; the Bible is the door itself.

sections.heading: 5. We Cannot Change Others, but We Can Change Ourselves
sections.html:
Humility means being willing to change ourselves first.

We cannot change people, because that is God’s work. The human heart is God’s territory; you and I cannot get in. You can persuade a person’s mind, but you can’t change his heart; you can suppress a person’s behaviour, but you can’t win over his soul.

What we can do is choose to adjust our own attitude, tone, expression and reactions. Every one of these four is within our control, and every one of them is in plain view of others.

The Lord Jesus put it even more strongly: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). “You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5). The Lord did not say there is no speck in your brother’s eye. He said the order cannot be reversed: deal with yourself first, and then you can see others clearly.

When we are willing to soften and to adapt, God moves the other person through our humility; and often, after we have changed, the other person is changed by the Holy Spirit too. Many people have experienced this first-hand: you stop pushing him, and he relaxes; you stop arguing your case, and he starts reflecting on himself.

So don’t be in a hurry to change others; be quick to change yourself.

This kind of “changing first” is not weakness; it is humility that springs from faith. Weakness keeps quiet because it is afraid of the other person; humility gives way willingly because it trusts God. We believe God can use our change to bring about a turnaround in someone else. As Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18).

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Humility Draws Out Humility, and Both Sides Win
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this point is at the very heart of the 321 vision.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a conflict, whoever humbles himself first overcomes first, because he is the first to break out of the cycle Satan has set up. You say something hard, I answer with something harder — that is “the cycle of pride.” You soften one step, I soften one step too — that is “the cycle of humility.” Both cycles start with one person. This morning God is asking us: are you willing to be the one who starts it?

The 321 vision also teaches us an order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Many rifts between co-workers happen not because the doctrine was wrong but because we put the “task” before the “person,” and being “right” before love. We won that argument but lost that brother.

Then there is the 920 practice: every person connected to us is our “2.” The co-worker you find hardest to get along with, the family member who most easily makes you impatient — that is exactly the “2” God has measured out to you. As you practise the “0” — the selfless life — with him, God produces in you the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, remember this: the hardest person to get along with is not your problem but your lesson; not your obstacle but your altar.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: I Am Really Nothing Special — Laying Down the Right to “Be Seen”
sections.html: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6)

sections.heading: 1. The Door Pride Loves to Come In By
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if the first practice is learned in “conflict,” the second is learned in “success.”

Many people think pride comes in through failure, but it doesn’t. Failure often makes people humble; it is success that most easily makes people proud. When we have something to show for our work, or when people praise us, pride slips quietly into the heart. It doesn’t knock; it comes in by the back door, and when it comes in it is usually wearing a very respectable coat called “I earned this on my own merit.”

We think to ourselves, “I worked hard to get where I am!” “If I hadn’t held it together, this small group would have fallen apart long ago.” “They have no idea how much I’ve given.” We may never say these things out loud, but while they circle around in our hearts, that “I” has already quietly taken the throne.

One brother put it very honestly: “My most dangerous moment isn’t when people criticise me. It’s the drive home after people have praised me.” Brothers and sisters, do you have a drive home like that?

sections.heading: 2. Neither the One Who Plants nor the One Who Waters Is Anything
sections.html:
The background to 1 Corinthians chapter 3 is the factions in the Corinthian church. One said, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos” (1 Corinthians 3:4). The church was being carved up by people’s names.

How did Paul handle it? He didn’t argue about who was more spiritual; he simply took everyone’s name down. “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants” (1 Corinthians 3:5). “Servants” in the original is διάκονος (diakonos), a “waiter, the one who serves the food.” Is the one who serves the food important? Yes. But no one thanks the hand that carried the plate for a good dish.

Then comes our key sentence: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Notice the tenses and the subjects of the three verbs. Planting was done by Paul, watering was done by Apollos; both are things people can do. And the growing? Growing is not something people can do. You can put a seed in the soil, you can water it every day, but you cannot make a single seed sprout. That faint force that pushes the seed coat open belongs to God.

In the next verse Paul says it right to the end: “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

Paul understood that he was only a tool; the one who really makes people grow is God. All he did was his “duty.” The Lord Jesus said the same thing: “Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty’” (Luke 17:10).

Without God’s grace, nothing is possible. Paul’s most famous confession is this: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Paul admits that he “worked more than all of them”; he doesn’t pretend he gave nothing. But he immediately adds: “yet not I, but the grace of God.”

This is what true humility looks like: not denying that we had a part, only acknowledging that we are not the source.

sections.heading: 3. “I Am Really Nothing Special” Is Not False Modesty
sections.html:
“I am really nothing special” is not a polite formula, nor is it false modesty; it is a recognition of the truth.

What is false modesty? False modesty says out loud, “Oh, not at all,” while inwardly waiting for the other person to say it again. False modesty is really still self-centred; it has simply found another way to ask for applause. True humility is not like that. True humility sees one fact clearly: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Brothers and sisters, stop and think quietly for a moment. Who gave you your mind? Who keeps you in health? Which family you were born into, which person led you to the Lord, at what moment you heard the gospel — which of these did you arrange yourself? Even the fact that we are breathing right now is no credit of ours. At rest, a person breathes roughly twelve to twenty times a minute, about twenty thousand times in a day. Of those twenty thousand breaths, which one did you put in your diary in advance?

Without Jesus I can do nothing; with Jesus I can do all things. I didn’t make these two sentences up; the Lord himself said the one, and Paul said the other: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

The one who is truly remarkable is not me but the Lord who is at work in me. So when people praise me, I say, “Thank the Lord!” — because I know that everything is his grace.

That “Thank the Lord” doesn’t bat the praise away; it passes the praise upward. People’s praise is like a ball thrown into your hands. You can hold on to it, or you can pass it on to the Lord. Those who hold on to it have their hands full and can’t catch anything else; those who pass it upward always have empty hands, so they can always catch again.

sections.heading: 4. The Picture of the Moon and the Illusion of Being “Better Than Average”
sections.html:
I love comparing Christians to the moon.

The moon is beautiful at night. It lights up the wilderness, it lights up the sea, it lights up the path in front of the lost traveller. But there is one fact about the moon: it gives off no light of its own. Moonlight is sunlight, reflected off the surface of the moon. If one day the moon decided, “This light is mine,” it would not grow any brighter in that moment; it would simply have lost its grasp of the facts.

More important still: when is the moon at its brightest? When it is directly facing the sun with nothing in between — that is the full moon. When is it at its darkest? When the earth squeezes in between — then there is a lunar eclipse. Brothers and sisters, our light is just the same. When we are facing the Lord directly, with no “self” blocking the way, we shine brightest; when we squeeze ourselves in between the Lord and people, we go into eclipse.

John the Baptist put it most beautifully: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Psychology also tells us how easily people overestimate themselves. In a classic study published in Acta Psychologica in 1981, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that among the American drivers he tested, more than nine in ten believed their driving skill was better than average. The phenomenon later came to be called the “better-than-average effect.” Yet by definition it is impossible for nine in ten people to be above average.

Brothers and sisters, the marks we give ourselves are naturally too high. This is not a moral accusation; it is simply the reality of human nature. So we need a mirror — not other people’s opinions, but God’s word. And God’s word says: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Galatians 6:3).

sections.heading: 5. A Channel of Grace: Humility Doesn’t Deny Our Worth, It Recognises Our Source
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, please hear something very important: humble people do not deny their own worth; they are clear about where it comes from.

Some people mistake humility for low self-esteem. They go around all day saying, “I can’t do it, I’m useless, I’m no good at anything.” In fact that is also a form of self-centredness; it has simply turned the camera onto its own flaws. Truly humble people know: I am precious, because God bought me at a great price; I am useful, because I am a vessel in God’s hand; but I am not the source. I am only a “channel of grace.”

A water pipe carries cool water to a field. The field is refreshed, and nobody thanks the pipe. If the pipe is in good condition, it has only one wish: not to clog, not to rust, not to leak, so that the water can flow through freely. Brothers and sisters, our worth lies not in how wide a pipe we are, but in what kind of water is flowing through us.

The glory belongs to God, not to man. That sentence is not a courteous deferral; it is a declaration of ownership.

Paul goes even further: “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). What a free man! He has no need to cover up his cracks, because he knows that the light shines out precisely through the cracks.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing, but Entering the Limitless
sections.html:
The 321 vision tells us: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

But notice: selflessness is not having nothing. It is not erasing yourself, not becoming a person with no thoughts, no feelings, no gifts. Selflessness is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. Because the “self” is limited, once it steps aside, the limitless Lord can move freely within us.

Paul gives us the best commentary on this: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness. “But Christ lives in me” — that is the limitless.

The second of the 321 vision’s Two Core Values is “let Jesus receive all the glory.” Brothers and sisters, the word “all” is very strict. Not ninety per cent to the Lord and ten per cent kept back for ourselves; not the glory on the platform to the Lord and the glory off it to me. When we say, “I am really nothing special,” we are not putting ourselves down; we are completing a piece of paperwork: transferring the title deed of the glory entirely into the Lord’s name.

This is exactly the shift of perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from man’s point of view to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s applause is temporary; God’s approval is eternal. This morning, which one do you want?

sections.heading: Key Point 3: I Don’t Understand Anything — Laying Down the Right to “Think I Already Understand”
sections.html: “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know.” (1 Corinthians 8:2)

sections.heading: 1. Spiritual Pride Is More Dangerous Than Worldly Pride
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the third practice is the hardest, because it deals with the deepest and hardest-to-detect kind of pride — spiritual pride.

Worldly pride boasts of wealth, status and ability. That kind of pride is easy to spot; even unbelievers can see it. Spiritual pride, though, wears the coat of godliness: boasting that I understand the truth, that I understand the church, that I understand spiritual principles, that I’ve been attending meetings for years, that I’ve read the Bible through so many times. And so that person is no longer teachable and no longer depends on God.

This was exactly the problem in the Corinthian church. The context of 1 Corinthians chapter 8 is whether food sacrificed to idols may be eaten. Paul says: “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). “Puffs up” in the original is φυσιόω (physioō), which literally means “to inflate by blowing air into,” like blowing up a balloon. Brothers and sisters, how vivid that word is: knowledge without love is like pumping in air — the size grows, the weight doesn’t increase, it is hollow inside, and one pin will burst it.

Then Paul says that piercing sentence: “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2). The truly wise are those who know what they don’t understand.

In the very next verse Paul gives the right way: “But if anyone loves God, the same is known by him” (1 Corinthians 8:3). Notice this astonishing turn — Paul doesn’t say “the one who loves God knows God”; he says “the one who loves God is known by God.” In spiritual knowledge, what matters is not how much I have grasped but by whom I have been grasped.

sections.heading: 2. The Lord Jesus’ Prayer: Revealed to Infants
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus himself stated this principle with great clarity: “At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight’” (Matthew 11:25–26).

Notice that the Lord does not say cleverness is a sin, nor that study is bad. “The wise and understanding” here are those who think they already have the answers and no longer need to be taught. Earlier in the same chapter the Lord had just rebuked Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum — the towns that had seen the most miracles yet refused to repent (Matthew 11:20–24). They knew everything, except how to turn back.

“Infants” in the original is νήπιος (nēpios), a child who cannot yet speak. What abilities does an infant have? None. The reason an infant can receive revelation is that he is simple, dependent and willing to learn. He never says, “I already knew that.”

Elsewhere the Lord says it even more strongly: “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

Brothers and sisters, spiritual “understanding” doesn’t come from the brain; it comes from humility. When we feel we “understand it all,” we lose the heart that learns and depends. If a cup is already full, however good the tea you pour into it, it only overflows and messes up the table. Only an empty cup can be filled.

sections.heading: 3. The Dunning–Kruger Effect and the “Illusion of Knowledge”
sections.html:
Modern psychology has made some rather interesting discoveries about this.

In a study published in 1999 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University showed that those least competent in a given area tend to be the most likely to overestimate their performance — because the very ability they lack is the ability needed to judge how well they are doing. This later became widely known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect.”

Another intriguing study comes from an experiment by Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil, published in Cognitive Science in 2002. They asked participants to rate how well they understood everyday objects — how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, for example. Most gave themselves fairly high marks. Then the researchers asked them to write out in detail how the thing actually works. The moment they started writing, the game was up: their self-ratings dropped sharply at once. The researchers called this phenomenon “the illusion of explanatory depth.”

Brothers and sisters, if we can overestimate ourselves about a flush toilet, how much more about the God who sits enthroned above the heavens?

Psychologists also offer us a positive reminder. In his 2021 book Think Again, the organisational psychologist Adam Grant puts forward “confident humility” — being confident in your abilities while staying humble about your judgements, and so always ready to rethink. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what Paul was like: utterly unshakeable about the gospel, and not in the least overestimating himself.

sections.heading: 4. God Is Never Boxed In: Three Times the Waters Parted
sections.html:
There is an even deeper reason why we are willing to admit, “I don’t understand anything”: God’s works are limitless. In every age and every setting he displays his power in new ways.

Scripture records three occasions when the waters were parted, and they are well worth our attention.

The first time, Moses raised his rod and the Red Sea parted. God said to Moses: “Lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it. Then the children of Israel shall go into the middle of the sea on dry ground” (Exodus 14:16).

The second time, Joshua led the priests into the water and the Jordan stopped flowing. God commanded: “You shall command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, saying, ‘When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan’” (Joshua 3:8). Notice that this time there was no rod, and they had to step into the water first before it stopped. Had they raised a rod on the strength of their Red Sea experience, the Jordan would not have dropped by a single drop.

The third time, Elijah struck the water with his cloak. “Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters, and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground” (2 Kings 2:8). This time there was neither rod nor ark, only a rolled-up cloak.

The same parting of waters, yet three completely different ways. Why? Because God is never boxed in by our experience. God says: “Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” (Isaiah 43:19). And again: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways … For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:8–9).

Brothers and sisters, yesterday’s method cannot guarantee today’s results. The person whose rod has worked before is the one most likely to stand at the riverbank raising it with all his might. We often say, “This is how we’ve always done it.” Sometimes that is faithfulness; sometimes it is locking God up inside our memories.

Even the universe we are able to observe is something humanity keeps rewriting. In 2016, on the basis of deep-field data from the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers estimated that the observable universe may contain as many as two trillion galaxies, far more than previous estimates. If our knowledge of one starry sky is being updated day by day, how dare we say of the God who created that sky, “I understand it all”?

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves
sections.html:
So when we are willing to admit, “I don’t understand anything,” we will depend more on the Holy Spirit and let him guide us into God’s limitless purposes.

The Lord Jesus promised: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming” (John 16:13).

This is precisely one of the 321 vision’s Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The other two are: Jesus is my role model, and the Bible is my standard. Brothers and sisters, not one of these three foundations can be left out. Some want only the Holy Spirit’s promptings without the Bible’s standard, and they easily go astray; some want only Bible knowledge without the Holy Spirit’s guidance, and they easily dry up. Humble people want both, because they know they need both.

The 321 vision also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. “Out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). This is not opposing thinking; it is saying that our thinking should stand inside obedience, not in front of it. Solomon put it most clearly: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6).

Humility keeps us teachable, and it keeps us walking in God’s fresh works. The psalm says: “He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way” (Psalm 25:9). Brothers and sisters, it is not that God won’t teach; it is that God teaches only those who are willing to learn.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Three Practices, Three Times Tying On the Apron
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us put today’s three practices back into the whole picture of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he tied on a towel and washed his disciples’ feet; he emptied himself and was made in human likeness. The Bible is my standard — not my feelings, not my face, not other people’s opinions. The Holy Spirit is my guide — not my experience, not yesterday’s method. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — King over my emotions, King over my achievements, King over my opinions; and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system — a system made up of selfless people, with Christ as its head.

Paul condenses this picture into one passage: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

Today’s three practices take aim at exactly three strongholds of the “self.”

The first stronghold is “my rights” — I have the right to demand that others change. What breaks it down is “I will change myself to fit in with you.”

The second stronghold is “my achievements” — I have the right to be seen. What breaks it down is “I am really nothing special.”

The third stronghold is “my opinions” — I have the right to think I’m right. What breaks it down is “I don’t understand anything.”

Three times laying down is three times tying on the apron; three times tying on the apron is three times letting Jesus reign as King.

The 321 vision says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. These three sentences today change precisely our mindset. Once our mindset changes, the way we treat people changes; once the way we treat people changes, our relationships change; once our relationships change, God naturally uses our ministry. So the order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry; first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things.

The 321 vision also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. In a conflict, if our focus is on the other person, we see only his faults; if our focus is on ourselves, we attend only to our own pain; only when our focus is on Jesus can we see the work God wants to accomplish through the situation.

Finally there are the 235 relationships: becoming a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions who can speak the truth to each other; building a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, willing to be taught and willing to teach; becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, serving together and used by the Lord together. Brothers and sisters, a person who won’t say “I don’t understand anything” will never find spiritual parents; a person who won’t say “I will change myself” will never keep a spiritual companion.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living Out the Three Sentences
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four concrete practices. Please hold them in your heart and start today.

First, adjust yourself: in a conflict today, ask first, “What can I change to fit in with him?”

Second, give the glory to God: when others praise you, respond, “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.”

Third, admit your limits: pray every day, “Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me.”

Fourth, look to the Holy Spirit: in everything, ask the Holy Spirit first; don’t go by experience, don’t rely on yourself.

The 321 vision tells us there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Let us use these eight stages to take these four practices deeper.

1. Information: this morning’s devotion is the information. We have heard three sentences, and we have heard their scriptural basis — 1 Corinthians 9:22, 3:6 and 8:2. Information must be accurate, so we go back to the Chinese Union Version and read it word by word.

2. Revelation: information enters the head; revelation enters the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to put his finger on it in your heart: of these three practices, which one are you speaking to me about today? Usually it is the one that makes your heart tighten, even makes you a little uncomfortable.

3. Conviction: conviction is being won over heart and mouth; it is saying, “Lord, you are right and I am wrong.” Without conviction, practice is mere willpower, and it won’t last three days.

4. Implementation: do it today. Make it specific to a person, specific to a situation. Not “I’ll try to be a bit more humble from now on,” but “Tonight when I get home, I’ll start by apologising to him for my tone yesterday.”

5. Evaluation: before bed tonight, take three minutes to look back: was there any moment today when my “self” took the throne again? What were my tone, my expression and my reaction at the time?

6. Correction: when you find something, change it; don’t let it pile up. Today’s evaluation is tomorrow’s correction. If you have wronged someone, while it is still called today, go and mend the relationship.

7. Repetition: humility is not a one-off decision but a daily choice. That is why this lesson is called “Practising Humility Every Day.” Every day means repetition; only repetition becomes character.

8. Multiplication: once you have experienced the release that humility brings, go and walk alongside someone. Take him along the road you have travelled, and walk it again with him. This is the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and it is the true expansion of God’s kingdom.

Brothers and sisters, these eight stages are not a syllabus; they are the rhythm of life. May we not merely finish a lesson but step into a cycle.

A Gentle Reminder: Humility Is Not Putting Yourself Down but Seeing Yourself Rightly

Before we come to the closing, let me remind you once more, because this is the point most easily misunderstood.

Humility is not putting yourself down; it is seeing yourself rightly — I am only a vessel, not the master; I am only a worker, not the owner.

Truly humble people are not “self-negating”; they are “God-centred.” Self-negating people still have the camera pointed at themselves; they are just filming their flaws. God-centred people have turned the camera towards the Lord, so they need neither to lift themselves up nor to trample themselves down.

When C. S. Lewis describes a truly humble person in Mere Christianity, the gist is this: if you meet a really humble person, you probably won’t think of him as humble; he won’t keep thinking about humility — he won’t keep thinking about himself at all. Brothers and sisters, this is selflessness — not straining to press ourselves down, but no longer revolving around ourselves.

Paul also says, “Now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:12). If even Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven, could say that, what do we have to boast about?

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Less and Less of Self, More and More of Christ
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the practice of humility is not about how much we do but about each willing choice we make.

God is not up in heaven holding a scoreboard, counting how many times you gave way today and how often you held your tongue. He is looking at your heart — at that crossroads where you could have argued your case, which road did you take? At that moment when you could have caught the applause, to whom did you pass the ball? On that occasion when you could have said, “I knew that already,” did you close your mouth and listen one more time?

When we say, “Lord, I am willing to change myself,” “I am really nothing special,” “I don’t understand anything” — a heart like that is where revival begins.

Revival has never begun with big meetings; revival begins with a heart willing to go low. Every true revival in history has begun with someone willing to say, “Lord, it’s me.”

So this morning I issue this call to you: let Jesus reign as King over your emotions, let Jesus reign as King over your achievements, let Jesus reign as King over your opinions. Lay on the altar your expectation that others should change; lay on the altar your longing to be seen; lay on the altar, too, your confidence that you already understand it all.

Let us practise humility every day; let us have less and less of self and more and more of Christ. May all the glory go to Jesus Christ, who sits on the throne.

keyVerses: “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:5–6)
“To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.” (1 Corinthians 9:22)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
Lord, I am willing to practise humility, willing to change myself first, and no longer to demand that others accommodate me.
I acknowledge that I am really nothing special; everything is your grace.
Lord, I also acknowledge that I don’t understand anything. May the Holy Spirit teach me and guide me,
so that I live every day in humility and dependence, a vessel pleasing to you and fit for your use.
practices: In a conflict, ask first: “What can I change to fit in with him?”
When praised, respond: “Thank the Lord — it’s his grace.”
Pray every day: “Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me.”
Ask the Holy Spirit first in everything; don’t go by experience or rely on yourself.
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for shining your light on us through your word this early morning.

Lord, we confess that we often ask you to change others but refuse to change ourselves first; we often treat your grace as our own achievement; we often think we understand and stop looking to you. Please forgive us.
Lord Jesus, you are our role model. You existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. Please place that humble heart of yours within us.

Holy Spirit, please be our guide all through this day. When conflict comes, remind us to ask first, “What can I change?” When praise comes, remind us to say, “Thank the Lord — it’s your grace.” When we think we understand, remind us to grow quiet and say, “Lord, please teach me.”
Lord, make us vessels fit for your use, living out the selfless life at home, at work and in the church, so that you receive all the glory through us.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: Paul says, “To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). In your current relationships, for whom does God want you to “change yourself to fit in with him”? What are you willing to adjust first — your attitude, your tone, your expression, or your reactions?

Question 2: The Lord Jesus says, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25). In what matter have you discovered that you only “think you understand”? This week, how will you concretely practise “Lord, I don’t understand anything; please teach me”?
